items.passage:
Dear Ms. Howard,

My name is Daniel Reyes, and I am a junior at Lakeview High School. For the past three years, I have used the Maple Street Public Library almost every weekend, and its quiet reading room and helpful staff have made it my favorite place to study. Recently, however, many of my classmates and I have found it difficult to finish our work because the library closes at 1 p.m. on Sundays. With final exams approaching in December, Sunday afternoons are exactly when we most need a calm place to concentrate. Many of us share small rooms with siblings, so studying at home is not always possible. I understand that longer hours require additional staff, and several students, including me, would gladly volunteer at the front desk if that would help. I am writing to ask whether the library could stay open until 6 p.m. on Sundays during the exam season. Thank you for considering this request.

Sincerely,
Daniel Reyes
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 시험 기간 일요일 도서관 운영 시간 연장을 요청하려고
도서관 열람실의 소음 문제 해결을 건의하려고
items.exp: 필자는 시험 기간 동안 일요일에 도서관을 오후 6시까지 열어 줄 수 있는지 묻고 있어요. 자원봉사 의사는 요청을 돕기 위한 제안일 뿐 글의 목적은 아니에요.

items.passage: Clara checked the bowl for the third time. Two hours earlier, she had mixed the flour, water, and yeast exactly as her grandmother's old recipe described, but the dough still sat flat and pale, as if it had fallen asleep. Her grandfather's eightieth birthday dinner would begin at six, and she had promised him a loaf just like the ones his late wife used to bake. Clara bit her lip and glanced at the clock. Had the yeast been too old? Had the kitchen been too cold? She wrapped the bowl in a warm towel, set it near the oven, and paced around the table, unable to sit still. When she lifted the towel forty minutes later, she gasped. The dough had swelled into a soft, round dome. An hour after that, a golden loaf came out of the oven, filling the house with a sweet smell. Clara clapped her hands and laughed out loud, already picturing her grandfather's face.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Clara의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 처음에는 반죽이 부풀지 않아 입술을 깨물고 서성일 만큼 걱정했지만, 반죽이 부풀고 빵이 노릇하게 구워지자 손뼉을 치며 웃었어요. 따라서 worried → delighted가 알맞아요.

items.passage: In most classrooms, questions travel in only one direction: teachers ask, and students answer. Students who answer quickly and correctly are praised, so they learn that the goal of school is to have answers ready. Yet outside school, the people who make real progress in science, business, or art are usually not those who know the most answers but those who ask better questions. A good question points to what is missing, and that is where new learning begins. If students never practice forming questions, they reach adulthood skilled at responding to problems that others have defined but unsure how to define problems for themselves. Teachers can change this with small steps. Before a new unit, they might show students a puzzling image or fact and ask them to write down as many questions as they can. Later, the class can choose the most promising questions to investigate together. When teachers treat students' questions as valuable material for lessons, they are teaching the skill that matters most beyond the classroom.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 교사는 학생의 정답에 대해 즉각적으로 칭찬해야 한다.
학생들은 수업 전에 배울 내용을 미리 예습해야 한다.
교사는 학생 스스로 문제를 해결할 때까지 기다려야 한다.
학교는 과학과 예술 교육의 비중을 늘려야 한다.
교사는 수업에서 학생이 직접 질문을 만들어 보게 해야 한다.
items.exp: 필자는 학생이 질문을 만드는 연습을 해야 스스로 문제를 정의할 수 있다며, 교사가 학생의 질문을 수업 재료로 삼아야 한다고 주장해요. 정답을 빨리 말하는 학생을 칭찬하는 것은 필자가 비판하는 현재 수업 방식이에요.

items.passage: Many people open a dictionary to settle an argument, believing it tells them how a word should be used. Lexicographers, the people who write dictionaries, see their work differently. They collect millions of examples from newspapers, books, conversations, and websites, and then they describe the meanings that speakers actually give to each word. When enough people begin to use a word in a new way, the dictionary eventually adds that meaning, even if some readers complain. The word "awful," for instance, once meant "full of awe" before speakers gradually shifted it toward "very bad." No committee voted on that change; it simply happened through use, and dictionaries followed. In this sense, a dictionary is [a record of the crowd, not a judge's ruling]. Its authority comes not from any power to decide what is correct but from the care with which it observes what millions of speakers have already decided together.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a record of the crowd, not a judge's ruling]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Dictionaries should be revised by a committee of language experts.
The meanings of words are fixed by their original forms.
Dictionaries describe how people actually use words rather than ruling on correctness.
Popular opinion often leads speakers to misuse words.
Readers have the right to reject new meanings added to dictionaries.
items.exp: 사전 편찬자는 사람들이 실제로 쓰는 의미를 수집해 기술하고, 사전의 권위는 무엇이 옳은지 정하는 힘이 아니라 관찰의 정성에서 나온다고 했어요. 따라서 사전은 옳고 그름을 판정하지 않고 실제 쓰임을 기록한다는 뜻이에요. ①은 위원회가 투표하지 않았다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: When winter arrives, the surface of a lake freezes first while the water below remains liquid. This happens because of an unusual property of water. Most substances become denser as they cool, but water is densest at about 4°C. As cold air chills a lake in autumn, the cooling surface water sinks until the whole lake reaches roughly that temperature. After that, water that cools further becomes lighter and stays at the top, where it eventually turns into ice. Ice itself is less dense than liquid water, so it floats instead of sinking to the bottom. The floating layer then acts like a lid, slowing the loss of heat from the water beneath it. As a result, fish, insects, and plants can survive the winter in water that stays just above freezing. If water behaved like most other liquids, lakes might freeze from the bottom up, and many could become solid blocks of ice, leaving little room for life.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: how a special property of water allows lake life to survive winter
why fish move to deeper water before lakes freeze
the process by which lakes lose heat during autumn
differences in density among various liquids
the dangers of thin ice for people in winter
items.exp: 물은 약 4도에서 가장 밀도가 높고 얼음은 물보다 가벼워 위에 뜨기 때문에, 얼음층이 뚜껑 역할을 해 호수 생물이 겨울을 날 수 있다는 내용이에요. ③과 ④는 글의 일부 내용에 그쳐요.

items.passage: For decades, many products have been designed in ways that make repairing them difficult. Screws are hidden, parts are glued together, and replacement components are hard to find, so when a phone or washing machine breaks, buying a new one often seems cheaper than fixing the old one. However, this calculation ignores costs that never appear on the price tag. Every discarded device becomes waste, and producing its replacement requires new materials and energy. Recently, a growing number of governments and consumers have begun to push back. Some regions now require manufacturers to make spare parts and repair manuals available for several years after a product is sold. Small repair shops are reopening in neighborhoods, and community "fix-it" events invite volunteers to help people mend toasters, lamps, and bicycles for free. These changes suggest that a product's true value may depend not only on how well it works when new but also on how long it can be kept working.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why New Products Are Always Better Than Old Ones
The Hidden Dangers of Repairing Devices at Home
How Manufacturers Lower Prices Through Clever Design
Fixing Over Replacing: Rethinking the Value of What We Own
Volunteers Who Changed the History of Technology
items.exp: 고치기 어렵게 만든 제품 대신 수리해서 오래 쓰려는 움직임이 늘고 있고, 제품의 진짜 가치는 얼마나 오래 쓸 수 있는가에도 달려 있다는 내용이에요. ⑤는 자원봉사 수리 행사라는 일부 사례만 다뤄요.

items.passage: Elsbeth Marrow (1841–1912) was a mapmaker known for her detailed charts of coastal waters. She was born in a small harbor town, where her father repaired fishing boats. As a child, she spent hours copying the shapes of the shoreline into notebooks. Because women were not admitted to the naval school in her region, she taught herself mathematics and surveying from borrowed books. In 1868, she began working as an assistant to a local surveyor, though her name did not appear on the maps she helped produce. After the surveyor died in 1875, she completed his unfinished chart of the eastern bay on her own, and it was published under her name. Sailors praised the chart for its accuracy, and it remained in use for more than forty years. In her later years, she trained young surveyors, many of whom were women. Her personal notebooks are now kept in a maritime museum.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 어린 시절 해안선의 모양을 공책에 옮겨 그렸다.
1868년부터 측량사의 조수로 일하며 지도에 이름을 올렸다.
그녀의 개인 공책은 해양 박물관에 보관되어 있다.
items.exp: 1868년부터 측량사의 조수로 일했지만, 그녀가 만든 지도에는 이름이 실리지 않았다고 했어요. 그녀의 이름으로 출판된 것은 1875년 이후 혼자 완성한 해도예요.

items.passage: Every autumn, millions of small birds fly thousands of kilometers to their winter homes, often at night and over unfamiliar land. Scientists have long wondered how they ①[manage] to stay on course. One important tool appears to be the Earth's magnetic field. Experiments have shown that birds ②[kept] in cages during the migration season tend to hop in the direction they would normally fly, and that this direction shifts when researchers change the magnetic field around the cage. Some researchers believe that special molecules in the birds' eyes are sensitive to magnetism, ③[allowing] the birds to "see" the field as a pattern laid over their normal vision. Birds also rely on the position of the sun and stars, as well as on familiar landmarks such as rivers and coastlines. Having several sources of information is useful, because when one becomes unavailable, as on a cloudy night, the others can still guide them. This combination of senses helps explain ④[why] young birds on their first journey can reach places they have never seen, a feat ⑤[what] still amazes the scientists who study it.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 앞의 명사 a feat를 수식하는 관계절을 이끌어야 하므로 선행사를 포함하는 what이 아니라 that이나 which로 고쳐야 해요. ②는 새가 우리에 갇힌 것이므로 수동의 과거분사 kept가 맞고, ③은 결과를 나타내는 분사구문이에요.

items.passage: Many students and office workers spend most of the day sitting, often for several hours without a break. Research suggests that long periods of uninterrupted sitting can ①[slow] the body's ability to process sugar and fat, even in people who exercise regularly. The good news is that the solution does not have to be ②[simple]. Standing up and moving for just two or three minutes every half hour can ③[improve] blood flow and help keep energy levels steady. Some studies have even found that short walks between study sessions ④[sharpen] attention, making it easier to focus when people sit back down. Because these breaks are brief, they rarely ⑤[interfere] with work; in fact, they may make the remaining time more productive. Setting a timer is one easy way to build the habit. Drinking water regularly also helps, since it naturally leads to trips away from the desk. Over time, such tiny movements can add up to a real difference in how the body feels at the end of the day.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 바로 뒤에 2~3분만 움직여도 된다는 간단한 해결책이 나오므로, 해결책이 복잡할 필요가 없다는 뜻이 되도록 ②의 simple을 complicated로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: Why do we keep promises even when breaking them would be more convenient? One answer is that a promise is a strange kind of tool: it allows us to give others control over a small part of our future. When I promise to help you move on Saturday, I am not just guessing what I will do; I am giving you the right to count on it. This matters because human cooperation depends on our ability to plan around one another. Without promises, every person's future actions would be a matter of guesswork, and large projects requiring many people over long periods would be nearly impossible. A promise turns an uncertain individual into someone others can build plans upon. Seen this way, keeping a promise is not merely about being polite or avoiding guilt. It is about maintaining the very thing that makes trust possible: by binding ourselves, we become ___ to others, and that is what allows them to rely on us.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 약속이 없으면 사람의 미래 행동은 짐작의 문제가 되지만, 약속은 불확실한 개인을 남들이 계획을 세울 수 있는 사람으로 바꾼다고 했어요. 따라서 스스로를 묶음으로써 남들에게 예측 가능한 사람이 된다는 predictable이 알맞아요. flexible은 정반대 방향이에요.

items.passage: Social norms are often described as the shared beliefs of a group, but this description can be misleading. What guides behavior is not what people actually believe but what they think others believe. Because private attitudes are hidden while public behavior is visible, individuals usually infer the group's views from what others do and say. This creates a curious possibility. Suppose most members of a group privately dislike a custom but, seeing others follow it, assume they are alone in their doubts. Each person then conforms in order to avoid disapproval, and that conformity in turn becomes evidence for everyone else that the custom is widely supported. The result is a norm that survives even though ___. Researchers studying such cases have found that simply revealing the real distribution of opinions, for example by publishing anonymous survey results, can cause long-standing practices to collapse with surprising speed, since the support that seemed to hold them up was largely imaginary.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: most members openly argue against it in public
it has been handed down for many generations
outsiders consider it strange and unnecessary
few of those who practice it actually endorse it
the group has no formal rules to enforce it
items.exp: 구성원 대부분이 속으로는 관습을 싫어하면서도 남들이 지지한다고 믿고 따르기 때문에, 실제 지지가 거의 없는데도 규범이 유지된다는 내용이에요. 익명 조사로 실제 의견이 드러나면 관습이 무너지는 것도 그 지지가 상상에 불과했기 때문이에요. ①은 사람들이 공개적으로는 따른다는 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. This extra heat is more than a matter of comfort; it raises energy demand and can be dangerous for elderly residents during summer. ① Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and rooftops absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly at night. ② In addition, tall buildings block cooling winds, and the heat produced by cars and air conditioners adds to the problem. ③ Air conditioners were first developed in the early twentieth century to control humidity in factories rather than to cool people. ④ One promising response is to cover rooftops with plants, which provide shade and cool the air as water evaporates from their leaves. ⑤ Cities that have planted green roofs and street trees on a large scale report lower surface temperatures and reduced energy use during heat waves.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 도시 열섬 현상의 원인과 해결책을 설명하는 글인데, ③은 에어컨이 처음 개발된 목적에 관한 역사 이야기로 흐름에서 벗어나요. ②의 에어컨은 열을 내는 원인으로 언급되어 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage:
The GPS receiver in your phone does not send any signal to the satellites overhead. It only listens.

(A) Each GPS satellite continuously broadcasts a message stating its position and the exact time the message was sent, measured by an extremely precise atomic clock on board. By comparing that time with the moment the message arrives, the receiver can calculate how far away the satellite is.

(B) In practice, though, a fourth satellite is needed. The clock inside your phone is far less accurate than those in space, and even a tiny timing error would produce a large error in distance. The extra signal allows the receiver to correct its own clock and fix its position precisely.

(C) A single distance, however, is not enough. Knowing that you are, say, 20,000 kilometers from one satellite only places you somewhere on a huge imaginary sphere around it. With distances from three satellites, these spheres overlap at only a couple of points, and one of them is your location.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 수신기가 듣기만 한다는 주어진 글 뒤에 위성이 보내는 메시지로 거리를 계산하는 (A)가 와요. (C)의 A single distance는 (A)에서 구한 거리를 가리키고, (B)의 a fourth satellite는 (C)의 세 개의 위성 다음이므로 (A)–(C)–(B) 순서예요.

items.passage: In many parts of the world, meals are served on shared plates placed in the middle of the table, and everyone takes food from the same dishes. ( ① ) In other places, each person receives an individual portion arranged on his or her own plate. ( ② ) These two styles may seem like a simple matter of convenience, but they reflect different ideas about what it means to eat together. ( ③ ) Shared dishes encourage diners to pay attention to one another, since taking too much of a favorite food means that others get less. ( ④ ) People often offer the best pieces to elders or guests, turning the meal into a quiet exercise in consideration. ( ⑤ ) That freedom, however, comes at a small cost: the meal can feel less like a shared event and more like several people eating alone at the same table. Neither style is simply better; each quietly teaches its own lesson about sharing a table.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Individual portions, by contrast, let each person eat at his or her own pace and choose exactly how much to have.
items.exp: ⑤ 뒤 문장의 That freedom은 자기 속도대로 먹고 양을 정할 수 있는 자유를 가리키므로, 개인 접시의 장점을 말하는 주어진 문장이 ⑤에 와야 해요. 그 앞까지는 함께 나누는 접시의 장점을 설명하고 있어 by contrast로 전환되는 자리도 ⑤예요.

items.passage: When we listen to music, we naturally focus on the notes: the melody we hum and the rhythm we tap our feet to. Yet the moments when no note is played are just as carefully planned. Composers write rests into their scores with the same precision as notes, marking exactly how long each pause should last. A short break after a rising phrase gives listeners time to absorb what they have just heard, while a sudden stop in the middle of a fast passage can create tension that makes the next chord feel far more powerful. Experienced performers know this well. When nervous beginners rush through the pauses, the music may contain every correct note and still sound flat and breathless. Conductors therefore spend rehearsal time not only on how the orchestra plays but also on how it stops playing. The empty spaces, in other words, do work of their own, guiding attention and shaping emotion.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

In music, (A) ___ is not simply the absence of notes but plays a(n) (B) ___ role in shaping how listeners experience what they hear.
items.exp: 음표가 연주되지 않는 쉼표와 멈춤이 음표만큼 정밀하게 계획되며, 그 빈 공간이 주의를 이끌고 감정을 만드는 일을 스스로 한다고 했어요. 따라서 (A)에는 silence, (B)에는 active가 알맞아요. optional은 멈춤을 대충 넘기면 음악이 밋밋해진다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
For much of the twentieth century, farmers in many regions treated bare soil between harvests as a sign of good management. After the crop was gathered, fields were plowed and left empty until the next planting season, giving them a neat, (a)[clean] appearance. Today, a growing number of farmers are questioning this habit and planting what are called cover crops: plants such as clover, rye, or radishes that are grown not for sale but to protect and feed the soil.

The reasons become clear when we consider what happens to an empty field. Without roots to hold it in place, the top layer of soil is easily (b)[carried] away by wind and heavy rain. This layer is the most fertile part of the field, and once it is lost, it can take centuries to rebuild. Cover crops act like a living blanket, shielding the surface and binding the soil together with their roots.

They also improve the soil from within. Some cover crops, such as clover, can take nitrogen from the air and store it in the ground, (c)[increasing] the amount of chemical fertilizer the next crop will need. Others have deep roots that break up hard ground, allowing water to (d)[soak] into the soil rather than running off the surface.

Of course, cover crops are not free. Seeds cost money, planting takes time, and the benefits may not appear in the first year. For this reason, some farmers remain (e)[hesitant] to try them. But those who have used them for many seasons often report healthier fields, steadier harvests during dry years, and lower costs over time. Their experience suggests that the most productive field may not be the one that looks cleanest but the one that is never left uncovered.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Never Bare: Why Farmers Are Covering Their Fields Between Harvests
The Hidden Costs of Chemical Fertilizers
How Plowing Made Modern Farming Possible
Clover and Rye: New Crops for Growing Markets
Why Soil Erosion Can No Longer Be Stopped
items.exp: 수확 사이에 밭을 비워 두지 않고 피복 작물을 심어 흙을 보호하고 기름지게 하는 이유를 설명하는 글이에요. ④는 피복 작물이 판매용이 아니라는 내용과 맞지 않고, ②는 일부 내용에 그쳐요.

Some cover crops, such as clover, can take nitrogen from the air and store it in the ground, (c)[increasing] the amount of chemical fertilizer the next crop will need. Others have deep roots that break up hard ground, allowing water to (d)[soak] into the soil rather than running off the surface.

Of course, cover crops are not free. Seeds cost money, planting takes time, and the benefits may not appear in the first year. For this reason, some farmers remain (e)[hesitant] to try them. But those who have used them for many seasons often report healthier fields, steadier harvests during dry years, and lower costs over time. Their experience suggests that the most productive field may not be the one that looks cleanest but the one that is never left uncovered.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 클로버가 공기 중의 질소를 땅에 저장하면 다음 작물에 필요한 화학 비료의 양이 줄어들므로 (c)의 increasing을 reducing으로 바꿔야 해요. 이 문단은 피복 작물이 흙을 안에서부터 좋게 만든다는 내용이에요.

items.passage:
(A)
The Riverside Hawks had lost three games in a row, and everyone on the team seemed to blame someone else. Their striker, Leo, was the best scorer in the league, but he rarely passed the ball. Whenever he got it, he charged toward the goal alone, even when two or three defenders surrounded him. The day before the semifinal, Coach Rivera gathered the players and read out the starting lineup. Leo waited for his name, but it never came. "You'll start on the bench tomorrow," the coach told him quietly afterward. (a)[He] walked home without a word, his face burning with anger.

(B)
Leo jogged onto the field for the second half, and from the first moment he played differently. Instead of shooting from impossible angles, he kept his head up and looked for open teammates. Ten minutes later, he dribbled toward the penalty area, drew two defenders toward (b)[him], and slipped the ball sideways to Daniel. Daniel struck it cleanly into the corner of the net. It was his first goal of the season, and the score was now tied at 1–1.

(C)
The next afternoon, Leo sat on the bench with his arms crossed. At first, he barely watched the game. But as the minutes passed, he began to notice things he had never seen while playing. Daniel, the smallest midfielder on the team, kept sprinting into open space and waving his hands, yet no one passed to him. With a sinking feeling, Leo realized that (c)[he] had ignored Daniel in exactly the same way all season. At halftime, the Hawks were losing 0–1. Leo walked up to Coach Rivera and described what he had seen. The coach listened, then smiled. "Then go out there and show them," he said.

(D)
With three minutes left, Daniel won the ball near the sideline and looked up. This time Leo did not shout for it. He ran toward the far post and waited. Daniel's cross curved over the defenders, and Leo leaped and headed it into the net. The Hawks had won, 2–1. As his teammates lifted Daniel onto their shoulders, Leo found Coach Rivera. "I learned more on the bench than I ever did on the field," (d)[he] admitted. The coach nodded. "That was the whole point," (e)[he] replied with a grin.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 벤치에서 시작하라는 말을 들은 (A) 다음에 다음 날 벤치에서 경기를 지켜보다 후반에 투입되는 (C)가 와요. 이어서 후반에 Daniel에게 패스해 동점을 만드는 (B), 경기 막판 결승골과 경기 후 대화의 (D) 순서예요.

items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Leo는 리그 최고의 득점원이었지만 패스를 거의 하지 않았다.
Daniel은 후반전에 이번 시즌 첫 골을 넣었다.
전반전이 끝났을 때 Hawks는 0대 1로 지고 있었다.
결승골은 Daniel이 Leo의 패스를 받아 넣은 것이었다.
Leo는 코치에게 벤치에서 더 많은 것을 배웠다고 말했다.
items.exp: (D)에서 결승골은 Daniel의 크로스를 Leo가 헤딩으로 넣은 것이라고 했어요. Leo의 패스를 받아 Daniel이 골을 넣은 것은 (B)의 동점골이에요.

items.passage:
Dear Principal Morgan,

I am writing on behalf of the Student Environmental Club at Westbrook High School. Over the past year, the number of students who ride bicycles to school has more than doubled, partly because of the new bike lane on Cedar Avenue. This is wonderful news for our community, but it has created a practical problem. The school has only one small bike rack near the gym, which holds about fifteen bicycles. As a result, many students lock their bikes to fences, trees, and even stair railings, which blocks walkways and sometimes damages the bikes. Some students have told us that they have stopped cycling because they have nowhere safe to leave their bikes. Our club has measured the empty space beside the main entrance and believes it could fit two additional racks for about forty bicycles. We would be grateful if you could approve the installation of these racks before the spring semester begins.

Respectfully,
Hannah Wells, Club President
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 자전거 통학 학생들의 안전 교육을 제안하려고
환경 동아리의 새 회원 모집을 알리려고
학교에 자전거 거치대 추가 설치를 요청하려고
자전거를 울타리에 묶어 둔 학생들에게 주의를 주려고
items.exp: 자전거 통학생이 늘었는데 거치대가 부족하다는 문제를 설명한 뒤, 정문 옆에 거치대 두 개를 추가로 설치하도록 승인해 달라고 요청하고 있어요. ⑤의 내용은 문제 상황을 설명하는 부분일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: The train doors slid shut behind me, and I had taken only a few steps along the platform when I felt how light my shoulders were. My backpack was still on the luggage rack. Inside it were my laptop, my passport, and the notes for the presentation I was supposed to give the next morning. I spun around just in time to watch the last car disappear into the tunnel. My heart pounded, and my hands went cold. I rushed to the station office, barely able to explain what had happened. The clerk calmly asked for the train number and my seat, then picked up the phone. For ten long minutes, I stood at the counter, imagining every terrible possibility. Finally, the clerk put down the phone and smiled. "A conductor found it," she said. "It will be here on the next train back, in about half an hour." I let out a long breath, my shoulders loosening at last, and sank into a chair by the window to wait.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 기차에 가방을 두고 내린 것을 알고 심장이 뛰고 손이 차가워질 만큼 당황했지만, 차장이 가방을 찾았다는 말을 듣고 긴 숨을 내쉬며 안도했어요. 따라서 panicked → relieved가 알맞아요.

items.passage: When people imagine how the writings of the ancient world were lost, they often picture a single dramatic fire consuming a great library. Such disasters did occur, but historians now believe they explain only a small part of the loss. Most ancient texts were written on papyrus or parchment, materials that slowly decay, and a manuscript usually lasted only a few generations before it crumbled. A work survived only if someone, somewhere, decided it was worth copying by hand, a slow and expensive task. Each time tastes changed, works that no longer interested readers simply stopped being copied, and within a century or two they quietly vanished. Many texts we still read today exist because a single monastery or scholar made one more copy at the right moment. In this sense, for an ancient writer, [a book that no one copied was already burning]. The real threat was not sudden destruction but gradual neglect.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a book that no one copied was already burning]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Ancient libraries lacked protection against fire.
Copying by hand often introduced errors into texts.
Writers burned their own works when readers lost interest.
Papyrus was more likely to catch fire than parchment.
A work that was not reproduced was bound to disappear over time.
items.exp: 파피루스와 양피지는 서서히 썩기 때문에 누군가 손으로 베껴 쓰지 않으면 작품은 한두 세기 안에 조용히 사라졌다고 했어요. 따라서 복제되지 않은 책은 이미 사라지는 중이었다는 뜻이에요. ①과 ④는 '불'이라는 낱말만 빌린 오답이에요.

items.passage: Some decisions deserve long reflection: choosing a university, accepting a job, or moving to a new city. Many others do not. Yet people often spend surprising amounts of time and energy on choices whose outcomes hardly matter, such as which of two similar shirts to buy or which restaurant to visit on a Tuesday night. Part of the reason is that small choices feel safe to think about. Their options are easy to compare, so weighing them gives a pleasant sense of control. The cost, however, is real. Mental effort is limited, and every minute spent comparing nearly identical options is a minute not spent on matters that truly shape our lives. Moreover, when two options are so close that we struggle to choose between them, that very difficulty is a sign that either one would probably be fine. A useful habit, then, is to ask before deciding how much the choice will matter a month from now and to limit our effort to match the answer.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 중요한 결정일수록 다른 사람의 조언을 구하는 것이 좋다.
선택지가 많을수록 결정에 대한 만족도는 낮아진다.
결과가 크게 중요하지 않은 결정에는 노력을 적게 들이는 것이 바람직하다.
작은 선택을 자주 연습하면 큰 결정을 더 잘 내릴 수 있다.
비슷한 선택지를 꼼꼼히 비교하는 습관은 통제감을 높여 준다.
items.exp: 결과가 별로 중요하지 않은 사소한 결정에 시간과 에너지를 쓰는 것은 한정된 정신적 노력을 낭비하는 일이므로, 결정의 중요도에 맞춰 노력을 제한하라는 내용이에요. ⑤는 사람들이 작은 선택에 매달리는 이유로 제시된 것이지 필자의 요지가 아니에요.

items.passage: Elephants are famous for their loud trumpeting, but much of their conversation takes place in sounds that humans cannot hear. They produce deep rumbles at frequencies below the range of human hearing. These low sounds lose little energy as they travel, so they can carry several kilometers across open land, far beyond the distance at which elephants can see one another. Researchers using special recording equipment have found that family groups use such rumbles to coordinate their movements, to find one another after separating, and to signal danger. Some of the vibrations also travel through the ground, and elephants appear to detect them through sensitive cells in their feet and trunks. When an elephant suddenly freezes, leans forward, and presses its foot firmly against the earth, it may be listening to a message from a herd far out of sight. This hidden channel helps explain how scattered groups seem to act together across large areas.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: reasons elephants trumpet loudly when they sense danger
how elephants communicate over long distances with low-frequency sounds
the structure of elephant family groups in open land
the equipment scientists use to record animal sounds
why elephants have difficulty seeing distant objects
items.exp: 코끼리가 사람이 들을 수 없는 낮은 진동음과 땅의 진동으로 먼 거리에서도 서로 소통한다는 내용이에요. ①의 trumpeting은 첫 문장에서 대조로만 언급되었어요.

items.passage: Many young athletes believe that the harder and more often they train, the faster they will improve. Taking a day off can feel like falling behind rivals who keep practicing. Yet sports scientists point out that muscles do not grow stronger during training itself. Intense exercise creates tiny tears in muscle fibers and uses up stored energy; it is during the hours and days of rest that the body repairs this damage and builds tissue slightly stronger than before. When athletes skip rest, the repair process never finishes, and each new session starts from a weaker point. Over weeks, this can lead to lasting tiredness, falling performance, and injuries that keep athletes away from their sport far longer than any planned break would have. For this reason, many coaches now schedule recovery days as carefully as training sessions, treating sleep, light stretching, and good meals as part of the program rather than interruptions to it.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Train Every Day to Stay Ahead of Your Rivals
Rest Days: Where Athletic Progress Is Actually Made
Stretching: The Secret to Avoiding All Injuries
The Best Foods for Young Athletes
How Coaches Choose Their Best Players
items.exp: 근육은 훈련 중이 아니라 휴식하는 동안 회복되며 더 강해지므로, 휴식일을 훈련만큼 신중하게 계획해야 한다는 내용이에요. ①은 글이 반박하는 통념이에요.

items.q: Greenfield Teen Cooking Class 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 앞치마와 조리 도구는 각자 가져와야 한다.
네 번 모두 참석하면 요리책을 받는다.
items.exp: 안내문에 앞치마와 조리 도구는 제공된다고 했으므로 각자 가져와야 한다는 ④가 일치하지 않아요.

items.passage: Almost everyone has noticed that the full moon looks enormous when it ①[rises] above the horizon and much smaller a few hours later, high in the sky. Photographs, however, show that the moon's size in the sky barely changes during the night. The difference exists only in our minds, which is why scientists call it the moon illusion. No single explanation has been accepted by everyone, but one popular idea involves the way the brain ②[judges] distance. Near the horizon, the moon appears behind trees, buildings, and hills, and these familiar objects suggest that it is very far away. Because the brain assumes that something so distant must be huge to look as large as it ③[does], it enlarges our impression of the moon's size. High in the empty sky, there are no such clues, so the moon seems smaller. Interestingly, the illusion often weakens when people look at the rising moon through a narrow tube, which hides the objects ④[surrounding] it. This simple test suggests that the background, not the moon itself, ⑤[being] responsible for the effect.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 suggests의 목적어인 that절의 동사 자리이므로 being이 아니라 is로 고쳐야 해요. ③의 does는 앞의 동사 look을 대신하는 대동사로 맞고, ④는 objects를 수식하는 현재분사예요.

items.passage: Subscription services have changed the way many people pay for music, movies, software, and even meals. Instead of buying a product once, customers pay a small fee every month. For businesses, this model is attractive because it provides a ①[steady] stream of income that is easier to predict than one-time sales. For customers, the low monthly price makes services feel ②[affordable]. Yet the same feature that makes subscriptions convenient can also make them ③[noticeable]. Because payments are taken automatically, people often forget how many services they have signed up for. Surveys suggest that many consumers ④[underestimate] their monthly subscription spending, sometimes by a large amount. Some companies take advantage of this by making it easy to join but complicated to cancel. In response, financial advisers recommend reviewing bank statements every few months and canceling any service that has not been used recently. A few minutes of attention can ⑤[prevent] small charges from quietly adding up to a large yearly expense.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 자동으로 결제되기 때문에 사람들이 몇 개의 서비스에 가입했는지 잊어버린다고 했으므로, 구독이 눈에 잘 띄지 않게 된다는 뜻이 되어야 해요. ③의 noticeable을 invisible로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: When adults listen to a foreign language, the speech often sounds like one continuous stream, with no clear breaks between words. Babies face the same problem with their first language, yet within their first year they begin to pick out individual words. How do they do it? Studies suggest that infants are remarkably sensitive to how often sounds appear together. In the phrase "pretty baby," for example, the syllable "pre" is followed by "tty" almost every time it is heard, but "tty" can be followed by many different syllables. By unconsciously tracking these patterns across thousands of hours of speech, babies learn that sounds which reliably occur together probably belong to the same word, while places where the next sound is hard to guess probably mark a boundary. In other words, babies discover words not by being told where they begin and end but by ___ the patterns hidden in what they hear.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 아기는 소리들이 얼마나 자주 함께 나오는지를 무의식적으로 추적해 단어의 경계를 찾아낸다고 했어요. 따라서 숨은 패턴을 찾아낸다는 detecting이 알맞아요. imitating이나 memorizing은 함께 나오는 빈도를 따지는 과정을 나타내지 못해요.

items.passage: A common complaint about scientific models is that they are unrealistic. An economic model may assume that every buyer has perfect information, and a model of planetary motion may treat each planet as a single point with no size at all. Critics conclude that such models must be flawed, since the world plainly does not work that way. This criticism, however, misunderstands what a model is for. A map that included every tree, stone, and blade of grass would be as large as the land itself and therefore useless for finding one's way. In the same manner, a model earns its value by leaving things out, so that the few factors that matter for a particular question stand out clearly. The real test of a model, then, is not whether its assumptions are true in every detail but whether ___. A planet-as-point model fails badly if we wish to study earthquakes on Mars, yet it predicts the planet's orbit with astonishing accuracy.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: it includes as many real-world factors as possible
experts in other fields are able to understand it easily
its predictions can be checked without experiments
it was built by observing the world directly
what it ignores is irrelevant to the question being asked
items.exp: 모델은 특정 질문에 중요한 몇 가지 요소를 드러내기 위해 나머지를 생략함으로써 가치를 얻으며, 점으로 본 행성 모델도 궤도 예측에는 정확하지만 지진 연구에는 쓸모없다고 했어요. 따라서 모델의 진짜 시험은 생략한 것이 해당 질문과 무관한가라는 ⑤가 알맞아요. ①은 지도 비유가 반박하는 생각이에요.

items.passage: Parents often complain that teenagers stay up too late and cannot get out of bed in the morning, and they tend to blame laziness or smartphones. Research suggests that biology plays a larger role than many people assume. ① During adolescence, the body begins to release melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy, about two hours later in the evening than it did in childhood. ② As a result, many teenagers simply do not feel tired until close to midnight, even if they go to bed earlier. ③ Because most schools start early, these students are forced to wake up before their bodies have had enough sleep. ④ Taking short naps after lunch is a common custom in several countries with hot climates. ⑤ Some school districts that have moved their starting times later have reported better attendance, fewer car accidents involving teen drivers, and improved grades.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 청소년의 늦은 수면이 생물학적 원인 때문이며 등교 시간을 늦추면 효과가 있다는 흐름인데, ④는 더운 나라의 낮잠 풍습에 관한 내용이라 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
Until the nineteenth century, nearly every town set its clocks by the sun. Noon was simply the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky over that particular place.

(A) To solve this, railway companies agreed to divide the country into a small number of zones, each sharing one official time. Towns resisted at first, unwilling to give up their own noon, but the convenience of the system soon won them over, and governments later made it law.

(B) This worked well enough when travel was slow. A town a few dozen kilometers to the east might keep time several minutes ahead, but people on horseback hardly noticed the difference.

(C) The arrival of the railway changed everything. Trains covered those distances in less than an hour, and each station posted its departures in its own local time. Timetables became a confusing puzzle, and errors in timing sometimes led to dangerous near-collisions.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 각 마을이 태양으로 시계를 맞췄다는 주어진 글 다음에, 그 방식(This)이 느린 여행 시절에는 문제가 없었다는 (B)가 와요. 이어서 철도가 모든 것을 바꾸어 혼란이 생겼다는 (C), 그 문제를 해결하려고(To solve this) 시간대를 나눴다는 (A) 순서예요.

items.passage: For most of history, the night sky was filled with thousands of visible stars, and the Milky Way stretched across it like a pale cloud. ( ① ) Today, more than half of the world's population lives where artificial light makes the Milky Way impossible to see. ( ② ) Bright light at night confuses many animals that depend on darkness. Young sea turtles, for example, find the ocean after hatching by moving toward the brighter horizon over the water, but streetlights and hotels along the shore can lead them inland instead. ( ③ ) Migrating birds that travel at night may circle lit buildings until they become exhausted. ( ④ ) Fortunately, light pollution is one of the easiest environmental problems to reduce. ( ⑤ ) Shielding lamps so that they shine only downward, choosing warmer colors, and switching off unnecessary lights can restore much of the darkness within a single night, often while saving money on electricity as well.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

The loss of these views is not only a problem for stargazers, however.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 these views는 앞 문장의 보이지 않게 된 은하수와 별을 가리키고, 별을 보는 사람만의 문제가 아니라는 말 뒤에 동물이 겪는 피해가 이어지므로 ②가 알맞아요. ①에 넣으면 아직 경관을 잃었다는 내용이 나오기 전이라 these views가 가리킬 것이 없어요.

items.passage: In one neighborhood study, researchers compared two similar apartment complexes. In the first, residents entered their homes directly from a parking lot. In the second, every resident passed through a shared courtyard with benches and a small playground on the way to the front door. After a year, residents of the second complex knew far more of their neighbors by name, were more likely to borrow tools or watch one another's children, and reported feeling safer at night. Their incomes, ages, and backgrounds were nearly the same as those in the first complex. The main difference, the researchers concluded, was the courtyard. Because people kept crossing paths there, brief greetings gradually turned into conversations, and conversations turned into relationships. No one had planned to become friends; the space simply made casual meetings hard to avoid. Over time, these countless small encounters created a network of people who felt they could count on one another.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Shared spaces that create (A) ___ casual encounters among residents can gradually build (B) ___ within a community.
items.exp: 공유 안뜰 때문에 주민들이 자주 마주치며 인사가 대화와 관계로 이어졌고, 서로 의지할 수 있다고 느끼는 관계망이 생겼다고 했어요. 따라서 (A)에는 frequent, (B)에는 trust가 알맞아요. planned는 아무도 친구가 되려고 계획하지 않았다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Before electric air conditioning existed, builders in hot regions had to keep people cool using nothing but the design of the building itself. Many of their solutions were remarkably effective. In parts of the Middle East, tall towers called windcatchers rose above houses, capturing breezes high above the street and directing them down into the rooms below. Thick walls of stone or mud absorbed the heat of the day and released it slowly at night, keeping indoor temperatures far more (a)[stable] than those outside.

Other traditions relied on shade and water. Narrow streets lined with high walls kept sunlight from reaching the ground for much of the day, and inner courtyards with small fountains or pools cooled the air through evaporation. Light-colored surfaces (b)[reflected] sunlight instead of absorbing it. None of these features required fuel, and many buildings that used them remained comfortable for centuries.

In the twentieth century, cheap electricity made such methods seem (c)[unnecessary]. Architects could design glass towers that would be unbearably hot without machines, knowing that air conditioners would solve the problem. Buildings began to look similar from one climate to another, and the knowledge built up over generations was often (d)[preserved] as old-fashioned.

Today, as cooling accounts for a growing share of the world's energy use, many architects are returning to these older ideas. Modern versions of windcatchers, shaded courtyards, and heavy walls are being combined with new materials and computer models that predict how air will move through a space. The goal is not to reject technology but to let the building do as much of the work as possible, so that machines are needed only for what design alone cannot (e)[achieve].
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Glass Towers Became the Symbol of Modern Cities
How Air Conditioning Changed Daily Life Forever
Cooling by Design: Old Building Wisdom for a Warming World
The Rising Cost of Electricity in Hot Regions
Fountains and Courtyards: Decorations of the Ancient World
items.exp: 기계 없이 건물 설계만으로 시원함을 유지하던 전통 건축 방식이 값싼 전기로 잊혔다가, 냉방 에너지 문제 때문에 다시 주목받고 있다는 내용이에요. ⑤는 분수와 안뜰을 장식으로만 본 오답이고, ②는 일부 내용에 그쳐요.

items.exp: 값싼 전기 때문에 전통 방식이 불필요해 보이고 건물들이 비슷해졌다는 흐름이므로, 대대로 쌓인 지식이 구식이라며 무시되었다는 뜻이 되어야 해요. (d)의 preserved를 dismissed로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
Mina had been preparing for the city's youth painting contest for two months. The theme was "My Neighborhood," and she had chosen to paint the old market near her apartment, with its crowded stalls and colorful umbrellas. On the morning of the contest, she packed her brushes carefully and hurried to the park where hundreds of students were setting up their easels. As she unrolled her paper, she noticed the girl at the next easel, Sora, searching through (a)[her] bag with a worried look. Mina could tell that something was wrong, so she leaned over and asked if Sora needed help.

(B)
When the winners were announced that evening, Mina's name was not called for first place. It was Sora who walked up to the stage to receive the top prize. For a moment, Mina felt a sharp sting of disappointment. Then, to her surprise, Sora asked the judges if she could say something. "I couldn't have painted anything today without the girl next to me," she said, pointing at Mina. The crowd turned and applauded, and Mina realized that (b)[she] was smiling.

(C)
With only her black and white paints left, Mina had to rethink her whole plan. At first, she nearly gave up. Then she remembered the market on rainy evenings, when the colors faded and everything turned gray and silver. Slowly, (c)[she] began to paint that scene instead: wet stones shining under the streetlights and shadows of people hurrying home. When the time was up, Sora looked at Mina's painting and gasped. "It's beautiful," Sora whispered. "It looks like a memory."

(D)
Sora had forgotten her paints at home. The contest rules did not allow anyone to leave the park once it began, and there were only three hours to finish. Without thinking twice, Mina opened her own box and pushed half of her colors toward Sora. "Take the reds and yellows," (d)[she] said. "I'll manage." It was only after Sora had thanked her and started working that Mina realized (e)[she] had given away nearly all the bright colors she had planned to use for her umbrellas.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: Sora가 가방을 뒤지며 걱정하는 (A) 다음에, 물감을 두고 왔다는 사실과 Mina가 물감을 나눠 주는 (D)가 와요. 이어서 남은 흑백 물감으로 비 오는 시장을 그리는 (C), 수상 발표와 Sora의 소감이 나오는 (B) 순서예요.

대회 도중에는 공원 밖으로 나갈 수 있었다.
items.exp: (D)에서 대회 규칙상 대회가 시작되면 아무도 공원을 떠날 수 없었다고 했어요.

items.passage:
Dear Director Hwang,

I am writing on behalf of the parents' association of Maple Hill Middle School. Every morning, more than three hundred students cross Oakridge Avenue at the intersection in front of our main gate. Since the road was widened last spring, it has gained two extra lanes, but the walking signal has stayed exactly the same length. Many of our younger students, especially those carrying instruments or heavy bags, are still in the middle of the road when the light turns red. Last week, a driver turning right had to brake suddenly to avoid a group of sixth graders. Fortunately, no one was hurt, but we fear that next time we may not be so lucky. We therefore ask that your office extend the walking signal at this crossing by at least ten seconds during school hours. We would be happy to meet with your staff and share the observations our volunteers have recorded.

Sincerely,
Grace Mendel
Parents' Association Chair
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 학교 앞 도로 확장 공사의 중단을 요구하려고
학교 앞 횡단보도의 보행 신호 시간 연장을 요청하려고
우회전 차량에 대한 단속 강화를 건의하려고
items.exp: 도로가 넓어졌는데도 보행 신호 길이가 그대로라 학생들이 위험하다고 설명한 뒤, 등교 시간에 보행 신호를 최소 10초 늘려 달라고 요청하고 있어요. 봉사자들의 관찰 기록은 요청을 뒷받침하는 자료일 뿐 보고가 목적은 아니에요.

items.passage: I had spent six weeks on the vase, shaping it on the wheel, trimming its base, and painting the glaze in thin layers late into the night. Now it sat somewhere inside the kiln with forty other pieces, and there was nothing more I could do. When Ms. Ortega finally unlocked the kiln door, I stood at the back of the crowd, my fingers twisted together. I had heard stories of glazes running and of pots cracking in the heat and coming out in pieces. One by one, my classmates lifted out their bowls and cups. Mine was the last to appear. Ms. Ortega held it up to the window, and the afternoon light passed through the blue glaze, which had melted into a pattern like waves on a shallow sea. There was not a single crack. Someone behind me whistled. I took the vase in both hands, still warm, and could not stop grinning as I turned it again and again.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 처음에는 손가락을 꼬고 유약이 흐르거나 도자기가 깨질까 걱정하다가, 금 하나 없이 아름답게 나온 꽃병을 보고 계속 웃음 짓고 있으므로 anxious → delighted가 알맞아요. 결과가 좋았으므로 disappointed는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: In many cities, public drinking fountains have quietly disappeared. Old ones break and are removed rather than repaired, and new parks and stations are often built without any at all. Officials explain that few people use them now that bottled water is sold on every corner. Yet this reasoning runs backward. People stopped using fountains largely because the remaining ones were dirty, broken, or hard to find, not because they no longer needed water. When a city removes them, it turns a basic need into something that must be bought. That choice falls hardest on those with the least money: children playing outside, elderly people on long walks, and workers who spend the day on the street. It also adds to the mountain of plastic bottles that cities must later collect at public expense. Cities should therefore install clean, well-maintained drinking fountains in parks, stations, and busy streets, and treat them as essential public equipment, just like benches and streetlights. Free water should be as easy to find as a place to sit down.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 도시는 공공장소에 깨끗한 식수대를 설치하고 관리해야 한다.
시민들은 생수 대신 개인 물병을 들고 다녀야 한다.
도시는 플라스틱 병 재활용 시설을 늘려야 한다.
공원과 역에 노인과 어린이를 위한 쉼터를 늘려야 한다.
고장 난 공공시설은 수리하지 말고 새로 지어야 한다.
items.exp: Cities should therefore install clean, well-maintained drinking fountains ...라는 문장에 필자의 주장이 드러나 있어요. 플라스틱 병 문제는 식수대가 필요한 이유 중 하나로 언급되었을 뿐이라 ③은 주장이 아니에요.

items.passage: In many offices, the most admired employee is the one whose coat is still on the chair at eight in the evening. Managers rarely see the work itself, which happens inside documents and conversations, so they rely on what they can see: who arrives first, who leaves last, who answers messages at midnight. Employees quickly learn what is being rewarded. They schedule meetings that could have been emails, send updates that no one needs, and stay late to be noticed rather than to finish anything. Before long, many of them are [performing work for an audience of one]. The cost is real. Hours spent looking busy are hours not spent thinking, resting, or solving the problems the company actually cares about, and tired workers make more mistakes. Organizations that want better results, then, must change what they pay attention to. When managers judge people by what they produce rather than by how long they are seen at their desks, the need to act out effort begins to fade.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [performing work for an audience of one]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: competing with coworkers for a single promotion
serving one important customer at a time
making their effort visible to the boss rather than productive
working alone without any support from the team
presenting their results to a small group of experts
items.exp: 관리자는 일 자체가 아니라 보이는 것(늦게까지 남기, 한밤중 답장)으로 판단하고, 직원들은 끝내려고가 아니라 눈에 띄려고 늦게 남는다고 했어요. 따라서 밑줄은 상사 한 사람에게 보여 주기 위해 일하는 척하는 것을 뜻해요. ①의 승진 경쟁은 글에 나오지 않아요.

items.passage: We usually associate falling leaves with autumn, but in many dry regions trees drop their leaves in the middle of the hot season. This is not a sign of illness. Leaves are the main places where a plant loses water, since the tiny pores that let in carbon dioxide also let water vapor escape. During a long drought, keeping a full crown of leaves would drain the tree faster than its roots could refill it. By shedding them, the tree gives up the ability to make food for a while, but it greatly reduces its water loss and protects its trunk and roots from fatal damage. Some species in tropical dry forests can stand bare for months, living on stored sugars until the rains return. Then, often within days of the first heavy storm, they push out new leaves and begin growing again. For these trees, losing their leaves is less a defeat than a carefully timed retreat.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the process by which leaves change color in autumn
the effect of tropical storms on forest growth
the role of roots in storing water for dry seasons
ways in which diseases spread among dry-forest trees
leaf shedding as a strategy for surviving drought
items.exp: 건조 지역의 나무가 가뭄 동안 잎을 떨어뜨려 수분 손실을 줄이고 살아남는다는 내용이므로 주제는 ⑤예요. 잎을 떨어뜨리는 것이 질병의 신호가 아니라고 했으므로 ④는 틀리고, 단풍(①)은 도입에만 잠깐 나와요.

items.passage: Many people imagine that a lightning rod works like a magnet, pulling bolts from the sky toward a building that would otherwise be left alone. In fact, a rod does not make lightning more likely to strike; a tall building in an open area is already a likely target. What the rod changes is what happens after the strike. Lightning carries an enormous electric current that must find a way into the ground. If it passes through brick, wood, or the wiring inside walls, it can heat these materials in an instant, starting fires or blowing pieces off stone. A lightning rod offers the current an easier route: a metal rod at the highest point, connected by a thick cable that runs down the outside of the building to metal plates buried in the earth. Because metal conducts electricity far better than building materials, the current follows the cable and passes harmlessly into the soil. The protection, in other words, comes not from attracting danger but from guiding it safely away.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Tall Buildings: Natural Targets of Storms
Not a Magnet but a Path: How Lightning Rods Protect
Why Lightning Never Strikes the Same Place Twice
Metal Versus Wood: Choosing Safer Building Materials
Predicting Where Lightning Will Strike Next
items.exp: 피뢰침은 번개를 끌어당기는 것이 아니라 번개의 전류를 금속 케이블로 땅까지 안전하게 흘려보내 건물을 보호한다는 내용이라 ②가 알맞아요. ①은 높은 건물이 원래 표적이 되기 쉽다는 일부 내용일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: Agnes Torvik was born in 1862 in a mining town in central Sweden, where her father worked underground and her mother sewed for neighbors. As a girl, she noticed that miners' families paid high prices at the only shop in town, which was owned by the mining company. At twenty-four, she persuaded thirty families to pool their savings and buy flour, salt, and coffee directly from a wholesaler in Stockholm. The small cooperative store they opened in 1887 sold goods at fair prices and returned its profits to members at the end of each year. Although the mining company at first threatened to fire any worker who shopped there, membership grew to more than six hundred families within a decade. Torvik later traveled throughout the country, helping workers in other towns start similar stores. In 1919 she published a practical guide to running a cooperative, which was reprinted many times. She died in 1940.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 마을의 유일한 상점은 광산 회사 소유였다.
협동조합 상점의 이익은 광산 회사에 돌아갔다.
items.exp: 협동조합 상점은 해마다 이익을 조합원에게 돌려주었다(returned its profits to members)고 했으므로 ④가 일치하지 않아요. 광산 회사는 오히려 그 상점을 이용하는 노동자를 해고하겠다고 위협했어요.

items.passage: Tea arrived in Britain in the seventeenth century as an expensive curiosity from China, ①[sold] in coffee houses and in tiny amounts by apothecaries who praised its supposed health benefits. For decades it remained a luxury, partly because the government taxed it heavily. High taxes, however, ②[encouraged] a huge smuggling trade, and by the 1770s more tea may have entered the country illegally than legally. When the tax was cut sharply in 1784, smuggling became unprofitable almost overnight, and tea ③[becoming] affordable for ordinary families. Workers soon drank it several times a day, often with sugar, ④[which] provided cheap energy for long hours in factories. By the nineteenth century, the drink was so central to British life that the country began growing its own supply in India, ⑤[where] a vast new industry of plantations developed. A drink that had once been a rare medicine had become an everyday habit for almost everyone in the country.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: and 앞의 smuggling became과 나란히 이어지는 절의 동사가 필요하므로 ③ becoming은 became으로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 curiosity를 꾸미는 과거분사, ②는 주어 High taxes의 동사, ④는 sugar를 받는 관계대명사, ⑤는 India를 받는 관계부사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: For centuries, the white marble statues of ancient Greece were admired as the ①[perfect] expression of classical beauty. Artists and architects copied their pale surfaces, and white came to be seen as a sign of elegance and good taste. Yet the statues the Greeks themselves looked at were far from white. Scientists using ultraviolet light and chemical analysis have found tiny ②[traces] of paint on many sculptures: red lips, blue and green clothing, patterned borders, and skin in warm tones. Over two thousand years, wind, rain, and soil wore most of this color away, and some later collectors even scrubbed off what ③[remained], believing it to be dirt. When researchers have built painted copies based on these findings, many visitors find the results surprising or even unpleasant. Their reaction shows how ④[strongly] our idea of the ancient world has been shaped by what time left behind rather than by what was originally made. The colorless marble we admire is, in a sense, a ⑤[faithful] record of how the Greeks wanted their statues to be seen.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 그리스 사람들은 조각에 색을 칠했고 지금의 흰 대리석은 세월이 색을 지운 결과라고 했으니, 흰 대리석은 그리스인이 원한 모습을 충실히 보여 주는 기록이 아니라 잘못 전하는 기록이에요. 그래서 ⑤ faithful을 misleading 같은 말로 바꿔야 해요. 남은 물감을 먼지로 여겨 문질러 없앴다는 ③과 우리의 생각이 크게 영향받았다는 ④는 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: Why do people believe some claims more readily than others? Part of the answer has little to do with evidence. In many experiments, participants rated statements as more likely to be true simply because they had seen them before, even when they had been told at first that some of the statements were false. A claim repeated several times starts to feel easy to process, and the mind tends to treat that ease as a signal of truth. This is why rumors grow stronger as they travel and why advertisers repeat the same slogan endlessly. The effect is hard to escape, because it works below the level of conscious reasoning; we rarely notice that we are judging a sentence by how smoothly it slides into our thoughts. In short, we often mistake ___ for accuracy, and the more often we hear something, the less we think to question it.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 전에 본 적이 있다는 이유만으로, 즉 반복되어 익숙해진 주장을 사실이라고 믿는다는 내용이므로 familiarity가 알맞아요. novelty(새로움)는 반대 의미이고, 권위(authority)나 감정(emotion)은 글에서 다루지 않아요.

items.passage: It is tempting to think that the best explanation is the one that can account for everything. A theory that fits every possible outcome seems powerful; whatever happens, it has an answer ready. Yet this flexibility is precisely what should make us suspicious. Suppose a fortune teller predicts that you will "face a change soon." Whether you change jobs, move house, or merely change your mind, the prediction appears confirmed. It can never fail, but for that very reason it tells you nothing. A serious scientific claim behaves very differently. It says, in effect, "If I am right, you will observe this and not that," and thereby ___. When the observation comes and the claim survives, we have learned something, because it could have lost. The value of an idea, then, lies not in how many events it can be stretched to cover, but in how many it rules out — and in its willingness to be judged by them.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: frees itself from the need for any further observation
explains every result that might appear in the future
borrows the language of prediction to sound more convincing
exposes itself to the risk of being proven wrong
persuades readers through a confident and authoritative tone
items.exp: 과학적 주장은 무엇이 관찰되고 무엇이 관찰되지 않을지 미리 밝히고, 살아남았을 때 '질 수도 있었기 때문에' 의미가 있다고 했으므로 틀렸다고 입증될 위험에 스스로를 내놓는다는 ④가 알맞아요. ②는 필자가 비판한 점쟁이식 설명이고, ⑤처럼 확신에 찬 말투로 설득하는 것은 글의 핵심과 관련이 없어요.

items.passage: In many cultures, the way a gift is offered carries as much meaning as the gift itself. ① In parts of East Asia, for example, a gift is traditionally handed over with both hands, a gesture that shows respect for the person receiving it. ② The receiver, in turn, may politely refuse once or twice before accepting, so as not to appear greedy. ③ The modern gift card industry has grown rapidly, as busy shoppers prefer to let recipients choose items for themselves. ④ In some Middle Eastern households, guests are expected to bring something small, such as sweets, and to present it to the host at the door. ⑤ Even the choice of wrapping paper can send a message, since certain colors are linked to celebration in one culture and to mourning in another. Paying attention to these customs helps travelers avoid giving offense when they intend only kindness.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 선물을 건네는 방식에 담긴 문화별 의미를 다루는 글인데, ③은 상품권 산업의 성장이라는 소비 경향을 말하고 있어 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤의 포장지 색깔은 선물을 전하는 방식의 일부라 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage:
Noise-cancelling headphones seem almost magical: they make the roar of an airplane engine fade without blocking your ears completely. Their trick relies not on thick padding but on a simple fact of physics.

(A) This method, however, works best on steady, low sounds such as the hum of an engine. Sudden or high-pitched noises, like a baby's cry, change too quickly to be predicted, which is why they still slip through.

(B) The headphones put this cancellation to work. A tiny microphone on the outside of each ear cup picks up incoming noise, and a chip calculates a mirror-image wave. The speaker then plays this opposite wave along with your music.

(C) Sound travels as a wave of pressure, with peaks and valleys following one another through the air. When two waves meet, they combine. If the peaks of one wave line up with the valleys of another, the two cancel out, and the result is near silence.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 '물리학의 사실'을 (C)에서 파동이 서로 상쇄되는 원리로 설명하고, (B)가 this cancellation으로 그 상쇄 원리를 헤드폰에 적용하는 방법을 말해요. 이어 (A)가 This method, however로 그 방법의 한계를 덧붙이므로 (C)–(B)–(A)예요.

items.passage: Two passengers sitting side by side on the same flight may have paid very different prices for their seats. ( ① ) This is not an error but the result of a strategy called dynamic pricing, in which the price of a product changes constantly according to demand. ( ② ) As seats fill up or the departure date approaches, the system raises the prices of the remaining seats; when sales are slow, it lowers them to attract more buyers. ( ③ ) The same approach is now common for hotel rooms, concert tickets, and taxi rides ordered through apps. ( ④ ) For companies, the benefit is clear: they can earn more from customers who are willing to pay more, while still filling seats and rooms that would otherwise stay empty. ( ⑤ ) Many customers, however, feel uneasy when they discover that the person next to them paid half as much for exactly the same thing. To them, a price that depends on timing rather than on the product itself can seem less like a fair market and more like a guessing game.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Airlines use computer programs that track how many tickets have been sold and how quickly new bookings are coming in.
items.exp: ② 뒤 문장의 the system은 주어진 문장의 computer programs를 가리키므로, 판매 현황을 추적하는 프로그램이 먼저 소개되어야 해요. ①에 넣으면 바로 뒤 This is not an error의 This가 가리킬 '서로 다른 가격' 내용과 끊어져요.

items.passage: Parents often try to teach young children new words by pointing at objects and naming them: "Look, a spoon!" But researchers who recorded families at play noticed that this approach works less well than one might expect. When a parent names an object that the child is not paying attention to, the child must first stop what he is doing, shift his gaze, and figure out what the word refers to. Many toddlers simply fail to make the connection. In contrast, when a parent waits to see what has caught the child's interest — a ball rolling under a chair, a dog in the window — and names that, the word lands on a mind that is already focused. Children whose parents frequently followed their attention in this way knew noticeably more words a year later than children whose parents usually tried to direct it. The lesson is that the timing of a word may matter as much as the word itself.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Young children learn new words more effectively when adults (A) ___ the child's current focus than when they try to (B) ___ it.
items.exp: 아이가 이미 관심을 둔 대상에 이름을 붙여 줄 때(관심을 활용할 때) 단어를 더 잘 배우고, 부모가 주의를 다른 곳으로 이끌려 할 때는 덜 배운다고 했으므로 (A) build on, (B) steer가 알맞아요. set aside는 아이의 관심을 무시한다는 뜻이라 반대예요.

items.passage:
For a long time, scientists pictured memory as a kind of storage room. An experience was recorded, placed on a shelf in the brain, and later taken down when needed, ideally in the same condition it was put away. Forgetting, in this view, was simply a matter of things getting lost or fading with age. Research over the past few decades has (a)[challenged] this picture. Experiments with animals showed that when an established memory is recalled, it becomes briefly unstable, as if it had been taken off the shelf and unpacked. To be kept, it must be stored again, and during this window it can be strengthened, weakened, or altered by new information. Studies with people point in the same direction. Witnesses who are asked leading questions about an event often later remember details that were only (b)[suggested] to them, and they do so with complete confidence. Each act of remembering, then, is less like replaying a recording than like retelling a story, which (c)[remains] identical each time it is told.

This discovery is unsettling, since it means that our most treasured memories may drift over the years without our noticing. Yet it may also be useful. A memory that can be updated allows us to (d)[revise] what we know as the world changes, rather than clinging to outdated information. Some researchers are even exploring whether the window after recall could be used to (e)[reduce] the emotional pain attached to frightening memories. The shelf, it turns out, was never a shelf at all; it is closer to a workshop, where each memory is rebuilt every time we visit it.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why We Forget Things as We Grow Older
Animal Experiments: The Key to Human Behavior
How to Train Your Memory Like a Muscle
items.exp: 기억은 꺼낼 때마다 불안정해져 다시 저장되며 바뀔 수 있으므로, 저장된 것을 그대로 꺼내는 것이 아니라 다시 만드는 것이라는 내용이에요. 그래서 ⑤가 제목으로 알맞고, 목격자가 확신을 갖고 잘못 기억한다고 했으므로 ④는 반대 내용이에요.

items.passage:
(A)
The snow had begun as a few lazy flakes when Mr. Dawson left the school with eleven children on his bus. By the time he reached the long climb toward Pine Ridge, the wind was driving it sideways in thick white sheets. The wipers could barely keep up, and the road ahead had become a pale blur. Behind him, the children's chatter had faded into an uneasy silence. (a)[He] gripped the wheel and told himself the village was only twenty minutes away.

(B)
Halfway up the hill, the rear wheels slipped, and the bus slid gently toward the ditch before stopping at an angle. No one was hurt, but when Mr. Dawson tried to move forward, the tires only spun. His radio crackled with a message that the road above them had been closed. Through the swirling snow, he could just make out a light in a farmhouse window about a hundred meters away. Taking the youngest child's hand, (b)[he] led the line of students through the knee-deep drifts, calling out names every few steps so that no one would wander off.

(C)
Early the next morning, the roar of a snowplow woke everyone. Parents arrived behind it in a line of trucks, hugging their children and thanking Mrs. Keller again and again. When the last family had gone, Mr. Dawson stood at the door, unsure how to repay her. She only pressed a jar of homemade jam into (c)[his] hands and told him to bring the children back in summer, when the road was clear and the strawberries were ripe.

(D)
A woman named Mrs. Keller opened the door before he could knock. Without asking a single question, she pulled the children inside, sat them near the wood stove, and began heating a large pot of soup. Mr. Dawson called the school to report that everyone was safe, and then, for the first time that afternoon, (d)[he] allowed himself to sit down. The children, warm again, soon turned the farmhouse into a noisy playground. Mrs. Keller brought out old board games and quilts, and as (e)[she] spread blankets across the living room floor, she laughed that her house had not been this lively in years.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A) 눈보라 속 운전 다음에 버스가 미끄러져 농가로 걸어가는 (B), 그 농가의 Mrs. Keller가 문을 열어 주는 (D), 다음 날 아침 제설차가 오고 작별하는 (C)의 순서예요. (C)의 Mrs. Keller는 (D)에서 처음 소개되므로 (D)가 (C)보다 앞서야 해요.

choices: Mr. Dawson의 버스에는 열한 명의 아이들이 타고 있었다.
버스가 도랑 쪽으로 미끄러지면서 아이 한 명이 다쳤다.
무전으로 위쪽 도로가 폐쇄되었다는 소식이 들려왔다.
Mr. Dawson은 아이들을 이끌고 농가까지 걸어갔다.
Mrs. Keller는 Mr. Dawson에게 직접 만든 잼을 건넸다.
items.exp: (B)에서 버스가 미끄러졌지만 No one was hurt라고 했으므로 ②가 일치하지 않아요. 열한 명의 아이, 도로 폐쇄 무전, 농가로 걸어간 일, 직접 만든 잼은 모두 글과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear members of the Eastbrook Youth Orchestra,

I hope you are all enjoying the cooler weather and practicing your parts for our winter concert. I am writing about an important change to our rehearsal plans. As many of you know, the main hall of the Eastbrook Arts Center will be closed throughout November so that its old heating system can be replaced. Our Saturday rehearsals, which were scheduled to take place there, will instead be held in the gymnasium of Northfield High School, just two blocks away. The starting time will remain 10 a.m., but please arrive fifteen minutes early during the first week, as we will need extra time to set up chairs and music stands. Parking is available behind the school building. The winter concert itself will still take place in the main hall on December 12, as planned. If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me.

Best regards,
Daniel Ruiz
Orchestra Manager
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 예술 회관 난방 시설 교체 공사에 대해 사과하려고
연주회 무대 설치를 도울 단원을 모집하려고
11월 토요일 연습 장소가 바뀐 것을 알리려고
새 연습 장소의 주차 문제 해결을 요청하려고
items.exp: 예술 회관 공사로 11월 토요일 연습을 Northfield 고등학교 체육관에서 하게 되었다고 알리는 글이에요. 겨울 연주회는 예정대로 12월 12일 본관에서 열린다고 했으므로 ①은 틀려요.

items.passage: The train from the coast was supposed to arrive at 6:10, and Mina had been standing on the platform since six. By 6:40, it had come and gone, and her friend Hana had not stepped off. Mina checked her phone for the fifth time. No message. They had planned this weekend for months, and now Hana could not even bother to text. Mina folded her arms and began composing in her head the sharp words she would say. Then her phone buzzed. "So sorry! I got off one stop early to pick something up. Taking the next train. Don't be mad!" Twenty minutes later, Hana came running down the platform, out of breath, holding a small paper bag. Inside was a jar of the honey cookies from the tiny bakery near their old elementary school, the same ones they used to share every day after class. "I remembered you said you missed these," Hana said. Mina felt her anger melt away, and her eyes grew warm.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Mina의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: Mina는 연락 없이 늦는 친구에게 화가 나 날카로운 말을 준비하다가, 친구가 추억의 과자를 사 오느라 늦은 것을 알고 화가 풀리며 눈시울이 뜨거워지므로 annoyed → touched가 알맞아요. 처음부터 화가 나 있었으므로 relaxed는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Some of the most admired paintings in museums are, in a sense, unfinished. Look closely at a portrait by a skilled painter, and you may find that the lace on a collar is only a few quick strokes, or that a hand fades into a blur of brown. Up close, these areas look careless. Step back, however, and the mind fills them in: the strokes become delicate lace, and the blur becomes a hand resting in shadow. Painters discovered long ago that a viewer who is given every detail tends to glance and move on, while one who must complete the image becomes involved in it. The work is no longer something seen but something partly made. In this way, great artists are often not those who say everything, but those who know exactly where to stop. Their genius lies partly in [leaving the last few steps to the viewer], trusting that the eye and imagination will travel the remaining distance.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [leaving the last few steps to the viewer]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: guiding visitors through the museum in a fixed order
allowing the audience to complete the image in their minds
asking critics to judge whether a work is finished
letting students copy the final parts of a master's work
hiding their mistakes from those who view the painting
items.exp: 대충 칠한 듯한 부분을 관람자의 마음이 채워 넣어 작품의 일부를 함께 만든다고 했으므로, 밑줄은 관람자가 상상으로 그림을 완성하도록 남겨 둔다는 뜻이에요. 가까이서 보면 부주의해 보이지만 의도된 것이라 했으므로 실수를 숨긴다는 ⑤는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: When a city wants people to spend time in a public square, it often focuses on what it can add: fountains, sculptures, colorful paving. Yet observers who have spent long hours watching how people actually use such spaces report something simpler. People go where they can sit, and they sit where they can watch other people. A plaza with beautiful design but no seating near the busy edges will remain empty at lunchtime, while a plain strip of steps beside a sidewalk may be crowded. Movable chairs are especially popular, because they let people adjust their position slightly, toward the sun or away from a stranger, which gives them a sense of control. Shade, a nearby food stand, and a view of passing crowds matter more than any decorative feature. The lesson for planners is that a successful public space is shaped less by how it looks from above on a drawing than by how comfortable it feels to an ordinary person looking for a place to rest.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 도시 광장은 지역의 역사와 문화를 반영하도록 꾸며야 한다.
공공장소의 장식물은 시민의 의견을 모아 결정해야 한다.
이동식 의자는 관리가 어려워 공공장소에 적합하지 않다.
광장의 크기가 클수록 더 많은 사람이 모이게 된다.
공공장소의 성공은 외관보다 사람들이 편히 머물 수 있는지에 달려 있다.
items.exp: 사람들은 앉을 수 있고 다른 사람을 볼 수 있는 곳에 모이며, 성공적인 공공장소는 도면상의 외관보다 쉴 곳을 찾는 사람이 느끼는 편안함에 달려 있다는 것이 요지예요. 이동식 의자는 인기가 많다고 했으므로 ③은 반대 내용이에요.

items.passage: London lies farther north than most of Canada's major cities, yet its winters are far milder than Montreal's. One important reason lies in the ocean. In the tropical Atlantic, the sun heats the surface water, and winds and the rotation of the Earth push this warm water northward along the coast of North America and then across the ocean toward Europe. As it flows, the water gives off its heat to the air above it, and westerly winds carry that warmth over the land. By the time the current reaches the cold waters near Iceland and Norway, it has cooled and become saltier, which makes it heavy enough to sink and flow back south along the ocean floor. This vast loop works like a conveyor belt, moving heat from the equator toward the poles. Scientists watch it closely, because a slowdown in this circulation could make the climate of western Europe noticeably colder.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the reasons why ocean water becomes saltier near the poles
the effect of the Earth's rotation on daily wind patterns
the role of an ocean current in warming western Europe
differences in city planning between Canada and Europe
the danger rising sea levels pose to coastal cities
items.exp: 적도의 따뜻한 바닷물이 북쪽으로 흘러 열을 공기에 내주어 서유럽의 겨울을 온화하게 만든다는 내용이므로 ③이 주제예요. 바닷물이 짜지는 것(①)은 순환을 설명하는 일부일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: When online stores offer "free shipping," customers often feel they are getting something for nothing. Of course, someone still pays to move the package from a warehouse to a front door. Usually the cost is quietly built into product prices, so shoppers who live near the store help pay for those who live far away, and people who buy one item at a time are supported by those who buy in bulk. The effects reach beyond the price tag. Because shipping seems costless, many shoppers order items they are unsure about, planning to send back whatever does not fit. Returned goods travel twice, and a surprising share of them are never resold, since checking and repackaging them costs more than they are worth. Delivery trucks making many small trips add to traffic and air pollution in crowded neighborhoods. None of this means that free shipping is wrong, but it does suggest that the word "free" hides a long list of costs that are simply paid by someone else.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Online Shopping: The End of Local Stores
How to Return Items Without Paying Extra
Why Delivery Trucks Need Cleaner Fuel
Free Shipping Is Never Really Free
The Growing Joy of Buying in Bulk
items.exp: 무료 배송의 비용은 상품 가격, 반품 낭비, 교통과 대기 오염의 형태로 다른 누군가가 결국 부담한다는 내용이라 ④가 알맞아요. 반품과 배송 트럭은 그 비용의 예로 나올 뿐 글 전체의 중심은 아니에요.
