items.q: Lakeview Star-Gazing Night 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 7세 미만 어린이는 학생 요금을 내야 한다.
items.exp: 7세 미만 어린이는 무료(Children under 7 free)라고 했으므로 ②가 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 시간, 프로그램, 신청 기한, 손전등 안내와 모두 일치해요.

items.passage: The octopus is one of the ocean's most skilled masters of disguise. Within a fraction of a second, it can change not only the color of its skin but also its texture, ①[raising] small bumps to imitate rough coral or smoothing them out to match sand. This ability depends on thousands of tiny sacs of pigment, each of ②[which] is surrounded by muscles connected directly to the nervous system. When the muscles pull, a sac stretches and its color spreads; when they relax, the sac shrinks to a nearly invisible dot. What makes this ③[even more] puzzling is that most octopuses appear to be color-blind, with only one type of light receptor in their eyes. Some researchers suspect that the skin itself ④[may sense] light, since proteins similar to those in eyes have been found there. If this is correct, the octopus may match its background partly by "seeing" through its skin, a possibility that, if confirmed, ⑤[changing] our understanding of animal vision.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 a possibility를 꾸미는 관계절 that ...의 동사 자리이므로 changing을 would change처럼 시제를 갖춘 동사로 고쳐야 해요. ②는 전치사 of 뒤의 관계대명사 which, ④는 조동사 뒤의 동사원형으로 맞아요.

items.passage: Lithium-ion batteries power our phones, laptops, and a growing number of cars, yet only a small share of them are recycled at the end of their lives. One reason is that recycling them is technically ①[easy]. The batteries contain a complex mixture of metals, plastics, and liquids, and they can catch fire if they are crushed carelessly. Traditional methods melt the batteries down at very high temperatures, which recovers some metals but ②[wastes] others and consumes large amounts of energy. Newer approaches instead take the batteries apart and use chemical solutions to ③[separate] valuable materials such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel. These methods can recover a much higher proportion of the metals, making recycling more ④[profitable]. As the number of electric cars on the road rises, so will the pile of worn-out batteries, and engineers hope that recovered metals will one day ⑤[reduce] the need to mine new ones.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 재활용률이 낮은 이유로 배터리가 복잡한 혼합물이고 불이 날 수도 있다는 점을 들고 있으므로 ① easy는 difficult로 바꿔야 해요. ③ separate, ④ profitable, ⑤ reduce는 모두 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: Waiting in line is rarely pleasant, but some waits feel far worse than others, even when they last exactly the same amount of time. In one study, customers at a bank were less upset by a long single line than by several shorter lines in which they kept watching people in neighboring lines move ahead. In another, diners who saw newcomers seated before them complained bitterly, even if they themselves were seated only a few minutes later. What seems to bother people most is not the delay itself but the feeling that the rules are being broken — that someone has gained an advantage they did not earn. This is why a "take a number" system can calm a crowded office, and why airlines that let some passengers board first often hide that process from those still waiting. When it comes to lines, people will accept a surprising amount of inconvenience, as long as they are convinced of the ___ of the process.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 사람들이 가장 싫어하는 것은 지연 자체가 아니라 규칙이 깨지고 누군가 부당한 이득을 얻는다는 느낌이라고 했으므로 fairness(공정성)가 알맞아요. 대기 시간이 같아도 느낌이 다르다고 했으므로 speed는 답이 될 수 없어요.

items.passage: Historians depend on written records, and it is tempting to assume that what appears often in the archives was common in the past, while what appears rarely was rare. But records were not produced by chance. For most of history, writing was a skill held by a small group — officials, priests, merchants — and they wrote about what concerned them: taxes, laws, trade, and the deeds of rulers. The daily work of farmers, the knowledge passed between mothers and daughters, and the songs of people who never learned to read left few marks on paper, not because they were unimportant but because no one with a pen thought them worth recording. A historian who counts mentions in documents may therefore end up measuring not what people did, but ___. Careful historians try to correct for this by reading the records against their grain, asking who is silent in them and why, and turning to other evidence, such as tools, buildings, and oral traditions, that ordinary people left behind.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: how accurately ancient languages have been translated
what the writers of the time considered worth noting
how many documents have been destroyed by war and fire
which events ordinary people remembered most clearly
what modern readers find most interesting about the past
items.exp: 기록은 글을 쓸 줄 아는 소수가 자신들의 관심사만 적은 것이므로, 기록 속 언급 횟수를 세면 사람들이 실제로 한 일이 아니라 기록자가 적을 가치가 있다고 여긴 것을 재게 된다는 ②가 알맞아요. ④의 평범한 사람들이 기억한 것은 오히려 기록에 남지 않은 쪽이고, ③의 기록 소실은 글에서 다루지 않아요.

items.passage: In the late nineteenth century, several large cities found a fast way to deliver messages without using the streets at all: they sent them through pipes. ① Networks of underground tubes connected post offices, and letters rolled into small metal containers were pushed from one station to the next by compressed air. ② Paris, Berlin, and other capitals built systems hundreds of kilometers long, and a message could cross the city in under an hour, far faster than any messenger on foot or on horseback. ③ For decades, people used these "pneumatic posts" much as we use text messages today, to arrange meetings, send quick replies, or share urgent news. ④ Compressed air is also used today to power many tools, such as the heavy drills that workers use to break up old pavement. ⑤ As telephones spread into homes and offices, however, fewer people needed to send short written notes, and the tubes gradually fell silent. By the late twentieth century, most of the city networks had closed, although similar tubes still carry samples and documents inside many hospitals.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 19세기 말 도시들이 압축 공기로 편지를 보내던 관 우편(기송관 우편)의 등장과 쇠퇴를 다루는 글이에요. ④는 압축 공기로 움직이는 오늘날의 공구 이야기라서 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤는 전화의 보급으로 관 우편이 쇠퇴했다는 내용으로 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage:
Many of the world's largest caves were carved not by rushing rivers or earthquakes but by something as gentle as rainwater. The process begins in the sky, as falling rain absorbs a small amount of carbon dioxide from the air.

(A) Over thousands of years, these tiny openings grow into passages and then into great halls. Eventually, when the water table drops, the passages drain, leaving behind empty chambers through which air instead of water can flow.

(B) This dissolved gas turns the water into a weak acid. As it soaks into the soil, it picks up even more carbon dioxide from decaying plants, becoming slightly stronger before it reaches the rock below.

(C) If that rock is limestone, the acid slowly dissolves it, especially along cracks where water can move easily. Each drop removes only an invisible amount, but it widens the cracks a little at a time.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 이산화탄소를 (B)가 This dissolved gas로 받아 약한 산이 된다고 하고, (C)가 그 산이 닿는 that rock(석회암)을 녹여 틈을 넓힌다고 해요. (A)의 these tiny openings는 (C)의 넓어진 틈을 가리키므로 (B)–(C)–(A)예요.

items.passage: When people who share no common language must work together, they often create a simple mixed language to get by. Such a language, called a pidgin, usually has a small vocabulary and few grammar rules, borrowing most of its words from whichever group holds the most power in the region. ( ① ) Speakers use it for trade or work, but nobody speaks it as a first language. ( ② ) Something remarkable can happen, however, when children grow up hearing a pidgin around them. ( ③ ) Rather than simply copying the broken speech of the adults, the children begin to add regular patterns of their own, such as consistent ways of marking time or forming questions. ( ④ ) Within a generation or two, the pidgin can develop into a full language, known as a creole, with a rich grammar. ( ⑤ ) For linguists, this transformation offers rare evidence that children do not merely absorb the language around them but actively build it.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Such a language can express ideas as complex as those of any other language in the world.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 such a language는 완전한 언어로 발전한 creole을 가리키고, 그 언어가 어떤 언어 못지않게 복잡하다는 내용은 ④ 뒤 creole 설명 바로 다음에 와야 해요. 이어 언어학자에게 이 변화가 갖는 의미로 글이 마무리되므로 ⑤가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Music students often believe that practicing a difficult passage at full speed, again and again, is the quickest way to master it. Teachers who have studied how skills are learned suggest the opposite. When a passage is played faster than a student can control, small errors creep in — a wrong finger here, an uneven rhythm there — and each repetition strengthens those errors along with the correct notes. The hands learn exactly what they practice, including the mistakes. By contrast, playing the same passage slowly enough to get every note right gives the brain a clean pattern to store. Once the passage can be played accurately at a slow pace, the speed can be increased step by step, and the accuracy tends to carry over. Students who follow this method often find, to their surprise, that they reach full speed sooner than classmates who rushed from the beginning.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Practicing a difficult passage slowly with (A) ___ before increasing the tempo leads to mastery that is often (B) ___ than repeating it at full speed.
items.exp: 느리게 쳐서 모든 음을 정확하게 익힌 뒤 속도를 올리면 처음부터 서두른 학생보다 오히려 더 빨리 제 속도에 도달한다고 했으므로 (A) precision, (B) faster가 알맞아요. 빠르게 반복하면 실수까지 굳는다고 했으므로 (A)에 speed는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Walk through a carefully managed park, and you will rarely see a dead tree. Fallen trunks are removed, and standing dead trees are cut down for safety or simply because they look untidy. For a long time, forest managers did the same, believing that dead wood was a sign of poor health and a waste of space. Ecologists now see it very differently. In a natural forest, a large share of all living species (a)[depend] on dead and dying wood at some point in their lives. Woodpeckers carve their nests in standing dead trunks, and the holes they leave behind later shelter owls, bats, and squirrels. As a fallen log slowly decays, fungi and insects break down its tough fibers, and the log becomes a soft, moist bed in which seedlings can take root. In dry seasons, these logs act like sponges, (b)[holding] water long after the surrounding soil has dried out.

Removing dead wood, therefore, does not make a forest healthier; it (c)[strengthens] the web of life that depends on it. In some managed forests in Europe, beetles that live only in old decaying trunks have become so (d)[rare] that they are now protected by law. In response, a growing number of foresters deliberately leave some dead trees standing and allow fallen logs to remain where they drop. The change requires patience, since a log may take decades to decay completely. But the reward is a forest that is (e)[richer] in life, one in which death is not the end of a tree's usefulness but the beginning of a new role.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How to Plant Trees in Dry Seasons
Why Forest Fires Begin in Dead Wood
Keeping Parks Clean and Safe for Visitors
Dead Trees: Hidden Engines of Forest Life
items.exp: 죽은 나무가 새, 곰팡이, 곤충, 묘목 등 수많은 생물을 떠받치므로 숲의 생명에 꼭 필요하다는 내용이라 ⑤가 알맞아요. 딱따구리(④)는 예시 중 하나일 뿐이에요.

items.passage:
Walk through a carefully managed park, and you will rarely see a dead tree. Fallen trunks are removed, and standing dead trees are cut down for safety or simply because they look untidy. For a long time, forest managers did the same, believing that dead wood was a sign of poor health and a waste of space. Ecologists now see it very differently. In a natural forest, a large share of all living species (a)[depend] on dead and dying wood at some point in their lives. Woodpeckers carve their nests in standing dead trunks, and the holes they leave behind later shelter owls, bats, and squirrels. As a fallen log slowly decays, fungi and insects break down its tough fibers, and the log becomes a soft, moist bed in which seedlings can take root. In dry seasons, these logs act like sponges, (b)[holding] water long after the surrounding soil has dried out.

Removing dead wood, therefore, does not make a forest healthier; it (c)[strengthens] the web of life that depends on it. In some managed forests in Europe, beetles that live only in old decaying trunks have become so (d)[rare] that they are now protected by law. In response, a growing number of foresters deliberately leave some dead trees standing and allow fallen logs to remain where they drop. The change requires patience, since a log may take decades to decay completely. But the reward is a forest that is (e)[richer] in life, one in which death is not the end of a tree's usefulness but the beginning of a new role.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 죽은 나무를 없애면 숲이 건강해지지 않는다는 흐름이므로 그에 의존하는 생명의 그물망을 '강화한다'는 (c) strengthens는 weakens로 바꿔야 해요. (d) rare는 법으로 보호될 만큼 드물어졌다는 뜻으로 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Every Saturday in summer, twelve-year-old Leo helped his grandfather sell peaches at the farmers' market in the town square. Grandpa Joe had grown peaches for fifty years, and he knew each of his trees the way other people knew their neighbors. Leo loved the early drive into town, the smell of coffee from the stalls, and the regular customers who always asked about the harvest. That morning, a sudden hailstorm two days earlier had left small brown marks on nearly half of the fruit. As they unloaded the crates, Leo frowned. "Nobody will buy these," (a)[he] said, holding up a spotted peach.

(B)
Leo stared at the sign, worried that his grandfather would be upset. Instead, the old man chuckled and handed (b)[him] a knife. "Let's give them a taste," he said. They cut the spotted peaches into slices and set them out on a plate. Within minutes, a small crowd had gathered, drawn first by the strange sign and then by the sweet smell of the fruit. People who bit into the sweet, juicy slices began reaching for paper bags, and some asked specifically for the marked fruit.

(C)
Grandpa Joe suggested selling the damaged peaches at half price, but Leo had another idea. While his grandfather arranged the perfect fruit in neat rows, Leo took a piece of cardboard and a marker. "Hail-kissed peaches," (c)[he] wrote in big letters. "Ugly outside, extra sweet inside. Same price as the pretty ones." When he propped up the sign, Grandpa Joe raised an eyebrow but said nothing.

(D)
By noon, the spotted peaches were gone, while a few perfect ones still remained in their rows. A woman who ran a bakery nearby even asked whether she could order ten crates of "hail-kissed" fruit for her pies the following week. On the drive home, Grandpa Joe was quiet for a while. Then (d)[he] patted Leo's shoulder and said that, after fifty years of farming, he had just learned something new from his grandson. Leo looked out the window, smiling, already thinking about what (e)[he] might write on next week's sign.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 우박 자국 난 복숭아를 걱정한 뒤, Leo가 반값 대신 '우박이 입 맞춘 복숭아' 팻말을 쓰는 (C), 그 팻말(the sign)을 보고 할아버지가 시식을 제안하는 (B), 정오에 흠집 난 복숭아가 다 팔리는 (D)의 순서예요. (B)의 the sign은 (C)에서 만든 팻말을 가리키므로 (C)가 먼저 와야 해요.

items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 우박으로 복숭아의 거의 절반에 갈색 자국이 생겼다.
복숭아 조각을 맛본 사람들이 봉투를 집어 들기 시작했다.
Leo는 흠집 난 복숭아를 반값에 팔자고 제안했다.
근처 빵집 주인이 다음 주에 쓸 복숭아 열 상자를 주문하려 했다.
items.exp: (C)에서 반값 판매를 제안한 사람은 할아버지였고, Leo는 예쁜 복숭아와 같은 가격으로 팔자는 팻말을 썼으므로 ④가 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 모두 글의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Dr. Whitmore,

My name is Jaeho Lim, and I am a second-year student at Brookside High School. I have visited the Brookside Planetarium almost every month since I was ten, and the evening shows there are what first made me dream of studying astronomy. Last week, I noticed on your website that the planetarium now offers guided tours of its exhibition hall for elementary school groups every Saturday. I would very much like to take part in this program as a volunteer guide. I have read most of the books sold in your gift shop, and I recently completed an online course on the solar system offered by a national university. I am available every Saturday morning and could also help out during school vacations. If there is an application form or an interview, I would be glad to complete it at any time. Thank you for considering my request.

Sincerely,
Jaeho Lim
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 천문관 견학 안내 자원봉사자로 참여하게 해 달라고 요청하려고
천문학 온라인 강좌의 수료 사실을 알리려고
기념품 가게에 판매할 도서의 확충을 건의하려고
items.exp: 초등학생 단체를 위한 토요일 전시관 안내 프로그램에 자원봉사 안내원으로 참여하고 싶다고 밝히고 지원 방법을 묻고 있어요. 온라인 강좌 수료나 기념품 가게 책 이야기는 자신이 적합하다는 근거로 든 것이에요.

items.passage: The fog had rolled in faster than Mina expected. Twenty minutes earlier, she could see the whole valley below the ridge; now she could barely make out the rocks at her feet. She stopped and checked her phone. No signal. Her heart began to pound as she turned in a slow circle, trying to remember which way the trail had bent. Every direction looked the same, gray and silent. She told herself not to panic, but her hands were shaking as she zipped up her jacket. Then, through the mist, she heard a faint sound, the clink of a metal bell. She walked toward it carefully, step by step, until a wooden post appeared in front of her. Hanging from it was the small bell that marked the shelter at the halfway point, and painted on the post was a bright yellow arrow. Mina let out a long breath and laughed quietly at herself. The path home was right where it should be.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Mina의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 안개 속에서 길을 잃고 심장이 뛰고 손이 떨리던 Mina는 종소리를 따라가 이정표를 찾고 긴 숨을 내쉬며 웃어요. 그래서 불안함에서 안도감으로 바뀐 거예요.

items.passage: Most writers revise by staring at the screen and reading silently, but this is one of the least effective ways to find problems in your own writing. When you read silently, your brain already knows what you meant to say, so it quietly fills in missing words and smooths over awkward phrases. Your eyes move across the page, but you are really reading the version that exists in your head. Reading aloud breaks this habit. Your mouth cannot skip a missing word as easily as your eyes can, and your ear immediately notices a sentence that runs out of breath or a rhythm that sounds clumsy. If you stumble over a sentence, your reader will probably stumble too. So before you call a draft finished, read it out loud from beginning to end, slowly, as if you were presenting it to an audience. It may feel strange at first, but the mistakes you hear will surprise you, and your writing will become clearer for it.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 글을 쓰기 전에 개요를 꼼꼼히 작성해야 한다.
글은 짧고 간결한 문장 위주로 써야 한다.
다른 사람의 글을 소리 내어 읽으며 문체를 익혀야 한다.
퇴고할 때는 충분한 시간 간격을 두고 다시 읽어야 한다.
글을 고칠 때는 자신의 초고를 소리 내어 읽어 보아야 한다.
items.exp: 속으로 읽으면 머릿속 문장을 읽게 되므로, 초고를 끝내기 전에 처음부터 끝까지 소리 내어 읽으라고 주장해요. 시간 간격을 두라는 말이나 남의 글을 읽으라는 말은 없어요.

items.passage: Digital tools have made saving information almost effortless. With a single click, we can store an article, a photo of a lecture slide, or a quote we liked. Many people now keep thousands of notes, bookmarks, and screenshots, and they feel reassured that everything is safely kept somewhere. Yet when they actually need a particular idea, they often cannot find it, or they find it without remembering why it mattered. The problem is not a lack of storage but a lack of connection. A note that is never reviewed, labeled, or linked to other ideas simply sits in place, and as the collection grows, each item becomes harder to reach. Without someone deciding what belongs together and what can be thrown away, such a collection turns into [a library with no librarian]. The real value of a note-taking system, therefore, comes less from how much it holds than from the regular effort of sorting, connecting, and revisiting what is inside it.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a library with no librarian]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a large collection of saved information that is hard to use because no one organizes it
a digital space where information is free for anyone to access
a storage system that automatically deletes information no longer needed
a place where people learn better when they study without a teacher
a collection that loses value because it contains too little information
items.exp: 사서가 없는 도서관은 무엇을 함께 묶고 버릴지 정하는 사람이 없어 자료가 많아도 찾아 쓰기 어려운 모음을 뜻해요. 글은 저장 공간이 아니라 정리와 연결이 부족한 것이 문제라고 하므로 정보가 너무 적다는 ⑤는 반대예요.

items.passage: Hummingbirds live life at an extreme pace. Their wings beat dozens of times per second, and their hearts can race at more than a thousand beats per minute. Such an engine burns fuel quickly, so during the day a hummingbird must visit hundreds of flowers to drink nectar. The real danger comes at night, when the bird cannot feed. If it kept its body at daytime temperature until morning, it could use up all of its energy reserves before sunrise. To avoid this, many hummingbirds enter a state called torpor. Their body temperature drops sharply, sometimes by more than twenty degrees, and their heartbeat and breathing slow dramatically. In this deep rest, a bird may use only a small fraction of the energy it would otherwise need. The cost is that it cannot respond quickly to danger, and waking up takes time. Yet for a tiny animal with a huge appetite, switching off for the night is often the only way to survive until dawn.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the role of hummingbirds in pollinating flowers
the reason hummingbirds migrate long distances at night
a strategy that helps hummingbirds save energy overnight
the dangers hummingbirds face from night predators
how fast wing beats allow hummingbirds to hover in the air
items.exp: 먹이를 먹을 수 없는 밤에 에너지가 바닥나지 않도록 체온과 심장 박동을 크게 낮추는 torpor 상태에 들어간다는 내용이므로 밤사이 에너지를 아끼는 전략이 주제예요. 꽃가루받이나 날갯짓 속도는 도입부의 배경일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: At the 2008 Olympic Games in Beijing, swimmers broke world records at an astonishing rate, and by the end of the following year more than a hundred world records had fallen. The main reason was not a new training method but a new kind of swimsuit. Made partly or entirely of polyurethane, these full-body suits trapped air to keep swimmers higher in the water and squeezed their bodies into a smoother shape that cut through it with less drag. Some swimmers even wore two suits at once for extra effect. Soon, critics complained that races were being decided by technology rather than by athletes, and that swimmers who could not obtain the newest suit had little chance. In 2010, the sport's international governing body responded by banning the suits and setting strict rules on material and coverage. Records stopped falling for several years. The decision reflected a basic belief about sport: equipment may help, but the contest should remain a test of the human body.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How Swimmers Train to Break World Records
The Hidden Health Risks of Competitive Swimming
Why Olympic Pools Are Getting Faster
Technology Always Makes Sports More Exciting
When the Suit Swims Faster Than the Swimmer
items.exp: 기록이 쏟아진 원인이 선수보다 첨단 수영복이었고, 결국 경기가 인간의 몸을 겨루는 것이어야 한다는 이유로 금지되었다는 내용이므로 '수영복이 선수보다 빨리 헤엄칠 때'가 알맞아요. 기술이 늘 스포츠를 흥미롭게 만든다는 ④는 글의 결론과 반대예요.

items.passage: Elsbeth Varga was born in 1871 in a small village in Hungary, where her father worked as a gardener on a large estate. As a child, she spent hours drawing the flowers he grew, and by the age of fifteen she was selling her sketches to visitors. In 1893, she moved to Vienna to study painting, but the art academy did not accept women at the time, so she took private lessons instead. Her big chance came in 1901, when a botanist hired her to illustrate a guide to the wild plants of the Danube region. The book's detailed watercolors were praised for being both beautiful and scientifically accurate. Over the next thirty years, Varga produced more than two thousand plant illustrations, many of which she painted while traveling through the mountains. Later in life, she lost much of her eyesight but continued to teach young artists in her home. She died in 1948, and her original paintings are now kept in a university library in Budapest.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 1893년에 빈의 미술 학교에 입학하여 그림을 공부했다.
1901년에 다뉴브 지역 야생 식물 안내서의 삽화를 맡았다.
시력을 상당 부분 잃은 후에도 젊은 화가들을 가르쳤다.
items.exp: 1893년에 빈으로 갔지만 미술 학교가 여성을 받지 않아 개인 교습을 받았다고 했으므로 ②가 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 지문 내용과 같아요.

items.passage: Many people choose the first day of a new year, a new month, or even a new week ①[to begin] a diet or an exercise plan. Psychologists suggest that such dates work as mental dividing lines. When a new period starts, people tend to see their past failures as ②[belonging] to an "old self," a person who is no longer quite the same as who they are now. This sense of distance makes it easier to look at the future with optimism. A birthday or the start of a school term can have a similar effect, ③[which] helps explain why gyms are often crowded in early January. However, the motivation created by a fresh start fades quickly unless it is supported by concrete plans. A person who decides to "read more" on January 1 is far less likely to succeed than one who ④[plans] to read ten pages every night before bed. The new date provides the spark, but daily habits ⑤[keeping] the fire burning.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 but 뒤 절에서 주어 daily habits의 동사 자리이므로 keeping이 아니라 keep이 되어야 해요. ③ which는 앞 절 전체를 받는 계속적 용법이라 맞아요.

items.passage: The Venus flytrap catches insects with leaves that snap shut in a fraction of a second. Yet closing the trap is ①[costly]: it uses a great deal of energy, and each trap can close only a limited number of times before it dies. So the plant must avoid wasting effort on raindrops or falling bits of leaves. Its solution is surprisingly ②[clever]. Inside each trap are a few tiny trigger hairs. When something touches one hair, nothing happens at first; the plant simply 'remembers' the touch for about twenty seconds. Only if a second touch follows within that time does the trap close. A single drop of rain is therefore ③[likely] to set it off, while a struggling insect, which keeps brushing against the hairs, almost certainly will. Even after closing, the plant keeps ④[counting]. Further touches signal that the prey is alive and worth digesting, and only then does the trap seal tightly and begin to release digestive juices. In this way, a plant without a brain manages to ⑤[distinguish] a meal from a false alarm.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 두 번 건드려야 닫히므로 빗방울 한 번으로는 덫이 닫히기 어렵다는 내용이 되어야 해요. 뒤의 while a struggling insect ... almost certainly will과 대조되므로 ③ likely는 unlikely로 바꿔야 해요. 나머지는 에너지 비용, 영리한 해결책, 접촉 횟수 세기, 먹이와 헛경보 구별이라는 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage: Economists often describe markets in terms of prices, supply, and demand. Yet beneath every exchange lies something that rarely appears in economic charts: ___. When you order a product online, you pay before it arrives, believing the seller will actually ship it. The seller, in turn, assumes that your payment will not suddenly be canceled. A farmer delivers vegetables to a restaurant expecting to be paid at the end of the month. If each side had to check, guard, and verify every step, transactions would become slow and costly, and many would never happen at all. This is why societies in which people can rely on strangers to keep their promises tend to have more active economies. Rating systems, contracts, and courts exist largely to support this foundation when personal relationships are absent. Without it, even the most efficient market would grind to a halt.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 먼저 돈을 내거나 물건을 보내는 예와 낯선 사람이 약속을 지킬 것이라 믿을 수 있는 사회라는 내용으로 보아 빈칸은 신뢰예요. 계약과 법원은 그 기초를 받쳐 주는 장치일 뿐이라 regulation은 답이 될 수 없어요.

items.passage: Drivers caught in a sudden traffic jam usually assume that something must have caused it: an accident, a closed lane, a slow truck. Often, however, when the traffic finally clears, there is nothing to be seen. Such jams can arise from almost nothing. On a crowded highway, one driver touches the brakes a little harder than necessary; the driver behind, reacting a moment late, brakes harder still, and the effect grows as it passes backward through the line of cars. Within minutes, a wave of stopped traffic is traveling backward along the road, even as the cars inside it creep forward, and it may last long after the first driver has continued on, unaware of having started anything. Researchers have recreated such waves on circular test tracks with no obstacles and with far fewer cars than the track could hold, simply by asking drivers to keep a steady speed. What this suggests is that a jam is better understood as ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a result of careless drivers who ignore the rules of the road
a problem that wider roads and more lanes would easily solve
an event that can be traced back to a single accident
a pattern produced by the interaction of many small reactions
a sign that the number of cars has exceeded the road's capacity
items.exp: 한 운전자의 약간 강한 제동이 뒤차들의 늦은 반응으로 커지며 뒤로 퍼지고, 장애물도 없고 차가 적은 원형 트랙에서도 정체 파동이 생겼다고 했으므로 정체는 수많은 작은 반응이 서로 작용해 생기는 패턴이에요. ③은 원인을 사고 하나로 보는 통념이고, ⑤는 차가 트랙 수용량보다 훨씬 적었다는 실험 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Spending long hours in front of screens can leave your eyes feeling tired, dry, and sore by the end of the day. ① One reason is that people blink far less often than usual when they concentrate on a screen, so the surface of the eye is not kept moist and slowly dries out. ② Screens have also become an important tool for learning, allowing students to watch lessons and join classes from almost anywhere. ③ In addition, focusing on something at a fixed, close distance for a long time keeps the small muscles inside the eye tense, and they rarely get a chance to relax. ④ A simple habit can help with both problems: every twenty minutes, look at something about six meters away for at least twenty seconds and blink a few times on purpose. ⑤ Adjusting the screen's brightness to match the light in the room and placing the screen slightly below eye level can further reduce discomfort.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 글은 화면을 오래 볼 때 눈이 피로해지는 이유와 줄이는 방법을 다루는데, ②는 화면이 학습 도구가 되었다는 장점을 말해 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
Today it seems natural that every house has a number, but for most of history, homes had none. People found one another by asking neighbors or by describing landmarks, such as the house beside the church or across from the well.

(A) Over time, however, residents discovered unexpected benefits of the system. Visitors could find unfamiliar addresses easily, and when regular postal delivery spread in the nineteenth century, numbered houses made it possible to bring letters directly to each door.

(B) This worked well enough in small villages where everyone knew everyone else. As cities grew and governments wanted to collect taxes and call young men for military service, officials needed a reliable way to identify each household.

(C) Their answer was to paint a number on every building. Not surprisingly, many people disliked this idea, fearing that the numbers existed only so the authorities could find them and take their money or their sons.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (B)의 This가 주어진 글의 이웃에게 묻거나 지형지물로 집을 찾던 방식을 받고, (C)의 Their answer는 (B)에서 가구를 식별할 방법이 필요했던 관리들(officials)의 해결책이에요. (A)는 however로 (C)의 사람들의 반감과 대조되는 뜻밖의 이점을 말하므로 마지막이에요.

items.passage: When you pour a soda into a glass, you may notice that streams of tiny bubbles keep rising from the same few spots on the inside of the glass, again and again. ( ① ) This is not a coincidence. ( ② ) A carbonated drink contains carbon dioxide that was dissolved into the liquid under high pressure, and once the bottle is opened, that gas begins to escape. ( ③ ) To leave the liquid, however, the gas needs a place where a bubble can begin to form. ( ④ ) Each pocket gives the dissolved gas an easy entrance, so a bubble grows there until it breaks free and rises, leaving a little air behind for the next one. ( ⑤ ) That is why a perfectly smooth and clean glass produces fewer bubbles, and why some beer glasses have tiny marks cut into the bottom on purpose to keep a steady line of foam rising to the top.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Tiny scratches in the glass or specks of dust provide such places, because each one holds a small pocket of trapped air.
items.exp: ④ 앞에서 기체가 거품이 생길 자리가 필요하다고 했고, 주어진 문장이 그 자리(긁힌 자국·먼지)를 소개하며 작은 공기 주머니를 처음 언급해요. ④ 뒤의 Each pocket이 그 공기 주머니를 받으므로 ④가 알맞아요.

items.passage: A neighborhood association in a mid-sized city once struggled to find volunteers. Its newsletter regularly asked residents to "get involved in improving the community," but almost no one responded. Then the organizers tried a different approach. Instead of a general appeal, they posted a list of small, clearly defined jobs: water the flower boxes on Elm Street for one week, bring two folding tables to the spring fair, or spend an hour helping seniors set up their new phones. Within days, nearly every task was taken, and many of the new volunteers later signed up for more. The organizers concluded that people are rarely unwilling to help. What holds them back is uncertainty: a vague request leaves them wondering how much time it will take, whether they have the right skills, and where to even begin. A concrete task removes those questions and makes saying yes feel easy.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

People are more likely to volunteer when a request is (A) ___, because it reduces the (B) ___ that keeps them from taking part.
items.exp: 막연한 부탁 대신 작고 분명한 일을 제시하자 지원자가 몰렸으므로 (A)는 specific이에요. 사람들을 막는 것은 시간·능력·시작점에 대한 불확실성이므로 (B)는 doubt예요.

items.passage:
In many industrialized societies, daily life is organized by the clock. Meetings begin at 9:00, lunch lasts an hour, and arriving fifteen minutes late is considered (a)[disrespectful]. Anthropologists call this "clock time": a system in which the hour on the watch decides when an activity starts and ends. Yet for much of human history, and in many communities today, people have lived by what researchers describe as "event time." In this system, an activity begins when the necessary conditions are in place and ends when it is naturally complete. A village meeting starts when enough people have gathered, not at a fixed hour, and a meal ends when the conversation winds down.

Outsiders often misread event time as a sign of laziness or poor organization. Anthropologists who live within such communities, however, report something quite different. Event time reflects a set of (b)[priorities] in which relationships and the quality of an activity matter more than its schedule. Cutting a conversation short simply because the clock says so would seem (c)[rude], much as arriving late seems rude in a clock-time culture. Each system, in other words, has its own idea of what it means to be polite.

The distinction matters more than ever in a connected world. Business partners, aid workers, and students abroad frequently find themselves moving between the two systems, and frustration on both sides is (d)[rare] when no one recognizes what is happening. One person feels kept waiting; the other feels rushed. Studying how communities experience time reminds us that even something as seemingly (e)[universal] as an hour is shaped by culture.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Punctuality Leads to Economic Success
The Disappearance of Event Time in Modern Villages
Clock or Event? How Cultures Shape Our Sense of Time
How Anthropologists Learn to Live in Other Cultures
Lateness: A Universal Sign of Disrespect
items.exp: 시계 시간과 사건 시간이라는 두 체계를 비교하며 시간 감각도 문화가 만든다고 말하므로 ③이 알맞아요. ⑤는 글의 결론과 반대이고, ④는 연구 방법만 다뤄요.

items.exp: 아무도 무슨 일이 일어나는지 모를 때 양쪽의 좌절은 드문 것이 아니라 흔하므로 (d) rare를 common으로 바꿔야 해요. 뒤의 '한쪽은 기다렸다고, 다른 쪽은 재촉당했다고 느낀다'가 근거예요.

items.passage:
(A)
Friday evenings were always the busiest time at Han's Kitchen, the small noodle restaurant Jiho's family had run for twenty years. That Friday, however, his father came out of the kitchen holding his right wrist, his face pale. He had slipped while carrying a heavy pot, and he could barely move his hand. The dining room was already half full. Jiho, who was fifteen, took a deep breath and said, "Let me cook tonight, Dad. I've watched you do it a thousand times." His father hesitated, looking at the line of customers waiting at the door.

(B)
Finally, he nodded. "All right. But I'll stand next to you and tell you every step." For the next hour, Jiho worked faster than (a)[he] ever had. His father called out instructions: how long to boil the noodles, when to add the green onions, how much broth to pour. Jiho's mother took orders and carried bowls, smiling at customers as if nothing were wrong. The first bowls went out, and the room filled with the familiar sound of people eating happily.

(C)
On the following Friday, Jiho's father's wrist was still wrapped in a bandage, so Jiho stepped up to the stove again. This time, he tasted the broth before every bowl went out. Near closing time, the same elderly customer came in, ordered noodles, and ate slowly. When he finished, he called Jiho over and said, "Now this tastes like Han's Kitchen." Jiho looked toward the doorway, where his father was standing. (b)[He] had been watching the whole time, and his eyes were shining. That night, Jiho wrote the recipe in a notebook of (c)[his] own.

(D)
Then a regular customer, an elderly man who came in every week, sent his bowl back. "Too salty," he said. Jiho realized that in the rush (d)[he] had added salt twice. After the last customer left, Jiho sat on a stool in the empty kitchen, feeling that he had let everyone down. His father sat beside him and laughed. "The first time I cooked here, your grandfather threw out a whole pot of my broth," he said. "Mistakes teach you what instructions can't." Jiho smiled for the first time all evening, and (e)[he] asked his father to show him the recipe again, step by step.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (B)의 Finally, he nodded가 (A) 끝에서 망설이던 아버지의 결정을 이어요. (D)의 Then으로 단골손님이 국물이 짜다고 돌려보내고, (C)에서 다음 주 금요일에 같은 손님이 칭찬하므로 (B)-(D)-(C)예요.

choices: Jiho의 가족은 20년 동안 식당을 운영해 왔다.

items.passage:
Dear Director Kim,

I am writing on behalf of the residents of Maple Hill Apartments, which are located next to Greenway Park. Many of us walk through the park every evening, as it is the shortest route between our building and the subway station. Over the past two months, however, at least six of the streetlights along the main path have stopped working. After sunset, the section near the pond becomes almost completely dark, and several residents, including elderly people and students coming home from evening classes, have tripped on the uneven ground. Some parents now refuse to let their children use the path at all. We reported the problem through the city's online system in early September, but we have not yet received a reply, and nothing has changed. We kindly ask that you send a team to repair the lights as soon as possible, before the days grow even shorter this winter. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,
Grace Yoon
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 공원 내 연못 주변의 쓰레기 문제를 알리려고
야간 수업을 듣는 학생들을 위한 셔틀버스를 요청하려고
고장 난 공원 가로등의 신속한 수리를 요청하려고
items.exp: 공원 산책로의 가로등 여러 개가 꺼져 주민들이 넘어지고 있으니 빨리 수리팀을 보내 달라고 요청하는 글이에요. 온라인 신고에 답이 없었다는 것은 사정 설명일 뿐 시스템 개선을 건의하는 것은 아니에요.

items.passage: For weeks, Leo had been counting the days until Saturday. His uncle had managed to get two tickets to his favorite band's outdoor concert, and their seats were right in front of the stage. Leo had even learned the words to every song on the band's new album, sure that he would be singing along all night. On Saturday morning he woke up before his alarm, put on the band's T-shirt, and ran to the window. The sky was dark gray, and rain was hammering against the glass. He turned on the television and waited nervously for the local news. Finally, the announcement came: because of the heavy storm, the concert had been called off, and no new date had been set. Leo sat down on the edge of his bed, still holding the tickets. The T-shirt suddenly felt silly on him. He looked out at the empty, soaking backyard and sighed. All those weeks of waiting had ended in nothing.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Leo의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 몇 주 동안 공연 날을 손꼽아 기다리며 들떠 있던 Leo가 폭우로 공연이 취소되자 한숨을 쉬며 낙담해요. 뉴스를 기다리며 초조해한 것은 잠깐이고 결국 안도하지 않았으므로 ③은 틀려요.

items.passage: Every time you install an app or buy a new phone, it arrives with hundreds of settings already chosen for you: how often it sends notifications, whether it shares your location, how bright the screen is. In theory, you are free to change any of them. In practice, studies show that most users never do. Changing a setting requires knowing that the option exists, finding it in a menu, and deciding what you prefer, and most people have better things to do. As a result, the choices made by a small group of designers quietly become the habits of millions of users. A messaging app that turns on read receipts by default creates a world in which people feel pressure to reply immediately; one that turns them off creates a more relaxed one. Nobody voted for these outcomes, and few users even notice them. This is [the quiet power of the preset]: decisions that look neutral end up shaping how we behave.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the quiet power of the preset]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the ability of users to freely customize their devices
the tendency of people to resist technology that is too complicated
the hidden influence of designers' preset choices on users' behavior
the growing pressure on companies to protect users' personal data
the way devices automatically learn the preferences of their users
items.exp: 대부분의 사용자는 설정을 바꾸지 않아 소수의 설계자가 정한 기본값이 수많은 사람의 습관이 된다는 것이 밑줄의 의미예요. ①은 이론상 가능할 뿐 실제로는 일어나지 않는다고 했고, 기기가 스스로 학습한다는 ⑤는 언급이 없어요.

items.passage: When students get back an assignment, most of them look first at the grade and then put the paper away. Many teachers have noticed this, and research on classroom feedback supports what they see. A number or letter tells students where they stand, but it says nothing about what to do next. Worse, once a grade appears, students tend to ignore any written comments beside it, because the grade feels like the final word. In contrast, comments that point to a specific strength and a specific next step, such as "Your examples are vivid, but your second paragraph needs a clear topic sentence," give students something they can actually act on. When teachers return work with comments only and reveal the grade later, students read the feedback more carefully and are more likely to apply it in their next assignment. Feedback improves learning not when it judges past work but when it guides the work that comes next.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 학생들은 성적보다 교사와의 관계에서 더 큰 동기를 얻는다.
과제의 수를 줄여야 학생들이 피드백을 꼼꼼히 읽는다.
구체적으로 다음 단계를 안내하는 피드백이 학습 향상에 도움이 된다.
성적은 학생의 실력을 객관적으로 보여 주는 가장 좋은 수단이다.
학생들은 서로의 과제에 의견을 주고받으며 더 많이 배운다.
items.exp: 점수는 다음에 할 일을 알려 주지 못하지만 구체적인 강점과 다음 단계를 짚어 주는 의견은 학생이 실행할 수 있어 학습을 돕는다는 것이 요지예요. 동료 피드백이나 과제 수 이야기는 없어요.

items.passage: For a long time, scientists wondered how certain birds could fly across oceans for days without stopping to rest. The answer turned out to be surprising: they sleep while flying, but only with half of their brain at a time. Recordings of brain activity in birds such as frigatebirds have shown that one side of the brain can enter a sleeplike state while the other side remains awake, keeping the bird balanced and alert. The eye connected to the waking side often stays open, watching for danger or obstacles. Such birds may sleep for only a few seconds at a time, adding up to less than an hour per day while in the air, far less than they sleep on land. A similar ability is found in dolphins, which must keep swimming to the surface to breathe. Sleeping with half the brain thus allows these animals to rest without giving up the activities that keep them alive.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the dangers birds face when they migrate across oceans
how some animals rest by letting only half the brain sleep
why dolphins need more sleep than birds
the effects of lack of sleep on animal behavior
how scientists measure brain activity in wild animals

items.passage: If rain is fresh and rivers are fresh, why is the ocean salty? The answer begins on land. As rain falls, it picks up a little carbon dioxide from the air, which makes it slightly acidic. When this water runs over rocks and soaks into soil, it slowly breaks down minerals and carries away tiny amounts of dissolved salts. Rivers then deliver these salts to the sea, where they remain. The sun heats the ocean surface, and water evaporates into the air, but the salts are left behind. Over hundreds of millions of years, this one-way traffic has built up the saltiness we taste today. Smaller amounts of salt also come from hot springs and volcanoes on the sea floor. River water does contain salt, but so little that we cannot taste it. The ocean, in other words, is the end of a very long journey, a place where minerals collect but rarely leave.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How Rivers Quietly Made the Ocean Salty
Why Rainwater Is Unsafe to Drink
Undersea Volcanoes: The Main Source of Sea Salt
Why Rivers Grow Saltier Every Year

items.passage: A popular story claims that glass is actually a very slow liquid, and that this is ①[why] old church windows are thicker at the bottom than at the top. Over centuries, the story goes, the glass has gradually flowed downward. Scientists, however, have shown that this explanation cannot be true. Calculations suggest that glass at room temperature flows so slowly that a visible change would take far longer than the age of the universe. The real reason lies in how window glass ②[was] made before modern factories. Glassmakers spun melted glass into a large disk, ③[which] was naturally uneven in thickness. When pieces were cut from it and fitted into frames, builders often placed the thicker edge at the bottom, perhaps because it seemed more stable. Some old windows even have their thick edge at the top or the side, a fact that the flowing-glass story cannot explain. Glass, then, is better described as a solid ④[lacks] the orderly structure of crystals, and uneven old windows ⑤[tell] us more about early craftsmanship than about physics.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ④는 앞의 a solid를 뒤에서 꾸며야 하므로 동사 lacks가 아니라 현재분사 lacking이 되어야 해요. ③ which는 a large disk를 받는 계속적 용법이고, ⑤ tell은 and 뒤 절의 주어 uneven old windows에 맞는 동사예요.

items.passage: In many professional sports, video replay now helps referees review difficult decisions. Supporters argue that the technology makes games ①[fairer]: a goal scored from an offside position or a ball that clearly crossed the line can be judged correctly instead of being left to a single glance in real time. Yet replay has also brought new problems. Reviews can take several minutes, ②[interrupting] the flow of the game and cooling the excitement of fans in the stadium. Some players complain that they no longer know whether to celebrate a goal immediately or wait for the decision. Moreover, slow-motion images can ③[exaggerate] contact between players, making an ordinary challenge look like a serious foul. For these reasons, many leagues limit replay to a few types of decisions and ask referees to overturn a call only when the original decision is clearly wrong. The goal is to ④[correct] obvious mistakes while ⑤[sacrificing] the natural rhythm that makes sports enjoyable to watch.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 분명한 실수는 바로잡되 경기의 자연스러운 흐름은 지키려는 것이 목적이므로 sacrificing이 아니라 preserving이 되어야 해요. ③ exaggerate는 느린 화면이 접촉을 부풀려 보이게 한다는 뜻으로 맞아요.

items.passage: When photography became widely available in the nineteenth century, many painters feared their art would become unnecessary. For centuries, one of painting's main jobs had been to record how people and places looked, and a camera could now do this faster, cheaper, and more accurately than any brush. Yet instead of disappearing, painting changed direction, and some of the most celebrated art movements in history grew out of this crisis. Freed from the duty of copying reality exactly, artists began to explore what a photograph could not easily capture: the feeling of a moment, the movement of light across a scene, or the inner world of the painter. Colors became bolder, brushstrokes became visible, and shapes were simplified or even broken apart. In this sense, the camera did not end painting but pushed it toward ___, encouraging artists to ask not "What does this look like?" but "What does this mean to me?"
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 사진이 사실을 기록하는 역할을 맡게 되자 화가들은 순간의 느낌과 내면 세계를 탐구했고, '나에게 무엇을 의미하는가'를 묻게 되었으므로 표현이 알맞아요. accuracy와 imitation은 사진이 가져간 역할이에요.

items.passage: Organizations love numbers because numbers seem objective. A hospital tracks how long patients wait, a school tracks test scores, and a call center tracks how many calls each worker completes per hour. These figures begin as useful signals: shorter waits, higher scores, and more calls usually suggest that things are going well. The trouble starts when the numbers are turned into goals and attached to rewards or punishments. Suddenly, people have reasons to improve the figure itself rather than the reality it was meant to reflect. Call-center workers may rush customers off the phone without solving their problems; a school may spend weeks drilling test formats instead of teaching deeper understanding. The numbers look better and better, while the service they were supposed to measure quietly gets worse. The lesson is not that measurement is useless, but that ___. A number works best as a window onto what is happening, and it loses that power the moment people start aiming at the window instead of looking through it.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: once a measure becomes a target, it stops telling us what we wanted to know
numbers should be replaced by personal opinions whenever possible
rewards are the most effective way to improve an organization's performance
only experts should be allowed to collect and interpret data
the more figures an organization tracks, the more accurate its picture becomes

items.passage: A paper cut is one of the smallest injuries a person can suffer, yet it often hurts far more than its size would suggest. ① Most paper cuts happen on the fingertips, which contain a remarkably dense network of nerve endings that allow us to feel fine textures and handle small objects. ② Because so many pain receptors are packed into such a small area, even a shallow cut there sends a strong signal to the brain. ③ The edge of a sheet of paper also looks smooth but is actually rough at a tiny scale, so it tears the skin unevenly rather than slicing it cleanly. ④ Paper was first made in China about two thousand years ago, and for centuries it remained a costly material used mainly for official records. ⑤ Finally, since the cut is usually too shallow to bleed much, the damaged nerve endings stay exposed to the air, and every movement of the finger stretches the wound open again.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 작은 종이 베인 상처가 유난히 아픈 이유(손끝의 많은 신경 말단, 거친 종이 가장자리, 피가 적게 나 노출된 신경)를 설명하는 글이에요. ④는 종이의 역사 이야기로 통증의 원인이라는 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
In the early 1800s, armies often struggled more with hunger than with their enemies, because fresh food spoiled long before it could reach soldiers far from home. Hoping to solve this problem, the French government offered a large cash prize to anyone who could find a reliable way to preserve food.

(A) His glass containers, however, were heavy and broke easily on rough roads. Within a few years, inventors in England began sealing food in cans made of iron coated with tin, which were far sturdier and soon replaced the jars.

(B) The winner was a confectioner named Nicolas Appert. After years of experiments, he showed that food sealed tightly in glass jars and then heated in boiling water could stay edible for months.

(C) These early cans, though, were so thick and heavy that opening them was a challenge in itself. Soldiers often had to use knives, bayonets, or even rocks, and a practical can opener did not appear until several decades later.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (B)의 The winner가 주어진 글의 상금을 받고, (A)의 His glass containers는 Appert의 유리병을 가리켜요. (C)의 These early cans는 (A)에서 나온 주석 도금 철제 통조림이므로 (B)-(A)-(C)예요.

items.passage: Throwing away leftover food may seem harmless. After all, it is natural material that will simply rot, unlike plastic bottles or metal cans that remain for centuries. ( ① ) However, the way food breaks down depends greatly on where it ends up. ( ② ) In a landfill, by contrast, food scraps are buried under layers of other waste, where there is almost no oxygen. ( ③ ) Under these conditions, the bacteria that break the food down release methane, a gas that traps far more heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide does over the short term. ( ④ ) That is why food waste in landfills is now considered a significant contributor to climate change. ( ⑤ ) Composting at home or using a city's food waste collection program can therefore make a real difference, turning yesterday's dinner into rich soil for gardens and farms instead of a source of greenhouse gas.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

In a garden or compost pile, for example, plenty of air reaches the scraps, and they break down mainly into water, carbon dioxide, and nutrients for the soil.
items.exp: ② 앞의 '음식이 어디로 가느냐에 따라 분해 방식이 달라진다'에 대한 예로 주어진 문장(for example)이 오고, ② 뒤의 In a landfill, by contrast가 정원과 대조를 이뤄요. 그래서 ②에 들어가야 해요.

items.passage: Before an important match, a tennis player may bounce the ball exactly four times. A pianist may rub her hands together and touch the edge of the piano before a concert. To outsiders, such pre-performance rituals can look like mere superstition. However, researchers who study performance anxiety have found that they serve a real purpose. In one experiment, participants were asked to sing in front of strangers, a task that made most of them nervous. Those who first performed a short, meaningless routine of drawing a picture, sprinkling salt on it, and counting to five reported feeling less anxious and actually sang more accurately than those who simply waited. The researchers suggested that rituals work by giving people a sense of control in situations that feel uncertain. By following steps they have chosen themselves, performers shift their attention away from worries about the outcome and toward something they can manage.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Even (A) ___ rituals performed before a stressful task can reduce anxiety and improve performance by giving people a feeling of (B) ___ over an uncertain situation.
items.exp: 짧고 의미 없는 동작만으로도 효과가 있었으므로 (A)는 simple, 의식이 불확실한 상황에서 통제감을 주기 때문이라고 했으므로 (B)는 control이에요. 의식이 행운을 가져온다는 미신과는 다르다고 했으니 luck은 틀려요.

items.passage:
In 1835, the French philosopher Auguste Comte offered what seemed like a safe example of something humans could never know. We might measure the distances and movements of the stars, he argued, but we would never learn what they are made of, since no one could ever travel there to collect a sample. Within a few decades, his prediction proved (a)[accurate] in a way he could not have imagined: the knowledge had arrived without anyone leaving Earth.

The key was light. When sunlight passes through a prism, it spreads into a band of colors called a spectrum. In the early nineteenth century, scientists noticed that this band was crossed by thin dark lines. Laboratory experiments later revealed their meaning. Each chemical element, when heated, gives off light only at certain colors, and when light passes through a cooler gas of that element, those same colors are (b)[absorbed]. The pattern of lines works like a fingerprint, (c)[unique] to each element.

By comparing the dark lines in sunlight with the fingerprints of elements in the laboratory, astronomers could identify sodium, iron, and hydrogen in the Sun. Soon they turned their instruments toward distant stars and found the same familiar elements, a (d)[discovery] that showed the universe is built from the same basic materials as our own planet. The method even revealed an element that had never been seen on Earth: helium was first detected in the Sun's spectrum, nearly thirty years before it was found here.

Today, the same technique allows astronomers to study the atmospheres of planets orbiting other stars. Comte's example reminds us that the limits of knowledge are often limits of (e)[method], not of possibility.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Some Questions About the Universe Have No Answers
The Life and Philosophy of Auguste Comte
Reading Starlight: How We Learned What Stars Are Made Of
How Helium Became Useful in Modern Industry
Prisms and Rainbows: The Beauty of Colored Light
items.exp: 빛의 스펙트럼에 나타나는 어두운 선을 이용해 별의 성분을 알아낸 과정을 설명하므로 ③가 알맞아요. ①은 Comte의 예측처럼 글이 반박하는 생각이고, ②는 도입부의 인물만 다뤄요.

items.passage:
(A)
When Ms. Ortiz announced that the chess club would play in the city tournament, every member raised a hand except Dylan. He had joined the club only a month earlier and had never played against anyone outside school. "I'll just lose in five minutes," he told his friend Priya after the meeting. Priya, who had been the club's top player for two years, shook her head. "Everyone loses at first. That's how you learn the game," she said, and she wrote his name on the sign-up sheet herself.

(B)
On the day of the tournament, Dylan's hands were cold as he sat down across from his first opponent, a tall boy wearing a jacket covered in medals. Within twenty minutes, Dylan had lost his queen and then the game. In the second round, he lost again. During the break, he found Priya and said quietly that (a)[he] wanted to go home. Priya simply opened her notebook and showed him the line she had taught him. "Play this," she said. "Don't think about winning. Just think about your next move."

(C)
In the final round, Dylan faced a girl about his age who seemed just as nervous as he was. He used the opening Priya had taught him and played slowly, checking each move twice. After more than an hour, his opponent's king was trapped. Dylan stared at the board, hardly believing it, until the girl smiled and offered (b)[her] hand. When the results were posted, Dylan had won only one game out of four, but Priya hugged him as if (c)[he] had won the whole tournament.

(D)
For the next three weeks, Priya stayed after club meetings to practice with Dylan. Instead of playing full games, she showed (d)[him] one simple opening again and again, until he could play the first ten moves without thinking. Whenever he made a mistake, she asked him to explain why he had chosen that move. At first Dylan found this boring, but slowly he began to see patterns on the board that he had never noticed before. By the end of the third week, (e)[he] was even beating some of the older members.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Priya가 Dylan을 대회에 등록시킨 뒤, (D)에서 3주 동안 함께 연습해요. (B)는 대회 당일 두 판을 진 장면이고, (C)의 In the final round로 마지막 판을 이기므로 (D)-(B)-(C)예요.
