items.passage:
Dear Ms. Grant,

My name is Laura Kim, and my nine-year-old son Ethan has autism. Like many children with autism, he is very sensitive to noise and bright light. Ethan loves water, and swimming is one of the few activities that truly calms him. Unfortunately, the Riverside Swimming Pool is always crowded on weekends, and the echoing shouts and loud music often overwhelm him within minutes. Several other parents in our support group face the same problem. I am writing to ask whether the pool could offer a "quiet swim" hour once a week, perhaps early on Sunday mornings, with the music turned off, the lights dimmed, and fewer swimmers allowed in the water. Pools in some nearby cities already run similar sessions, and families say the results have been wonderful. Our group would be happy to help spread the word and to volunteer during the sessions. Thank you for considering this request.

Sincerely,
Laura Kim
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 수영장의 주말 이용 요금 인하를 요청하려고
감각이 예민한 아이들을 위한 조용한 수영 시간 운영을 요청하려고
자폐 아동 부모 모임의 자원봉사자를 모집하려고
수영장의 소음과 조명 문제에 대해 항의하려고
다른 도시 수영장의 프로그램 운영 결과를 문의하려고
items.exp: 소음과 빛에 예민한 자폐 아동을 위해 일주일에 한 번 음악을 끄고 조명을 낮춘 조용한 수영 시간을 운영해 달라고 부탁하는 편지예요. 자원봉사는 요청을 돕겠다는 제안일 뿐이고, 소음 문제는 요청의 배경이지 항의가 목적은 아니에요.

items.passage: It was my first game as a referee, and the players were only ten years old, but the whistle felt heavy in my hand. Twenty minutes in, a boy in a red shirt went down near the goal, and I pointed to the penalty spot. At once, parents on the blue team's side began shouting. "That was a dive!" "Are you even watching?" My face burned, and my heart pounded so loudly I could barely hear anything else. I wondered whether I had made a terrible mistake and whether I should simply walk off the field. Then the blue team's coach walked over to the parents. "She had the best view of anyone here," he said firmly. "Let her do her job." The shouting stopped. After the game, the coach shook my hand and told me I had kept the match fair and safe. As I walked to my bike, I realized I was already looking forward to next Saturday.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 학부모들의 고함에 얼굴이 달아오르고 경기장을 떠나고 싶을 만큼 흔들렸다가, 코치가 편을 들어 주고 공정했다고 칭찬하자 다음 경기를 기대하게 되었어요. 처음부터 호루라기가 무겁게 느껴졌으므로 confident로 시작하는 ⑤는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Watch almost any youth soccer game and you will hear a second set of coaches: parents standing along the sideline, shouting "Shoot!" "Pass it!" "Get back!" Most of them mean well. They want their children to succeed, and they believe their advice helps. In reality, it usually does the opposite. A young player who is trying to read the game, listen to her coach, and decide what to do next now has a crowd of adult voices telling her different things at once. Rather than learning to make her own decisions, she learns to wait for instructions, or she freezes, afraid of disappointing someone in the stands. Children play sports to have fun and to grow, and both depend on the freedom to try things and make mistakes. So, parents, keep your cheers loud and your instructions at home. Clap for effort, stay quiet about tactics, and leave the coaching to the coach. Your child will play better, and probably enjoy the game more, too.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 부모는 경기 중 자녀에게 지시하지 말고 응원에 그쳐야 한다.
어린 선수는 코치보다 부모의 조언을 더 따라야 한다.
유소년 경기에서는 실수를 줄이는 훈련을 우선해야 한다.
부모는 자녀가 참여할 운동 종목을 직접 골라 주어야 한다.
코치는 경기 전에 부모와 전술을 미리 공유해야 한다.
items.exp: 경기장 옆에서 부모가 외치는 지시가 아이의 판단을 방해하므로 응원은 크게 하되 지시는 하지 말고 지도는 코치에게 맡기라고 주장해요. 실수할 자유가 중요하다고 했으므로 실수를 줄이는 훈련을 앞세운 ③은 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: After a difficult choice turns out badly, people often torture themselves with the thought of what might have been. If only I had taken the other job, studied a different subject, or moved to another city, things would surely be better. Yet this comparison is rarely fair. The life we actually live comes with every detail attached: the boring meetings, the unexpected bills, the small disappointments that fill an ordinary week. The life we did not choose, on the other hand, exists only as a brief sketch, and we tend to fill that sketch with the best possible outcomes. We forget that the other job would have had its own difficult boss and the other city its own lonely winters. In this sense, the road not taken is [a road with no potholes on the map]. It looks smooth only because no one has ever had to travel it. Recognizing this does not erase regret, but it can stop us from measuring our real lives against a perfect fiction.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a road with no potholes on the map]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: an option that would have been better if chosen earlier
a decision based on accurate information about the future
an alternative that seems flawless because it was never experienced
a goal that requires careful planning to achieve
a choice that other people would have regretted as well
items.exp: 선택하지 않은 삶은 직접 겪어 보지 않아 문제점이 보이지 않기 때문에 완벽해 보일 뿐이라는 뜻이에요. 바로 뒤의 아무도 그 길을 가 본 적이 없어서 매끄러워 보인다는 문장이 근거예요.

items.passage: For decades, many economists believed that any resource shared by a whole community, such as a pasture, a fishing ground, or a forest, was doomed. Since each user gains the full benefit of taking a little more while the cost of overuse is spread among everyone, the resource would eventually be destroyed unless the government took control or divided it into private property. Yet researchers who studied real communities found a different story. In mountain villages in Switzerland, farmers had grazed cattle on shared meadows for centuries without ruining them, and many fishing communities had managed their waters for generations. What these groups had in common was a set of rules they had made for themselves: clear limits on who could use the resource and how much, ways of watching one another, and penalties that grew heavier for repeated violations. Because the users designed and enforced the rules, they understood them and saw them as fair. Shared resources, it turns out, can survive when the people who depend on them are trusted to govern them.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: reasons why private ownership protects natural resources best
the role of governments in preventing the overuse of pastures
difficulties faced by fishing communities in coastal regions
economic benefits of dividing shared land among villagers
how communities can manage shared resources through their own rules
items.exp: 공동 자원은 정부 통제나 사유화 없이는 망가진다는 통념과 달리, 이용자들이 스스로 만든 규칙으로 오랫동안 자원을 지켜 온 사례를 들어 설명하므로 ⑤가 주제예요. ①②④는 글이 반박하는 기존 견해에 해당해요.

items.passage: When a word travels from one language into another, it rarely arrives unchanged. Its sounds are reshaped to fit the new language, but its meaning often shifts as well. In Japanese, for instance, the English word "mansion" became "manshon," which refers not to a grand house but to an ordinary apartment in a concrete building. The English word "robot," borrowed from Czech, originally carried the sense of forced, tiring labor, an association most English speakers no longer hear. Such changes happen because a borrowed word enters a vocabulary that already has words for many things. To survive, it must find an empty space: a meaning not yet covered by existing words, or a slightly different shade of one. Speakers then use it in their own situations, and over time its meaning settles into whatever role it has come to play. A loanword, in other words, is less a copy of a foreign word than a new word built from foreign material.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Some Languages Refuse to Borrow Words
Borrowed Words, New Meanings: How Loanwords Transform
The Sounds That Every Language Shares
Learning Foreign Words Through Their Origins
How English Became a Global Language
items.exp: 다른 언어에서 빌려 온 낱말은 소리뿐 아니라 뜻도 바뀌어 새로운 낱말이 된다는 내용이에요. 마지막 문장의 외국 재료로 만든 새 낱말이라는 표현이 제목의 근거예요.

items.passage: Hedda Calloway (1872–1950) was a teacher who devoted her life to educating working adults. She was born in a mill town, where she began working in a cotton factory at the age of twelve. Determined to keep learning, she read borrowed books by candlelight after her long shifts. At twenty, she earned a teaching certificate through evening classes and took a job at a primary school. In 1901, she opened a free night school in a rented room above a bakery, offering reading and arithmetic lessons to factory workers. The school grew so popular that within ten years it had five branches across the region. Calloway also wrote a series of simple textbooks designed for adults, which were used in night schools for decades. Although she was offered a position at a university, she declined it, saying that her place was with the workers. She continued teaching until the age of seventy-five.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 열두 살에 면직 공장에서 일하기 시작했다.
야간 수업을 통해 교사 자격증을 땄다.
1901년에 빵집 위층의 방에서 무료 야간 학교를 열었다.
성인용 교재를 썼지만 널리 쓰이지는 못했다.
items.exp: 그녀가 쓴 성인용 교재는 수십 년 동안 야간 학교에서 쓰였다고 했으므로 널리 쓰이지 못했다는 ④가 틀려요. 나머지는 글의 순서대로 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage: Before electric lighting became cheap, architects had no choice but to design buildings around the sun. Rooms ①[were] arranged so that the spaces used most during the day faced the brightest sky, and ceilings were built high so that light could travel deep into the interior. Narrow buildings with windows on both sides ②[allowed] daylight to reach every desk. When electric lamps spread in the twentieth century, many of these habits disappeared. Deep office floors, ③[which] workers sat far from any window, became common because lamps could light them at any hour. Today, however, designers are returning to older ideas. Studies have found that people working near natural light often report ④[feeling] more alert and sleeping better at night. Modern tools such as light shelves, which bounce sunlight off a ceiling, and glass that ⑤[adjusts] its tint automatically make it possible to enjoy daylight without suffering from glare or heat. In a sense, the future of lighting may look a lot like its past.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③ 뒤에 workers sat far from any window라는 완전한 절이 오므로 관계대명사 which가 아니라 관계부사 where(또는 in which)를 써야 해요. ①은 Rooms에 맞춘 수동태, ②는 복수 주어 buildings의 동사, ④는 report의 목적어인 동명사, ⑤는 단수 glass에 맞춘 동사라 맞아요.

items.passage: When people apologize, they often focus on the words "I'm sorry," as if those words alone could repair the damage. Research on apologies, however, suggests that the words matter far less than what surrounds them. An effective apology usually ①[acknowledges] exactly what went wrong, rather than referring vaguely to "what happened." It also accepts responsibility instead of ②[shifting] blame onto circumstances or onto the person who was hurt. The phrase "I'm sorry if you were offended," for example, tends to make listeners angrier, because it suggests that the real problem lies in their own ③[sensitivity]. Perhaps most important is an offer to repair the harm, whether by replacing what was broken or by changing future behavior. Such an offer shows that the apology is more than a ④[performance]. Interestingly, people often overestimate how much a hurt person wants to hear explanations; long explanations can easily sound like excuses. In apologizing, then, being ⑤[vague] about one's own mistake is usually the wisest course.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 효과적인 사과는 무엇이 잘못되었는지 정확히 인정하는 것이라고 했으므로 자신의 실수에 대해 모호하게 말하는 것이 현명하다는 ⑤ vague는 specific이나 clear로 바꿔야 해요. ①~④는 책임을 인정하고 보상을 제안하라는 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage: On a clear day, you may see long white lines stretching across the sky behind airplanes. These contrails, short for "condensation trails," are not smoke. Jet engines burn fuel and release hot, moist exhaust. High above the ground, where the air can be colder than minus forty degrees, the water vapor in that exhaust freezes almost instantly into tiny ice crystals, much like the cloud of breath you see on a winter morning. Whether a contrail lasts depends on the air around it. In dry air, the ice crystals quickly turn back into vapor, and the trail disappears within seconds. In air that is already close to saturation, however, the crystals survive and may spread for hours into thin, feathery clouds. For this reason, weather forecasters treat long-lasting contrails as a clue: they reveal that the upper air is ___, and that a change in the weather may be coming.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 공기가 이미 포화에 가까울 때 얼음 결정이 남아 비행운이 오래 퍼진다고 했으므로, 오래 남는 비행운은 높은 곳의 공기가 습하다(humid)는 것을 보여 줘요. ③ warm은 영하 40도보다 차가운 공기라는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Organizations often try to improve behavior by making their rules more precise. A vague instruction such as "keep the workplace safe" seems weak, so it is replaced by a detailed checklist: inspect the fire extinguishers monthly, mark exits with green signs, store chemicals on the lowest shelf. Precision has real advantages; everyone knows what is expected, and failures are easy to identify. But it also changes the question people ask themselves. Under a vague goal, workers must think about what safety actually requires in each situation. Under a checklist, the question becomes whether every box has been ticked. A danger that the list did not foresee can then go unnoticed, not because anyone is careless, but because no one feels responsible for anything beyond the list. In this way, a rule that defines exactly what counts as success can lead people to ___. The more completely a rule spells out its demands, the more easily its original purpose disappears from view.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: question whether the rule should exist at all
take greater personal responsibility for their mistakes
ignore the rule whenever it becomes inconvenient
meet its requirements while losing sight of its aim
spend more time inspecting their equipment
items.exp: 규칙이 정밀해지면 사람들은 칸을 모두 채웠는지만 따지게 되어 본래 목적인 안전을 놓친다는 흐름이므로 ④가 알맞아요. 사람들은 규칙을 무시하는 것이 아니라 오히려 그대로 지키기 때문에 ③은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: In many cities, young people and the elderly rarely spend time together outside their own families, and both groups are often lonely as a result. Some communities have responded by creating programs that bring the generations together on purpose. ① In one model, a preschool is placed inside a care home, and children and residents share meals, art projects, and storytelling sessions every week. ② Many care homes also struggle to hire enough staff, since the work is demanding and wages are often low. ③ Older residents in such programs report feeling more useful and less isolated, and some even show improvements in memory and mood. ④ The children, for their part, become more patient and more comfortable with people who move slowly or use wheelchairs. ⑤ Organizers say the key is to give both groups real tasks to do together, rather than simply placing them in the same room.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 어린이와 노인을 일부러 함께 지내게 하는 세대 통합 프로그램과 그 효과를 설명하는 글이에요. 요양원이 직원을 구하기 어렵다는 ②는 요양원 이야기이긴 하지만 세대 간 교류라는 흐름과 관계가 없어요.

items.passage:
In many legal systems, a person accused of a crime is presumed innocent until proven guilty. This principle sounds simple, but it shapes almost every part of a criminal trial.

(A) Most importantly, it decides who must prove what. The accused does not have to show that he or she is innocent. Instead, the prosecution must prove guilt, and it must do so beyond a reasonable doubt.

(B) Their reasoning is that wrongly punishing an innocent person is a far greater harm than failing to punish a guilty one. As an old legal saying puts it, it is better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent person suffer.

(C) This heavy burden means that some guilty people will go free when the evidence against them is not strong enough. Critics see this as a serious weakness, but supporters of the principle accept the cost willingly.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 무죄 추정 원칙을 it으로 받아 누가 무엇을 증명해야 하는지 설명하는 (A)가 먼저 와요. (A)의 합리적 의심이 없을 정도의 입증을 This heavy burden으로 받는 (C)가 이어지고, (C)의 supporters를 Their로 받는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Bakers have long known that bread made slowly tastes better than bread made quickly, even when the ingredients are exactly the same. ( ① ) The reason lies in what happens inside the dough while it rises. Yeast feeds on sugars and releases the gas that makes the dough expand, but at the same time, enzymes and bacteria are breaking down starches and producing acids and other compounds that give bread its flavor. ( ② ) At a warm room temperature, the yeast works so quickly that the dough is ready to bake before much flavor has developed. ( ③ ) This difference explains why many bakers leave their dough in the refrigerator overnight. ( ④ ) By the next morning, the dough has risen only modestly. ( ⑤ ) Yet it has had many hours to develop the deep, slightly sour taste and the rich aroma that customers love, qualities no amount of extra yeast can quickly create.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Cooling the dough, however, slows the yeast far more than it slows these flavor-producing processes.
items.exp: 따뜻하면 효모가 너무 빨리 일해 풍미가 생기기 전에 반죽이 부푼다는 문장 뒤에, 그러나 반죽을 차갑게 하면 효모만 크게 느려진다는 주어진 문장이 와야 해요. 그래야 This difference가 가리키는 대상이 생겨 냉장고에 넣어 두는 이유로 이어져요.

items.passage: When choosing a gift, many people avoid buying the item the recipient has openly asked for. Picking something from a wish list feels too easy, even a little lazy, so they search for an unexpected present that shows how well they know the other person. Studies of gift exchanges, however, suggest that this effort is often misplaced. In several experiments, people who received exactly what they had requested rated their gifts as more thoughtful and were more pleased than those who received a surprise item of similar price. Givers, meanwhile, predicted the opposite, expecting their unrequested choices to be appreciated more. The gap seems to arise because givers focus on the moment of exchange, when a surprise might create a burst of delight, while recipients think about the weeks and months in which they will actually use the gift. An item they chose themselves is simply more likely to fit their needs.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Although gift givers tend to believe that (A) ___ presents will be valued more, recipients usually prefer the gifts they asked for because they care more about a gift's long-term (B) ___.
items.exp: 주는 사람은 요청받지 않은 깜짝 선물이 더 환영받으리라 믿으므로 (A)는 unexpected이고, 받는 사람은 앞으로 실제로 쓸 몇 주와 몇 달을 생각하므로 (B)는 usefulness예요. 비싼 선물이나 겉모습은 글의 근거가 없어요.

items.passage:
When students are asked to judge whether a website is trustworthy, most do what they have been taught: they stay on the page and examine it closely. They read the "About" section, check whether the design looks (a)[professional], and look for spelling errors or a list of references. These clues feel sensible, but they are easy to fake. A polished layout costs little, and an organization with a hidden agenda can describe itself in perfectly neutral language.

Researchers who watched professional fact-checkers at work noticed a very different habit. Faced with an unfamiliar site, the fact-checkers barely read it at all. Within seconds, they opened new tabs and searched for what others said about the source: who funded it, what reporters had written about it, and whether experts treated it as reliable. This approach, sometimes called lateral reading, allowed them to reach (b)[accurate] conclusions far more quickly than students or even university professors, who often spent long minutes studying a single page and were still fooled.

The lesson is somewhat (c)[surprising]. We usually think of careful reading as deep reading, staying with a text until we understand it fully. When the question is whether to trust a source, however, depth can be a trap. The longer we stay inside a page, the more we see the world through the frame its authors have built. Leaving the page, by contrast, lets us (d)[accept] that frame and compare it with outside views.

Of course, lateral reading is not a cure for every problem. Other sites can be wrong too, and searching well takes some skill. But as information grows more (e)[abundant] and design tools grow cheaper, the habit of asking "What do others say about this source?" may matter more than the ability to inspect a single page closely.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Leave the Page to Judge the Source
Why Website Design Matters More Than Content
Deep Reading: The Best Defense Against False Information
How Professors Teach Students to Spot Spelling Errors
The Rising Cost of Building Trustworthy Websites
items.exp: 사이트를 믿을지 판단할 때는 그 페이지 안에 머물기보다 밖으로 나가 다른 곳에서 그 출처를 어떻게 평가하는지 찾아보는 편이 낫다는 글이에요. 깊이 읽기는 오히려 함정이 될 수 있다고 했으므로 ③은 반대 내용이에요.

A polished layout costs little, and an organization with a hidden agenda can describe itself in perfectly neutral language.

Researchers who watched professional fact-checkers at work noticed a very different habit. Faced with an unfamiliar site, the fact-checkers barely read it at all. Within seconds, they opened new tabs and searched for what others said about the source: who funded it, what reporters had written about it, and whether experts treated it as reliable. This approach, sometimes called lateral reading, allowed them to reach (b)[accurate] conclusions far more quickly than students or even university professors, who often spent long minutes studying a single page and were still fooled.

The lesson is somewhat (c)[surprising]. We usually think of careful reading as deep reading, staying with a text until we understand it fully. When the question is whether to trust a source, however, depth can be a trap. The longer we stay inside a page, the more we see the world through the frame its authors have built. Leaving the page, by contrast, lets us (d)[accept] that frame and compare it with outside views.

Of course, lateral reading is not a cure for every problem. Other sites can be wrong too, and searching well takes some skill. But as information grows more (e)[abundant] and design tools grow cheaper, the habit of asking "What do others say about this source?" may matter more than the ability to inspect a single page closely.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 페이지를 떠나면 작성자가 만든 틀에서 벗어나 바깥의 시각과 비교할 수 있다는 흐름이므로 (d) accept는 escape 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요. 바로 앞 문장의 페이지 안에 오래 머물수록 그 틀로 세상을 보게 된다는 내용과 대비돼요.

items.passage:
(A)
Every Saturday morning, Daniel pushed a cart of picture books down the long hallway of the children's ward at Westbrook Hospital. The sixteen-year-old had signed up as a volunteer reader, hoping to bring a little cheer to young patients, and most of the children greeted him eagerly. One boy, however, never did. Eight-year-old Theo, who had been in the hospital for nearly a month, turned toward the wall whenever Daniel knocked on his door. Before long, Daniel noticed that (a)[he] had begun to dread knocking on that door.

(B)
In early spring, the doctors told Theo that he was well enough to go home. On the boy's final morning, Daniel came to say goodbye, and (b)[he] found the finished notebook waiting on the bed. On the last page, Theo had drawn a dragon flying beside a tall boy holding a pencil. Underneath, in shaky letters, were the words "For Daniel, who listened." Daniel stood there for a long while, unable to speak. Years later, after (c)[he] became a teacher himself, Daniel kept the notebook on his desk as a reminder that the best way to reach someone is sometimes to stop talking and start listening.

(C)
The next Saturday, Daniel arrived without his cart. Instead, (d)[he] brought a blank notebook and a box of colored pencils. "I can't draw at all," he admitted, "but I can write. What if we made a book about Ember together?" Theo studied him for a long moment and then nodded. Week after week, Theo drew while Daniel wrote down the story Theo told him, adding words only when the boy asked for help. Before long, the nurses began stopping by to see the newest page.

(D)
For three weeks, Daniel tried every book on his cart, from funny animal stories to tales of brave knights. Nothing worked. Then, one afternoon, he noticed a stack of papers on Theo's bedside table, covered with careful pencil drawings of dragons, each with scales, claws, and wings drawn in remarkable detail. Instead of opening a book, Daniel picked up a drawing and asked what the dragon's name was. Theo hesitated, then muttered, "Ember. She guards a mountain." It was the first thing (e)[he] had ever said to Daniel.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: Theo가 말을 하지 않던 (A) 뒤에 3주 동안 애쓰다 용 그림을 발견하고 Ember라는 이름을 듣는 (D)가 오고, Ember에 관한 책을 함께 만들자는 (C), 완성된 공책을 받는 마지막 날의 (B) 순서예요.

choices: Daniel은 토요일 아침마다 어린이 병동에서 책 읽어 주는 봉사를 했다.
Theo는 마지막 날 완성된 공책을 Daniel에게 남겼다.
Daniel은 그림을 잘 그려서 Theo 대신 용 그림을 그려 주었다.
간호사들이 새로 완성된 페이지를 보러 들르기 시작했다.
Theo의 침대 옆 탁자에는 용 그림이 쌓여 있었다.
items.exp: (C)에서 Daniel은 그림을 전혀 못 그린다고 말했고 그림은 Theo가 그리고 Daniel은 이야기를 받아 적었으므로 ③이 틀려요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Whitfield,

I am a science teacher at Oakridge High School, and I am writing about the field trip we booked at the Norton Natural History Museum for Friday, May 14. Thirty-two of my students were scheduled to join your guided tour of the fossil hall at 10 a.m. Last week, however, our school district moved the date of the state science exam to that same Friday, and all of my students are required to take it. I know that your guided tours fill up quickly in spring, and I apologize for the short notice. Would it be possible to move our reservation to Friday, May 21, or to any weekday during the following week? We are flexible about the time of day, and the number of students will stay the same. My students have been preparing questions about the dinosaur exhibit for weeks, so I truly hope we can still visit. I look forward to your reply.

Best regards,
Laura Bennett
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 박물관 단체 관람의 인원 변경을 알리려고
주 과학 시험 일정이 바뀐 이유를 설명하려고
박물관 견학 예약 날짜의 변경을 요청하려고
공룡 전시에 관한 학생들의 질문을 전달하려고
봄철 가이드 투어의 추가 개설을 건의하려고
items.exp: 시험 날짜가 견학일과 겹치게 되어 5월 21일이나 그다음 주 평일로 예약을 옮겨 달라고 부탁하는 편지예요. 인원은 그대로라고 했으므로 ①은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Jiho ran the last few meters to the bus stop, but the red taillights were already disappearing around the corner. He checked his phone: 11:42 p.m. That had been the last bus. His phone battery showed two percent, and before he could call his mother, the screen went black. The street was empty, the shops had pulled down their metal shutters, and the cold wind cut through his thin jacket. Home was more than an hour away on foot, along a road he barely knew. He sat down on the bench, his mind racing through every bad possibility. Then a small car pulled up to the curb, and the window rolled down. It was Mrs. Kang, the woman who ran the bakery below his apartment. "Jiho? What are you doing out here so late? Get in, I'm heading home anyway." Warm air poured out of the car. As he sank into the seat, Jiho felt his shoulders relax, and he thanked her again and again all the way home.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Jiho의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 막차를 놓치고 휴대폰까지 꺼져 온갖 나쁜 상황을 떠올리며 걱정하다가, 이웃 Kang 씨가 태워 주자 어깨의 긴장이 풀리고 거듭 고마워해요. 그래서 worried → grateful이 알맞아요.

items.passage: In Japan, there is a traditional way of repairing broken pottery called kintsugi. Instead of hiding the cracks, the craftsperson joins the pieces with a special lacquer mixed with powdered gold, so that every line of breakage shines across the surface of the bowl. A repaired cup does not pretend that nothing happened to it. On the contrary, its history becomes the most visible part of its beauty, and some collectors value such pieces more highly than ones that were never broken. This approach reflects a way of thinking that differs from the common wish to make damaged things look new again. We usually treat a crack as a mistake to be erased, as if an object's worth depended on its remaining perfect. Kintsugi suggests the opposite: that damage, honestly shown and carefully mended, can add meaning rather than take it away. In this sense, the gold lines [turn the break into part of the story] rather than the end of it.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [turn the break into part of the story]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: make broken pottery more useful in daily life
allow the damage to become a valued part of the object's history
prevent the object from ever breaking again
hide the evidence that the object was once broken
show how skilled the craftsperson was at making new pottery
items.exp: 킨츠기는 금으로 깨진 선을 드러내어 손상의 역사를 아름다움의 일부로 만든다고 했으므로, 깨짐을 대상의 가치 있는 역사의 일부로 만든다는 ②가 알맞아요. 금 선은 흔적을 숨기는 것이 아니라 드러내므로 ④는 반대예요.

items.passage: Conservation programs often raise endangered animals in captivity and then release them into the wild. The idea seems simple: breed enough healthy animals, and the population will recover. Yet many releases fail, not because the animals are weak or sick, but because they do not know what to fear. An animal raised safely behind fences has never had to escape a predator, and when it meets a fox or a hawk for the first time, it may simply watch with curiosity. For this reason, some programs now train animals before release. In one approach, young animals are shown a stuffed predator or a trained dog while hearing the alarm calls of their own species, sometimes along with a mildly unpleasant experience such as a squirt of water. Animals that receive this training are noticeably more likely to survive their first months in the wild. Releasing an animal, in other words, should be seen not as the end of a program but as the final lesson of an education that must begin long before the gate opens.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 멸종 위기 동물은 야생보다 보호 시설에서 기르는 것이 더 안전하다.
멸종 위기종을 지키려면 무엇보다 포식자의 수를 줄여야 한다.
인공 번식은 동물의 건강을 해칠 수 있으므로 신중하게 해야 한다.
방사할 동물에게 미리 천적을 알아보는 법을 가르치면 생존율이 높아진다.
동물을 방사한 뒤에는 오랜 기간 추적 관찰해야 한다.
items.exp: 보호 시설에서 자란 동물은 무엇을 두려워해야 할지 몰라 방사 후 실패하는데, 방사 전 천적을 알아보도록 훈련하면 생존 가능성이 높아진다는 것이 요지예요. 포식자 수를 줄이자거나 방사 후 추적하자는 내용은 글에 없어요.

items.passage: Most of us learned that ice is slippery because a skate's pressure melts a thin layer of water beneath it. This explanation is neat, but it does not hold up well. Calculations show that the pressure from a person's weight lowers the melting point of ice by only a tiny amount, far too little to explain why we slip on ice that is many degrees below freezing. Friction from moving across the surface does produce some heat, but it cannot explain why ice is slippery even for someone standing still. A more promising answer lies in the ice surface itself. The water molecules at the very top of a block of ice are not held in place by neighbors above them, so they are bound less tightly than those inside. As a result, the outermost layer behaves less like a rigid solid and more like a loose, almost liquid film, even at low temperatures. Scientists are still studying the details, but this restless surface appears to be the main reason ice is so hard to stand on.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the effect of temperature on the speed of skaters
ways to prevent accidents on icy roads
the process by which water turns into ice
the role of friction in winter sports
a revised explanation of why ice is slippery
items.exp: 압력이 얼음을 녹인다는 기존 설명이 맞지 않으며, 표면 분자가 느슨하게 묶여 액체 같은 막을 이루는 것이 미끄러운 주된 이유라는 내용이에요. 마찰은 기존 설명의 한계를 보여 주려고 잠깐 나올 뿐이에요.

items.passage: Today the fork seems like an obvious tool, but for much of history, many Europeans regarded it with suspicion. For centuries, people ate with knives, spoons, and their fingers, and a small two-pronged fork was used mainly in the kitchen to hold meat while it was carved. When forks began to appear at dining tables, some observers mocked them as a needless luxury, and certain religious writers even claimed that it was improper to avoid touching food that had been given by God. Travelers who returned from places where forks were common were sometimes laughed at for their foreign manners. Only gradually, as ideas about cleanliness and politeness changed and as forks gained a third and fourth prong that held food more securely, did they become a normal part of meals. By the eighteenth century, eating with one's hands at a formal table had become a sign of bad manners rather than a natural habit.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Forks Have Four Prongs Instead of Two
The Kitchen Tools That Changed Cooking Forever
From Mocked Luxury to Table Manners: The Fork's Slow Rise
How Travelers Spread Foreign Foods Across Europe
Religious Rules That Shaped European Diets
items.exp: 포크가 처음에는 사치품이라며 조롱받다가 청결과 예절 관념이 바뀌면서 점차 식사 예절의 일부가 되었다는 내용이에요. 갈래가 늘어난 것은 보급 이유 중 하나일 뿐이라 ①은 너무 좁아요.

items.passage:

items.q: Lakeside Robotics Workshop 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 참가비에는 이틀 중 첫째 날 점심만 포함된다.
첫째 날에는 짝과 함께 로봇 키트를 조립한다.
items.exp: 참가비에 모든 재료와 이틀 동안의 점심이 포함된다고 했으므로 첫째 날 점심만 포함된다는 ②가 틀려요. 나머지는 안내문의 순서대로 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage: Most world maps hung in classrooms ①[are] based on a projection designed centuries ago for sailors. Since the surface of a sphere cannot be flattened without being stretched, every flat map must distort something. This projection keeps the shapes of small areas accurate, ②[making] it ideal for plotting a compass course, but it greatly enlarges regions far from the equator. Greenland, for instance, appears about as large as Africa, although Africa is actually about fourteen times ③[bigger]. Such distortions are not merely technical details. Some educators worry that maps showing northern countries larger than they really are ④[shape] students' sense of which parts of the world matter most. Alternative projections that preserve the relative sizes of countries do exist, but they make continents look stretched or squashed, and many viewers find them strange at first. In the end, no map is perfectly neutral; each one reflects choices about ⑤[that] its makers considered most important to show accurately.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤ 전치사 about의 목적어 자리이고 뒤에 considered의 목적어가 빠진 절이 오므로 선행사를 포함한 관계대명사 what을 써야 해요. ①은 복수 주어 maps의 동사, ②는 결과를 나타내는 분사구문, ③은 times 뒤 비교급, ④는 that절의 복수 주어 maps의 동사라 맞아요.

items.passage: A gecko can race up a glass window and hang from a ceiling by a single toe, yet its feet produce no glue at all. For a long time, this ability seemed ①[ordinary] to scientists, who could not explain how it worked. The answer turned out to lie in structures far too small to see. Each toe is covered with millions of tiny hairs, and each hair splits into hundreds of even finer tips. These tips come so ②[close] to the surface that weak attractive forces between molecules begin to act. Any single force is extremely small, but added together over billions of contact points, the forces are ③[strong] enough to hold the animal's whole weight. Just as remarkable is how easily the gecko lets go. By peeling its toes away at an angle, it breaks the contact one row of hairs at a time, so it can take each step without ④[effort]. Engineers have tried to copy this design to create tapes that grip firmly yet can be removed cleanly and ⑤[reused] many times.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 과학자들이 오랫동안 원리를 설명하지 못했다(could not explain)고 했으므로 이 능력은 평범한 것이 아니라 불가사의해 보였어야 해요. ① ordinary는 mysterious 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요. 나머지는 미세한 털이 표면에 가까이 붙어 힘을 모으고, 쉽게 떼어져 다시 쓸 수 있다는 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage: Teams in almost every sport win more often at home than away, and fans usually credit their own cheering for lifting the players. Some studies suggest, however, that the crowd's strongest effect may fall not on the players but on the officials. In one experiment, experienced referees watched video clips of tackles in soccer matches and decided whether each was a foul. Half of them watched with the original crowd noise; the other half watched the same clips in silence. Referees who heard the crowd called fewer fouls against the home team, apparently reacting to the roar of the home fans whenever a visiting player made contact. Supporting this idea, records from matches played without spectators showed that the usual advantage for home teams in fouls and penalties largely disappeared. Referees try hard to be neutral, but the evidence suggests that a loud crowd can leave their judgments slightly ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 관중 소음을 들은 심판들이 홈팀에 반칙을 덜 선언했으므로, 관중이 심판의 판정을 한쪽으로 기울게 만든다는 biased가 알맞아요. 판정이 무작위가 아니라 홈팀 쪽으로 일관되게 기울었으므로 random은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: We often trust experts who can make quick, confident judgments without being able to explain them. A firefighter senses that a floor is about to collapse; an experienced nurse notices that a patient is getting worse before any test confirms it. Such intuitions are real, but they are not magic. They are patterns stored from thousands of past cases in which a judgment was followed by clear and rapid feedback. The nurse who misjudged a patient learned of it within hours; the firefighter's mistakes had immediate consequences. Not every field offers such lessons. A stock picker or a long-range political forecaster may wait years to learn whether a call was right, and by then so many other factors have changed that the outcome teaches little. Experts in these areas can feel just as confident as the firefighter, yet their confidence rests on far less. An expert's intuition, then, ___. Before trusting a gut feeling, we should ask not how sure the expert is, but whether that expert's world ever offered the chance to learn from mistakes.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: improves steadily with the number of years spent in a profession
is only as trustworthy as the environment in which it was learned
becomes more accurate when it is explained in detail to others
should be replaced by careful analysis in every situation
depends mainly on the confidence with which it is expressed
items.exp: 직관은 빠르고 분명한 피드백이 있는 환경에서 쌓여야 믿을 만하고, 피드백이 늦은 분야의 직관은 근거가 약하다는 흐름이므로 ②가 알맞아요. 경력 연수(①)나 자신감(⑤)은 오히려 직관의 신뢰도를 보장하지 못한다고 했어요.

items.passage: Almost everyone has felt a small shock on hearing a recording of their own voice: it seems higher, thinner, and somehow less pleasant than the voice they know. The main reason lies in how sound reaches our ears. ① When we speak, we hear our voice not only through the air but also through the bones of the skull, which carry the lower tones especially well. ② A recording captures only the sound traveling through the air, so it lacks the deep, rich quality we are used to. ③ Psychology adds another layer: because we have heard the inner version of our voice all our lives, any difference strikes us as unfamiliar, and the unfamiliar often feels wrong. ④ Professional singers spend years training their voices, and many of them warm up for half an hour before every performance. ⑤ Interestingly, other people usually find our recorded voice perfectly normal, since the recording is exactly what they hear every day.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 녹음된 자기 목소리가 낯설고 어색하게 들리는 이유(뼈 전도, 익숙함의 차이)를 설명하는 글인데, ④는 전문 가수의 발성 훈련과 준비 운동 이야기여서 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
A year, as we usually count it, has 365 days. Yet the time it takes Earth to travel once around the Sun is a little longer, about 365 days and six hours.

(A) Even so, the fix was not perfect. Adding a full day every four years slightly overcorrected the error, and over many centuries the calendar drifted again, until a later reform decided to skip the extra day in most years ending in 00.

(B) Those extra hours may seem too small to matter. But if they were simply ignored, the calendar would fall about a quarter of a day behind the seasons every year, and after a few centuries summer months would arrive in cold weather.

(C) To prevent this, calendar makers in ancient Rome began adding one extra day every fourth year. This leap day gathers the four missing quarters into a single day and pulls the calendar back into step with the Sun.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (B)의 Those extra hours가 주어진 글의 약 6시간을 받고, (C)의 To prevent this는 (B)의 달력이 계절보다 밀리는 문제를 받아요. (A)의 the fix는 (C)의 윤일 도입을 가리키며 그 한계를 덧붙이므로 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Farmers in many parts of the world have long known that a field of wheat grows better if beans or peas had been planted there the year before. ( ① ) The secret lies underground, in the roots of these crops. ( ② ) All plants need nitrogen to build proteins and grow, and although the air is mostly nitrogen, most plants cannot use it in that form. ( ③ ) In exchange for sugars from the plant, the bacteria turn nitrogen from the air into compounds the plant can absorb. ( ④ ) When the bean plants die or are plowed into the soil, much of this nitrogen remains behind, ready for the next crop. ( ⑤ ) Rotating crops in this way allows farmers to keep their fields fertile while using less chemical fertilizer, an advantage that has drawn renewed interest as fertilizer prices rise and concerns grow about the pollution it causes in rivers.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Beans and peas, however, form a partnership with bacteria that live in small swellings on their roots.
items.exp: 대부분의 식물은 공기 중 질소를 그대로 쓰지 못한다는 문장 뒤에, 그러나 콩류는 뿌리의 세균과 협력한다는 주어진 문장이 와야 해요. 그래야 다음 문장의 the bacteria가 가리키는 대상이 생겨요.

items.passage: Commuters on trains and buses usually sit in silence, staring at their phones or out the window. When asked why, many say that strangers would not want to be disturbed and that a conversation would be awkward. To test these beliefs, researchers asked some commuters to start a conversation with the person next to them, while others were told to keep to themselves as usual. Before the ride, the talkers predicted that their experience would be less pleasant than sitting alone. Afterward, it was the reverse: those who had talked reported a noticeably more positive journey, and almost none had been rejected. The strangers they approached, it turned out, were just as interested in chatting but had held back for the same reason. Each person assumed that others preferred solitude, and so everyone stayed quiet, missing a small but real source of enjoyment.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Commuters avoid talking to strangers because they (A) ___ how willing others are to talk, even though such conversations turn out to be more (B) ___ than they expect.
items.exp: 통근자들은 상대도 대화를 원한다는 것을 모른 채 남들이 혼자 있기를 원한다고 여기므로 (A)는 underestimate이고, 실제 대화는 예상보다 즐거웠으므로 (B)는 enjoyable이에요. 대화가 어색하거나 피곤했다는 근거는 없어요.

items.passage:
Nutrition labels list foods as collections of separate parts: so many grams of fat, so many milligrams of calcium, so much fiber. This way of thinking has been enormously (a)[useful]. It helped scientists discover vitamins and explain diseases caused by their absence. Yet it rests on an assumption that is now being questioned: that a nutrient behaves the same way in the body no matter what food it comes in.

When whole almonds are eaten, a considerable share of their fat is never absorbed, because it stays locked inside cell walls that chewing does not fully break. The same amount of fat in almond oil, by contrast, is taken up almost (b)[completely]. Sugar in a whole apple enters the bloodstream more slowly than the same sugar in apple juice, since the fruit's structure must be broken down first. Researchers call this surrounding structure the food matrix, and they increasingly argue that it can matter as much as the list of nutrients itself.

This idea helps explain a long-standing puzzle. For decades, studies that observed people's eating habits linked diets rich in fruits and vegetables to better health. But when researchers gave people the same nutrients in pill form, the benefits often (c)[disappeared]. A vitamin taken alone, outside the company of the fiber, water, and countless other compounds it normally travels with, may simply not act the way it does in a carrot or an orange.

None of this means that nutrient labels are (d)[valuable]. They remain a quick way to compare products. But they describe what a food contains, not how the body will experience it. For everyday choices, the practical lesson is fairly simple: when a food reaches us in a form close to the way it grew, its label tells only (e)[part] of the story.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Almonds Are Healthier Than Almond Oil
Read the Label Carefully Before You Buy
Supplements: A Cheaper Path to Good Health
More Than the Sum of Its Nutrients: Why Food Structure Matters
items.exp: 같은 영양소라도 어떤 음식 구조 속에 들어 있느냐에 따라 몸에서 다르게 작용한다는 식품 매트릭스 개념을 다룬 글이에요. 아몬드는 예시 하나일 뿐이라 ①은 너무 좁아요.

items.exp: 영양 성분표는 여전히 제품을 빠르게 비교하는 수단이라고 이어지므로, 성분표가 쓸모없다는 뜻이 아니라는 흐름이 되어야 해요. 따라서 (d) valuable은 worthless로 바꿔야 해요. (b)는 통아몬드와 대조되어 기름의 지방이 거의 완전히 흡수된다는 뜻이라 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Hana had been looking forward to the camping trip at Pine Lake for weeks, but her younger brother Minsu had not. The nine-year-old was afraid of the dark, and the thought of spending a night in the woods without streetlights made him miserable. As their father unloaded the car, Minsu sat on a rock with his arms folded. "What if something is out there?" (a)[he] asked. Hana rolled her eyes, but she promised to stay beside him all night.

(B)
By morning, the storm had passed. Sunlight sparkled on the lake, and the air smelled of wet pine needles. Their father cooked pancakes on the camp stove while Hana hung the soaked sleeping bags on a branch to dry. Minsu was already at the water's edge, skipping stones. When Hana asked whether (b)[he] still wanted to go home, he grinned and shook his head. "Next time," he said, "I'm bringing a stronger tent pole, and I'm in charge of the songs."

(C)
Around midnight, a storm swept across the lake. Rain hammered the tent, and a sudden gust snapped one of the poles with a loud crack. The roof sagged over their heads. Their father told the children to hold up the sides while he ran through the downpour to the car for a spare pole and some rope. Hana gripped the wet fabric, her heart pounding. Beside her, Minsu had gone completely silent, and (c)[he] pressed close to her side. Every flash of lightning showed the trees bending, and for the first time, she was the one who felt afraid.

(D)
Then, to her surprise, she heard Minsu's voice in the dark. Pressing his small hands against the tent wall, he began to sing the silly song their grandmother used to sing on long car rides. His voice shook at first, but (d)[he] kept going, and soon Hana was singing too. By the time their father returned, soaked to the skin, both children were laughing. (e)[He] quickly fixed the pole, and as the wind died down, Minsu fell asleep with his flashlight still in his hand.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 캠핑장에 도착한 (A) 뒤에 한밤중 폭풍으로 텐트 기둥이 부러지는 (C), 어둠 속에서 Minsu가 노래를 부르는 (D), 폭풍이 지나간 아침의 (B) 순서예요.

choices: Minsu는 캠핑을 몇 주 동안 손꼽아 기다렸다.
아침에 Hana는 젖은 침낭을 나뭇가지에 널었다.
한밤중의 돌풍으로 텐트 기둥 하나가 부러졌다.
Minsu는 손전등을 쥔 채 잠이 들었다.
items.exp: (A)에서 캠핑을 몇 주 동안 기다린 사람은 Hana이고 Minsu는 어둠이 무서워 캠핑을 싫어했으므로 ①이 틀려요.

items.passage:
Dear Principal Moore,

My name is Sofia Mendes, and I volunteer at the Family Welcome Center in our neighborhood, which supports families who have recently moved here from other countries. Many of these families have children at Cedar Park Elementary School, and the parents care deeply about their children's education. However, the school's weekly newsletters and notices are sent home only in English. As a result, some parents miss important information about field trips, vaccination schedules, and parent-teacher meetings, and their children are sometimes the only ones who arrive unprepared. I am writing to ask whether the school could provide translated versions of its main notices in Spanish, Vietnamese, and Arabic, the three most common languages among these families. Our center has trained volunteers who would be glad to translate the documents free of charge within two days of receiving them. Thank you for your time and for your support of every family in our community.

Sincerely,
Sofia Mendes
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 학교 가정통신문의 발송 일정 변경을 요청하려고
이주 가정을 위한 학부모 상담 시간을 늘려 달라고 요청하려고
학교 안내문을 여러 언어로 번역해 제공해 달라고 요청하려고
가족 지원 센터의 번역 자원봉사자를 모집하려고
현장 학습과 예방 접종 일정을 문의하려고
items.exp: 영어로만 나가는 가정통신문 때문에 이주 가정 부모들이 중요한 정보를 놓치므로 주요 안내문을 스페인어·베트남어·아랍어로 번역해 달라고 부탁하는 편지예요. 자원봉사자는 이미 있어서 번역을 돕겠다고 제안한 것이므로 ④는 목적이 아니에요.

items.passage: Mina sat at the back of the student council room, watching the vice principal unfold the ballots one by one. She had run for class president against two popular classmates, and for a week she had given speeches, put up posters, and talked to anyone who would listen. Now the count on the whiteboard was painfully close. Each time an opponent's name was read, her stomach tightened. She twisted the strap of her bag until her fingers ached and tried not to look at anyone. With only ten ballots left, she was behind by three votes. Then the vice principal read her name, again and again. When the final ballot was opened and the last mark went up beside "Mina Park," the room erupted. Her friends rushed over, shouting her name. Mina covered her mouth with both hands, laughing and blinking back tears, hardly able to believe that she had won.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Mina의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 개표 중 상대 이름이 나올 때마다 속이 조이고 가방끈을 비틀며, 세 표 뒤처진 모습에서 초조함이 드러나요. 마지막 표로 당선이 확정되자 웃으며 눈물을 참았으므로 몹시 기쁜 마음으로 바뀌었어요. 그래서 anxious → overjoyed가 알맞아요.

items.passage: When a student raises a hand and says, "I don't get it," a caring teacher's first instinct is to explain right away. The explanation usually works, at least in the short term: the confusion disappears and the class moves on. But something valuable is lost in that quick rescue. Research on learning suggests that students who wrestle with a problem for a while, trying different approaches and even failing, understand the concept more deeply when the explanation finally comes. The struggle prepares their minds, making clear exactly which part they did not understand and why the answer matters. A student who is rescued too quickly, on the other hand, learns that the way to deal with difficulty is to wait for someone else to solve it. Teachers, therefore, should learn to hold back. Instead of immediately giving the answer, they can offer a hint, ask a guiding question, or simply allow a few minutes of silence. Help is most powerful when it arrives after students have had a real chance to think.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 교사는 학생이 스스로 고민할 시간을 준 뒤에 도움을 주어야 한다.
교사는 학생의 질문에 즉시 명확한 설명을 제공해야 한다.
학생들은 어려운 문제를 친구들과 함께 해결해야 한다.
교사는 수업 진도보다 학생의 흥미를 우선해야 한다.
학생은 이해하지 못한 부분을 숨기지 말고 질문해야 한다.
items.exp: Teachers, therefore, should learn to hold back 이후 바로 답을 주지 말고 힌트나 질문, 침묵의 시간을 주라고 하며, 학생이 생각할 기회를 가진 뒤의 도움이 가장 효과적이라고 주장해요. ②는 필자가 경계하는 즉각적인 구조에 해당해요.

items.passage: Navigation apps have made it nearly impossible to get lost. Type in an address, and a calm voice will guide you turn by turn to your destination. Yet this convenience comes at a hidden cost. Studies of drivers and walkers have found that people who follow step-by-step directions remember far less about the places they pass through than those who work out routes for themselves. They arrive successfully, but if the phone dies on the way home, many have no idea which direction to head. The reason is that building a mental map requires effort: noticing landmarks, judging distances, and relating one street to another. When an app handles all of this, the brain simply stops doing it. The driver's hands may still be on the wheel, but in an important sense such travelers have [handed the steering wheel to the screen]. Using an app now and then to check one's own sense of direction, rather than to replace it, may be the wiser approach.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [handed the steering wheel to the screen]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: stopped paying close attention to the traffic around them
spent too much time looking at their phones while driving
let the device take over the work of understanding their surroundings
relied on self-driving functions to control their cars
started to trust paper maps more than digital ones
items.exp: 앱이 랜드마크 파악, 거리 판단, 길 연결 같은 마음속 지도 만들기를 대신하면 뇌가 그 일을 멈춘다고 했으므로, 밑줄은 주변을 이해하는 일을 기기에 넘겼다는 뜻이에요. 손은 여전히 핸들 위에 있다고 했으니 실제 자율 주행이나 운전 중 휴대폰 사용을 말하는 것이 아니에요.

items.passage: Most birds work hard to raise their young, but the common cuckoo leaves the job to others. A female cuckoo watches a smaller bird, such as a reed warbler, building its nest. When the owner leaves, she quickly lays a single egg there, often removing one of the host's eggs. Remarkably, her egg usually matches the color and pattern of the host's own. Soon after hatching, the cuckoo chick pushes the other eggs and chicks out of the nest. The host parents, unaware of the trick, feed the stranger as if it were their own, even when it grows much larger than they are. The chick's loud begging calls, which sound like those of a whole nest of hungry chicks, make the parents work even harder. Some host species, however, have begun to fight back by learning to recognize foreign eggs and throw them out, leading to an ongoing evolutionary contest between deceiver and deceived.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the reasons birds migrate long distances
the role of song in bird communication
how cuckoos trick other birds into raising their young
why some birds lay eggs of different colors

items.passage: In most industries, a company that drives its competitors out of business is considered a success. Professional sports leagues are different. A league in which one team wins every game would soon lose its fans, because much of the excitement of sport comes from not knowing who will win. For this reason, many leagues deliberately limit how strong any single team can become. The most common tool is the salary cap, a limit on how much each team may spend on player wages. Without it, the richest clubs could simply buy all the best players. Some leagues also use a draft system, which gives the weakest teams from the previous season the first chance to choose new young players. These rules may seem to punish success, but they protect something every team depends on: a competition whose result is uncertain. In sports, rivals are not only opponents but also partners in producing a show that people will pay to watch.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why the Richest Clubs Always Win Championships
How Players Decide Which Team to Join
The Draft System: A Reward for Last Season's Champions
Can Fans Change the Rules of Professional Leagues?
Keeping Rivals Strong: Why Leagues Limit Their Best Teams
items.exp: 승부를 예측할 수 없어야 리그가 살아남으므로 샐러리캡과 드래프트로 한 팀이 지나치게 강해지는 것을 막는다는 내용이라 ⑤가 제목으로 알맞아요. 드래프트는 지난 시즌 가장 약한 팀에게 먼저 기회를 주는 제도이므로 ③은 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: Ruth Imboden (1903–1981) was a Swiss trainer of mountain rescue dogs. She grew up in a village high in the Alps, where her father ran a small inn for travelers crossing the pass. As a teenager, she watched a search team spend two days looking for a climber buried under snow, and the experience convinced her that dogs could find people far faster than humans could. With no formal training, she began working with her family's farm dogs, hiding friends in snow caves and rewarding the dogs with play when they dug them out. In 1931, she founded a small training school in her village, which accepted dogs of any breed as long as they showed curiosity and stamina. Her method of using games rather than punishment was at first dismissed by army trainers, but it was widely adopted after the war. Imboden trained more than two hundred dogs during her career and wrote a handbook that remained in use for decades.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 아버지는 고개를 넘는 여행자들을 위한 작은 여관을 운영했다.
십대 시절 눈에 묻힌 등반가를 직접 구조했다.
놀이를 활용한 훈련법은 처음에 군 훈련사들에게 무시당했다.
items.exp: she watched a search team spend two days looking for a climber라고 했으므로 십대 때 수색대가 등반가를 찾는 모습을 지켜보았을 뿐 직접 구조한 것이 아니에요. 나머지는 지문 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage: Long before coins became common, salt ①[were] one of the most valued goods in the ancient world. For people without refrigerators, it was the main way ②[to preserve] meat and fish through long winters, and armies could not march far without it. Cities that controlled salt supplies grew rich, and roads ③[built] to carry it across deserts and mountains became some of the earliest trade routes. One of them, the Via Salaria, or "Salt Road," led into Rome itself. Roman soldiers are often said to have received part of their pay in salt, a story ④[that] historians now doubt but that survives in the English word "salary." Governments, too, saw salt as an easy source of income. In ancient China, a state monopoly on salt helped pay for armies and public works for centuries, and in many other lands rulers taxed it heavily, since everyone needed it no matter how high its price ⑤[rose].
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: 주어 salt는 셀 수 없는 단수 명사이므로 ①은 were가 아니라 was로 고쳐야 해요. ② 명사 the main way를 꾸미는 to부정사, ③ roads를 꾸미는 과거분사, ④ a story를 선행사로 하는 관계대명사, ⑤ no matter how 절의 동사 rose는 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: In many countries, a person cannot be prosecuted for most crimes once a certain number of years has passed. This rule, known as a statute of limitations, can seem ①[unfair] at first: why should time excuse wrongdoing? Yet there are sound reasons behind it. As years go by, evidence ②[disappears]. Witnesses move away or forget details, documents are lost, and memories that once seemed clear become ③[unreliable]. A trial held decades after the events may therefore be more likely to convict an innocent person, who can no longer find the records or witnesses needed for a defense. The rule also encourages police and prosecutors to investigate cases ④[promptly] instead of leaving them untouched for years. Nevertheless, most legal systems set no time limit for the most serious crimes, such as murder, because society's interest in punishing such acts is considered too ⑤[weak] to fade with time.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 살인 같은 중대 범죄에는 시효를 두지 않는다고 했으므로 처벌에 대한 사회의 관심이 시간이 지나도 사라지지 않을 만큼 강하다는 흐름이에요. 따라서 ⑤ weak는 strong으로 바꿔야 해요. 시간이 지나면 증거가 사라지고 기억이 믿기 어려워져 수사를 서두르게 된다는 나머지는 알맞아요.

items.passage: In a 4×100-meter relay, it seems obvious that the team with the four fastest sprinters should win. Yet major championships regularly produce upsets in which a team of individually slower runners crosses the line first. The reason lies in the exchange zones. Each runner must pass a baton to the next within a marked stretch of track, and the handoff has to happen while both athletes are moving at nearly full speed. If the receiving runner starts too late, the two collide or slow down; if she starts too early, she may leave the zone before the baton reaches her, and the team is disqualified. A well-drilled team practices these handoffs hundreds of times, learning exactly when to start and where to reach back, so that the baton seems to travel at a constant speed around the track. A team of stars who rarely train together, however, often loses precious tenths of a second at every exchange. In the relay, victory belongs less to raw speed than to ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 개인 기록이 느린 팀이 이기는 이유는 바통 터치 구간에서 언제 출발하고 어디서 손을 뻗을지 수백 번 연습해 손발을 맞추기 때문이라고 했어요. 따라서 승리는 순수한 속도보다 연습으로 다진 호흡(practiced coordination)에 달려 있어요. individual talent는 글이 부정한 스타 선수들의 능력이에요.

items.passage: Consider what happens when a stranger steps into a crowded elevator and stands facing the back wall. No rule has been broken and no one has been harmed, yet the other passengers feel a sharp discomfort they can hardly explain. The episode reveals something about how social norms operate. The norms that govern our daily lives most firmly are seldom the ones written in laws or posted on signs. A written rule, after all, can be read, questioned, and argued against; its very visibility invites people to ask whether it is fair. The unspoken norm about which way to face in an elevator enjoys no such exposure. Because people absorb it without ever being told, it never becomes an object of debate, and so it is rarely challenged. Paradoxically, then, the power of such a norm comes not from enforcement but from ___. It is only when someone breaks it, as the stranger did, that we suddenly become aware of a rule we had been obeying all along.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the strict penalties attached to violating it
our failure to recognize it as a rule at all
the open discussion it receives in society
its being clearly stated in public places
the respect people feel toward those who created it
items.exp: 글로 쓰인 규칙은 눈에 보이기 때문에 의심받고 논쟁의 대상이 되지만, 말없이 흡수된 규범은 논쟁 대상이 되지 않아 도전받지 않는다고 했어요. 마지막 문장에서도 누군가 어길 때에야 그 규칙을 알아차린다고 했으므로, 힘의 원천은 그것을 규칙으로 인식하지 못한다는 점이에요. ③④는 오히려 규범을 약하게 만드는 요소예요.

items.passage: The body's internal clock does not keep perfect time on its own; each day it needs to be reset, and the most powerful signal for doing so is morning light. ① When bright light enters the eyes, special cells in the retina send a message directly to the part of the brain that controls daily rhythms. ② This message tells the brain to stop releasing melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, and to begin the processes that keep us alert. ③ It also starts a countdown, so that melatonin is released again roughly fourteen to sixteen hours later, preparing the body for sleep. ④ Sunlight also allows the skin to produce vitamin D, a nutrient that plays a key role in keeping bones strong. ⑤ For this reason, people who spend even twenty minutes outdoors soon after waking often find it easier to fall asleep at night, while those who stay in dim rooms all morning may find their clocks drifting later and later.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 아침 빛이 생체 시계를 재설정하는 과정을 설명하는 글인데, ④는 햇빛이 비타민 D를 만들어 뼈를 튼튼하게 한다는 내용이라 생체 시계와 관련이 없어요. ⑤의 For this reason은 ③의 멜라토닌 카운트다운을 이어받아요.

items.passage:
The value of most goods does not depend on who else owns them. A loaf of bread tastes the same whether one person or a million people buy the same brand.

(A) Yet network effects can also work against newcomers. A new app may be better designed than an established one, but if none of your friends use it, its superior features count for little. This is why markets shaped by network effects often end up dominated by one or two players.

(B) A telephone, however, is different. The first telephone ever sold was nearly useless, since its owner had no one to call. Each new buyer made every existing phone a little more valuable, because there was now one more person to reach.

(C) Economists call this a network effect. It explains why messaging services, online marketplaces, and even languages can grow rapidly once they pass a certain size, as each new user attracts still more users.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 빵과 대조되는 전화기를 however로 소개하는 (B)가 먼저 와요. (B)에서 설명한 현상을 this로 받아 network effect라고 이름 붙이는 (C)가 이어지고, 이미 소개된 network effects의 단점을 Yet으로 말하는 (A)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Long before anyone knew that microbes existed, people around the world were putting them to work, turning ordinary harvests into foods that could survive long journeys and hard seasons. ( ① ) Cabbage packed in salt became sauerkraut in Germany and kimchi in Korea; milk carried in warm leather bags became yogurt in Central Asia; soybeans became soy sauce and miso in East Asia. ( ② ) In each case, the method was discovered by trial and error and passed down through generations, often as closely guarded family recipes. ( ③ ) What these cultures had found was a way to let helpful bacteria and yeasts take over food before harmful ones could. ( ④ ) The friendly microbes produced acids or alcohol that made the food hostile to the organisms that cause spoilage, allowing it to last for months. ( ⑤ ) That is why fermented foods are not simply a way of storing food but a central part of how many cultures define their cuisine.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

But fermentation did more than keep food safe; it also created sharp, sour, and rich flavors that people came to love.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 keep food safe는 ⑤ 앞에서 설명한, 미생물이 부패를 막아 음식을 오래 보존하게 한다는 내용을 받아요. 또 주어진 문장의 맛 이야기가 있어야 발효 음식이 단순한 저장법이 아니라 요리의 중심이라는 마지막 문장이 자연스러워요.

items.passage: In one study, researchers asked participants to write a short letter of thanks to someone who had made a difference in their lives. Before sending it, the writers predicted how the recipient would feel: how surprised, how happy, and how uncomfortable. The recipients were then asked to report how they actually felt. The gap was striking. Writers consistently expected their letters to produce less pleasure than they actually did, and they imagined the recipients would feel far more uncomfortable than they reported. Part of the explanation lay in what each side paid attention to. Writers worried about finding the right words and feared their message would come out badly phrased or insincere. Recipients, by contrast, hardly noticed the wording at all; what moved them was the simple warmth of being thanked. Because of this mismatch, many people hold back from expressing gratitude that would have been gladly received.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

People tend to (A) ___ the positive impact of expressing thanks, partly because they focus too much on how (B) ___ their words might seem.
items.exp: 편지를 쓴 사람들은 받는 사람이 느낄 기쁨을 실제보다 적게 예상했으므로 (A)는 underestimate예요. 또 그들은 표현이 서툴게 나올까 걱정했으므로 (B)는 awkward가 알맞아요.

items.passage:
A popular picture of science holds that a theory is abandoned the moment it makes a false prediction. One failed test, the story goes, is enough to (a)[overturn] years of agreement. The actual history of science suggests something more complicated.

In the early nineteenth century, astronomers noticed that Uranus was not moving exactly as Newton's laws predicted. A strict reading of the popular picture would have required them to reject Newtonian physics. Instead, the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier assumed the theory was correct and asked what would have to be true for the (b)[observations] to fit it. His answer was an unseen planet pulling on Uranus. In 1846, astronomers pointed their telescopes where he had calculated and found Neptune. Protecting the theory had led to a (c)[discovery].

Le Verrier later tried the same strategy with Mercury, whose orbit also showed a small irregularity. He proposed another hidden planet, which was even given a name, Vulcan. This time, however, decades of searching turned up nothing. The irregularity was finally explained only in 1915 by Einstein's theory of general relativity, which replaced Newton's account of gravity.

The two cases look (d)[different] from the inside. In both, scientists faced an anomaly and chose to save their theory by adding something unseen. What separated success from failure was not the logic of the move but what the world turned out to contain. No simple rule, then, can tell scientists in advance whether to defend a theory or (e)[abandon] it. Such decisions call for judgment, which is often justified only in hindsight. Yet this willingness to hold on to a troubled theory is part of what makes science productive: a theory dropped at the first difficulty would never have led anyone to Neptune.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Newton's Physics Was Never Really Wrong
Rescuing a Theory: A Choice Logic Alone Cannot Make
How Neptune Was Discovered by Accident
Einstein's Long Search for the Planet Vulcan
One Failed Test Is Enough to End a Theory
items.exp: 해왕성은 이론을 지켜서 성공했고 불칸은 같은 방법으로 실패했으며, 이론을 지킬지 버릴지는 단순한 규칙이 아니라 판단의 문제라는 글이에요. 따라서 ②가 제목으로 알맞아요. 해왕성은 계산으로 예측해 찾았으므로 ③은 틀리고, ⑤는 글이 반박하는 통념이에요.

items.exp: 바로 뒤에서 두 경우 모두 이상 현상에 부딪혀 보이지 않는 것을 더해 이론을 지키려 했다고 했으므로, 안에서 보면 두 경우가 똑같아 보인다는 뜻이 되어야 해요. 따라서 (d) different는 identical이나 similar로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
The moving truck left on a gray Saturday, and Jun stood in the empty living room of the new apartment, listening to the traffic eleven floors below. Back in his small coastal town, he had known every street and nearly every face. Here, he knew no one. For the first week, he unpacked boxes slowly and spent most evenings at the window. Each evening he noticed the same thing in the park across the road: a tall boy alone on the basketball court, shooting free throws until the streetlights came on. Even when (a)[he] missed, the boy simply picked up the ball and tried again.

(B)
After that first game, the two boys met at the court almost every evening. Between shots, Marcus told (b)[him] that his own family had arrived in the city only a year earlier. "The first month was the worst," he said. "I used to come here because I didn't know where else to go." Jun was surprised; Marcus seemed so at ease. When school began, Marcus was waiting at the front gate, ready to introduce (c)[him] to his friends. Jun's first day, which he had dreaded for weeks, passed far more easily than he had expected.

(C)
Months later, Jun's best friend from his hometown called and asked whether he still missed the sea. Jun thought about it for a moment. He did, sometimes. But he also had a team now, a favorite noodle shop, and a friend who always knew how to cheer (d)[him] up. After hanging up, he glanced out the window. On the court stood a small boy he had never seen before, holding a ball and looking around uncertainly. Jun grabbed his jacket and headed for the door, ready to do what Marcus had once done for him.

(D)
The next evening, Jun took his old basketball and crossed the road. At the fence, (e)[he] hesitated, suddenly unsure. Just then the boy's shot bounced off the rim and rolled toward the gate. Jun picked it up and passed it back. "Want to play?" the boy called, waving him in. His name was Marcus, and he played with a calm patience that Jun admired. They played until it was too dark to see the hoop.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Jun이 창밖으로 혼자 농구하는 소년을 보았고, The next evening 그 코트로 가서 Marcus를 만나는 (D)가 이어져요. After that first game으로 시작하는 (B)가 그다음이고, Months later로 시작해 Jun이 새 아이에게 다가가는 (C)가 마지막이에요.

The next evening, Jun took his old basketball and crossed the road. At the fence, (e)[he] hesitated, suddenly unsure. Just then the boy's shot bounced off the rim and rolled toward the gate. Jun picked it up and passed it back. "Want to play?" the boy called, waving him in. His name was Marcus, and he played with a calm patience that Jun admired. They played until it was too dark to see the hoop.
items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Jun은 이사 후 첫 주에 대부분의 저녁을 창가에서 보냈다.
Marcus의 가족은 1년 전에 그 도시로 이사 왔다.
Jun의 첫 등교일은 예상보다 훨씬 힘들게 지나갔다.
몇 달 뒤 Jun의 고향 친구가 전화를 걸어왔다.
Marcus는 Jun에게 함께 농구를 하자고 제안했다.
items.exp: (B)에서 몇 주 동안 걱정했던 첫날이 예상보다 훨씬 수월하게 지나갔다고 했으므로 ③은 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 각각 (A), (B), (C), (D)의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Residents of Willow Court,

As many of you know, the water pipes in our building are more than forty years old, and over the past year we have had to repair leaks in several apartments. After careful review, the residents' committee has decided to replace the main pipes this spring. The work will take place from Monday, March 8 to Friday, March 19, 2027, between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. on weekdays only. During these hours, water will be shut off for one floor at a time, and each floor will be without water for no more than two days. A schedule showing the exact dates for each floor will be posted in the elevator and the main lobby by the end of this month. We recommend storing some water in advance for cooking and cleaning. We apologize for the inconvenience and thank you for your patience as we make our building safer.

Sincerely,
Grace Holloway
Building Manager
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 건물 배관 누수 신고 방법을 알려 주려고
배관 수리 비용 분담 방식을 설명하려고
배관 교체 공사 일정과 단수 계획을 안내하려고
items.exp: 배관 교체 공사가 언제 진행되는지, 층별로 며칠 동안 물이 끊기는지, 일정표를 어디에 게시하는지를 알려 주는 글이에요. 누수 수리는 공사 배경일 뿐이고, 엘리베이터는 일정표를 붙일 장소로 나왔을 뿐이에요.

items.passage: On the morning of the school cooking contest, I arranged my lemon tart on the judges' table and stepped back to admire it. The crust was golden, the filling smooth and bright, and I had decorated the top with thin slices of candied lemon arranged like the petals of a flower. I had practiced it six times that month, and each time my family had cleaned their plates. Looking at the other entries, I honestly thought mine was the best. When the head judge took her first bite, I leaned forward, waiting for her smile. Instead, she paused and reached for a glass of water. "It's beautiful," she said gently, "but I think there may be salt in here instead of sugar." My face went hot. I suddenly remembered the two identical jars on the kitchen shelf that morning and how quickly I had grabbed one. As the judges moved on to the next table, I stared at my perfect-looking tart, wishing I could disappear.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 자신의 타르트가 최고라고 생각하며 심사위원의 미소를 기다렸지만, 설탕 대신 소금을 넣었다는 말을 듣고 얼굴이 달아오르며 사라지고 싶어 했어요. 따라서 자신감에서 창피함으로 바뀌었어요.

items.passage: Writers of the Japanese haiku must fit an entire moment into three short lines with a fixed number of sound units. The sonnet demands exactly fourteen lines and a strict pattern of rhyme. To an outsider, such rules look like obstacles that a truly free artist would throw away. Yet poets have returned to these forms for centuries, and many describe the experience not as restriction but as release. When almost anything is possible, the mind tends to fall back on its most familiar habits, producing the first idea that comes along. A demanding form blocks those easy paths. Searching for a word with exactly the right sound and rhythm, the poet is pushed toward images and connections that would never have appeared otherwise. The limit does not reduce choices so much as force the writer to look beyond the obvious ones. In this sense, a strict form is [a cage that teaches the bird to fly], turning what seems like a barrier into the source of surprise.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a cage that teaches the bird to fly]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a limitation that drives the writer toward unexpected creativity
a tradition that young poets must escape to become original
a set of rules that only skilled poets are able to follow
a teacher who corrects the mistakes of beginning writers
a form that allows poets to copy the works of earlier masters
items.exp: 엄격한 형식이 익숙한 생각으로 가는 쉬운 길을 막아 시인을 뜻밖의 이미지와 연결로 이끈다고 했으므로, 밑줄은 제약이 오히려 예상치 못한 창의성을 이끌어 낸다는 뜻이에요. ②는 형식을 벗어나야 한다는 외부인의 시각이라 글의 논지와 반대예요.

items.passage: Shoppers who care about the climate are often told to buy local food, and the advice sounds obviously right: food that travels a shorter distance should produce fewer emissions. The reality is less simple. For most foods, transportation accounts for only a small share of the greenhouse gases released between the farm and the table, often around a tenth. The far larger share comes from how the food is produced: the land cleared for it, the fertilizer applied, the methane released by cattle, and the energy used to heat greenhouses. As a result, tomatoes grown in a heated greenhouse nearby may have a larger climate impact than tomatoes grown in an open field in a sunny country and shipped hundreds of kilometers. Likewise, a locally raised steak almost always carries a heavier climate cost than beans imported from abroad. Distance is easy to see on a label, but it is rarely the factor that matters most. What we eat usually matters far more than where it comes from.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 음식의 운송 거리를 줄이는 것이 기후 변화 대응의 핵심이다.
지역 농가를 지원하면 지역 경제가 살아난다.
음식의 기후 영향은 운송 거리보다 생산 방식과 종류에 더 크게 좌우된다.
온실 재배 채소가 노지 재배 채소보다 영양이 풍부하다.
식품 라벨에 탄소 배출량을 반드시 표시해야 한다.
items.exp: 운송은 배출의 작은 부분이고 생산 방식이 훨씬 큰 몫을 차지하며, 마지막 문장에서 무엇을 먹는지가 어디서 오는지보다 중요하다고 정리해요. 따라서 ③이 요지예요. ①은 글이 반박하는 통념이고, ⑤는 언급되지 않은 주장이에요.

items.passage: Most of the units we use to measure time come from nature. A day is one turn of the Earth, a month roughly matches the cycle of the moon, and a year follows the Earth's journey around the sun. The week, however, has no such basis. Nothing in the sky repeats every seven days, and different societies have experimented with very different lengths. Ancient Egyptians divided their months into ten-day periods, some West African markets operated on a four-day cycle, and in the late eighteenth century revolutionary France introduced a ten-day week, which proved deeply unpopular and was later abandoned. The seven-day week spread largely through religious traditions and trade, and it survives today not because it fits any natural rhythm but because nearly everyone else uses it. Once schools, shops, and workplaces are organized around the same cycle, changing it becomes almost impossible. The week, in this sense, is a shared agreement that holds only because we all keep it.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: natural cycles that determine the length of a day and a year
the week as a social convention rather than a natural unit of time
religious origins of rest days in ancient societies
failed attempts by revolutionary governments to reform society
the influence of the moon on early market schedules
items.exp: 하루·한 달·한 해와 달리 일주일은 자연에 근거가 없고, 모두가 같은 주기를 쓰기 때문에 유지되는 공동의 약속이라는 글이에요. 따라서 ②가 주제예요. ①은 도입부의 비교 대상일 뿐이고, ④ 프랑스의 실패는 예시 하나에 불과해요.

items.passage: Basic economic theory suggests that a company should pay workers no more than the market requires; any extra money seems to be simply lost profit. Yet some firms deliberately pay well above the usual wage, and many of them do so for strictly practical reasons. Replacing an employee is expensive. A company must advertise the job, interview candidates, and then train the new worker, who may need months to become as productive as the person who left. When wages are higher than elsewhere, fewer workers quit, so these costs shrink. Higher pay also gives employees a reason to protect their jobs by working carefully, since losing this position would mean accepting a worse one. In addition, a generous wage attracts more applicants, allowing the employer to choose the most skilled among them. Economists call this idea the efficiency wage. It suggests that, in the right circumstances, a higher payroll can lower total costs, because the money returns in the form of loyal, careful, and experienced workers.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Low Wages Always Mean Higher Profits
The Rising Cost of Job Advertisements
How Workers Choose Between Two Job Offers
Paying More to Spend Less: The Logic of Higher Wages
Training New Employees: A Waste of Time?
items.exp: 임금을 더 많이 주면 이직이 줄고, 직원이 성실해지며, 우수한 지원자를 고를 수 있어 오히려 전체 비용이 줄 수 있다는 효율 임금 이야기이므로 ④가 알맞아요. ①은 글이 반박하는 생각이고, 채용 광고 비용(②)은 일부 예시예요.

items.passage:
Hillcrest Teen Job Fair 2027
