items.q: Hillcrest Teen Job Fair 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
items.exp: Lunch will not be provided라고 했으므로 점심은 제공되지 않고, 밖에 푸드 트럭이 있을 뿐이에요. 이력서 워크숍은 오전 10시 30분, 모의 면접은 sign-up required로 안내문과 일치해요.

items.passage: Ask speakers of different languages what sound a dog makes, and you will get surprisingly different answers. English dogs say "woof," Korean dogs say "meong-meong," and French dogs say "ouaf." If these words simply copied real sounds, we ①[would expect] them to be nearly identical, since dogs everywhere bark in much the same way. The differences arise because each language can imitate a sound only with the set of sounds it already ②[possesses]. A noise that does not fit those patterns must be reshaped until it ③[sound] like a normal word. Children, moreover, learn these words from adults rather than from animals, so the imitations are handed down as part of the language, ④[changing] slowly over generations. Onomatopoeia, then, is less a recording of nature than a translation of it, and like all translations, it reveals as much about the language ⑤[doing] the translating as about the original sound.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③의 주어는 단수인 it(a noise)이므로 sound를 sounds로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 가정의 결과를 나타내는 would expect, ④는 분사구문, ⑤는 the language를 뒤에서 꾸미는 현재분사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Many people cannot imagine starting the day without coffee, but few know how caffeine actually keeps them awake. Throughout the day, the brain produces a substance called adenosine, which gradually ①[builds] up while we are awake. As adenosine attaches to receptors on brain cells, it slows their activity and makes us feel ②[sleepy]. Caffeine has a shape similar to adenosine, so it can fit into the same receptors and ③[block] them. The adenosine is still there, but it can no longer deliver its message, and we feel more alert. This explains why the effect is ④[temporary]: when the caffeine wears off a few hours later, the adenosine that has kept accumulating floods the receptors at once, sometimes causing a sudden crash. Regular drinkers face another problem. Over time, the brain responds to caffeine by growing additional receptors, so the same cup of coffee produces a ⑤[stronger] effect than it once did, and people need more to feel the same boost.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 뇌가 수용체를 더 만들어 같은 양의 커피로는 예전만큼 효과를 느끼지 못해 더 많이 마셔야 한다는 흐름이므로 ⑤ stronger는 weaker로 바꿔야 해요. ④ temporary는 몇 시간 뒤 효과가 사라진다는 내용과 맞아요.

items.passage: Why do skilled athletes sometimes fail at the very moment when the stakes are highest? A golfer who sinks short putts easily in practice misses one to win a championship; a pianist who has played a piece flawlessly a hundred times stumbles before an audience. Psychologists who study this "choking" have found that pressure often causes experts to pay close attention to movements they normally perform without thinking. A well-practiced skill is stored as a smooth, automatic sequence. When an anxious performer begins to monitor each step, asking whether the wrist is at the right angle or the fingers are pressing correctly, the sequence breaks into separate pieces and loses its flow. In one experiment, experienced golfers who were told to focus on the details of their swing performed worse than those who were given a distracting task, such as counting backward. For experts under pressure, the problem is often not too little effort but too much ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 압박을 받으면 전문가가 평소 생각 없이 하던 동작 하나하나를 의식적으로 감시하게 되어 실력이 무너진다고 했으므로 빈칸에는 conscious control이 알맞아요. 연습을 많이 한 기술이 자동화되어 있다고 했으므로 practice는 문제의 원인이 아니에요.

items.passage: A banknote is a small piece of printed paper, and the numbers in a bank account are only entries in a computer. Neither can be eaten, worn, or used to build a house. Why, then, will a baker hand over bread in exchange for them? It is tempting to answer that money is backed by something solid, such as gold or the power of the government. But most modern currencies cannot be exchanged for gold, and a government can declare a currency legal without making anyone eager to hold it, as the collapse of many currencies in history shows. The baker accepts money for a simpler reason: she is confident that the butcher and the landlord will accept it from her tomorrow. Each person takes money because they expect the next person to take it, and that person reasons in the same way. The value of money, then, rests less on any property of the money itself than on the fact that ___. Once that shared expectation weakens, even a currency issued by a powerful state can lose its worth almost overnight.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: it is printed with great care by a trusted central authority
it can be exchanged at any time for a fixed amount of gold
people need it to pay the taxes required by law
its supply is carefully limited so that it remains scarce
everyone expects everyone else to keep accepting it in exchange
items.exp: 제빵사가 돈을 받는 것은 다음 사람도 받아 줄 것이라 믿기 때문이고, 그 공유된 기대가 약해지면 돈의 가치가 사라진다고 했으므로 ⑤가 알맞아요. ②의 금 교환과 정부의 힘은 글이 그럴듯하지만 충분하지 않다고 부정한 설명이에요.

items.passage: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all known marine species. ① Their richness depends on a partnership between coral animals and tiny algae that live inside their tissues. ② The algae use sunlight to produce food, much of which they share with the coral, while the coral provides the algae with shelter and nutrients. ③ When water temperatures rise even slightly above normal for several weeks, however, this partnership breaks down and the coral expels the algae, turning white in a process called bleaching. ④ Divers from around the world travel to famous reefs every year, and many popular sites now limit the number of daily visitors. ⑤ If cooler conditions return quickly, the algae can recolonize the coral, but repeated or prolonged heat often leaves the reef dead and the creatures that depended on it without a home.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 산호와 조류의 공생, 그리고 수온 상승으로 그 관계가 무너지는 백화 현상을 설명하는 글이에요. ④는 다이버들의 관광과 방문객 제한에 관한 내용이라 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤의 the algae can recolonize는 ③의 백화 과정을 이어받아요.

items.passage:
Deep in the ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland lies one of the most detailed records of Earth's past climate. Each year, snow falls on the ice sheet and is gradually pressed down by the layers that fall after it.

(A) Over thousands of years, the snow turns to ice, trapping small bubbles of the air that existed at the time it fell. Each layer, therefore, contains a sealed sample of the atmosphere as it was in that particular year.

(B) Comparing these measurements layer by layer, researchers have reconstructed temperatures and gas levels going back more than 800,000 years, showing a close link between carbon dioxide and global temperature.

(C) To read this record, scientists drill long cylinders of ice, called cores, sometimes more than three kilometers deep. In laboratories, they release the trapped air and measure the amount of carbon dioxide and other gases it contains.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 눈이 쌓여 눌린다는 주어진 글 다음에, 눈이 얼음이 되며 공기 방울을 가둔다는 (A)가 와요. this record로 (A)의 기록을 받아 얼음 코어를 뚫어 기체를 측정하는 (C)가 이어지고, these measurements로 (C)의 측정을 받는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Almost everyone has experienced an earworm, a short piece of music that repeats itself in the mind for hours. ( ① ) Researchers who have collected thousands of reports find that earworms tend to share certain musical features, regardless of the listener's age or taste: a fairly fast tempo, a simple melody, and an unusual jump or repetition that makes the tune stand out. ( ② ) They also strike most often when the mind is not fully occupied, such as while walking, showering, or doing household chores. ( ③ ) Interestingly, another common remedy, trying hard not to think of the song, tends to backfire. ( ④ ) Deliberately pushing a thought away keeps the brain checking whether it has returned, which only brings it back more often. ( ⑤ ) Some people find that listening to the whole song from start to finish helps, perhaps because the brain is satisfied once the unfinished loop is completed.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

This may be why keeping the mind fully busy with an absorbing activity, like solving a puzzle or reading a challenging book, is one of the most reliable ways to make an earworm fade.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 This는 ③ 앞의, 귀벌레가 마음이 완전히 바쁘지 않을 때 자주 찾아온다는 내용을 가리켜요. 그래서 몰입하는 활동이 귀벌레를 없애는 방법이 된다는 결론이 이어지고, ③ 뒤의 another common remedy는 주어진 문장이 첫 번째 해결책을 제시해야 자연스러워요.

items.passage: A software company once ran an experiment with two groups of employees doing the same kind of work. The first group continued under the usual rules, arriving at nine and leaving at six. The second group was told that, as long as they met their deadlines and attended a few key meetings, they could decide for themselves when and where to work. Many managers expected the second group's output to fall, assuming that people without supervision would relax. The opposite happened. Over six months, the flexible group completed more projects, took fewer sick days, and reported higher job satisfaction. Several employees explained that being trusted to organize their own time made them feel personally responsible for the results. Some chose to work early in the morning, when they could concentrate best; others split their day around family needs. The freedom, it seemed, did not encourage laziness but brought out a stronger sense of commitment.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

When employees were given (A) ___ over their working hours, their performance improved rather than declined, because the trust they received increased their sense of (B) ___.
items.exp: 두 번째 집단은 언제 어디서 일할지 스스로 결정했으므로 (A)는 control, 신뢰를 받자 결과에 개인적 책임을 느꼈다고 했으므로 (B)는 ownership이 알맞아요. guidance는 감독이 줄어든 상황과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
For most of history, painters did not simply buy their colors; they made them. Pigments were ground by hand from minerals, plants, and even insects, then mixed with oil shortly before use. Because the mixture dried out within hours, paints were difficult to carry and store. Painters therefore worked mainly in studios, where they made sketches outdoors and (a)[completed] their landscapes later from memory.

In 1841, an American portrait painter named John Goffe Rand patented a small, squeezable tube made of tin that could be sealed with a cap. Paint stored inside stayed (b)[fresh] for weeks and could be carried in a box with a few brushes. At first the invention seemed like a minor convenience. Soon, however, color makers were selling ready-made paints in tubes, including bright new colors produced by the growing chemical industry.

The effect on painting was (c)[considerable]. For the first time, artists could set up an easel in a field or on a riverbank and finish an entire picture on the spot. The young painters later known as the Impressionists took full advantage of this freedom. Working outdoors, they tried to capture the way light changed from hour to hour, using quick, visible brushstrokes and colors straight from the tube. Their paintings looked (d)[polished] to critics used to smooth studio surfaces, but they recorded a direct experience of nature that earlier methods had made nearly impossible. Pierre-Auguste Renoir is often quoted as saying that without paint in tubes there would have been no Impressionism.

The story is a reminder that art history is not only a history of ideas and individual talent. New styles often (e)[depend] on humble tools that change what artists are able to do.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: The Forgotten Art of Grinding Pigments
How Critics Shaped the Rise of Impressionism
Studio or Field: Which Produces Better Paintings?
A Small Tube That Took Painting Outdoors
items.exp: 휴대 가능한 물감 튜브가 발명되어 화가들이 야외에서 그림을 완성할 수 있게 되었고 이것이 인상주의를 가능하게 했다는 글이므로 ⑤가 제목으로 알맞아요. 인상주의 화가들은 튜브에서 짠 밝은 색을 그대로 썼으므로 ①은 반대예요.

items.passage:
For most of history, painters did not simply buy their colors; they made them. Pigments were ground by hand from minerals, plants, and even insects, then mixed with oil shortly before use. Because the mixture dried out within hours, paints were difficult to carry and store. Painters therefore worked mainly in studios, where they made sketches outdoors and (a)[completed] their landscapes later from memory.

In 1841, an American portrait painter named John Goffe Rand patented a small, squeezable tube made of tin that could be sealed with a cap. Paint stored inside stayed (b)[fresh] for weeks and could be carried in a box with a few brushes. At first the invention seemed like a minor convenience. Soon, however, color makers were selling ready-made paints in tubes, including bright new colors produced by the growing chemical industry.

The effect on painting was (c)[considerable]. For the first time, artists could set up an easel in a field or on a riverbank and finish an entire picture on the spot. The young painters later known as the Impressionists took full advantage of this freedom. Working outdoors, they tried to capture the way light changed from hour to hour, using quick, visible brushstrokes and colors straight from the tube. Their paintings looked (d)[polished] to critics used to smooth studio surfaces, but they recorded a direct experience of nature that earlier methods had made nearly impossible. Pierre-Auguste Renoir is often quoted as saying that without paint in tubes there would have been no Impressionism.

The story is a reminder that art history is not only a history of ideas and individual talent. New styles often (e)[depend] on humble tools that change what artists are able to do.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 매끈한 화실 그림에 익숙한 비평가들에게 빠르고 눈에 보이는 붓질의 그림은 미완성처럼 보였을 것이고, 뒤의 but도 그런 대조를 이끌어요. 따라서 (d) polished는 unfinished로 바꿔야 해요. 나머지 낱말은 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
The sound was small, a sharp crack, but Hana felt it in her whole body. Her violin had slipped from the chair where she had carelessly left it and struck the corner of the desk. When she picked it up, a thin line ran across its top, and the bridge lay flat on the strings. The regional youth orchestra audition was only nine days away. The violin had belonged to her grandfather, who had played in a dance band for forty years before passing it on to (a)[her].

(B)
Inside, an old man with silver glasses was working under a lamp. Mr. Adler examined the violin for a long time without speaking. At last (b)[he] said that the crack could be repaired but that the glue needed time to set properly. "Five days, maybe six," he said. Then he noticed the worry on Hana's face and asked when she needed it. When she told him about the audition, he pulled a violin from a shelf behind him and handed it to (c)[her]. "Practice on this one in the meantime," he said.

(C)
Her teacher did not know anyone who could fix the instrument quickly, and the music store in town only sold new ones. Finally, Hana's mother remembered a small repair shop she had passed years ago, tucked behind a bakery in the old market. The next afternoon, Hana carried the violin case through the narrow lanes until she found a faded sign reading "Adler Strings." Holding her breath, (d)[she] pushed open the door, and a bell rang above her head.

(D)
The borrowed violin felt strange under her chin, and for the first two days every note sounded wrong. But by the end of the week, Hana had learned to listen more carefully than ever before. On the sixth day, Mr. Adler called. Her grandfather's violin was ready, the crack nearly invisible. At the audition, Hana played it with a confidence that surprised even (e)[her] teacher. Afterward, she returned to the shop with a box of pastries from the bakery next door and a promise to never again leave her violin on a chair.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 바이올린이 부서진 뒤, 고칠 곳을 찾다가 수리점에 들어가는 (C)가 이어져요. 수리점 안에서 Mr. Adler를 만나는 (B)가 다음이고, 빌린 바이올린으로 연습하고 오디션을 보는 (D)가 마지막이에요.

choices: Mr. Adler는 수리하는 동안 쓸 바이올린을 빌려주었다.
Hana의 선생님은 빨리 고쳐 줄 사람을 알지 못했다.
수리점은 오래된 시장의 빵집 뒤에 있었다.
items.exp: (D)에서 여섯째 날 할아버지의 바이올린이 수리되었고 오디션에서 그것을 연주했다고 했으므로 ⑤는 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 각각 (A), (B), (C), (C)의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Editor,

I am writing about the article "Old Mill Reopens as Art Center," which appeared in the Weekend section of your newspaper on March 6. As a member of the volunteer group that restored the building, I was delighted to see our project covered, and many of our members have already shared the article with friends. However, the article contains two errors that I would like to bring to your attention. First, it states that the restoration was paid for by the city, but in fact nearly all of the funds were raised through donations from local residents and small businesses. Second, the opening date of the center's first exhibition is given as April 2, while the correct date is April 12. Since many readers may plan their visits based on your article, I would be grateful if you could publish a correction in your next edition. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
Rachel Kim
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 신문 기사의 잘못된 내용을 바로잡아 달라고 요청하려고
건물 복원에 기부한 주민들에게 감사를 전하려고
지역 예술 단체에 대한 취재를 제안하려고
items.exp: 필자는 아트센터 기사에서 복원 비용의 출처와 첫 전시 날짜, 두 가지가 틀렸다고 지적한 뒤 다음 호에 정정 기사를 실어 달라고 부탁하고 있어요. 전시 날짜는 기사의 오류로 언급된 것이지 일정이 바뀐 것이 아니므로 ④는 알맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Jun set the old radio on his desk and stared at it. It had belonged to his grandfather, who used to listen to baseball games on it every summer evening, and it had been silent for more than ten years. For three weekends, Jun had been taking it apart, cleaning its dusty parts, and replacing a broken wire he had found with the help of an online guide. Twice he had put everything back together and turned the knob, and twice nothing had happened. Now his fingers were sore, and he was beginning to think he had wasted his time. "One last try," he muttered, tightening the final screw. He plugged it in and slowly turned the knob. At first there was only silence. Then came a soft crackle, and suddenly a clear voice filled the room, announcing the score of a game. Jun jumped up from his chair and laughed out loud. He grabbed his phone to call his grandfather, his heart racing with joy.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Jun의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 두 번이나 실패해 시간을 낭비했다고 생각하던 Jun은 낙담해 있었지만, 라디오에서 목소리가 흘러나오자 펄쩍 뛰며 웃고 기쁨에 가슴이 뛰었어요. 따라서 discouraged → thrilled가 알맞아요. 처음부터 즐겁거나 자랑스러운 상태가 아니었으므로 ②는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: When a new school building is planned, the decisions are usually made by architects, officials, and perhaps a few teachers. The students who will spend six or seven hours a day inside it are rarely asked anything. This is a costly mistake. Students know things about school spaces that adults easily overlook: which hallways become dangerously crowded between classes, which corners are too dark to read in, where they go when they need a quiet moment, and why the expensive lounge sits empty while the stairs are always full. When designers listen to these experiences, the solutions are often simple and inexpensive, such as wider doorways, benches near windows, or small rooms for group work. Just as important, students who help shape a building tend to treat it with more care, because it feels partly their own. If we want schools that truly work for the people inside them, we should invite students into the design process from the very beginning, not merely show them the finished plans.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 학교 건물을 설계할 때 처음부터 학생들의 의견을 반영해야 한다.
학교 건물은 비용보다 안전을 우선으로 설계해야 한다.
학생들은 학교 시설을 자기 것처럼 아껴 사용해야 한다.
학교에는 학생들이 쉴 수 있는 휴게 공간을 늘려야 한다.
건축가는 설계도를 완성한 뒤 학생들에게 공개해야 한다.
items.exp: 학생들은 어른들이 놓치는 학교 공간의 문제를 알고 있으므로, 설계 과정에 처음부터 학생들을 참여시켜야 한다고 마지막 문장에서 분명히 말해요. 완성된 설계도를 보여 주기만 하는 것은 안 된다고 했으므로 ⑤는 필자의 생각과 반대예요.

items.passage: When a new bridge opens, there is a ceremony. Officials cut a ribbon, cameras flash, and the engineers who designed it are praised in the local news. Yet a bridge is not finished on the day it opens; in a sense, its real life has only begun. For the next hundred years, someone must inspect its cables, repaint its steel to keep rust away, and replace worn joints before small cracks grow into dangerous ones. This work is rarely reported, because its success looks like nothing at all: the bridge simply keeps standing. Budgets reflect the same bias. Funding for new projects is easy to announce, while money for upkeep is often the first to be cut when times are hard. In many societies, [the applause stops at the ribbon], and the people who keep our roads, pipes, and power lines working remain invisible until something fails. A wiser culture would honor the patient work of keeping things running as much as the exciting work of building them.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the applause stops at the ribbon]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: public ceremonies are a waste of limited budgets
engineers prefer designing structures to inspecting them
recognition goes to creating structures, not to maintaining them
new bridges are built more safely than old ones
the media fails to report accidents caused by poor design
items.exp: 리본 커팅은 새 시설의 개통을 뜻하고, 박수가 거기서 멈춘다는 것은 건설에는 찬사를 보내지만 이후의 유지 보수 작업은 주목받지 못한다는 뜻이에요. 기념식 자체가 예산 낭비라는 말은 글에 없어요.

items.passage: In many forests and grasslands, a surprising partnership helps plants spread their seeds. The seeds of plants such as violets and trilliums carry a small, fatty attachment called an elaiosome. To an ant, this soft package is a valuable meal. Worker ants pick up the seeds and carry them back to their nest, where the elaiosome is removed and fed to the growing larvae. The seed itself, however, is too hard to eat, so the ants discard it, often in an underground waste chamber or just outside the nest. For the plant, this is an excellent result. Its seed has been moved away from the parent plant, where it would have competed for light and water, and has been placed in soil that is rich in nutrients from the colony's waste. Being buried also hides the seed from birds and mice that might eat it. In return for a small reward, the plant gains a careful and reliable delivery service.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: competition between ants and birds for plant seeds
the way ant larvae depend on underground chambers
why some seeds are too hard for animals to digest
the influence of soil nutrients on the growth of violets
a mutually beneficial relationship between plants and ants in seed dispersal
items.exp: 개미는 씨앗에 붙은 지방 덩어리를 먹이로 얻고, 식물은 씨앗을 멀리 영양이 풍부한 곳으로 옮겨 받으므로 씨앗 퍼뜨리기에서 서로 이익을 얻는 관계가 주제예요. 씨앗이 단단하다는 점이나 토양 영양분은 세부 내용일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: Parents who want their children to become top athletes are often told to start early and focus on a single sport. The logic seems obvious: the sooner a child begins specialized training, the more hours of practice he or she will collect. However, research on elite athletes tells a more complicated story. Many of them played several different sports throughout childhood and only committed to one in their mid-teens. Moving between soccer, swimming, and basketball, for example, exposes young bodies to a wide range of movements, which builds general coordination and reduces the repeated strain that causes overuse injuries. Variety also keeps sport enjoyable. Children who specialize too early are more likely to burn out and quit, sometimes before they ever reach their potential. In addition, trying several sports helps young people discover which one truly suits their body and personality, rather than staying with the first one their parents chose. Early focus may produce quick results, but broad experience tends to build longer and healthier careers.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How to Choose the Right Coach for Your Child
Why Young Athletes Benefit from Playing Many Sports
Overuse Injuries: An Unavoidable Cost of Elite Sport
The Earlier, the Better: The Secret of Champions
Team Sports Versus Individual Sports for Children
items.exp: 어릴 때 여러 종목을 경험하면 협응력이 길러지고 부상과 탈진이 줄며 자신에게 맞는 종목을 찾게 된다는 내용이므로 여러 종목을 하는 것의 이점이 제목으로 알맞아요. 조기 전문화를 지지하는 보기는 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: Ingrid Solheim (1889–1962) was a Norwegian glass artist known for her delicate bowls inspired by sea ice. Born in a small fishing village near Bergen, she spent her childhood collecting pieces of frosted glass that washed up on the shore. At the age of seventeen, she moved to Oslo to work as an assistant in a glass factory, where she first learned to shape melted glass. Unlike most artists of her time, she rarely used bright colors and instead mixed tiny amounts of ash into her glass to create soft, cloudy surfaces. Her first solo exhibition, held in Copenhagen in 1921, received little attention, but her work gradually gained admirers across northern Europe. In 1934, she opened a small workshop of her own and began training young women, who had few chances to enter the craft at the time. Today, more than two hundred of her works are kept in museums, and her workshop still operates as a school for glassmakers.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 어린 시절 해변에서 젖빛 유리 조각을 모았다.
유리에 재를 섞어 부드럽고 흐릿한 표면을 만들었다.
코펜하겐에서 열린 첫 개인전이 큰 주목을 받았다.
그녀의 작업장은 오늘날 유리 공예 학교로 운영되고 있다.
items.exp: 1921년 코펜하겐에서 열린 첫 개인전은 주목을 거의 받지 못했다고 했으므로 큰 주목을 받았다는 진술은 틀려요. 나머지는 해변의 유리 조각, 17세 오슬로 공장, 재를 섞은 유리, 학교로 운영되는 작업장 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage: The first bicycle had no pedals at all. In 1817, a German inventor named Karl Drais introduced a wooden machine ①[that] riders pushed along by kicking the ground with their feet, much like a child's balance bike today. Some historians link his idea to a disaster two years earlier: a huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia had filled the sky with ash, ②[causing] crop failures across Europe, and many horses starved or were killed for lack of feed. A vehicle that needed no oats ③[attracting] considerable interest. The "running machine," as Drais called it, could cover a distance faster than walking, and it soon appeared in Paris and London. Yet its popularity was brief. Riders crashed into pedestrians on crowded sidewalks, and several cities banned the machines within a few years. Not until the 1860s ④[were] pedals attached to the front wheel, and only in the 1880s did the chain-driven "safety bicycle," with two wheels of equal size, make cycling practical for millions of people ⑤[who] had never ridden before.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: 주어 A vehicle that needed no oats 뒤에 문장의 동사가 필요하므로 ③ attracting은 attracted로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 machine을 꾸미는 관계대명사, ②는 결과를 나타내는 분사구문, ④는 Not until로 시작해 도치된 동사, ⑤는 people을 받는 주격 관계대명사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Open an old book in a secondhand shop, and you may notice a sweet, slightly musty scent that some readers compare to vanilla. This smell is a sign of chemistry at work. Paper made from wood pulp contains lignin, a substance that helps trees stand upright, and over time lignin and other compounds in the paper slowly ①[break] down. As they do, they release small molecules into the air, including vanillin, the same compound that gives vanilla its flavor. The process is ②[accelerated] by heat, light, and moisture, which is why books stored in a warm attic age faster than those kept in a cool library. Interestingly, scientists working in archives have begun to treat the smell as useful ③[information]. By collecting the air around a book and analyzing which chemicals it contains, they can estimate how badly the paper has ④[deteriorated] without cutting off even a tiny sample. A scent that readers find charming is, for conservators, a sign that the pages are slowly ⑤[strengthening].
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 헌책 냄새는 종이 속 물질이 분해되면서 나는 것이므로 보존 전문가에게는 종이가 서서히 약해지고 있다는 신호예요. 그래서 ⑤ strengthening은 weakening으로 바꿔야 해요. 열·빛·습기가 분해를 빠르게 하므로 따뜻한 다락의 책이 더 빨리 낡는다는 ②는 알맞아요.

items.passage: Imagine two drivers who each run a red light late at night. One reaches home safely; the other hits a cyclist. Most people judge the second driver far more harshly, even though both made exactly the same choice. This tendency to evaluate decisions by their results rather than by the quality of the thinking behind them is understandable, but it can lead us badly astray. Results are shaped not only by our choices but also by luck, which we cannot control. A careful investor may lose money in an unexpected crash, while a careless one may get rich by accident. If we praise the careless investor and blame the careful one, we teach everyone the wrong lessons. Organizations that want better decisions over time should therefore look at what information was available, what options were considered, and how risks were weighed. In other words, a decision should be judged by its ___, not by how it happened to turn out.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 결정은 운에 좌우되는 결과가 아니라 어떤 정보를 보고 어떤 선택지를 고려하며 위험을 어떻게 따졌는지로 평가해야 한다는 글이므로 과정을 뜻하는 process가 알맞아요. outcome은 빈칸 뒤의 how it happened to turn out과 같은 뜻이라 글의 주장과 반대예요.

items.passage: A beginner who translates a poem often assumes that the most faithful version is the most literal one, matching each word with its nearest equivalent in the new language. Yet a poem does not live only in its dictionary meanings. A joke may depend on a double meaning that the other language lacks; a line moves readers partly through its rhythm and sound; an ordinary phrase in one culture may sound strangely formal in another. A word-for-word translation can preserve every meaning listed in the dictionary and still lose the laughter, the music, and the tone that made the original worth reading. Experienced translators therefore ask not only "What does this word mean?" but also "What did this line do to its first readers?" To recreate that effect, they may replace a pun with an entirely different pun or reshape a sentence from beginning to end. In this sense, ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a translation should follow the original word order as closely as possible
readers of translations should learn the original language first
poems are impossible to translate and should be read only in the original
being true to a poem sometimes requires being untrue to its words
the dictionary is the translator's most reliable guide to tone
items.exp: 낱말을 그대로 옮기면 웃음·운율·어조를 잃기 때문에, 숙련된 번역가는 원문이 독자에게 준 효과를 살리려고 말장난을 바꾸거나 문장을 새로 짠다고 했어요. 즉 시에 충실하려면 때로 낱말에는 충실하지 않아야 하므로 ④가 알맞아요. ③은 번역이 불가능하다고 단정해 글의 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Chili peppers contain capsaicin, a chemical that triggers the same pain receptors in the mouth that respond to real heat, yet millions of people eat them happily every day. ① Psychologists have suggested that part of the appeal lies in what they call "benign masochism": the pleasure of experiencing a threatening sensation while knowing that no real harm will follow. ② Chili plants were first grown as crops in the Americas thousands of years ago and later spread to Asia and Europe through trade. ③ Like riding a roller coaster or watching a frightening film, eating a hot pepper lets the body react to danger while the mind remains safely in control. ④ Repeated exposure also plays a role, as regular eaters gradually become less sensitive to the burn and learn to notice the flavors beneath it. ⑤ Over time, the very pain that first made people reach for a glass of water becomes part of what they look forward to.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 글은 고추의 매운맛이 통증인데도 사람들이 즐기는 이유를 '안전한 위협'의 즐거움과 반복 노출로 설명하고 있어요. ②는 고추를 다루긴 하지만 재배의 기원과 전파에 관한 역사라서 즐기는 이유라는 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
When the supply of a widely used material suddenly falls, its price rises, and at first this looks like nothing but bad news for buyers. Companies that depend on it see their costs climb, and many worry that they will have to raise prices or cut production.

(A) As a result, by the time the original material becomes plentiful again, many buyers no longer return to it. The shortage, painful as it was, has left behind a set of new options that might never have been developed otherwise.

(B) Yet the higher price also sends a powerful signal. Factories that once used the material without a second thought begin to look for ways to use less of it, and they start testing cheaper substitutes that had never seemed worth the trouble.

(C) Some of these experiments fail, but others succeed so well that the substitutes become permanent. Engineers improve them, production grows, and their cost steadily falls.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 가격 상승이 나쁜 소식처럼 보인다는 주어진 글 뒤에 Yet으로 반전하는 (B)가 오고, (B)의 대체재 시험을 these experiments로 받는 (C)가 이어져요. 대체재가 자리 잡은 결과 원래 재료로 돌아가지 않는다는 (A)가 As a result로 마무리해요.

items.passage: From Earth, we always see the same face of the Moon, and for a long time many people assumed that the Moon simply does not rotate. ( ① ) In fact, it does spin, but it turns exactly once in the time it takes to orbit Earth, so the same side always faces us. ( ② ) This match is no coincidence. ( ③ ) Earth's gravity pulls more strongly on the near side of the Moon than on the far side, stretching it slightly so that it bulges toward and away from Earth. ( ④ ) When the young Moon spun faster than it does today, these bulges were constantly dragged around its body, and the resulting friction worked like a brake. ( ⑤ ) Once that happened, the bulges stayed pointed toward Earth, and the braking stopped. Astronomers call this state tidal locking, and it is common among moons throughout the solar system.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Over a long period, this braking slowed the Moon's spin until one rotation took exactly as long as one orbit.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 this braking은 마찰이 브레이크처럼 작용했다는 ⑤ 앞 문장을 가리켜요. 또 ⑤ 뒤의 Once that happened는 자전과 공전 시간이 같아진 일을 가리키므로 주어진 문장이 그 사이에 와야 해요.

items.passage: Why does a comedy seem funnier in a packed theater than on a laptop at home? Researchers explored this question by showing the same film clips to viewers either alone or in groups of strangers. Those who watched with others laughed more often and later rated the clips as more enjoyable, even though the films were identical. Part of the reason is that emotions spread: hearing others laugh signals that something is funny and gives us permission to react openly. Watching together also shapes what we notice. When an audience gasps at a sudden scene, each viewer's attention is pulled to the same moment, and that moment becomes more memorable. Interestingly, the effect weakened when viewers could not hear one another, suggesting that it depends on sensing others' reactions rather than simply being in the same room. This may help explain why people continue to buy cinema tickets even when they could stream the same film at home.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Watching a film with an audience whose reactions we can (A) ___ tends to (B) ___ our emotional responses to it.
items.exp: 다른 관객과 함께 보면 더 많이 웃고 더 즐겁게 평가했으며, 서로의 소리를 들을 수 없을 때는 효과가 약해졌다고 했어요. 따라서 반응을 감지할(perceive) 수 있는 관객과 함께 보면 감정 반응이 강해진다(intensify)는 ①이 알맞아요. 효과는 반응을 느낄 때 생기므로 ignore가 들어간 보기는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Public health has an unusual problem: its greatest successes are almost impossible to see. When a doctor saves a patient in an emergency room, the result is dramatic and immediate. There is a person who was dying and is now alive, and family members who can say thank you. Prevention works differently. When clean water systems, vaccination programs, or food safety inspections do their job, the outcome is a disease that never appears. No one celebrates an outbreak that did not happen, because no one knows it was ever on its way.

This invisibility creates a dangerous cycle. When a prevention program works well for many years, people begin to wonder why they are still paying for it. The threat it guards against seems to have (a)[vanished], so funding is reduced and attention moves elsewhere. Then, after the protection has weakened, the old disease returns, and the public is (b)[shocked] by a danger it had forgotten. Experts sometimes call this the paradox of prevention: the better a measure works, the more (c)[unnecessary] it appears.

Breaking this cycle requires changing how success is measured and communicated. Rather than waiting for a crisis to prove their value, health agencies can show what would have happened without them, comparing current figures with the disease rates of earlier decades or of regions lacking similar programs. Such comparisons make the invisible (d)[obscure]. Communities, too, can learn to treat quiet years not as evidence that a program is pointless but as proof that it is working. A calm season, after all, is often the (e)[reward] of years of careful effort that no one noticed.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Emergency Medicine: The Front Line of Public Health
Why Diseases Return After Decades of Silence
Seeing the Unseen: Why Prevention Needs to Prove Its Worth
Clean Water: The Oldest Weapon Against Disease
How Funding Cuts Improve Health Agencies' Efficiency
items.exp: 예방의 성공은 눈에 보이지 않아 지원이 줄어드는 악순환이 생기므로, 예방이 없었다면 어땠을지 보여 주어 가치를 증명해야 한다는 글이에요. 질병이 다시 돌아온다는 보기는 악순환의 한 부분만 다룬 거예요.

items.exp: 과거나 다른 지역의 수치와 비교하면 보이지 않던 예방의 효과가 드러나므로 (d) obscure는 visible로 바꿔야 해요. 위협이 사라진 듯 보이고, 대중이 충격을 받고, 효과가 좋을수록 불필요해 보이며, 평온한 시기는 노력의 보상이라는 나머지 낱말은 알맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Every morning on his way to the bus stop, Leo passed a small bakery on Elm Street. He had moved to the neighborhood only a month before, and he still knew almost no one there. The smell of warm bread drifting from the bakery was the only thing that made the gray street feel friendly. One cold morning, he noticed a handwritten card in the window: "Weekend helper wanted. No experience needed." Leo stood in front of it for a long time. (a)[He] had never had a job, and he was not sure anyone would hire a quiet fifteen-year-old.

(B)
One Saturday in January, Leo arrived to find the bakery dark. His phone rang a moment later. It was Mr. Ortega, calling from home: he had slipped on the ice and hurt his ankle. "Just put a sign on the door saying we're closed," he said. But when Leo looked outside, he saw Mrs. Kim, who bought two loaves every Saturday, already waiting in the snow. (b)[He] took a deep breath, turned on the ovens, and tied on his apron.

(C)
The following Saturday, Leo finally pushed open the bakery door. The owner, a gray-haired man named Mr. Ortega, looked him up and down and simply handed him an apron. That morning, the baker showed Leo how to fold dough into rolls. Leo's first rolls came out lumpy and uneven, and (c)[he] wanted to hide them. Mr. Ortega only laughed. "Mine looked worse at your age," he said. Week after week, Leo's hands grew more confident, and the regular customers began to greet him by name.

(D)
By noon, every shelf was empty. A few rolls had burned, but no one complained. That evening, Leo carried the day's earnings and one leftover roll to Mr. Ortega's apartment. The old baker examined the roll, took a bite, and said, "Still a little lumpy." Then he smiled, and Leo realized (d)[he] had been holding his breath. The next Saturday, there was a new sign above the counter, painted by Mr. Ortega himself while (e)[he] rested his ankle at home: "Ortega & Leo."
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 구인 카드 앞에서 망설이던 (A) 뒤에 다음 토요일 빵집에 들어가 일을 배우는 (C)가 와요. 이어서 Mr. Ortega가 다쳐 Leo가 혼자 오븐을 켜는 (B), 빵이 다 팔리고 새 간판이 걸리는 (D) 순서예요.

items.passage:
Dear Mr. Okafor,

My name is Yerin Cho, and I lead the volunteer club at Crestwood High School. Every Saturday, our members help prepare lunch at the Eastside Community Kitchen, which serves about eighty elderly and low-income neighbors each week. Recently, rising food prices have made it difficult for the kitchen to buy enough fresh vegetables and fruit, and some weeks the meals have had to rely mainly on rice and canned food. Several of our members shop at your store, Green Basket Market, and have noticed that produce close to its sell-by date is thrown away each evening. Much of it is still perfectly good for cooking. We would like to ask whether your store would be willing to donate such produce to the kitchen instead. Our members would collect it from your store every Friday evening, so it would require no extra work from your staff.

Sincerely,
Yerin Cho
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 식료품 가격 인상에 대한 대책을 건의하려고
판매 기한이 임박한 농산물을 급식소에 기부해 달라고 요청하려고
매장의 음식물 쓰레기 처리 방식에 항의하려고
금요일 저녁 매장 아르바이트 자리를 문의하려고
items.exp: 급식소가 신선한 채소와 과일을 사기 어려워졌으니, 매일 저녁 버려지는 판매 기한 임박 농산물을 급식소에 기부해 달라고 부탁하는 편지예요. 버려지는 농산물은 기부를 부탁하는 이유로 나올 뿐 항의하는 글이 아니므로 ④는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: As the lights came up on the stage, Minseo stepped forward to deliver the first line of the play. She opened her mouth, and nothing came out. The words she had practiced a hundred times in front of her bedroom mirror had simply disappeared. Two hundred faces stared at her from the dark hall, and she could feel her cheeks burning. Somewhere in the back, someone coughed. She wished the floor would open and swallow her. Then, from behind the curtain, she heard a soft whisper: "The storm is coming." It was Joon, her classmate, holding the script. The moment she heard those words, the rest of the scene came rushing back. Her voice rang out clearly across the hall, and the audience leaned forward. When the curtain finally fell, the applause went on and on. Minseo let out a long breath and felt her shoulders relax at last.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Minseo의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 대사를 잊고 얼굴이 달아오르며 바닥이 꺼졌으면 할 만큼 당황했지만, 친구의 귓속말로 대사를 되찾고 공연을 마친 뒤 긴 숨을 내쉬며 마음을 놓았어요. 그래서 당황에서 안도로 바뀐 거예요.

items.passage: Every app on a smartphone wants the same thing: a moment of its user's attention. To get it, apps send notifications, small sounds and flashing messages that announce a new like, a sale, or a news update. Each one seems harmless, and many people leave all of them switched on because they do not want to miss anything important. Yet consider what happens over a day. A student sits down to study, and within ten minutes the phone buzzes three times. Each time, the student glances at the screen, and each glance breaks a line of thought that takes several minutes to rebuild. The phone was supposed to be a tool, something we pick up when we need it and put down when we are done. With notifications, the relationship is reversed: the device decides when we look at it, and [we are no longer the ones holding the leash]. Turning most notifications off is a simple way to take back the decision about where our attention goes.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [we are no longer the ones holding the leash]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: we have stopped using smartphones as tools for study
our attention is being directed by devices rather than by ourselves
apps can no longer attract our attention as they once did
we rely on others to tell us which messages are important
students spend less time on their phones than adults do
items.exp: 알림이 울리면 기기가 우리가 언제 볼지를 정하므로, 목줄을 쥔 쪽이 더 이상 우리가 아니라는 것은 우리의 주의가 스스로가 아닌 기기에 의해 끌려다닌다는 뜻이에요. 앱이 더는 주의를 끌지 못한다는 보기는 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: When we hear someone speak with an unfamiliar accent, we often form quick judgments about the speaker. Studies have found that listeners tend to rate the same statement as less believable, and the speaker as less capable, when it is spoken with a foreign or regional accent. Yet an accent tells us almost nothing about a person's knowledge or ability. Every speaker has an accent; what we call "no accent" is simply the one most common in our own community or the one we hear most often on television. Part of the problem is that unfamiliar speech takes more effort to process, and our minds mistake that effort for a weakness in the message itself. A doctor, scientist, or teacher who learned English as an adult may know far more than a native speaker, but listeners who judge by sound alone will never find that out. Recognizing this bias is the first step toward hearing what people actually say rather than how they say it.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 외국어를 배울 때는 원어민의 억양을 익히는 것이 중요하다.
낯선 억양은 메시지 이해를 어렵게 하므로 고쳐야 한다.
지역 방언은 공동체의 정체성을 지키는 역할을 한다.
전문가는 청중이 이해하기 쉬운 말로 설명해야 한다.
억양으로 화자의 능력이나 말의 신뢰성을 판단하는 것은 편견이다.
items.exp: 억양은 사람의 지식이나 능력에 대해 거의 아무것도 알려 주지 않는데도 듣는 사람은 낯선 억양의 말을 덜 믿는다는 편견을 지적하는 글이므로 ⑤가 요지예요. 낯선 말이 처리하기 더 힘들다는 내용은 편견의 원인일 뿐 억양을 고치라는 ②의 주장은 없어요.

items.passage: In some of the driest places on Earth, rain may not fall for years, yet the air is far from empty. Along the coasts of Chile, Peru, and Morocco, cold ocean currents produce thick fog that rolls inland almost every morning. For centuries, this moisture simply drifted past villages that had no reliable water supply. In recent decades, however, communities have begun to catch it. Large vertical nets made of fine plastic mesh are set up on hillsides facing the wind. As the fog passes through, tiny droplets stick to the threads, join together, and run down into gutters that lead to storage tanks. A single large net can collect hundreds of liters of water on a good day, enough for drinking, cooking, and small gardens. The systems need no electricity and are cheap to repair, so local residents can maintain them without outside experts. Fog collection will not turn deserts green, but it offers a practical lifeline where other sources fail.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the causes of long droughts along desert coasts
the effects of ocean currents on global climate
the difficulty of repairing water systems in remote villages
a simple method of gathering drinking water from fog in dry regions
the reasons deserts cannot be turned into farmland
items.exp: 비가 거의 오지 않는 해안 지역에서 그물로 안개 속 물방울을 모아 식수 등으로 쓰는 간단한 방법을 설명하는 글이에요. 해류나 가뭄의 원인은 배경 설명일 뿐 중심 내용이 아니에요.

items.passage: In most team sports, players expect referees to catch their fouls, and many treat getting away with a foul as part of the game. Ultimate, a fast-moving team sport played with a flying disc, takes a very different approach. Even in many serious competitions, games are played without referees. Instead, players call their own fouls. If a player believes she was pushed, she calls the foul herself, and the two players involved discuss what happened. If they cannot agree, the play is simply repeated. This system rests on a principle known as the "Spirit of the Game," which places respect for opponents and fair play above winning. At the end of many tournaments, teams even rate one another on sportsmanship, and an award goes to the fairest team, not just the strongest. Remarkably, the system works: deliberate cheating is rare, because a player who abuses it quickly loses the respect of the entire community.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Fair Play Without Referees: Ultimate's Honor System
Why Every Sport Needs More Referees
The Fastest Disc Sport in the World
Winning at All Costs: The Real Spirit of Ultimate
How Video Replay Changed Team Sports
items.exp: 얼티밋은 심판 없이 선수들이 스스로 반칙을 판정하고, 승리보다 공정함을 앞세우는 원칙 덕분에 이 방식이 잘 운영된다는 내용이라 ①이 제목으로 알맞아요. Spirit of the Game은 승리보다 존중과 공정함을 중시한다고 했으므로 ④는 반대예요.

items.passage: Shipwrecks are often described as time capsules, and for good reason. When a trading ship sank in ancient times, everything on board went down with it at the same moment: cargo, tools, coins, and even the crew's last meals. On land, by contrast, objects from different centuries usually ①[become] mixed together as cities are rebuilt layer upon layer. A wreck lying in cold, deep water can remain almost untouched for thousands of years, since there is little oxygen to support the creatures ②[that] destroy wood. Archaeologists studying such sites can therefore learn not only what goods were traded but also how sailors ③[lived] day to day. However, exploring a wreck is slow and costly work. Divers can stay at great depths for only short periods, and each object must be recorded carefully before it ④[is lifted] to the surface. Once removed from the salty water, wood and metal begin ⑤[decays] quickly unless they are treated immediately.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 begin 뒤에 오는 목적어 자리이므로 decays가 아니라 to decay 또는 decaying으로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 복수 주어 objects의 동사, ②는 the creatures를 꾸미는 주격 관계대명사, ③은 과거 시제 동사, ④는 시간 부사절의 수동태 현재형으로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Many students give up sleep before an exam, believing that every extra hour of study will improve their scores. Research on memory suggests that this strategy often ①[backfires]. During deep sleep, the brain replays the information gathered during the day and transfers it from short-term storage into more ②[temporary] networks, where it can be retrieved later. In experiments, people who learned a list of words and then slept recalled far more of them the next day than people who stayed awake for the same period. Sleep also ③[clears] away waste products that build up in the brain during waking hours, which helps explain why tired students feel slow and foggy. A lack of sleep, then, does not simply make learners feel worse; it ④[weakens] the very process that turns studying into lasting knowledge. A student who studies for six hours and sleeps well may ⑤[outperform] one who studies for nine hours and barely sleeps at all.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 잠자는 동안 정보가 단기 저장소에서 나중에 꺼내 쓸 수 있는 곳으로 옮겨진다고 했으므로 ② temporary는 permanent나 stable로 바꿔야 해요. 잠을 줄이는 전략이 역효과를 내고, 수면이 노폐물을 치우며, 수면 부족이 기억 과정을 약화시켜 잘 잔 학생이 더 잘할 수 있다는 나머지는 알맞아요.

items.passage: In many schools and universities, average grades have risen steadily over the past few decades, while there is little evidence that students have learned more. This trend, known as grade inflation, may seem harmless or even kind; after all, who is hurt when more students receive an A? The problem becomes clear when we consider what a grade is for. A grade is a signal, a short message to students, parents, and future employers about how well someone has mastered a subject. When nearly everyone receives the highest mark, the signal can no longer separate excellent work from merely adequate work. A student who truly excelled ends up with the same transcript as one who did the minimum. In this sense, grade inflation is much like printing too much money: the more freely grades are handed out, the less each one is worth. Grades that everyone receives ultimately lose their ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 성적은 학생이 얼마나 잘 익혔는지 알려 주는 신호인데, 모두가 최고 점수를 받으면 뛰어난 학생과 겨우 한 학생을 구별하지 못한다고 했어요. 따라서 모두가 받는 성적은 의미를 잃는다는 ④ meaning이 알맞아요. 성적이 후해질수록 인기가 떨어진다는 내용은 없으므로 ②는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Until the late nineteenth century, voters in many democracies cast their ballots in public, often by calling out their choice or by dropping a colored ticket printed by a party into the box while others watched. Under this system, buying votes was common and effective: a candidate could pay a voter and then simply watch to see whether he delivered. The secret ballot, first adopted in parts of Australia in the 1850s, changed this in a surprising way. It did not make voters more honest, nor did it make bribery illegal; bribery had been illegal already. What it did was to make a voter's promise ___. A voter could still accept money and say he would support the buyer's candidate, but no one could ever confirm what he had done behind the curtain. Since a bribe that buys nothing is a waste of money, vote buying declined sharply. The secrecy that protects the voter also protects the election, not by improving human nature but by removing the means of enforcing a corrupt deal.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: legally binding even when it was made in private
more expensive for candidates to purchase
impossible for anyone to check or enforce
publicly known to every member of the community
less important than the voter's own conscience
items.exp: 비밀 투표에서는 돈을 받은 유권자가 실제로 누구를 찍었는지 아무도 확인할 수 없어 뇌물이 아무것도 사지 못하게 되었다고 했어요. 따라서 유권자의 약속을 확인하거나 강제할 수 없게 만들었다는 ③이 알맞아요. 비밀 투표가 유권자를 더 정직하게 만든 것은 아니라고 했으므로 양심을 내세운 ⑤는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Crows are among the few animals that can make and adjust tools to solve new problems. ① On a Pacific island, one species shapes twigs and leaves into hooks that it uses to pull insects out of narrow holes in dead wood. ② In laboratory tests, crows have bent straight pieces of wire into hooks to lift a small basket of food from the bottom of a tube, a task they had never faced before. ③ Some birds even combine two short sticks into a longer one when neither piece alone is long enough to reach a reward. ④ Crows are also known for gathering in huge flocks in winter, sometimes numbering in the tens of thousands, to sleep together in the same trees each night. ⑤ Such behavior suggests that these birds can plan ahead and picture the result of an action before they perform it, an ability once thought to belong mainly to humans and great apes.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 글은 까마귀가 새로운 문제를 풀기 위해 도구를 만들고 고친다는 내용이에요. ④는 까마귀를 다루지만 겨울에 큰 무리를 지어 잠을 잔다는 이야기라 도구 사용이라는 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
The ancient Romans built more than 80,000 kilometers of paved roads across their empire, many of which remained in use for over a thousand years. Their durability was no accident; it came from a careful method of construction that was repeated wherever the empire expanded.

(A) On top of these layers came the surface itself: flat, closely fitted stone blocks. The center of the road was made slightly higher than its edges, so that rainwater would run off to either side instead of soaking into the layers below.

(B) This attention to drainage was especially important. Water is the greatest enemy of any road, and by keeping it away from the foundation, Roman engineers ensured that their roads would not crack or sink even after centuries of use.

(C) First, workers dug a deep trench along the planned route and filled the bottom with large stones. Over this base, they laid layers of smaller stones and gravel mixed with lime, pressing each layer down firmly.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 건설 방법을 소개한 주어진 글 뒤에 First로 기초 공사를 설명하는 (C)가 오고, these layers 위에 표면을 깐 (A)가 이어져요. (A)의 빗물 배수를 This attention to drainage로 받는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: In many legal systems, a contract signed by a minor is treated differently from one signed by an adult. ( ① ) If a sixteen-year-old agrees to buy an expensive motorcycle on credit, for example, he can usually cancel the agreement later, even though the seller could not. ( ② ) The law takes this position because young people are thought to lack the experience needed to judge the risks of a serious agreement, and adults might otherwise take advantage of them. ( ③ ) For this reason, many sellers refuse to sign major contracts with minors at all, or they insist that a parent sign as well. ( ④ ) However, the protection has limits. Contracts for necessities such as food, clothing, and housing are generally enforceable, so that minors can still obtain the things they need to live. ( ⑤ ) In this way, the law tries to balance two goals: protecting the young from bad deals while not shutting them out of everyday life entirely.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Such protection, though, puts businesses in a difficult position, since only one side of the deal is free to walk away.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 Such protection은 ③ 앞에서 설명한, 미성년자를 경험 많은 어른에게서 보호하는 법의 입장을 받아요. 또 ③ 뒤의 For this reason은 한쪽만 계약을 깰 수 있어 사업자가 곤란해진다는 주어진 문장을 이유로 받아 판매자들이 계약을 거절한다는 내용으로 이어져요.

items.passage: Many organizations reward employees for success and quietly punish them for failure. On the surface, this seems sensible. In practice, it often teaches people to hide their mistakes, so the same errors are repeated in other teams that never hear about them. Some companies have tried a different approach. They hold regular meetings in which employees describe a project that went wrong, what they had expected, and what actually happened. Managers are expected to speak first, describing their own failures, so that others feel safe to follow. The goal is not to celebrate mistakes but to make sure that the lesson from each one is learned only once. Companies that have adopted such practices report that problems are reported earlier, when they are still small and cheap to fix, and that employees become more willing to try new ideas. When people are not afraid to admit what went wrong, the whole organization grows wiser.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

When organizations encourage employees to (A) ___ their failures openly, mistakes are less likely to be repeated and people become more (B) ___ in their work.
items.exp: 직원들이 실패한 프로젝트를 회의에서 털어놓게 하자 같은 실수가 반복되지 않았으므로 (A)는 share예요. 직원들이 새로운 아이디어를 더 기꺼이 시도하게 되었다고 했으므로 (B)는 innovative가 알맞아요.

items.passage:
When parents fill a child's week with lessons, sports practice, and tutoring, they usually do so with the best of intentions. Each activity seems to promise a useful skill. Yet researchers who study child development have found that something important can be lost when every hour is planned by adults: the chance for children to organize their own time.

In unstructured play, no one tells children what to do next. They must decide which game to play, invent the rules, and settle arguments when someone feels the rules are unfair. A group building a fort in the backyard has to agree on a design, divide the jobs, and (a)[adjust] the plan when the walls keep falling down. These situations exercise what psychologists call executive function, the set of mental skills that allows a person to set goals, control impulses, and (b)[shift] strategies when something is not working. Studies have found that children who spend more time in self-directed activities tend to show (c)[stronger] executive function, even when family income and other factors are taken into account.

Structured activities have real value, of course. A piano lesson teaches discipline and a soccer team teaches cooperation. The problem arises when such activities leave (d)[abundant] room for anything else. In a fully scheduled life, the coach or teacher makes the decisions, and children learn to follow rather than to plan. As they grow older and adults step back, many find it (e)[difficult] to manage their own time. Protecting a few free afternoons each week may be one of the simplest gifts parents can give.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Free Time: Where Children Learn to Manage Themselves
How Music Lessons Build Discipline in Young Children
Family Income as the Key to Children's Success
Team Sports and the Value of Following Rules
Why Children Need More Tutoring After School
items.exp: 어른이 짜 주지 않은 자유 놀이 속에서 아이들이 목표를 세우고 충동을 조절하는 실행 기능을 기른다는 글이므로 자유 시간이 스스로를 관리하는 법을 배우는 곳이라는 제목이 알맞아요. 음악 수업이나 팀 스포츠는 구조화된 활동의 예로만 나와요.

items.passage:
(A)
The call reached the Pine Ridge Rescue Station just after four in the afternoon. A hiker named Owen Hale had phoned his sister from somewhere on Mount Calder, saying he had lost the trail in thick fog. Then the line had gone dead. Team leader Nora Banks looked at the darkening sky through the window. Within ten minutes, (a)[she] and two volunteers, Eli and Rosa, were loading ropes, a stretcher, and warm blankets into the truck.

(B)
Three weeks later, a man with a cane walked slowly into the rescue station. It was Owen, his ankle still in a brace. He placed a large box of cookies on the table and shook each volunteer's hand. When he reached Nora, he struggled to find the right words. "I thought no one would find me," he said at last. Nora smiled and pointed to the wall, where a map of Mount Calder hung. "Next time," (b)[she] said, "take this with you."

(C)
When they reached him, Owen was shaking with cold. He had twisted his ankle on a loose rock and could not stand. Rosa wrapped him in blankets while Eli prepared the stretcher. The trip down was slow and difficult. Twice the team had to stop and lower Owen with ropes over steep, wet stones. It was nearly midnight when they finally saw the lights of the station below. Only then did Nora, who had led every step of the way down the mountain, let (c)[herself] relax and breathe more easily.

(D)
The fog was even thicker on the mountain. The team moved slowly, calling Owen's name every few minutes and listening carefully for any reply. Nora knew the mountain well, and (d)[she] guessed that a lost hiker would likely follow the stream downhill. After an hour, Rosa spotted a red glove lying on a rock beside the water. Nora shouted again, and this time a weak voice answered from somewhere above them. Rosa, the youngest on the team, was so excited that (e)[she] almost slipped on the wet rocks as she rushed ahead.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 구조대가 출동하는 (A) 뒤에 안개 속에서 Owen을 찾는 (D)가 오고, When they reached him으로 그를 구조해 내려오는 (C)가 이어져요. 세 주 뒤 Owen이 구조대를 찾아오는 (B)가 마지막이에요.
