items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 가리키는 대상이 나머지 넷과 다른 것은?
items.exp: (e)는 들뜬 나머지 젖은 바위에서 미끄러질 뻔한 막내 대원 Rosa를 가리켜요. 나머지 (a), (b), (c), (d)는 모두 팀장 Nora예요.

items.passage:
(A)
The call reached the Pine Ridge Rescue Station just after four in the afternoon. A hiker named Owen Hale had phoned his sister from somewhere on Mount Calder, saying he had lost the trail in thick fog. Then the line had gone dead. Team leader Nora Banks looked at the darkening sky through the window. Within ten minutes, (a)[she] and two volunteers, Eli and Rosa, were loading ropes, a stretcher, and warm blankets into the truck.

(B)
Three weeks later, a man with a cane walked slowly into the rescue station. It was Owen, his ankle still in a brace. He placed a large box of cookies on the table and shook each volunteer's hand. When he reached Nora, he struggled to find the right words. "I thought no one would find me," he said at last. Nora smiled and pointed to the wall, where a map of Mount Calder hung. "Next time," (b)[she] said, "take this with you."

(C)
When they reached him, Owen was shaking with cold. He had twisted his ankle on a loose rock and could not stand. Rosa wrapped him in blankets while Eli prepared the stretcher. The trip down was slow and difficult. Twice the team had to stop and lower Owen with ropes over steep, wet stones. It was nearly midnight when they finally saw the lights of the station below. Only then did Nora, who had led every step of the way down the mountain, let (c)[herself] relax and breathe more easily.

(D)
The fog was even thicker on the mountain. The team moved slowly, calling Owen's name every few minutes and listening carefully for any reply. Nora knew the mountain well, and (d)[she] guessed that a lost hiker would likely follow the stream downhill. After an hour, Rosa spotted a red glove lying on a rock beside the water. Nora shouted again, and this time a weak voice answered from somewhere above them. Rosa, the youngest on the team, was so excited that (e)[she] almost slipped on the wet rocks as she rushed ahead.
items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Owen은 짙은 안개 속에서 길을 잃었다고 전화로 알렸다.
Owen은 구조대에 쿠키를 들고 오지 않았다.
구조대는 자정 무렵에 구조대 건물의 불빛을 보았다.
Rosa가 물가의 바위 위에서 빨간 장갑을 발견했다.
items.exp: 세 주 뒤 Owen은 쿠키 한 상자를 탁자 위에 놓고 대원들과 악수했으므로 쿠키를 들고 오지 않았다는 진술은 틀려요. 안개 속 전화, 발목 부상, 자정 무렵의 불빛, 빨간 장갑 발견은 모두 글과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Director Morales,

I am writing on behalf of the residents of Elmwood Terrace, a senior housing complex on Harlow Avenue. Many of our residents depend on the Route 12 bus to reach the clinic, the pharmacy, and the grocery store. The bus itself is reliable, and we are grateful for the frequent service. However, the stop in front of our building offers nothing but a pole and a sign. During the summer, people wait in direct sunlight, and in winter they stand exposed to wind and freezing rain. Several residents who use walkers have told me that they skip appointments rather than wait outside in bad weather. A simple covered shelter with a bench would make an enormous difference to their health and independence. Our residents' association would be happy to help keep the area clean. We kindly ask that your department consider installing a shelter at this stop as soon as possible.

Sincerely,
Gloria Pham
Elmwood Terrace Residents' Association
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 버스 정류장에 대기 시설 설치를 요청하려고
items.exp: 정류장에 기둥과 표지판뿐이라 노인들이 더위와 추위에 노출된다며, 벤치가 있는 지붕 덮인 쉼터 설치를 요청하고 있어요. 버스 서비스 자체는 믿을 만하고 자주 온다고 했으므로 배차 간격 단축 건의는 아니에요.

items.passage: Noah sighed as he dragged another dusty box across the attic floor. His family had moved into the old house a week earlier, and his parents had given him the dullest job of all: sorting through the things the previous owners had left behind. Most of it was broken furniture and stacks of yellowed newspapers. He yawned and was about to carry the box downstairs when something slipped out from between two newspapers: an envelope, still sealed, with the words "To whoever lives here next" written across it. Noah sat down on the floor and opened it carefully. The letter was dated May 1952. A girl named Ellen described the apple tree she had planted in the yard, the creaking third step on the staircase, and her hope that the next family would be happy there. Noah rushed to the window. The apple tree was still standing, taller than the roof. He read the letter again, his heart racing, and decided to write a reply of his own.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Noah의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 처음에 Noah는 가장 지루한 일을 맡아 한숨을 쉬고 하품을 해요. 그러다 1952년에 쓰인 편지를 발견하고, 편지 속 사과나무가 아직 서 있는 것을 보며 가슴이 뛰고 답장까지 쓰기로 하므로 지루함에서 매혹으로 바뀌었어요.

items.passage: When a neighborhood is redeveloped, its old street names are often among the first things to disappear. Developers prefer names that sound fresh and attractive, such as Sunrise Avenue or Green Park Road, and city officials rarely object, since a name seems like a small matter compared with new housing and wider roads. Yet a place name is one of the few records of the past that people use every single day. A lane called Tannery Street reminds residents that leather was once made there; a road named Ferry Lane marks a river crossing that existed long before the bridge. When such names are replaced, this quiet history vanishes without anyone ever deciding that it should. Cities should therefore treat historic place names as part of their heritage. Before approving a new name, officials should ask what the old one records and, wherever possible, keep it, so that even a completely rebuilt district can still tell people where it came from.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 재개발을 하더라도 역사적 지명을 유산으로 보고 가능한 한 유지해야 한다.
새로 개발된 지역에는 밝고 매력적인 이름을 붙여야 한다.
도로 이름은 주민 투표를 거쳐 결정해야 한다.
도시를 재개발할 때 옛 건물을 최대한 보존해야 한다.
거리마다 지역의 역사를 알리는 안내판을 세워야 한다.
items.exp: 옛 지명은 사람들이 날마다 쓰는 과거의 기록이므로, 도시는 역사적 지명을 유산으로 여기고 가능하면 지켜야 한다고 주장해요. 글은 건물이 아니라 이름을 지키자는 것이므로 옛 건물 보존은 알맞지 않아요.

items.passage: When your phone suggests the next word as you type, it seems like a small kindness. You write "Happy," and the screen offers "birthday"; you begin "Sorry I," and it proposes "missed your call." Accepting the suggestion saves a second or two, and most of us accept it without a thought. Yet these suggestions are not neutral. They are drawn from what millions of other users have typed most often, so they quietly steer each writer toward the most common way of saying things. Studies of people writing with such tools have found that their messages become shorter and more predictable, often containing words they would not have chosen on their own. Over time, the tool can turn each of us into [a speaker borrowing the voice of a crowd]. The convenience is real, but so is the cost: the odd phrase, the private joke, and the word only you would use are exactly the ones a prediction system is least likely to offer.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a speaker borrowing the voice of a crowd]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a writer who quotes famous people to sound more persuasive
a user who depends on others to correct spelling mistakes
a person whose messages echo the most common phrasing of many users
a speaker who reads messages aloud to a large audience
a reader who follows popular opinions found on the internet
items.exp: 자동 완성 제안은 수많은 사용자가 가장 자주 입력한 말에서 나오므로 각자를 가장 흔한 표현 쪽으로 이끈다고 했어요. 따라서 밑줄은 자기만의 말 대신 많은 사람의 흔한 표현을 그대로 따라 쓰는 사람을 뜻해요. 남의 의견을 따르는 것이나 유명인 인용은 지문과 관계없어요.

items.passage: To human eyes, the males and females of many bird species look almost exactly alike. For a long time, researchers assumed that such birds must rely on song or behavior, rather than appearance, to recognize suitable partners. That assumption changed once scientists began measuring feathers with instruments sensitive to ultraviolet light. Unlike humans, many birds have a fourth type of color receptor in their eyes that responds to ultraviolet wavelengths. When feathers were examined under this light, patterns invisible to us suddenly appeared: crowns that glowed brightly in males, wing patches that differed between individuals, and markings that seemed to change with a bird's health. In several species, females were found to prefer males whose feathers reflected more ultraviolet light, possibly because bright feathers are hard to maintain for a bird in poor condition. What looked like plain plumage, in other words, was a rich visual signal that we had simply been unable to see.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: difficulty of telling male and female birds apart by song
ways in which birds change feather color with the seasons
reasons why humans cannot detect certain wavelengths of light
influence of a bird's health on the quality of its songs
hidden ultraviolet signals in bird feathers that shape mate choice
items.exp: 사람 눈에는 똑같아 보이는 새의 깃털에 자외선으로만 보이는 무늬가 있고, 암컷이 자외선을 더 많이 반사하는 수컷을 고른다는 내용이에요. 따라서 짝 선택에 작용하는 깃털 속 숨은 자외선 신호가 주제예요. 사람이 자외선을 못 보는 이유는 글의 일부 배경일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: On Earth, the daytime sky is blue and sunsets glow orange and red. On Mars, the colors are almost exactly reversed. Photographs sent back by robotic rovers show a dusty, yellowish-brown sky during the day, while the area around the setting Sun turns a cool, pale blue. The difference comes from what fills each planet's air. Earth's sky is colored mainly by gas molecules, which are far smaller than the wavelength of light and scatter blue light in every direction. Martian air, by contrast, is very thin but full of fine dust. These dust particles spread reddish light widely across the sky, giving the day its warm color. Blue light, however, tends to be scattered only slightly forward, so it stays close to the direction of the Sun. At sunset, when sunlight passes through the longest stretch of dusty air, this blue glow around the Sun becomes easy to see. The same sunlight, passing through different kinds of air, paints two very different skies.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Mars Has Almost No Clouds
Blue Sunsets, Dusty Days: How Mars Colors Its Sky
How Rovers Take Pictures on Distant Planets
The Hidden Dangers of Martian Dust Storms
Why Earth's Sunsets Are Growing Redder
items.exp: 화성은 공기 속 미세한 먼지 때문에 낮 하늘은 누런 갈색이고 해 질 녘 태양 주위는 푸르게 보인다는 원리를 설명하므로 ②가 알맞아요. 탐사 로봇의 사진은 근거로 나올 뿐이고, 먼지 폭풍의 위험은 다루지 않아요.

items.passage: Greta Lindqvist (1902–1988) was a Swedish graphic designer best known for the lettering on her country's road signs. Born in the port city of Gävle, she spent much of her childhood copying letters from old books in her grandfather's print shop. After studying art in Stockholm, she designed posters for theaters and concert halls for twelve years. In 1951, the national road authority asked her to create a lettering style that drivers could read quickly at high speed. She tested her designs by placing sample signs along a country road and asking volunteers to read them from passing cars, first in daylight and later at night. The final lettering, introduced in 1955, used wide, open letters with simple shapes. It remained on Swedish roads for more than forty years. In her later years, she taught typography at a design school in Gothenburg and wrote a short book about lettering for public spaces.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 할아버지의 인쇄소에서 옛 책의 글자를 따라 쓰며 자랐다.
스톡홀름에서 미술을 공부한 뒤 극장과 공연장의 포스터를 디자인했다.
1951년에 국가 도로 당국으로부터 글자체 제작을 의뢰받았다.
견본 표지판을 낮 시간에만 시험해 보았다.
말년에 디자인 학교에서 글자 디자인을 가르쳤다.
items.exp: 견본 표지판을 처음에는 낮에, 나중에는 밤에도 시험했다(first in daylight and later at night)고 했으므로 낮 시간에만 시험했다는 설명은 틀려요. 나머지는 모두 글의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage: After a long bath, the tips of your fingers become covered in wrinkles. Most people assume that the skin simply ①[soaks] up water and swells, like a sponge. However, doctors noticed long ago that fingers whose nerves had been damaged ②[did] not wrinkle at all, no matter how long they stayed in water. This observation suggested that the wrinkles are not a passive effect but a reaction ③[controlling] by the nervous system: blood vessels beneath the skin narrow, and the surface folds inward. Why would the body bother to do this? One idea is that wrinkled fingers work like the tread on a tire, channeling water away so that we can hold wet objects more securely. In one experiment, volunteers with wrinkled fingers moved wet marbles from one container to another faster than those ④[whose] fingers were smooth. The advantage disappeared with dry objects, which suggests that the wrinkles may have developed for one purpose: ⑤[to help] us grip things in wet conditions.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③은 a reaction이 신경계에 의해 '조절되는' 것이므로 수동의 과거분사 controlled로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 주어 the skin에 맞춘 동사, ②는 과거 사실을 나타내는 조동사, ④는 those를 꾸미는 소유격 관계대명사, ⑤는 목적을 나타내는 to부정사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: For centuries, popular stories claimed that the great pyramids of Egypt were built by huge crowds of slaves driven by whips. Archaeological discoveries near Giza have ①[confirmed] this picture. In recent decades, researchers uncovered the remains of a town where the builders had lived, complete with bakeries, breweries, and storage rooms for grain. Animal bones found there showed that the workers ate large amounts of beef and other meat, a diet suggesting that they were ②[valued] rather than merely used. Nearby, the workers' own tombs were found. Burying laborers so ③[close] to the king's monument would have been unthinkable if they had been regarded as worthless. Their skeletons also revealed broken bones that had healed properly, evidence that injured workers ④[received] medical care. Most scholars now believe that the pyramids were built by organized teams of paid laborers, many of whom worked in rotating shifts. The new picture is less dramatic than the old legend, but it is far more ⑤[accurate].
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 뒤에 이어지는 발굴 결과(좋은 식사, 왕의 무덤 가까이 묻힌 무덤, 치료받은 뼈)는 노예가 피라미드를 지었다는 옛 이야기를 뒤집는 증거이므로 ①의 confirmed는 challenged(이의를 제기하다)나 overturned로 바꿔야 해요. ⑤ accurate는 새로운 모습이 덜 극적이지만 더 정확하다는 뜻으로 알맞아요.

items.passage: We tend to think of a surname as something deeply personal, a link to our ancestors and a symbol of family pride. Yet in many societies, surnames did not arise from families' own wishes. For centuries, most people in small villages needed only a single name, since everyone could tell from the situation which John was meant. Fixed family names became common when rulers began to count their populations, collect taxes, and call men up for military service. A tax collector facing hundreds of men named John could not do his work unless each one carried a second, permanent name that passed from parent to child. In some countries, laws even ordered citizens to adopt surnames, and officials assigned names to those who had none. The names themselves often came from a job, a place, or a father's first name, but the reason they became fixed was ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 고정된 성은 통치자가 인구를 세고 세금을 걷고 병사를 모으면서 흔해졌고, 법으로 성을 갖게 하거나 관리가 이름을 붙여 주기도 했다고 했어요. 따라서 성이 고정된 이유는 행정상의 필요예요. personal pride와 family loyalty는 글이 처음에 부정한 통념이에요.

items.passage: We often imagine that an invention arrives in the world with its purpose already attached, as if the inventor had written instructions that society simply follows. History suggests otherwise. When the telephone first appeared, its promoters were unsure what it was for. Some companies used it to send concerts and news reports to subscribers who listened at home, much as people would later use the radio. Others marketed it strictly as a business instrument and discouraged what they considered wasteful social calls. It was ordinary users, especially families in isolated rural homes who used the line to chat with distant neighbors, who turned it into a tool for personal conversation, and the companies eventually followed them, advertising the very use they had once dismissed. The telephone is hardly unusual in this respect. The inventor determines what a device can do, but ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: users rarely discover functions that the inventor did not plan
companies predict future needs better than ordinary users do
the most successful devices are those with a single clear purpose
what it finally becomes is decided by the people who take it into their lives
technical limits usually prevent a device from being used in new ways
items.exp: 전화는 처음에 방송이나 업무용으로 홍보되었지만, 시골 가정의 평범한 사용자들이 이웃과 대화하는 도구로 바꾸었고 회사들이 오히려 그 쓰임을 따라갔다고 했어요. 따라서 발명품이 결국 무엇이 되는지는 그것을 삶에 들이는 사람들이 정한다는 말이 알맞아요. ①과 ②는 글의 사례와 반대예요.

items.passage: Many experienced cooks insist that a roast or steak should rest for several minutes after it comes off the heat, and there is good science behind this habit. ① While meat cooks, its outer layers heat up much faster than the center, and the muscle fibers near the surface tighten and squeeze their juices toward the middle. ② If the meat is sliced at once, much of that liquid, still loosely held, simply runs out onto the cutting board. ③ During a short rest, the temperature evens out, the fibers relax slightly, and the juices thicken and spread back through the meat. ④ Grilling over charcoal, which became popular in many backyards during the twentieth century, gives meat a smoky flavor that gas grills cannot easily copy. ⑤ The result is a piece that stays moist when cut, which is why even a few minutes of patience can matter as much as the cooking itself. Cooks who skip this step often blame the recipe, when the real problem was timing.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 고기를 익힌 뒤 잠시 두면 육즙이 고르게 퍼져 촉촉해지는 과학적 이유를 설명하는 글인데, ④는 숯불구이의 유행과 훈연 향에 관한 내용이라 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤의 The result는 ③의 휴지 과정의 결과를 이어 받아요.

items.passage:
If you walk across a long steel bridge, you may notice metal plates with interlocking teeth crossing the road at regular intervals. These plates are neither decorations nor signs of repair work.

(A) They are expansion joints, gaps that allow the bridge to grow and shrink with the weather. Like most building materials, steel and concrete expand when they warm up and contract when they cool down.

(B) Without a way to absorb that much movement, the structure would push against its own supports until something cracked. The interlocking teeth solve the problem by letting the gap open and close while still giving cars a smooth surface to drive over.

(C) For a single meter of steel, this change is tiny, only a fraction of a millimeter for every ten degrees. Over a bridge hundreds of meters long, however, the total movement between a cold winter night and a hot summer afternoon can reach many centimeters.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: They가 주어진 글의 금속판을 가리키므로 (A)가 먼저 오고, (A)의 팽창·수축을 this change로 받는 (C)가 이어져요. 마지막으로 (C)의 수 센티미터 움직임을 that much movement로 받는 (B)가 와요.

items.passage: For most of the twentieth century, ski jumpers flew with their skis held tightly together and parallel, a position judges regarded as the mark of good technique. ( ① ) In the late 1980s, however, a few jumpers began spreading the front tips of their skis apart into the shape of a V. ( ② ) Yet the jumpers who used it often landed farther than anyone else. ( ③ ) Wind-tunnel tests later explained why: the V shape turned the skis and the jumper's body into a kind of wing, producing more lift and allowing the athlete to stay in the air longer. ( ④ ) Faced with such results, the judges could not hold out for long. ( ⑤ ) Within a few years, the old parallel style had all but disappeared from competition, and today nearly every top jumper flies in a V. The story offers a lesson that reaches beyond sport: a rule about what looks correct can sometimes stand in the way of what actually works.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

At first, judges considered the new style clumsy and took points away from those who used it.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 the new style은 바로 앞에서 소개된 V자 자세를 가리키고, 심판이 감점했다는 내용 뒤에 Yet으로 '그래도 더 멀리 날았다'는 대조가 이어져야 하므로 ②가 알맞아요. ①은 아직 새 자세가 나오기 전이고, ③ 이후는 이미 Yet의 대조가 끝난 뒤라 흐름이 어색해요.

items.passage: In one study, researchers gave two groups of high school students exactly the same set of geometry problems. One group was told that the task was a test that would measure their math ability. The other group was told that it was a puzzle game designed for fun. The students who believed they were playing a game solved noticeably more problems correctly, and the difference was largest among students who usually earned low grades in math. When asked afterward, the "test" group reported feeling more worried about making mistakes, and many said they had given up quickly on difficult items. The "game" group, by contrast, described the problems as challenging but enjoyable and kept trying different approaches. The researchers concluded that the label attached to a task can change how students feel about it, which in turn affects how well they perform.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Presenting a task as (A) ___ rather than as an evaluation can (B) ___ students' performance, especially for those who struggle with the subject.
items.exp: 같은 문제를 재미로 하는 퍼즐 게임, 즉 놀이(play)라고 소개받은 학생들이 더 많이 맞혔고, 평소 수학 성적이 낮은 학생에게서 차이가 가장 컸어요. 따라서 과제를 놀이로 제시하면 성적을 높일(improve) 수 있다는 ①이 알맞아요.

items.passage:
Many people enter a negotiation as if they were about to divide a pie of fixed size: every slice one side gains is a slice the other side loses. This view turns the process into a contest of strength, encouraging negotiators to hide information, make extreme demands, and give ground as (a)[slowly] as possible. Experienced negotiators, however, know that most real deals involve several issues at once, and that the two sides rarely value each issue (b)[differently].

Consider a small company hiring a designer. The company has a tight budget this year but expects strong growth; the designer wants a good salary but cares even more about working from home two days a week. If the two sides argue only about salary, every dollar becomes a battle. But if they put all the issues on the table, a different deal appears: a modest starting salary, a guaranteed raise next year, and a flexible schedule. Each side gives up something it values (c)[less] in exchange for something it values more, and both leave better off than a simple compromise would have left them.

Such trades are possible only when the parties understand each other's priorities. That is why skilled negotiators spend much of their time asking questions rather than making offers. "What matters most to you here?" and "What would make this hard for you to accept?" may seem like (d)[weak] moves, but the answers often reveal room for agreement that neither side could see at the start. Sharing one's own priorities carries some risk, of course, but keeping everything secret almost (e)[guarantees] that the pie stays exactly the size it seemed to be at the beginning.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Salary Should Always Come First in Hiring
Extreme Demands: The Fastest Route to a Deal
The Risks of Revealing What You Want
Growing the Pie by Trading on Different Priorities
items.exp: 협상을 고정된 파이 나누기로 보지 말고, 양측이 서로 다르게 중시하는 쟁점을 맞바꾸어 모두에게 더 나은 거래를 만들 수 있다는 내용이에요. 우선순위 공개의 위험은 마지막에 잠깐 언급될 뿐이고, 단순한 절충보다 낫다고 했으므로 ③도 답이 아니에요.

items.exp: 뒤의 예처럼 회사는 예산을, 디자이너는 재택근무를 더 중시하므로 양측이 각 쟁점을 똑같이 중시하는 경우가 드물다는 흐름이에요. 따라서 (b) differently는 equally로 바꿔야 해요. (d)는 질문이 약해 보이지만 실제로는 합의 여지를 드러낸다는 뜻으로 알맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Ethan had played the cello in the Westbrook High School orchestra for two years, always hidden safely in the back row. So when Mr. Lowell, the conductor, announced that Ethan would play the short solo in the final piece of the spring concert, the room went silent. Ethan felt his face burn. At the next rehearsal, when the moment came, (a)[he] played the first few notes so softly that the violinists turned around to see whether he had started at all.

(B)
When the last chord faded, the audience rose to its feet. Ethan sat frozen for a moment, unable to believe it was over. Backstage, Mr. Lowell shook his hand warmly and said nothing at all about the mistake. Later that evening, a ninth-grade cellist shyly asked Ethan how (b)[he] had managed not to panic. Ethan smiled and told her about the empty music room. "Next year," he said, "I'll practice with you there, if you like."

(C)
On the night of the concert, the hall was full. As the final piece began, Ethan pictured the empty room and tried to breathe slowly. The solo started well, but halfway through, (c)[his] bow slipped and a harsh note rang out. For one terrible second, he wanted to stop. Then he remembered what Mr. Lowell had told him, kept his eyes on the music, and played on. By the end of the solo, his sound had grown full and warm, and the orchestra joined him as if nothing had happened.

(D)
After rehearsal, Mr. Lowell asked Ethan to stay behind. Instead of criticizing him, the conductor described his own first solo as a young trumpet player, when (d)[he] had been so nervous that he forgot to breathe. "Every musician makes mistakes on stage," he said. "The audience remembers only whether you kept going." He then gave Ethan a key to the music room so that (e)[he] could practice the solo alone every morning before classes. For the next three weeks, Ethan played to rows of empty chairs until the notes felt like his own.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)의 리허설 직후 Mr. Lowell이 Ethan을 남게 하는 (D)가 오고, (D)에서 받은 조언과 빈 음악실을 떠올리며 공연하는 (C)가 이어져요. 공연이 끝나고 실수 이야기가 나오는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

리허설에서 Ethan은 솔로의 첫 음들을 매우 작게 연주했다.
공연이 끝난 뒤 Mr. Lowell은 Ethan의 실수를 지적했다.
공연 중 Ethan의 활이 미끄러져 거친 음이 났다.

items.passage:
Dear Guest Services Manager,

My family stayed at the Harborview Inn from March 3 to March 6, in Room 412. After returning home, I realized that I had left a small brown leather notebook in the drawer of the bedside table. It has little value to anyone else, but it contains handwritten recipes from my late grandmother, and it means a great deal to me. I called the front desk yesterday, but the staff member I spoke with was not sure whether the room had already been cleaned and could not find a record of lost items. Could you please check with your housekeeping team and let me know whether the notebook has been found? If it has, I would be very grateful if you could mail it to the address below. I will, of course, pay any shipping costs.

Sincerely,
Daniel Brooks
27 Willow Lane, Fairmont
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 두고 온 물건을 찾아 보내 줄 것을 요청하려고
items.exp: 객실 서랍에 두고 온 할머니의 요리법 수첩을 찾았는지 확인하고, 찾았다면 우편으로 보내 달라고 요청하는 편지예요. 직원이 분실물 기록을 찾지 못했다는 내용은 항의가 아니라 다시 확인을 부탁하는 배경이에요.

items.passage: For weeks, Hana had been counting down the days to the meteor shower. The news said this year's display would be the brightest in a decade, with up to a hundred shooting stars an hour. She convinced her father to drive her two hours away from the city lights to a hill famous for its dark skies. She packed blankets, hot chocolate, and a notebook to record every meteor she saw. As the car climbed the winding road, she pressed her face to the window, imagining the sky bursting with streaks of light. But when they finally spread their blankets on the grass, a thick layer of cloud rolled in from the west. They waited one hour, then two. Not a single star appeared. Hana closed her empty notebook and stared at the gray sky. "All that planning for nothing," she whispered, her voice heavy, as her father quietly began folding the blankets.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Hana의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 유성우를 기대하며 하늘이 빛줄기로 가득할 장면을 상상하다가, 구름 때문에 별 하나 보지 못하고 빈 수첩을 덮으며 힘없이 말해요. 그래서 들뜬 마음에서 실망으로 바뀐 것이에요.

items.passage: Imagine that twenty research teams independently test whether a certain vitamin improves memory. In reality, it has no effect. By chance alone, one or two teams will still observe a small improvement, while the rest will find nothing. The teams with exciting results write them up and send them to journals, which are eager to publish. The others, feeling that "nothing happened" is not worth reporting, put their data away and move on to new projects. Years later, a reader searching the published research finds only positive studies and concludes that the vitamin clearly works. No one has lied, and every published study may be perfectly honest. The distortion comes from [the drawer where the other eighteen studies sleep]. For this reason, many scientists now argue that experiments should be registered before they begin, so that their results, whatever they turn out to be, become part of the public record.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the drawer where the other eighteen studies sleep]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: research that was faked to make a product seem effective
results that went unpublished because they found no effect
experiments that were stopped before they could be finished
data that was stolen from teams with positive results
studies that are waiting to be reviewed by expert editors
items.exp: 효과를 발견하지 못한 나머지 팀들이 결과를 보고할 가치가 없다고 여겨 자료를 치워 두었고, 그래서 출판된 연구만 보면 비타민이 효과가 있는 것처럼 보인다는 내용이에요. 따라서 효과가 없어서 출판되지 않은 결과를 뜻해요. 아무도 거짓말하지 않았다고 했으므로 조작이라는 ①은 틀려요.

items.passage: Every time a major earthquake strikes, people ask why scientists did not warn them. The honest answer is that no one can yet predict the exact time and place of an earthquake. Seismologists can identify which regions sit on active faults and estimate how likely a large quake is within the next few decades, but the moment a fault finally slips depends on countless small conditions deep underground that cannot be measured. Claims of precise predictions, whether based on animal behavior or unusual clouds, have repeatedly failed when tested. For this reason, many experts argue that our energy is better spent on preparation than on prediction. Buildings designed to bend rather than break, emergency supplies kept at home, and regular evacuation drills have saved far more lives than any forecast. Some countries also detect the first, weaker waves of a quake and send alerts seconds before the strongest shaking arrives. We cannot know when the ground will move, but we can decide how ready we will be.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 동물의 행동을 관찰하면 지진을 미리 알아낼 수 있다.
지진 연구에 더 많이 투자해 예측의 정확도를 높여야 한다.
지진 경보 시스템은 피해를 줄이는 데 효과가 없다.
지진은 정확히 예측할 수 없으므로 대비에 힘쓰는 것이 더 효과적이다.
활성 단층 근처에는 건물을 짓지 말아야 한다.
items.exp: 지진의 정확한 시간과 장소는 예측할 수 없으니 예측보다 내진 설계, 비상용품, 대피 훈련 같은 대비에 힘을 쏟는 것이 낫다는 글이에요. 동물 행동에 근거한 예측은 실패했다고 했으므로 ①은 반대이고, 경보 시스템은 오히려 도움이 되는 예로 나와요.

items.passage: In a desert, rain is not only scarce but also unpredictable. A heavy shower in spring may be followed by months of drought, or by another shower a week later. For an annual plant that lives for only one season, this creates a serious gamble. If all of its seeds sprout after the first rain and the ground then dries out, the entire next generation dies before producing seeds of its own. Many desert annuals have solved this problem in a surprising way: their seeds do not all behave the same. Some seeds from a single plant germinate after the first good rain, while others remain dormant in the soil for one, two, or even several years, waiting for later rains. In a good year, the plant loses little by holding some seeds back; in a disastrous year, the sleeping seeds ensure that the family line continues. By spreading its offspring across time, the plant avoids putting all its eggs in one basket.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: ways desert plants store water in their thick leaves
effect of heavy spring rain on desert soil quality
reasons why desert annuals produce very few seeds
competition among desert plants for scarce water
staggered seed germination as a survival strategy in deserts
items.exp: 사막의 한해살이 식물이 씨앗 일부만 먼저 싹틔우고 나머지는 몇 년씩 휴면시켜 예측할 수 없는 비에 대비한다는 내용이에요. 따라서 사막에서 살아남기 위한 시차를 둔 발아 전략이 주제예요. 씨앗이 적다거나 잎에 물을 저장한다는 말은 없어요.

items.passage: Before electric refrigerators became common, ice was a valuable product, and in cold regions it was gathered much like a crop. Each winter, when lakes and ponds froze thick, workers marked the surface into a grid and cut huge blocks with saws pulled by horses. The blocks were floated along channels, lifted into tall wooden storehouses, and packed in sawdust or straw, which kept them from melting for months. By the nineteenth century, ice was being loaded onto ships and carried thousands of kilometers to hot cities, where it cooled drinks, preserved fish and meat, and helped hospitals treat patients with fevers. Surprisingly, a good share of the ice arrived intact, thanks to careful insulation. The trade employed tens of thousands of people at its peak. Within a few decades, however, factories that could make ice by machine, and later home refrigerators, made the frozen harvest unnecessary, and the great icehouses disappeared from the landscape.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Harvesting Winter: The Rise and Fall of the Ice Trade
Why Lakes Freeze from the Top Down
The Dangers Faced by Nineteenth-Century Sailors
items.exp: 냉장고가 없던 시절 겨울 호수의 얼음을 잘라 저장하고 배로 실어 날랐던 얼음 무역이 번성했다가, 제빙 기계와 냉장고로 사라졌다는 내용이에요. 병원이나 톱밥은 세부 내용일 뿐이에요.

items.q: Greenhill Bird-Watching Morning 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 쌍안경은 요금을 내고 빌릴 수 있다.
items.exp: 쌍안경은 방문자 센터에서 무료로(free of charge) 빌릴 수 있다고 했으므로 ④가 일치하지 않아요. 토요일 오전 6시 30분 시작, 14세 미만 성인 동반, 회원 5달러, 전화 신청은 모두 안내문과 같아요.

items.passage: When we are upset, putting our feelings into words can be surprisingly calming. In one kind of experiment, participants look at photos of angry or frightened faces while their brain activity ①[is recorded]. Some are simply asked to look; others are asked to choose a word, such as "angry" or "scared," that describes the emotion. Those who label the feeling show less activity in the brain region ②[associated] with alarm, and more activity in areas linked to careful thought. In everyday life, the same principle may explain why writing in a diary or talking with a friend ③[help] people recover from difficult events. Naming an emotion seems to turn a vague, overwhelming experience into something more ④[manageable]. The more precisely the feeling is described, the stronger the effect tends to be. Saying "I feel left out" rather than simply "I feel bad" gives the mind a clearer target, ⑤[making] it easier to decide what to do next.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③의 주어는 동명사구 writing in a diary or talking with a friend로 하나의 행동을 뜻하므로 단수 동사 helps로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 활동이 기록되는 수동태, ②는 region을 꾸미는 과거분사, ④는 something을 뒤에서 꾸미는 형용사, ⑤는 분사구문으로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: On a winter day, a thermometer may read zero degrees, yet the air can feel far colder when the wind is blowing. The reason is that our bodies are constantly ①[warming] a thin layer of air right next to the skin. When the air is still, this layer stays in place and works like a light blanket, slowing the ②[loss] of heat. Wind, however, sweeps the warm layer away and replaces it with cold air, so the body must heat new air again and again. As a result, exposed skin cools much more ③[quickly] than it would on a calm day. Weather services express this effect as a wind chill temperature, which describes how cold it feels to a person rather than what the air itself measures. The difference is not merely a matter of ④[comfort]: in a strong wind, uncovered fingers and ears can freeze within minutes. That is why, on windy days, a thin windproof jacket can be more ⑤[useless] than a thick sweater that lets the air pass through.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 바람을 막아 피부 옆 따뜻한 공기층을 지켜 주는 얇은 방풍 재킷이 바람이 통하는 두꺼운 스웨터보다 더 쓸모 있다는 흐름이므로 ⑤의 useless는 useful로 바꿔야 해요. ④ comfort는 '단순히 편안함의 문제가 아니라 동상 위험'이라는 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: Architects often imagine a building as a finished object, perfect on the day it opens. Yet buildings, unlike paintings, are used for decades or centuries, and the people inside them keep changing their needs. A house built for a young couple must later hold children, then perhaps an office, and finally a single elderly resident. A factory may become apartments; a bank may turn into a restaurant. Buildings that survive these shifts are rarely the most striking ones. They tend to have simple shapes, generous ceilings, and interior walls that can be moved without bringing the structure down. Their designers accepted that they could not predict every future use and left room for others to make changes. In contrast, buildings shaped tightly around one specific purpose often become hard to use once that purpose disappears, and many are torn down within a generation. The buildings that last longest, then, are often those designed to be ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 오래 살아남는 건물은 단순한 형태와 옮길 수 있는 벽을 갖추어 미래의 다른 용도로 바꿀 여지를 남겼다고 했어요. 따라서 적응할 수 있도록 설계된 건물이 알맞아요. 가장 눈에 띄는 건물이 아니라고 했으므로 admired는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: When we read about a war, an election, or an economic crisis from the past, we already know how the story ends. This knowledge quietly shapes our judgment. Leaders who chose badly seem foolish, warnings that turned out to be correct seem obvious, and the outcome itself appears to have been almost inevitable. But the people living through those events had no such advantage. They faced a cloud of possibilities, many of which looked just as likely as the one that actually occurred, and they had to act on incomplete and often contradictory information. A historian who forgets this will tend to judge past decisions by results that no one at the time could have seen. The more difficult but more honest task is to reconstruct the uncertainty that surrounded those decisions, to ask what was known, what was feared, and what seemed possible. In other words, to understand the people of the past, we must ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: try to forget, for a moment, the ending we already know
judge their choices strictly by the results they produced
focus on the leaders rather than on ordinary citizens
collect as many documents as possible from later periods
accept that the outcome of history was already determined
items.exp: 결말을 아는 지식이 판단을 왜곡하므로, 당시 사람들이 겪은 불확실성을 재구성해야 한다고 했어요. 따라서 이미 아는 결말을 잠시 잊으려 해야 한다는 말이 알맞아요. ②와 ⑤는 글이 경계하는 태도이고, ④는 오히려 사후 지식을 늘리는 일이에요.

items.passage: Every time synthetic clothing goes through a washing machine, it sheds thousands of tiny plastic fibers. ① These microfibers are too small to be caught by most washing machine filters, so they flow out with the wastewater. ② Treatment plants remove many of them, but a significant share still reaches rivers and eventually the ocean, where they are eaten by plankton and small fish. ③ Researchers have found that the amount shed depends on how clothes are washed: cooler water, shorter cycles, and fuller loads all reduce the rubbing that breaks fibers loose. ④ Synthetic fabrics were first developed in the early twentieth century as cheaper alternatives to silk, and they quickly became popular for stockings. ⑤ Some companies are also designing filters that can be attached to the drain hose, trapping fibers before they leave the home. Together, such small changes in everyday habits and equipment could greatly reduce the plastic that enters waterways.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 세탁 과정에서 나오는 미세 플라스틱 섬유와 이를 줄이는 방법을 다루는 글인데, ④는 합성 섬유가 처음 개발된 역사에 관한 내용이라 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤의 also는 ③의 세탁 방법에 이어 또 다른 해결책인 필터를 덧붙여요.

items.passage:
Walk along certain beaches and you may find smooth, frosted pieces of colored glass among the pebbles. These are known as sea glass, and each piece began its life as something quite ordinary.

(A) Both processes take a very long time, often twenty to fifty years. For this reason, collectors have grown worried: as more drinks are sold in plastic and fewer glass bottles end up in the sea, good pieces are becoming harder to find.

(B) Most of it comes from bottles and jars that were thrown away or broken near the shore decades ago. Once the sharp fragments reached the water, waves began to roll them back and forth against sand and stones.

(C) This constant tumbling gradually rounds off their edges. At the same time, chemicals in seawater slowly react with the surface of the glass, leaving tiny pits that give it a cloudy, frosted look.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 평범한 물건에서 시작되었다는 주어진 글 다음에 병과 유리병 조각이 파도에 굴려졌다는 (B)가 오고, 그 굴림을 This constant tumbling으로 받는 (C)가 이어져요. (C)의 마모와 화학 반응 두 과정을 Both processes로 받는 (A)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Newborn babies are remarkable listeners. ( ① ) In their first months, they can tell apart speech sounds from almost any language in the world, including differences that their parents cannot hear at all. ( ② ) A baby raised in an English-speaking home, for instance, can distinguish sounds that are important in Hindi but meaningless in English. ( ③ ) By the end of the first year, babies become better at the sound differences that matter in the language around them and worse at those that do not. ( ④ ) This narrowing is not a loss in any harmful sense. By focusing on the contrasts that carry meaning in their own language, infants can process the speech they hear more quickly and begin to pick out words. ( ⑤ ) It is a bit like a radio that gives up scanning every station in order to tune in clearly to the one that is actually playing.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

This wide-open ability, however, does not last long.
items.exp: ③ 앞까지는 아기가 거의 모든 언어의 소리를 구별하는 넓은 능력을 설명하고, ③ 뒤에서는 첫해 말에 모국어 외의 구별 능력이 약해진다고 해요. 주어진 문장의 however와 This wide-open ability가 그 전환을 이어 주므로 ③에 들어가야 해요. ④ 뒤의 This narrowing은 이미 ③ 뒤 문장을 받고 있어요.

items.passage: Museum visitors, studies suggest, spend an average of less than half a minute in front of a single artwork, and much of that time goes to reading the label or taking a photo. Some art teachers have begun to challenge this habit with an exercise they call slow looking. Students choose one painting and simply observe it for ten or even fifteen minutes, noting whatever they see without searching for the correct interpretation. At first, many find the task boring and uncomfortable. After a few minutes, however, details that were invisible at a glance begin to appear: a tiny figure in the background, a strange shadow, a brushstroke that suddenly changes direction. By the end, students typically describe the work in far richer terms and report that they enjoyed it more than they had expected. The painting, of course, has not changed. What has changed is the amount of attention they were willing to give it.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Giving a single artwork an extended period of (A) ___ allows viewers to (B) ___ features that a quick glance misses and to appreciate the work more.
items.exp: 한 작품을 10~15분 동안 그저 관찰하게 하자 처음엔 보이지 않던 세부가 드러나고 감상이 풍부해졌다고 했으므로 (A)는 observation(관찰), (B)는 discover(발견하다)가 알맞아요. 토론이나 사진 촬영은 활동 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Imagine two people who each receive an unexpected 200 dollars. The first finds it as a tax refund; the second wins it in an office raffle. Logically, the money is identical, yet studies suggest that the raffle winner is far more likely to spend it on a fancy dinner, while the refund receiver is more likely to pay bills or save it. Economists call this habit mental accounting: people sort money into separate mental "accounts" based on where it came from or what it is meant for, and then treat each account by (a)[different] rules.

Mental accounting can lead to choices that look odd from a purely economic point of view. Some families keep money in a savings account earning little interest while carrying credit card debt that charges far more, simply because the savings are labeled "for emergencies." Others will drive across town to save ten dollars on a forty-dollar jacket but would not make the same trip to save ten dollars on a thousand-dollar sofa, even though the saving is (b)[identical] in both cases.

Yet the habit is not purely a weakness. Labeling money can act as a (c)[barrier] against temptation. A jar marked "vacation" or a bank account named "college fund" makes it psychologically (d)[easier] to raid that money for an impulse purchase, because doing so feels like breaking a promise. Some financial programs now use this tendency on purpose, letting customers create many small, named savings goals rather than one large account. The lesson is not that we should erase our mental accounts, but that we should design them (e)[wisely], so that the very same bias that sometimes misleads us can also help us keep our commitments.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Tax Refunds Should Always Be Saved
Credit Card Debt: The Hidden Family Crisis
Saving Small Amounts Leads to Large Fortunes
Mental Accounts: A Bias That Can Mislead or Help
items.exp: 돈을 출처나 용도에 따라 마음속 계좌로 나누는 심리 회계가 비합리적 선택을 낳기도 하지만, 잘 설계하면 유혹을 막는 데 도움이 된다는 내용이에요. 세금 환급, 카드 빚, 경품은 예시일 뿐이에요.

items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 이름 붙인 돈을 충동구매에 쓰는 것은 약속을 깨는 느낌이 들기 때문이라고 했으므로, 그 돈을 꺼내 쓰기가 심리적으로 더 어려워진다는 흐름이에요. 따라서 (d) easier는 harder로 바꿔야 해요. (b)는 두 경우 모두 10달러로 절약액이 같다는 뜻이라 알맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Every summer, Liam's grandfather took him to Pine Lake for a three-day fishing trip, and every summer Liam caught almost nothing. This year, at thirteen, he was determined to change that. On the first morning, he cast his line again and again, reeling it in quickly whenever nothing happened. Watching him, Grandpa chuckled and said, "The fish can hear you hurrying." Liam frowned and asked what (a)[he] was doing wrong.

(B)
That evening, Grandpa showed him an old notebook. For forty years, (b)[he] had written down every trip: the weather, the water temperature, the spots where fish had bitten. Liam turned the pages slowly. Most entries ended with the words "caught nothing, good day." Some pages held pressed leaves or small sketches of birds. He realized that his grandfather had never been chasing fish at all, at least not only fish; he had been collecting quiet mornings. The next morning, Liam asked if he could keep a notebook of his own.

(C)
Instead of answering, Grandpa rowed them to a quiet cove shaded by tall pines. He baited Liam's hook, cast it gently near a fallen log, and handed (c)[him] the rod. "Now we wait," he said, and leaned back against the side of the boat. At first Liam fidgeted, but slowly he began to notice things he had never seen before: a heron standing perfectly still in the shallows, dragonflies skimming the water, the ripple of something large moving beneath the surface. The longer he sat without moving, the more the lake seemed to come alive around him, as if it had simply been waiting for him to be still.

(D)
Then the line tightened. Liam's heart jumped. Remembering Grandpa's words, (d)[he] did not yank the rod but let the fish pull for a moment before slowly reeling in. A fat silver trout flashed beside the boat. Grandpa helped him lift it, and they both laughed out loud. After a long look, Liam carefully slipped the trout back into the water and watched it disappear into the deep, feeling strangely proud that (e)[he] had let it go.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Liam이 무슨 뜻이냐고 묻자 Instead of answering으로 시작하는 (C)가 이어지고, (C)에서 기다리던 중 줄이 당겨지는 (D)가 와요. 그날 저녁 할아버지의 공책을 보는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.exp: (D)에서 Liam은 송어를 조심스럽게 물속에 다시 놓아주었다고 했으므로 ⑤가 틀려요. 나머지는 (A), (B), (C), (D)의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Whitfield,

My name is Daniel Osei, and I teach history at Bramley High School. This semester, my eleventh-grade students are working on a research project about how everyday tools changed during the early industrial period. Last month, our class visited your museum, and many students were fascinated by the collection of hand-forged farming tools in the East Gallery. Since then, several of them have asked whether they could return to study those pieces more closely. I understand that photography is normally not allowed in that gallery in order to protect the older items from light damage. However, I would like to ask whether a small group of four students could take photographs without flash for their project reports. We would be happy to visit at a quiet time, follow any rules your staff set, and use the images only for classroom purposes. Thank you for considering this request.

Sincerely,
Daniel Osei
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 학생들의 과제를 위한 전시품 촬영 허가를 요청하려고
산업 시대 농기구 전시회 개최를 제안하려고
박물관의 사진 촬영 금지 규정에 항의하려고
items.exp: 필자는 촬영이 보통 금지된 전시실에서 학생 네 명이 플래시 없이 사진을 찍을 수 있는지 묻고 있어요. 그래서 과제를 위한 촬영 허가 요청이 목적이에요. 촬영 금지 규정은 이해한다고 했으므로 항의하는 글은 아니에요.

items.passage: Jun arranged the bracelets on the table for the fifth time. She had spent two weeks weaving them from colored thread to raise money for the animal shelter, and she had imagined that they would sell out within an hour. But the school charity market had been open since nine, and while crowds gathered at the cookie stand next door, not a single person had stopped at her table. A few students glanced at the bracelets and walked on. Jun sat down, rested her chin on her hand, and wondered why she had bothered. Then a little girl tugged at her mother's sleeve and pointed. She tried on a blue and yellow bracelet, held up her wrist, and laughed. Her mother paid, and ten minutes later the girl came back with three friends, each holding coins. By noon, only two bracelets were left on the table. Jun counted the money for the shelter twice, smiling so widely that her cheeks hurt.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Jun의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 아무도 팔찌를 사지 않아 턱을 괴고 왜 이걸 했나 생각하던 Jun은 낙담했어요. 여자아이와 친구들이 팔찌를 사 가 거의 다 팔리자 볼이 아플 만큼 웃었으니 기뻐한 거예요. 옆 쿠키 가게를 부러워했다는 내용은 없어서 ③은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: In many youth soccer and basketball leagues, every game ends with a score, a winner, and a loser, even for players as young as six. Adults keep standings, award trophies to the top teams, and talk with excitement about who is in first place. The intention is usually good: competition is part of sport, and children will eventually have to learn to win and lose. But for young children, an emphasis on results changes how the game is played. Coaches give most of the playing time to the few children who are already skilled, and nervous players learn to pass the ball away quickly rather than risk a mistake. Many children quit before they ever discover what they might become with practice. Leagues for children under ten should therefore stop keeping official scores and standings, and focus instead on equal playing time and skill development. The children will still count goals on their own, of course. What changes is that the adults stop treating every Saturday morning as a championship.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 10세 미만 유소년 리그는 공식 점수와 순위를 기록하지 말아야 한다.
어린 선수들에게 이기고 지는 법을 일찍 가르쳐야 한다.
코치는 실력 있는 선수에게 출전 기회를 더 주어야 한다.
유소년 리그의 경기 수를 줄여 휴식 시간을 늘려야 한다.
부모는 자녀의 경기 결과에 더 많은 관심을 가져야 한다.
items.exp: Leagues for children under ten should therefore stop keeping official scores and standings에 필자의 주장이 드러나요. ②는 필자가 소개한 어른들의 의도일 뿐이고, ③은 필자가 문제로 지적한 모습이에요.

items.passage: Most of what we believe, we have never checked for ourselves. We accept that the Earth orbits the Sun, that a certain medicine is safe, or that a historical event happened in a particular way, largely because people we trust told us so. This is not a weakness; no one could verify everything personally. The problem begins when we forget that we are borrowing. Someone who has absorbed an opinion from friends or from a favorite commentator often speaks about it with the same confidence as someone who has studied the evidence carefully. But when a sharp question arrives, the difference quickly becomes visible. The borrower cannot explain why the view makes sense, what would count against it, or where its limits lie. Such a person is [holding a key to a door they have never opened]. Recognizing which of our beliefs are borrowed does not mean abandoning them. It simply reminds us to hold them more humbly and to look inside when it truly matters.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [holding a key to a door they have never opened]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: refusing to trust any information that comes from other people
changing one's opinion whenever a more popular view appears
being confident in a belief without understanding the reasons behind it
keeping one's true opinions hidden from friends and commentators
having the evidence for a view but lacking the courage to share it
items.exp: 남에게서 빌린 의견을 확신에 차서 말하지만, 그 견해가 왜 타당한지 설명하지 못하는 사람을 가리키는 표현이에요. 열쇠(믿음)는 가졌지만 문 안(근거)은 들여다본 적이 없다는 뜻이에요. 남을 믿지 않는다는 보기는 남의 말을 믿는 것은 약점이 아니라는 글의 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Bats that hunt by echolocation face a problem that rarely occurs to us. Each bat sends out high-pitched calls and listens for the echoes that bounce back from insects and obstacles. When a single bat hunts alone, this system works remarkably well. But many species leave their roosts in groups of hundreds or even thousands, and the air quickly fills with overlapping calls. In such a crowd, a bat could easily confuse a neighbor's call with its own echo and lose track of its prey. Researchers have found that several species handle this challenge by adjusting their calls. When another bat flies nearby using a similar pitch, some individuals shift their own call slightly higher or lower, creating a private channel that is easier to pick out. Others change the timing of their calls or briefly stay silent and listen to the echoes produced by their neighbors. These flexible strategies allow bats to keep hunting accurately even in the noisiest skies.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: reasons why bats prefer to hunt alone rather than in groups
the role of echolocation in helping bats avoid predators
the difficulty humans have in hearing high-pitched bat calls
how insects escape from bats by producing their own sounds
ways bats prevent their calls from being confused in crowds
items.exp: 무리 속에서 다른 박쥐의 소리와 자기 메아리가 섞이는 문제를, 음높이·타이밍 조절이나 잠시 침묵하기로 해결한다는 내용이에요. 그래서 무리 속에서 소리 혼동을 막는 방법이 주제예요. 박쥐가 혼자 사냥하기를 더 좋아한다는 내용은 나오지 않아요.

items.passage: Imagine that shoppers buy slightly more paper towels than usual for a week. The store manager notices and, to be safe, orders a little extra from the distributor. The distributor sees this larger order, assumes demand is rising, and orders even more from the factory, adding some extra of its own. The factory, seeing a sudden jump in orders, hires temporary workers and buys more raw materials. By the time the signal reaches the beginning of the supply chain, a small change in what customers bought has turned into a huge swing in production. Then, when shoppers return to their normal habits, everyone discovers that warehouses are full, orders collapse, and the factory must cut back sharply. Business researchers call this pattern the bullwhip effect, after the way a small flick of the wrist sends a large wave down a whip. It can be reduced when companies share actual sales data with one another instead of reacting only to the orders they receive from the next link in the chain.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Small Ripples, Big Waves: How Supply Chains Amplify Demand
Why Shoppers Suddenly Change Their Habits
The Factory Worker: Hero of the Supply Chain
Full Warehouses: A Sign of a Healthy Economy
How Advertising Creates Demand for Simple Goods
items.exp: 소비자의 작은 수요 변화가 소매점, 유통업체, 공장을 거치며 점점 커져 생산의 큰 변동이 되는 채찍 효과를 설명하므로 ①이 알맞아요. 가득 찬 창고(④)는 수요가 원래대로 돌아왔을 때 생기는 문제로 나왔어요.

items.passage: Wilhelmina Strand (1891–1969) was a Norwegian puzzle maker who turned the jigsaw puzzle from a classroom tool into a hobby for adults. The daughter of a carpenter in Bergen, she learned to handle a fine saw in her father's workshop before she was ten. In the 1910s, most jigsaw puzzles were simple maps designed to teach geography to schoolchildren, but Strand began cutting famous paintings into hundreds of irregular pieces, some shaped like animals or letters. Because each puzzle was cut by hand, no two were exactly alike, and she priced them according to how long they took to complete rather than by their size. During the economic hardship of the 1930s, when many families could not afford other entertainment, she opened a puzzle library that lent out sets for a small weekly fee. Although a large toy company offered her a generous contract, she turned it down, insisting that no machine could reproduce the surprise of a hand-cut edge. Her workshop tools are now displayed at a museum of everyday life in Bergen.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 열 살이 되기 전에 아버지의 작업장에서 실톱 다루는 법을 배웠다.
유명한 그림을 불규칙한 모양의 수백 개 조각으로 잘랐다.
퍼즐 가격을 크기가 아니라 완성에 걸리는 시간에 따라 매겼다.
1930년대에 퍼즐 세트를 무료로 빌려주는 도서관을 열었다.
대형 장난감 회사의 계약 제안을 거절했다.
items.exp: 1930년대에 연 퍼즐 도서관은 적은 주간 요금(a small weekly fee)을 받고 세트를 빌려주었으므로 무료로 빌려주었다는 ④가 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 실톱을 배운 일, 그림을 자른 조각, 시간에 따른 가격, 계약 거절로 모두 글과 일치해요.

items.passage: Before satellite navigation, sailors approaching a coast at night faced a dangerous problem: a light on the shore told them that land was near, but not which part of the coast they ①[were] looking at. To solve this, lighthouse builders gave each tower its own pattern. One light flashed once every five seconds, while another ②[gave] two quick flashes followed by a long pause. Some used colored glass so that a red or green light marked a particular rock or harbor entrance. Sailors carried printed lists ③[describe] the pattern of every light along their route, and by counting the seconds between flashes, a navigator could identify a lighthouse with confidence. In daylight, when the lamps were dark, towers were recognized by their shapes and painted stripes, ④[which] were also different from one another. Although modern ships rely mostly on electronic systems, many lighthouses still operate today, ⑤[serving] as a backup in case those systems fail.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③은 앞의 printed lists를 꾸며 '~을 설명하는 목록'이 되어야 하므로 현재분사 describing(또는 that described)으로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 복수 주어 they, ②는 주어 another의 과거 동사, ④는 shapes and painted stripes를 받는 관계대명사, ⑤는 분사구문으로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Many people have noticed that a hard green banana ripens faster when it is placed in a paper bag. The reason is a gas called ethylene, which fruits such as bananas, apples, and tomatoes ①[release] as they ripen. Ethylene acts as a signal, telling the fruit to soften, sweeten, and change color. Inside a bag, the gas is ②[trapped] around the fruit, so its concentration rises and ripening speeds up. Putting an apple in the bag adds even more ethylene, which makes the effect ③[stronger]. Farmers and shippers use the same principle on a large scale. They often pick bananas while they are still green and firm, which lets them travel long distances without ④[damage], and then expose them to ethylene in special rooms when they reach the market. On the other hand, people who want their fruit to last longer should keep ripe apples ⑤[close to] other fruits, since the gas will speed up their ripening.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 에틸렌이 다른 과일의 숙성을 빠르게 하므로, 과일을 오래 두고 싶다면 잘 익은 사과를 다른 과일과 멀리 두어야 해요. 따라서 ⑤ close to는 away from으로 바꿔야 해요. 나머지는 가스를 내뿜고, 가두고, 더 강하게, 손상 없이라는 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage: In many racing video games, a curious thing happens to the player in last place: the items that appear on the track suddenly become more powerful. A rocket that can push a car past several rivals rarely shows up for the leader, yet it is common for those far behind. Some players complain that this is unjust, since it seems to punish the very skill that put the leader ahead. Designers, however, defend the feature, known as "rubber banding," on practical grounds. A race whose winner is obvious after the first lap offers nothing to anyone but the person in front; everyone else simply waits for it to end, and many quit. By pulling trailing players back into contention, the game keeps every participant believing that the outcome remains open until the final turn. Skill is not erased, since the strongest racers still win most of the time, but the gap is narrowed enough to hold attention. What designers are protecting, in short, is not equal results but the ___ that makes players keep trying.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 뒤처진 선수를 다시 경쟁에 끌어들여 마지막 순간까지 결과가 열려 있다고 믿게 만든다고 했으므로, 설계자가 지키려는 것은 결과의 불확실성인 uncertainty예요. fairness는 오히려 이 장치가 불공평하다는 불만과 연결되고, 글은 결과의 평등이 목적이 아니라고 했어요.

items.passage: We often praise tolerance as if it simply meant being relaxed about other people's choices. But this common picture hides a puzzle. If I am completely indifferent to how my neighbor spends his weekends, it would be odd to say that I tolerate his hobbies; I merely do not care about them. Likewise, if I warmly approve of a friend's decision, my acceptance requires no effort at all. Tolerance enters the picture only at a particular point: when I judge something to be mistaken, unwise, or even distasteful, and yet deliberately choose not to interfere with it. In this sense, tolerance is not the absence of judgment but a disciplined response to it. A society in which everyone agreed on everything would have no need for tolerance, and a person who has no convictions has nothing to restrain. Paradoxically, then, the virtue depends on the very thing it seems to overcome. Tolerance, properly understood, is possible only where ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: there is something one genuinely disapproves of
people have learned to stop judging one another
everyone shares the same set of convictions
laws forbid any form of interference
items.exp: 관용은 무관심이나 찬성이 아니라, 잘못되었다고 판단하면서도 간섭하지 않기로 할 때만 생긴다고 했어요. 따라서 진심으로 반대하는 무언가가 있는 곳에서만 관용이 가능해요. 판단을 멈춘다는 보기와 모두가 같은 신념을 가진다는 보기는 글에서 관용이 필요 없거나 성립하지 않는 경우로 든 것이에요.

items.passage: Peatlands, the soggy wetlands found from cold northern regions to tropical forests, cover only about three percent of the Earth's land surface, yet they store more carbon than all the world's forests combined. ① In these waterlogged areas, dead plants decompose extremely slowly because the lack of oxygen limits the activity of bacteria and fungi. ② As a result, plant material builds up layer by layer over thousands of years, locking away the carbon it absorbed while it was alive. ③ When peatlands are drained for farming or development, however, oxygen reaches the buried material and decomposition speeds up dramatically. ④ In some regions, peat has also been cut and dried as a household fuel, and its smoky scent is still associated with certain traditional foods and drinks. ⑤ The stored carbon is then released into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, turning what was once a long-term carbon store into a steady source of emissions.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 이탄지가 탄소를 저장하는 원리와 배수 시 탄소가 배출되는 과정을 설명하는 글이에요. ④는 이탄을 연료로 쓰고 그 향이 전통 음식과 연결된다는 문화적 이야기로 흐름에서 벗어나요. ④를 빼면 ③의 분해 가속에서 ⑤의 탄소 배출로 자연스럽게 이어져요.

items.passage:
On a hot day, a refrigerator seems to be a machine that produces cold and pours it over our food. In fact, it does nothing of the kind. It works by collecting heat from inside the box and carrying it out into the kitchen, with the help of a special fluid called a refrigerant.

(A) Because of this, when the hot gas flows through the thin coils on the back of the machine, it gives off its heat to the cooler room and turns back into a liquid. The fluid then returns inside, and the cycle starts again, which is why the back of a refrigerator always feels warm.

(B) This fluid boils at a very low temperature. As it flows through pipes inside the fridge, it evaporates, and like sweat drying on the skin, it takes heat from the food and air around it.

(C) The resulting gas is then drawn to a pump called a compressor, which squeezes it into a much smaller space. Under this pressure, the gas becomes very hot, far hotter than the air in the kitchen.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 a refrigerant를 (B)가 This fluid로 받아 증발하며 열을 빼앗는다고 설명해요. (C)의 The resulting gas는 (B)에서 증발해 생긴 기체이고, (A)의 Because of this와 the hot gas는 (C)에서 압축되어 뜨거워진 기체를 가리켜요.

items.passage: When the cost of ingredients and packaging rises, food companies face a difficult choice. ( ① ) Raising the price of a familiar product is risky, since shoppers remember what they used to pay and may switch to a competitor. ( ② ) Instead, many companies keep the price the same and quietly put less inside the package. ( ③ ) A chocolate bar becomes a few millimeters thinner, or a box of cereal shrinks from 500 grams to 450. ( ④ ) Meanwhile, the package usually keeps its familiar size, colors, and design, with only a small number printed on the back revealing the change. ( ⑤ ) To help these unaware buyers, some countries now require stores to display the price per gram or per liter on shelf labels. Consumer groups, which call the practice "shrinkflation," argue that such labels allow people to compare products by what they actually contain rather than by how large the box looks.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Thanks to this disguise, the change is nearly invisible, and many shoppers keep paying the same amount for less without noticing.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 this disguise는 ④ 뒤에 나온, 포장의 크기와 디자인을 그대로 두는 것을 가리켜요. 또 ⑤ 뒤의 these unaware buyers는 주어진 문장의 '알아채지 못하는 소비자들'을 받으므로 ⑤가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Most households learn how much electricity they have used only once a month, when the bill arrives. By then, the connection between any particular action and its cost has disappeared; no one remembers how long the heater ran on a certain Tuesday. In one study, researchers installed small screens in a group of homes that showed, minute by minute, how much power the household was using and what it was costing. Other similar homes received only their usual monthly bills. Over the following months, the families with screens cut their electricity use by noticeably more than the others. Many reported that they had started switching off lights and unplugging devices once they saw the number jump each time an appliance came on. The researchers concluded that people do not waste energy simply because they do not care, but because the effects of their choices are normally hidden from them until it is too late to connect cause and effect.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

When people receive (A) ___ information about their energy use, they tend to (B) ___ how much they consume.
items.exp: 분 단위로 사용량과 요금을 보여 주는 화면이 있는 가정이 전기를 더 많이 줄였으므로 (A)에는 immediate(즉각적인), (B)에는 reduce(줄이다)가 알맞아요. monthly와 delayed는 효과가 적었던 월별 고지서 조건이에요.

items.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, city planners followed a simple rule: keep cars and people apart. Streets were divided into lanes for vehicles and raised sidewalks for pedestrians, with fences, signals, and signs telling everyone exactly where to go. The logic seemed (a)[obvious]: clear separation should mean fewer collisions. Yet some traffic engineers began to notice a surprising pattern. In places where the rules were most detailed, drivers often behaved as if the road belonged entirely to them, speeding up whenever the signals allowed it and paying little attention to their surroundings.

This observation led to an experiment known as "shared space." In certain town centers, planners (b)[removed] curbs, traffic lights, and most road markings, creating a single level surface used by cars, cyclists, and walkers alike. Critics predicted chaos. Instead, in many of these areas, vehicle speeds dropped and serious accidents declined. Without signals to rely on, drivers could no longer assume that they had the right of way. They had to make eye contact with pedestrians, slow down at uncertain moments, and negotiate their path. The (c)[uncertainty] of the street, in other words, made people more careful.

Shared space is not a perfect solution. People with visual impairments, for example, have pointed out that the lack of curbs and clear crossings can make such streets (d)[easier] to navigate safely, and many designs now include textured paving to guide them. Still, the experiment offers a valuable lesson for urban design. Safety does not always come from adding more control. Sometimes a street becomes safer when it (e)[invites] the people using it to pay attention to one another.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Traffic Signals Are the Key to Safer Cities
The Rise of Car-Free Town Centers
Fewer Rules, Safer Streets: The Logic of Shared Space
How Pedestrians Lost the Battle for the Road
Designing Streets for People with Visual Impairments
items.exp: 신호와 경계석을 없앤 공유 공간에서 오히려 속도와 사고가 줄었고, 안전이 늘 통제를 더하는 데서 오지는 않는다는 것이 글의 핵심이에요. 자동차가 사라진 것이 아니라 함께 쓰는 공간이므로 Car-Free는 맞지 않고, 시각 장애인 이야기는 일부 내용이에요.

This observation led to an experiment known as "shared space." In certain town centers, planners (b)[removed] curbs, traffic lights, and most road markings, creating a single level surface used by cars, cyclists, and walkers alike. Critics predicted chaos. Instead, in many of these areas, vehicle speeds dropped and serious accidents declined. Without signals to rely on, drivers could no longer assume that they had the right of way. They had to make eye contact with pedestrians, slow down at uncertain moments, and negotiate their path. The (c)[uncertainty] of the street, in other words, made people more careful.

Shared space is not a perfect solution. People with visual impairments, for example, have pointed out that the lack of curbs and clear crossings can make such streets (d)[easier] to navigate safely, and many designs now include textured paving to guide them. Sometimes a street becomes safer when it (e)[invites] the people using it to pay attention to one another.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 시각 장애인들이 지적한 문제점이고 그 때문에 안내용 질감 포장을 넣는다고 했으므로, 경계석이 없으면 거리가 안전하게 다니기 더 어려워진다는 뜻이어야 해요. 그래서 (d) easier를 harder로 바꿔야 해요. (c) uncertainty는 신호가 없어 조심하게 된다는 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
The rain had been falling all afternoon when Nora pushed open the door of Halvorsen Books, a narrow shop beside a bakery. A bell rang above (a)[her] head, and the smell of old paper filled the air. Behind a counter piled with books sat an elderly man, reading under a small lamp. Nora needed a copy of a classic novel for her literature class, and the new editions downtown cost more than she wanted to spend. "Fiction is on the left, near the back," the man said without looking up.

(B)
After twenty minutes of searching, Nora found the novel on the bottom shelf. Its cover was faded, and the price written inside in pencil was only two dollars. As she flipped through it, a dried violet slipped out from between the pages. The margins were filled with neat handwriting, comments on the characters and little drawings of birds. On the last page someone had written, "For the days when you forget how to be brave. R., 1968." Curious, Nora carried the book to the counter. When the old man saw it, (b)[he] put down his own book and was silent for a long moment.

(C)
Nora shook her head. "It was never really for sale," (c)[she] said, sliding the book across the counter. The old man offered her money, but she refused. A week later, when she returned, Mr. Halvorsen was waiting with a small package. Inside was a fresh copy of the novel she needed and a note: "For the girl who returned something I thought was lost." From then on, (d)[she] spent many rainy afternoons in the shop, listening to stories about Ruth.

(D)
"This belonged to my wife, Ruth," he said quietly. "She wrote in every book she loved." After she passed away three years earlier, he had not been able to keep her books at home, so he had put a box of them on the shelves without looking through them. Later he regretted it, but by then they had mixed with thousands of others, and he had no idea which ones were hers. He turned the pages slowly, touching the drawings of birds. Then he looked up and asked whether (e)[she] would let him buy it back for twice the price.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 소설을 찾으라는 안내를 받은 Nora가 (B)에서 메모가 적힌 책을 찾아 계산대로 가져가요. (D)에서 노인이 아내 Ruth의 책이라 밝히며 되사겠다고 하고, (C)에서 Nora가 원래 팔 물건이 아니었다며 책을 돌려줘요. (C)의 Ruth는 (D)에서 처음 소개되므로 (D)가 (C)보다 먼저예요.

The rain had been falling all afternoon when Nora pushed open the door of Halvorsen Books, a narrow shop beside a bakery. A bell rang above (a)[her] head, and the smell of old paper filled the air. Behind a counter piled with books sat an elderly man, reading under a small lamp. Nora needed a copy of a classic novel for her literature class, and the new editions downtown cost more than she wanted to spend. "Fiction is on the left, near the back," the man said without looking up.

After twenty minutes of searching, Nora found the novel on the bottom shelf. Its cover was faded, and the price written inside in pencil was only two dollars. As she flipped through it, a dried violet slipped out from between the pages. The margins were filled with neat handwriting, comments on the characters and little drawings of birds. On the last page someone had written, "For the days when you forget how to be brave. R., 1968." Curious, Nora carried the book to the counter. When the old man saw it, (b)[he] put down his own book and was silent for a long moment.

From then on, (d)[she] spent many rainy afternoons in the shop, listening to stories about Ruth.

"This belonged to my wife, Ruth," he said quietly. "She wrote in every book she loved." After she passed away three years earlier, he had not been able to keep her books at home, so he had put a box of them on the shelves without looking through them. Later he regretted it, but by then they had mixed with thousands of others, and he had no idea which ones were hers. He turned the pages slowly, touching the drawings of birds. Then he looked up and asked whether (e)[she] would let him buy it back for twice the price.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 가리키는 대상이 나머지 넷과 다른 것은?
items.exp: (b)는 책을 내려놓고 오래 말이 없던 서점 주인 노인을 가리켜요. 나머지 (a), (c), (d), (e)는 모두 Nora를 가리켜요.
