items.passage:
Dear Councilmember Ortiz,

My name is Hyunwoo Park, and I live on Linden Street, across from the small square in front of the old post office. At the center of that square stands a ginkgo tree that is believed to be more than two hundred years old. Generations of residents have met in its shade, and every November its golden leaves draw photographers from all over the city. Last week, however, a notice appeared on the tree announcing that it will be cut down next month so that the street can be widened for a new bus lane. I understand that better bus service is important, and I am not opposed to the project itself. According to the plan posted at the city office, though, the lane could be shifted slightly to the other side of the street, where there is an empty parking area. I respectfully ask that the council consider this option and spare the tree before it is too late.

Sincerely,
Hyunwoo Park
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 버스 전용 차로 신설 계획에 반대하려고
오래된 은행나무를 베지 않도록 차로 계획의 변경을 요청하려고
빈 주차장을 공원으로 바꿔 달라고 건의하려고
items.exp: 새 버스 차로 때문에 이백 년 된 은행나무가 베일 예정이니, 차로를 길 건너 빈 주차장 쪽으로 옮겨 나무를 살려 달라고 요청하는 편지예요. 필자는 사업 자체에는 반대하지 않는다고 했으므로 ①은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Seoyeon stood at the door of the apartment next to hers, going over the hand movements one more time. The girl who had moved in last week, Ayeon, was deaf, and for three nights Seoyeon had practiced simple greetings from a sign language video. Now her palms were damp, and every sign she had learned seemed to be slipping away. When the door opened, she raised her hands and carefully signed what she believed was "Nice to meet you." Ayeon blinked, then covered her mouth and burst out laughing. Seoyeon's face burned. Had she said something rude? Still smiling, Ayeon took Seoyeon's hands and gently reshaped them, showing her the correct sign. Then she typed a message on her phone and held it up: "You just told me your cat is purple! But thank you for trying. Nobody in this building has ever tried." Seoyeon laughed until tears came to her eyes, and she signed "Nice to meet you" again, this time perfectly. Ayeon clapped and signed it back.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Seoyeon의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 수화 인사를 앞두고 손바닥에 땀이 나고 배운 동작이 다 달아나는 것 같았으며, 상대가 웃자 얼굴이 달아올랐으니 긴장한 상태였어요. 이웃이 바른 동작을 알려 주고 고마워하자 눈물이 날 만큼 웃으며 다시 인사했으므로 기뻐한 거예요. 처음에 차분했던 것이 아니므로 ③은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: To a listener, a jazz solo can sound like pure freedom. The saxophonist closes her eyes, and melodies seem to pour out of nowhere, never repeated and never planned. It is tempting to conclude that improvisers simply abandon the rules that bind classical musicians. In fact, the opposite is closer to the truth. Before they can improvise well, jazz players spend years practicing scales, memorizing chord progressions, and copying the solos of earlier masters note by note. On stage, they work within a shared structure: everyone knows the key, the tempo, and the order of the chords, and a soloist who ignores them quickly loses the band. What sounds spontaneous is usually a fresh combination of patterns stored through long training, chosen in the moment to fit that structure. In this sense, [freedom on stage is built from rules in the practice room]. The surprises we hear in a performance are possible only because so much has been learned that it no longer needs to be thought about.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [freedom on stage is built from rules in the practice room]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Jazz musicians play better when they avoid practicing before a show.
Classical training prevents musicians from improvising freely.
Audiences prefer music that follows predictable patterns.
Soloists must follow the band leader's instructions on stage.
Creative improvisation depends on mastered patterns and shared structure.
items.exp: 재즈 연주자는 오랜 연습으로 음계·화음 진행·선배의 솔로를 익히고, 무대에서도 조성·박자·화음 순서라는 공유된 틀 안에서 연주한다고 했어요. 그래서 즉흥의 자유는 익힌 패턴과 공유된 구조에서 나온다는 뜻이에요. 클래식 훈련이 즉흥을 막는다는 내용은 없어요.

items.passage: When we think of scientific discovery, we usually picture professionals in laboratories, surrounded by expensive equipment. Yet some of the most valuable data in fields such as astronomy, ecology, and weather science are collected by ordinary people. Amateur astronomers with backyard telescopes have spotted new comets and recorded the sudden brightening of distant stars. Volunteers who count butterflies in their gardens, or note the first day a certain flower opens each spring, have built records that cover decades and entire continents, far more ground than any research team could cover alone. Professional scientists rarely have the time or money to watch so many places so often. What they need is not more experts but more eyes, and careful nonexperts can provide them. Of course, such observations must be checked, and volunteers need clear guidelines. But when projects are designed well, the contributions of amateurs are not a minor supplement to science; they are often the very foundation on which professional analysis is built.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 과학 연구의 정확성을 위해 전문가만 자료를 수집해야 한다.
아마추어 천문가도 고가의 장비를 갖추어야 성과를 낼 수 있다.
자원봉사자의 관찰 기록은 검증이 어려워 연구에 쓰기 어렵다.
잘 설계된 연구에서 일반인의 관찰은 과학 연구의 중요한 토대가 된다.
과학자들은 연구비를 늘려 관찰 지역을 넓혀야 한다.
items.exp: 일반인이 모은 관찰 기록이 전문가가 감당할 수 없는 넓은 범위를 채우며, 잘 설계된 연구에서는 과학 분석의 토대가 된다는 글이에요. 관찰 기록은 확인이 필요하다고 했을 뿐 쓰기 어렵다고 하지 않았으므로 ③은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Why are there no mountains on Earth much taller than Mount Everest? Mountains grow when the plates of Earth's crust collide and push rock upward, a process that can continue for tens of millions of years. Yet several forces work against this growth. As a mountain rises, its peaks meet colder temperatures, stronger winds, and heavier snowfall, and glaciers and rivers grind away rock faster than they do at lower levels. The mountain's own weight also matters. A huge mass of rock presses down on the softer layers beneath the crust, causing the whole region to sink slightly, much as a boat settles deeper in the water when it is loaded. Beyond a certain height, the rock near the base would even begin to flow under the pressure. Because of these limits, the highest ranges reach a point where uplift is roughly balanced by erosion and sinking. On Mars, where gravity is weaker and erosion is slight, one volcano has grown about two and a half times as tall as Everest.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: how glaciers carved the world's deepest valleys
the natural limits on how tall Earth's mountains can grow
the dangers that climbers face at high altitudes
why volcanoes on Mars are still active today
methods used to measure the height of Mount Everest
items.exp: 산은 판의 충돌로 솟아오르지만 높아질수록 침식이 빨라지고 자체 무게로 가라앉아, 일정 높이 이상 자랄 수 없다는 내용이에요. 빙하의 침식이나 화성의 화산은 이를 설명하는 근거나 비교일 뿐 중심 내용이 아니에요.

items.passage: The zipper seems so simple that it is hard to believe it took decades to perfect. In 1893, an American inventor introduced a "clasp locker," a device of hooks and eyes meant to fasten shoes quickly. It worked poorly, often jamming or springing open at the worst moment, and few people bought it. The real breakthrough came in 1913, when a Swedish-American engineer designed rows of small metal teeth that locked together tightly as a slider moved over them. Even then, the public was slow to accept the new fastener, and it was used mainly on boots and tobacco pouches. Clothing makers worried that it would break or look cheap, and many people distrusted anything that could be opened with a single pull. Only in the 1930s, when tailors began putting zippers in children's clothes and men's trousers, did the device become common. Today, billions are produced every year, and few people stop to think about the small invention holding their clothes together.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Metal Is Better Than Buttons
A Slow Start: The Long Road to the Modern Zipper
items.exp: 1893년 처음 나온 잠금장치는 잘 작동하지 않았고, 1913년에 개선된 뒤에도 사람들이 쉽게 받아들이지 않다가 1930년대에야 널리 쓰였다는 내용이에요. 그래서 ④가 제목으로 알맞아요. ③의 부츠는 지퍼가 처음 쓰인 곳의 예일 뿐이에요.

items.q: Eastbrook Youth Podcast Workshop 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 도서관 안내 데스크에서 등록할 수 있다.
items.exp: 참가비 40달러는 다섯 번의 수업 전체에 대한 금액(for all five sessions)이므로 ③이 일치하지 않아요. 나머지 일정, 대상, 장비 제공, 등록 장소는 안내문과 같아요.

items.passage: Most people assume that bread becomes hard simply because it ①[drying] out. In fact, staling is mainly ②[caused] by changes in starch, the main substance in flour. When dough bakes, heat and water make starch molecules loosen and spread out, ③[which] gives fresh bread its soft, springy texture. As the loaf cools and sits on the counter, these molecules slowly pull back together and form tight, crystal-like structures. The crumb becomes firm and tastes dry even when very little water has actually been lost. Surprisingly, this process happens ④[faster] at refrigerator temperatures than at room temperature, so keeping bread in the fridge often makes it stale sooner, not later. Freezing, on the other hand, almost stops the change. This also explains why briefly warming a day-old roll in the oven can bring back much of its softness: the heat is enough ⑤[to loosen] the starch structures once again, at least until the bread cools down.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ① 앞의 it이 주어이고 because절에 동사가 필요하므로 drying을 dries로 고쳐야 해요. ②는 staling이 변화에 의해 일어나는 수동태, ③은 앞 절 전체를 받는 관계대명사, ④는 than과 짝을 이루는 비교급, ⑤는 enough to 구문으로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Restaurant owners have long known that the prices on a menu influence one another. Consider a menu on which the most expensive dish, a seafood platter, costs ninety dollars. Few customers actually order it, and the owner may not ①[expect] them to. Its real job is to change how the other prices look. Next to a ninety-dollar platter, a forty-dollar steak suddenly seems ②[reasonable], even though the same steak might have felt costly on its own. Psychologists describe this effect as anchoring: the first or most noticeable number people see becomes a ③[reference] point for judging everything that follows. Designers also arrange menus so that the eye lands on high-priced items first, setting the anchor early. Customers who believe they are carefully comparing options are often being ④[freed] by numbers they never intended to consider. Knowing this will not make anyone immune, but it can help diners pause and ask whether a dish is worth its price, rather than merely ⑤[cheaper] than the one above it.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 손님들은 스스로 신중하게 비교한다고 믿지만 실제로는 고려할 생각도 없던 숫자에 영향을 받고 있다는 흐름이에요. 그래서 ④ freed는 guided나 influenced 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요. ⑤ cheaper는 바로 위 요리보다 싸 보일 뿐이라는 뜻으로 알맞아요.

items.passage: Visitors to museums are sometimes disappointed by how dim the galleries holding old drawings, photographs, and textiles are. Curators keep the lights low for a good reason. Light, especially its ultraviolet part, slowly breaks down the dyes and fibers in paper and cloth, causing colors to fade and materials to grow weak. What makes this damage hard to manage is that it does not depend on any single moment of exposure. A watercolor shown under bright light for one month suffers roughly as much harm as the same painting shown under light half as strong for two months. Every hour of display adds to the total, and none of the harm can be undone later, however carefully the work is stored in darkness afterward. For this reason, many museums rotate fragile works, showing them for a few months and then resting them for years. In the eyes of a conservator, light damage is ___, a debt that grows a little every time the work is seen.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 빛의 손상은 한순간의 노출이 아니라 전시 시간마다 더해져 쌓이고 되돌릴 수 없다고 했으므로 cumulative(누적되는)가 알맞아요. 나중에 어둠 속에 보관해도 되돌릴 수 없다고 했으니 reversible과 temporary는 반대이고, 색이 바랜다고 했으니 invisible도 아니에요.

items.passage: Many customs that seem to have existed forever turn out, on closer inspection, to be surprisingly young. A national costume proudly worn at festivals may have been designed by a committee barely a century ago, and a ceremony described as ancient may have been created to celebrate a new government. Historians who study such cases do not conclude that these traditions are fake. Rather, they point out that people living through rapid change often look for symbols that make a new community feel old and stable. A newly formed nation, a growing city, or a recently merged school may invent rituals, songs, and uniforms and then present them as inherited from the distant past. The claim of age is part of what gives a custom its power, since something that seems to have always existed is harder to question. Within a generation or two, the origins are forgotten, and the practice is handed down as if it had never been otherwise. In this sense, many traditions are less a record of the past than ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a faithful copy of how earlier generations actually lived
an obstacle that keeps communities from accepting change
an answer to present needs dressed in the clothing of history
a set of stories that historians have proven to be false
an accident of memory that nobody intended to create
items.exp: 오래된 것처럼 보이는 전통 중 상당수는 급변기에 새 공동체를 안정되게 느끼게 하려고 최근에 만들어진 뒤 옛것으로 포장되었다고 했어요. 그러니 전통은 과거의 기록이라기보다 역사의 옷을 입은 현재의 필요에 대한 응답이에요. 역사가들은 가짜라고 결론 내리지 않는다고 했으므로 ④는 틀리고, 의도적으로 만들었다고 했으니 ⑤도 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: A hiccup may seem like a meaningless annoyance, but it is actually a carefully coordinated reflex. ① It begins when the diaphragm, the muscle beneath the lungs that drives breathing, suddenly tightens and pulls air rapidly into the chest. ② The diaphragm is also the muscle that singers learn to control, and they train for years to make a single breath last through a long phrase. ③ A fraction of a second later, the vocal cords snap shut, stopping the rush of air and producing the familiar sound. ④ Common triggers include eating too quickly, swallowing air, and drinking fizzy beverages, all of which stretch the stomach and irritate nerves that run close to it. ⑤ Most episodes end on their own within a few minutes, although scientists still debate why the reflex exists at all, since it seems to serve no clear purpose in adults.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 딸꾹질이 횡격막 수축과 성대 닫힘으로 일어나는 과정, 원인, 경과를 설명하는 글이에요. ②는 같은 횡격막을 다루지만 가수의 호흡 훈련 이야기로 딸꾹질의 흐름에서 벗어나요. ③의 A fraction of a second later는 ①의 횡격막 수축에 바로 이어져요.

items.passage:
Hail can fall even on a hot summer afternoon, which seems strange, since hailstones are solid balls of ice. The explanation lies several kilometers above the ground, inside the towering clouds that produce thunderstorms.

(A) These pellets do not fall straight down. The rising currents keep tossing them up and down within the cloud, and each trip through areas full of extremely cold water droplets adds a fresh coating of ice. If you cut a large hailstone in half, you can often see these layers, much like the rings of a tree.

(B) Eventually, a hailstone grows too heavy for the air currents to hold, and it drops toward the ground. Because it falls quickly and is large, it has little time to melt on the way down, even when the air near the surface is warm.

(C) In these clouds, powerful currents of rising air, called updrafts, carry raindrops far above the level where the temperature drops below freezing. Up there, the drops freeze into tiny pellets of ice.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (C)의 these clouds는 주어진 글의 뇌우 구름을 가리키고, 물방울이 얼어 작은 얼음 알갱이가 된다고 해요. (A)의 These pellets가 그 알갱이를 받아 층이 쌓이는 과정을 설명하고, (B)의 Eventually에서 무거워진 우박이 떨어지며 끝나요.

items.passage: Many cities have installed countdown timers at crosswalks, which show how many seconds remain before the signal changes. The idea is simple: people make better decisions when they have more information. ( ① ) This benefit, however, is not the whole story. ( ② ) The numbers are visible not only to people on foot but also to drivers approaching the intersection, and some drivers use them in a way the designers never intended. ( ③ ) Seeing that only three or four seconds remain, they speed up to get through before the light turns red. ( ④ ) Studies in several cities have linked this behavior to a rise in rear-end crashes, when the car in front stops suddenly, and in near misses with walkers who are still crossing. ( ⑤ ) For this reason, some cities now place the timers where mainly pedestrians can see them, or choose not to install them at busy intersections where cars travel fast.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

For pedestrians, the advantage is clear: they can judge whether there is enough time to cross, and fewer people end up stranded in the middle of the road.
items.exp: ② 앞의 This benefit은 보행자가 건널 시간을 판단할 수 있다는 이점을 가리켜야 하는데, 주어진 문장이 ①에 들어가야 그 대상이 생겨요. ② 이후는 운전자가 숫자를 보고 속도를 높이는 부작용으로 이어지므로 다른 자리는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Many people set goals such as "I will exercise more" or "I will study harder," yet fail to act on them. Psychologists have found that a small change in how a goal is stated can make a large difference. Instead of simply deciding what to do, people decide exactly when and where they will do it, in the form "If it is 7 a.m. and I have finished breakfast, then I will go for a run." In many studies, those who made such if-then plans were far more likely to carry out their intentions than those who set only general goals, even when both groups were equally motivated. The reason seems to be that the plan connects the action to a particular situation in advance. When that situation arrives, the decision has already been made, so the person does not need to rely on willpower or to remember the goal at the right moment. The situation itself becomes the reminder.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Linking a goal to a (A) ___ situation in advance makes people more likely to act on it, since it reduces their (B) ___ on willpower in the moment.
items.exp: 언제, 어디서 할지 정한 '만약 ~라면 ~하겠다' 계획이 행동을 특정 상황에 미리 연결해 준다고 했으므로 (A)는 specific(구체적인)이에요. 그 순간 의지력에 기댈 필요가 없어진다고 했으므로 (B)는 dependence(의존)가 알맞아요. general은 효과가 적었던 쪽이에요.

items.passage:
Many parents assume that a child's food preferences are fixed from birth: one child simply loves broccoli, while another will never touch it. Humans do arrive with a few built-in tendencies. Newborns everywhere prefer sweet tastes and reject bitter ones, a sensible (a)[defense] in a world where many poisonous plants taste bitter. Beyond these basics, however, most of what we like to eat is learned, and the learning begins earlier than most people imagine.

Flavors from a mother's diet pass into the fluid that surrounds the baby before birth and later into breast milk. In one line of research, babies whose mothers had regularly drunk carrot juice during pregnancy made fewer unhappy faces when they were later fed cereal (b)[flavored] with carrot. In other words, the first lessons about which foods are familiar, and therefore safe, are delivered before a child ever sits at a table.

After infancy, the most powerful teacher is repetition. Young children are naturally (c)[suspicious] of new foods, and a single refusal often leads parents to give up. Studies suggest, however, that a child may need to taste a new vegetable eight to fifteen times before accepting it. Each small, pressure-free taste makes the food a little less strange. Children also watch closely what the adults and older children around them eat, and they are more willing to try a dish when they see others (d)[enjoying] it.

This helps explain why food preferences differ so widely across cultures. A taste for fermented fish, bitter greens, or fiery chili is not something people are born with; it is (e)[discouraged] by the meals they grow up with. Our palates, it turns out, are shaped as much by our kitchens as by our genes.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Children Are Born Hating Vegetables
Learned Palates: How Experience Shapes What We Like to Eat
The Hidden Dangers of Bitter Plants
Breast Milk or Formula: Which Is Healthier?
Traditional Recipes That Changed the World
items.exp: 단맛·쓴맛에 대한 몇 가지 타고난 경향을 빼면 음식 취향은 태아기의 맛 경험, 반복된 맛보기, 주변 사람 관찰, 자라면서 먹는 식사로 배워진다는 내용이에요. 그래서 경험이 입맛을 만든다는 ②가 알맞아요. 아이가 채소를 싫어하게 태어난다는 ①은 글과 반대예요.

items.exp: 삭힌 생선이나 매운 고추를 좋아하는 입맛은 타고나는 것이 아니라 자라면서 먹는 식사로 길러진다는 흐름이에요. 그래서 (e) discouraged는 developed나 encouraged로 바꿔야 해요. (c) suspicious는 아이들이 새 음식을 경계한다는 뜻으로 알맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Ben had trained for six months for his first marathon, getting up before dawn to run along the river in all kinds of weather. His older sister, Hannah, had finished five marathons herself, and on the morning of the race (a)[she] hugged him at the start line. "Don't chase anyone in the first half," she said. "Run your own race, and I'll be waiting at the finish." Ben nodded, but when the starting horn sounded and thousands of runners surged forward, he forgot her advice almost at once.

(B)
Ben would never have reached the line on his own. When he crossed it, Hannah ran to hug him, and he turned to introduce his new friend, but Grace had already slipped away into the crowd. That evening, checking the official results, Ben found her name. She had finished just one second behind him. Later, a race volunteer told him that Grace had once run the same course twenty minutes faster. Ben realized that she had given up her own race to save (b)[his].

(C)
Carried along by the energy of the crowd, Ben ran the first fifteen kilometers far faster than he had planned. For a while, (c)[he] felt wonderful. But around the thirtieth kilometer, his legs grew heavy, and a sharp cramp gripped his right calf. He slowed to a walk and then stopped at the side of the road, wondering whether he should give up. Runners streamed past without a glance, and the finish line suddenly felt impossibly far away.

(D)
Then a gray-haired woman in a faded blue cap stopped beside (d)[him]. "First marathon?" she asked. Her name was Grace, and she showed him how to stretch the cramp out. "We'll walk one minute and jog four," she said. "Just to the next water station." At the station, she said the same thing again, and then again. Little by little, the kilometers passed, and Ben found that (e)[his] breathing had settled into a steady rhythm. With five hundred meters left, Grace told him to go ahead and finish strong.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 누나의 충고를 잊고 앞으로 달려 나간 Ben은 (C)에서 너무 빨리 달리다 30km 지점에서 쥐가 나 멈춰요. (D)에서 Grace가 다가와 함께 걷고 뛰며 결승선 근처까지 데려가고, (B)에서 결승 후 Grace가 자신의 기록을 포기했다는 것을 알게 돼요.

items.exp: (B)에서 Ben이 새 친구를 소개하려고 돌아섰을 때 Grace는 이미 사람들 속으로 사라진 뒤였어요. 그래서 Grace가 결승선에서 함께 Hannah를 만났다는 ②가 틀려요.

items.passage:
Dear Principal Harris,

I am the president of the Gardening Club at Westfield High School. Since September, our members have been growing herbs, tomatoes, and flowers in the school greenhouse, and many of the seedlings are now just a few weeks away from being ready to plant in the community garden. Unfortunately, the school building will be locked for the whole winter break, which lasts three weeks. Without regular watering, most of our plants will die long before classes begin again. Our members have already made a schedule so that two students, together with our advisor, Ms. Kim, can come in every other morning for about thirty minutes. We would only need to use the side entrance that leads directly to the greenhouse. I am therefore writing to ask whether you would allow our club to enter the greenhouse during the break to care for the plants. Thank you for considering our request.

Sincerely,
Noah Bennett
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 원예 동아리의 신입 회원 모집 일정을 안내하려고
지역 공동체 정원에 모종을 기부하겠다고 제안하려고
방학 중 온실에 들어가 식물을 돌볼 수 있게 허락을 요청하려고
방학 기간 학교 건물의 개방 시간 연장을 건의하려고
items.exp: 겨울 방학 동안 건물이 잠겨 식물이 죽을 것을 걱정하며, 담당 교사와 함께 온실에 들어가 식물을 돌볼 수 있게 허락해 달라고 부탁하고 있어요. 건물 전체의 개방 시간 연장이 아니라 옆문으로 온실에만 들어가겠다는 요청이에요.

items.passage: For three days, the gray cat that Sora's family had adopted from the shelter had not come out from under the bed. Every evening, Sora lay on the floor, holding out a piece of chicken and calling the cat's name softly, but all she ever saw were two yellow eyes in the dark. 'Why won't she trust me?' she muttered, pushing the plate a little closer and sighing. 'I've done everything right.' On the fourth night, tired of waiting, she simply sat against the wall with a book and stopped calling. Half an hour passed. Then she felt something soft brush against her ankle. She held her breath and looked down. The cat was standing beside her, sniffing the edge of the book. Slowly, it climbed into her lap, turned around twice, and settled down with a low, rumbling purr. Sora bit her lip to keep from laughing out loud and gently stroked its back, her heart full.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Sora의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 사흘 동안 고양이가 나오지 않자 한숨을 쉬며 '왜 나를 믿지 않지?'라고 중얼거리다가(frustrated), 고양이가 무릎에 올라와 가르랑거리자 웃음을 참으며 마음이 벅차올라요(delighted). 처음부터 들뜨거나 안심한 상태가 아니므로 다른 보기는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Every summer, news reports tell of young people who drown in rivers, lakes, and the sea, often within a few meters of safety. Many of them could swim a little, at least in a calm pool. But open water is different: it is cold, currents pull in unexpected directions, and a sudden drop in depth can cause panic. In such moments, the ability to swim a neat lap matters far less than knowing how to stay calm, float on one's back, and wait for help. That is why I believe every student should learn basic water survival skills before finishing school. These lessons do not require athletic talent. Students practice floating while fully dressed, recognizing a dangerous current, and signaling for help instead of struggling until they are exhausted. A few hours of training spread over a school year could save lives that no lifeguard is close enough to reach. Schools already teach students how to escape a fire; teaching them how to survive in water deserves the same priority.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 수영장에서 정확한 영법을 익히는 데 집중해야 한다.
여름철 물가에는 반드시 안전 요원을 배치해야 한다.
운동에 재능이 있는 학생에게 수영 대회 참가를 권해야 한다.
모든 학생이 학교에서 기본적인 수상 생존 기술을 배워야 한다.
학교 화재 대피 훈련의 횟수를 늘려야 한다.
items.exp: 'That is why I believe' 뒤에 모든 학생이 졸업 전에 기본적인 수상 생존 기술을 배워야 한다는 주장이 나와요. 깔끔한 영법보다 침착하게 떠 있는 법이 중요하다고 했으므로 ①은 반대이고, 화재 대피는 비교의 예일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: When someone asks us to join a project next month, we often say yes far more easily than we would if the same request were for tomorrow. Tomorrow is crowded with obligations we can see clearly: the report that is due, the dentist appointment, the groceries we still need to buy. Next month, by contrast, looks strangely empty. Its calendar has not yet filled with the small tasks that always appear, so we imagine that we will have more hours, more energy, and more patience then. In effect, we schedule our commitments as if the future will be lived by [a richer version of ourselves]. But when next month finally arrives, it turns out to be just as busy as today, and the person who must keep all those promises is the same tired person who made them. A useful test, therefore, is to ask: 'Would I agree to this if it were happening this week?' If the answer is no, the future probably won't be any different.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a richer version of ourselves]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a person who will earn more money in the future
someone imagined to have more spare time and energy than we will
a self who has learned from past scheduling mistakes
a more generous person willing to help others
someone whose calendar is managed by other people
items.exp: 앞 문장에서 다음 달에는 시간·에너지·인내심이 더 많을 것이라고 상상한다고 했으므로, 밑줄 친 표현은 실제보다 여유 시간과 에너지가 많다고 상상된 미래의 자신을 뜻해요. richer를 돈으로 해석한 ①은 매력적인 오답이에요.

items.passage: Why do zebras have stripes? For more than a century, scientists suggested answers ranging from camouflage in tall grass to confusing lions during a chase. Recent studies, however, point to a much smaller enemy: biting flies. In Africa, horseflies and tsetse flies carry serious diseases, and zebras, with their short coats, are especially easy targets. To test the idea, researchers watched flies approaching zebras and horses kept in the same field. The flies flew toward both animals about equally often, but when they came close to a zebra, they failed to slow down properly and often bumped into it or flew past without landing. The researchers even put striped coats on horses, and the number of successful landings dropped sharply compared with horses wearing plain coats. It seems that the bold pattern disrupts the way flies judge their approach in the final moments before landing. If this explanation is correct, the zebra's famous stripes are less a disguise against lions than a shield against insects.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the way stripes help zebras hide in tall grass
how lions are confused by the movement of a herd
the diseases that flies spread among horses in Africa
differences in coat length between zebras and horses
stripes as a defense that keeps biting flies from landing
items.exp: 얼룩말과 줄무늬 옷을 입힌 말에 파리가 제대로 내려앉지 못했다는 실험을 통해, 줄무늬가 무는 파리를 막는 방어 수단이라는 내용을 다루고 있어요. 풀숲 위장이나 사자를 혼란시킨다는 설명은 기존 가설로 소개되었을 뿐이에요.

items.passage: In 1816, a young French doctor named René Laennec faced an awkward problem. A patient with heart trouble needed to be examined, but the usual method, in which the doctor pressed an ear directly against the patient's chest, felt improper, and the patient's size made the sounds hard to hear anyway. Laennec remembered seeing children send signals to each other through a long piece of wood, one scratching at one end while the other listened at the other. He rolled a sheet of paper into a tight tube, placed one end on the patient's chest, and put his ear to the other. To his surprise, the heartbeat sounded far clearer than it ever had through direct contact. He soon replaced the paper with a wooden tube and spent years linking the sounds he heard to the diseases he later found. His simple instrument, the stethoscope, allowed doctors to listen inside the body without cutting it open, and it remains a symbol of medicine today.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Doctors Stopped Examining Patients by Touch
Children's Games That Changed Modern Science
A Rolled-Up Paper That Let Doctors Hear the Heart
The Long History of Heart Disease in France
How Wood Became the Best Material for Medical Tools
items.exp: Laennec이 종이를 말아 환자의 심장 소리를 더 또렷하게 들은 일이 청진기 발명으로 이어졌다는 내용이므로 ③이 알맞아요. 아이들의 놀이는 발상의 계기였을 뿐이고, 나무 재질이나 심장병의 역사는 중심 내용이 아니에요.

items.passage: Teresa Valli (1891–1967) was an Italian meteorologist and the first woman to present weather forecasts on Italian radio. Born in a mountain village near Trento, she kept a notebook of daily temperatures and cloud shapes from the age of nine. Because her family could not afford university, she worked as a telegraph operator while studying physics at night. In 1921, she joined the national weather office, where at first she was allowed only to copy data sent from other stations. Her careful analysis of mountain storms soon impressed her supervisors, and she was given her own forecasting area. In 1934, a radio station invited her to read the evening forecast, and her calm, clear voice made the program popular across the country. She also wrote a guidebook that taught farmers how to read the sky. After retiring in 1956, she continued to record the weather in her village until her death.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 아홉 살 때부터 매일의 기온과 구름 모양을 기록했다.
전신 기사로 일하면서 밤에 물리학을 공부했다.
기상청에 들어가자마자 자신만의 예보 구역을 맡았다.
농부들에게 하늘을 읽는 법을 알려 주는 안내서를 썼다.
items.exp: 기상청에 들어간 처음에는 다른 관측소에서 보낸 자료를 옮겨 적는 일만 허락되었다(allowed only to copy data)고 했으므로 ④가 글과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 어린 시절의 기록, 야간 공부, 1921년 입사, 농부를 위한 안내서로 모두 일치해요.

items.passage: Early golf balls were smooth, and players noticed something strange: old balls covered in nicks and scratches seemed to fly farther than new ones. Today almost every golf ball ①[is covered] with hundreds of small, shallow dents called dimples, and the reason has to do with the way air flows around a moving object. When a smooth ball flies through the air, the thin layer of air next to its surface separates from the ball early, leaving a wide, swirling area of low pressure behind it ②[what] pulls the ball backward. Dimples stir up this layer and make it cling to the surface a little longer before ③[letting] go. As a result, the low-pressure area behind the ball becomes much smaller, and the drag on the ball is greatly ④[reduced]. Together with the spin given by the club, which also helps lift the ball, dimples allow a well-struck ball to travel nearly twice as far as a smooth ball ⑤[hit] in exactly the same way.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: 앞의 명사 a wide, swirling area를 꾸미는 관계대명사 자리이므로 선행사를 포함하는 ② what은 that이나 which로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 공이 덮이는 수동태, ③은 전치사 before 뒤의 동명사, ④는 drag가 줄어드는 수동태, ⑤는 a smooth ball을 꾸미는 과거분사라서 맞아요.

items.passage: Walk through almost any city and you may notice that similar businesses tend to gather in the same area: furniture stores line one street, and restaurants crowd another. At first, this seems ①[strange]. Why would a shop choose to open right next to its competitors? The answer lies in how customers behave. People shopping for something important, like a sofa, want to compare options before deciding. A street full of furniture stores therefore ②[attracts] far more shoppers than any single store could on its own. Each shop may lose some customers to its neighbors, but it gains access to a much ③[larger] crowd. Clustering also helps businesses in less visible ways. Suppliers and skilled workers move to the area, making it ④[easier] for shops to find materials and staff. Over time, the district gains a reputation, and that reputation becomes a shared asset that ⑤[discourages] new visitors from coming.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 명성은 가게들이 함께 누리는 자산(shared asset)이므로 새 방문객을 '오지 못하게 하는' 것이 아니라 끌어들여야 해요. ⑤ discourages를 draws나 attracts 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: Most falls on stairs do not happen because a staircase is too steep or too narrow. They happen because one step is slightly different from the others. When we climb or descend stairs, we do not look carefully at each step. After the first two or three, the brain learns the height and depth of the steps and moves the feet automatically, lifting them just high enough to clear the next edge. If a single step is even a centimeter taller or shorter than the rest, the foot arrives too early or too late, and a person can trip or lose balance before noticing anything is wrong. For this reason, building codes in many countries pay less attention to the exact size of steps than to their ___, allowing only tiny differences between one step and the next within the same flight. A staircase, in other words, is safe not when each step is ideal but when every step keeps the promise made by the ones before it.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 뇌가 처음 몇 계단의 높이를 익혀 발을 자동으로 움직이므로 한 계단만 달라도 넘어진다고 했어요. 따라서 건축 규정은 계단의 크기보다 계단끼리 같은지, 즉 균일성(uniformity)을 중시한다는 말이 알맞아요. 가파름이나 폭은 첫 문장에서 주된 원인이 아니라고 했어요.

items.passage: We usually assume that experts see more than beginners. In one sense, this is true: an experienced doctor notices signs in an X-ray that a student would miss. Yet research on expert perception suggests that what distinguishes skilled people is often not the quantity of information they take in but the quality of their filtering. A beginner looking at a chessboard, a radar screen, or a patient tries to attend to everything at once and is quickly overwhelmed, because every detail seems equally likely to matter. The expert, by contrast, has learned through years of experience that most details are irrelevant to the decision at hand, and so attention flows almost automatically to the few features that carry meaning. This is why experts often find it hard to explain their judgments: much of their skill lies in what they no longer notice. Expertise, then, may be best understood as ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the ability to remember every detail one has observed
a habit of checking each decision more than once
a trained sense of which details can safely be ignored
the courage to trust one's first impression over evidence
a talent for explaining complex judgments in simple words
items.exp: 전문가의 차이는 받아들이는 정보의 양이 아니라 '걸러 내는 질'이며, 대부분의 세부가 무관하다는 것을 배워 더 이상 알아차리지 않는다고 했어요. 그래서 '무시해도 되는 세부를 아는 훈련된 감각'이 알맞아요. 전문가는 판단을 설명하기 어려워한다고 했으므로 ⑤는 반대예요.

items.passage: An apple that has been cut in half turns brown within minutes, and the change is the result of a chemical reaction rather than of spoiling. ① When the knife breaks open the apple's cells, substances that were kept apart inside them suddenly mix together. ② An enzyme from one part of the cell meets certain compounds from another, and in the presence of oxygen from the air, it turns them into brown pigments. ③ In the living fruit, this reaction may help protect damaged tissue from insects and germs. ④ Apples come in thousands of varieties, and growers continue to develop new ones that are sweeter, crunchier, or better suited to cold climates. ⑤ Knowing how browning works also explains the tricks cooks use to slow it, such as brushing the fruit with lemon juice, whose acid weakens the enzyme, or keeping cut pieces in cold water, which limits their contact with oxygen. So a brown apple is not necessarily a bad apple; it is simply one whose chemistry has been exposed to the air.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 잘린 사과가 효소와 산소의 반응으로 갈색으로 변하는 원리와 이를 늦추는 방법을 설명하는 글인데, ④는 사과 품종 개발 이야기라 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤의 browning은 ①~③에서 설명한 갈변 반응을 이어 받아요.

items.passage:
Schools often set up tutoring programs in which older students help younger ones. The main goal is usually to support the younger students who are struggling with a subject, and the older tutors are seen simply as volunteers giving their time.

(A) This process also reveals gaps. When tutors discover that they cannot explain a certain step, they realize they never fully understood it, and they go back to fill in what is missing. In this way, teaching becomes one of the most powerful ways of learning.

(B) But teachers who run such programs frequently report a surprising side effect: the tutors themselves often improve as much as, or even more than, the students they help.

(C) One reason is that explaining an idea forces the tutor to organize knowledge that was previously loose and unconnected. To answer a younger student's simple question, the tutor must find the core of the concept and put it into clear, simple words.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 튜터가 단순한 자원봉사자로 여겨진다는 주어진 글 뒤에 But으로 튜터 자신도 향상된다는 (B)가 오고, 그 이유(One reason)를 설명하는 (C), 그 설명 과정(This process)이 빈틈도 드러낸다는 (A)가 이어져요.

items.passage: In the early 1950s, the world's first jet airliner entered service, promising passengers faster and smoother flights than ever before. ( ① ) Investigators set out to find the cause, testing a whole aircraft on the ground by filling its cabin with air pressure again and again. ( ② ) After thousands of these cycles, they concluded that the problem began at the corners of windows and other openings in the body of the plane. ( ③ ) Each time the plane climbed and the cabin was pressurized, the metal around these sharp corners was stretched far more than elsewhere. ( ④ ) Over many flights, tiny cracks formed at the corners and slowly grew until the structure suddenly failed. ( ⑤ ) The solution was simple: give the windows round corners, because a rounded edge spreads the stress evenly so that no single point carries too much of the load. This painful lesson is why every passenger window you look through today has curved corners.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Within two years, however, several of these planes broke apart in the air, and at first no one understood why.
items.exp: 첫 문장은 제트 여객기의 등장이라는 긍정적 내용이고, ① 뒤의 Investigators set out to find the cause는 원인을 알 수 없는 사고가 먼저 나와야 자연스러워요. 따라서 however로 사고를 알리는 주어진 문장은 ①에 들어가야 해요. ② 이후는 이미 원인 조사가 진행 중이라 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Museums usually keep their treasures behind glass, and signs everywhere warn visitors not to touch. Yet a study at one history museum suggests that this rule may limit how much people take away from a visit. Researchers divided visiting students into two groups. One group looked at a collection of old tools, such as a farmer's sickle and a blacksmith's hammer, in a display case while a guide explained their use. The other group heard the same explanation but was allowed to pick up and handle exact copies of the tools, feeling their weight and trying the motions of using them. A week later, the students who had held the copies remembered far more details about the objects and the work they were made for, and many described the tools in terms of how they felt in the hand. The researchers concluded that touch gives the mind something to hold on to, linking information to a physical experience that is harder to forget than words alone.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Museum visitors who are able to (A) ___ copies of objects tend to (B) ___ more about them than those who only see them and hear explanations.
items.exp: 복제품을 직접 들어 보고 다룬(handle) 학생들이 일주일 뒤 훨씬 많은 세부 내용을 기억했다(recall)고 했어요. 만진 쪽이 더 많이 잊었다는 ④는 결과와 반대이고, 사진 찍기는 실험 조건에 없어요.

items.passage:
Why does a piece of music give us chills at certain moments? One influential explanation focuses on prediction. As we listen, our brains constantly guess what will come next: which note will follow, when the beat will fall, how a phrase will end. These guesses are based on years of (a)[exposure] to the music of our culture, so even listeners with no musical training have surprisingly accurate expectations. When a prediction is confirmed, we feel a small sense of satisfaction, as if the music has kept a promise. When it is broken in an interesting way, by a sudden pause or an unexpected chord, we feel a jolt of surprise that can be deeply (b)[pleasurable].

Composers have long used this mechanism, often without thinking of it in scientific terms. They set up patterns, let listeners settle into them, and then (c)[delay] the expected resolution, building tension that is released only when the familiar ending finally arrives. Brain imaging studies support this view: activity in reward-related areas rises not only at the emotional peak of a song but also in the moments just before it, as the listener anticipates what is coming.

This explains why music that is entirely predictable quickly becomes boring, while music that is entirely random feels like noise. Enjoyment seems to lie in a middle zone, where the music is familiar enough for us to form expectations and (d)[surprising] enough to challenge them. It also explains a curious fact: we can enjoy a favorite song hundreds of times, even when we know exactly what will happen. Our brains, it seems, still respond to the pattern of tension and release, so knowing the ending in advance (e)[ruins] the pleasure.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Musical Training Improves Listening Skills
Expect, Then Surprise: How Prediction Shapes Musical Pleasure
The Brain Areas That Produce Musical Sounds
Random Notes: The Future of Modern Composition
Why Familiar Songs Eventually Lose Their Charm
items.exp: 음악을 들으며 뇌가 다음을 예측하고, 그 예측이 맞거나 흥미롭게 어긋날 때 즐거움을 느낀다는 내용이므로 ②가 알맞아요. 좋아하는 곡을 수백 번 들어도 즐길 수 있다고 했으므로 ⑤는 반대예요.

items.passage:
(A)
Minho had spent three months building a water filter for the regional science fair. Layers of gravel, sand, and charcoal were packed inside a clear plastic tube, and in every test so far, muddy water had come out the bottom almost as clear as tap water. His science teacher, Mr. Hayes, had studied the design and said that (a)[he] had rarely seen such careful work from a first-year student. But on the night before the fair, Minho ran one final test, and the water that dripped out was gray and cloudy. He stared at the jar in disbelief. The fair started at nine the next morning.

(B)
The next morning, the hall was full of students, posters, and nervous chatter. When a judge in silver glasses stopped at Minho's table, she asked whether the filter had ever failed. Minho hesitated. It would have been easy to say no. Instead, (b)[he] told her the whole story of the cloudy water and the late-night repair, and showed her the notebook where every failed test was recorded. The judge listened carefully, writing notes without saying a word.

(C)
That afternoon, the winners were announced. Minho's name was not called for first, second, or third place, and he felt his chest tighten. Then the judge in silver glasses stepped forward with one more certificate: a special award for honesty and problem-solving. "Science is not about never failing," she said, looking at (c)[him]. "It is about what you do when you fail." Walking out of the hall, Minho realized that the cloudy jar had taught (d)[him] more than any successful test had.

(D)
In a panic, Minho called his friend Clara, who lived two streets away. She arrived twenty minutes later with a flashlight. Together they took the tube apart and found the problem: the charcoal layer had cracked, letting dirty water rush straight through. There was no extra charcoal in the house, so Clara ran home and returned with a bag her father used for his fish tank. By midnight, (e)[he] and Clara had rebuilt the filter, and the water ran clear again. Exhausted but relieved, Minho fell asleep at his desk.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 대회 전날 밤 물이 흐리게 나온 (A) 뒤에, 당황해 Clara에게 전화해 밤새 고친 (D), 다음 날 아침 심사위원에게 실패와 밤늦은 수리(the late-night repair)를 털어놓는 (B), 그날 오후 특별상을 받는 (C)가 이어져요.

choices: Minho는 세 달 동안 정수 필터를 만들었다.
대회 전날 밤 마지막 실험에서 물이 맑게 나왔다.
심사위원은 필터가 실패한 적이 있는지 물었다.
Clara는 아버지가 어항에 쓰던 숯을 가져왔다.
items.exp: 대회 전날 밤 마지막 실험에서 나온 물은 회색으로 흐렸다(gray and cloudy)고 했으므로 ②가 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 지문 내용과 같아요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Whitfield,

My name is Ethan Brooks, and I am the president of the Film Club at Linwood High School. Every spring, our club holds an open-air movie night for students and families in the community. Last year, more than a hundred people came, bringing blankets and snacks to watch a classic film together under the sky. This year, however, we face a problem. The school field we have always used will be under construction until the fall, and there is no other open space nearby that is quiet and large enough. We have learned that the rooftop of the Linwood Public Library offers a wide, flat area with plenty of room for a screen and seating. We would be very grateful if you would allow us to use the rooftop for one evening in April. We promise to follow all safety rules and to leave the space exactly as we found it.

Sincerely,
Ethan Brooks
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 야외 영화 상영회에 지역 주민을 초대하려고
도서관 옥상을 행사 장소로 사용하게 해 달라고 요청하려고
도서관에 상영 장비 기증 의사를 밝히려고
items.exp: 학교 운동장을 쓸 수 없게 된 상황을 설명한 뒤 4월 하루 저녁 도서관 옥상을 쓰게 해 달라고 부탁하고 있어요. 상영회 소개는 배경 설명이고, 주민 초대가 목적은 아니에요.

items.passage: When our homeroom teacher asked me to guide a group of exchange students from Spain around the school, I said yes before I could think. By the morning of their visit, I deeply regretted it. My English was fine in class, but I had never spoken it with strangers for a whole hour. As the eight students stepped off the bus, I gripped my notes so tightly that the paper wrinkled, and my first sentence came out as a whisper. Then one of them, a tall girl named Lucía, pointed at the mural on the cafeteria wall and asked, in slow, careful English, who had painted it. I explained that our art club adds a new section every year, and soon everyone was asking questions. I forgot about my notes. By the time we reached the gym, we were laughing about our favorite snacks, and I was answering without stopping to think. When the bus pulled away, I waved until it disappeared, already looking forward to their next visit.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 낯선 사람들과 한 시간 동안 영어로 이야기해야 해서 후회하고, 메모를 꽉 쥔 채 첫 문장을 속삭이듯 말한 데서 긴장한 마음이 드러나요. 질문에 답하다 메모를 잊고 거침없이 대답하며 다음 방문을 기다리게 되었으므로 자신감 있는 마음으로 바뀌었어요. 그래서 nervous → confident가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Streaming services and online shops are remarkably good at recommending things we will like. They study what we have watched, read, and bought, and they offer more of the same, often with impressive accuracy. It is easy to see this as a kind of personal guide. But a system that learns only from our past choices can do little more than return those choices to us in slightly different forms. If you watched three detective dramas last month, you will be shown a fourth and a fifth, until your screen becomes [a mirror that only reflects yesterday]. What gets lost is the chance encounter: the strange documentary a friend mentions, the book with an odd cover in a used bookstore, the song playing in a café that you would never have searched for. These unexpected finds are often how our tastes grow. A recommendation engine can satisfy who we have been, but it is far less able to introduce us to who we might become.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a mirror that only reflects yesterday]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a device that records our daily habits for later review
a screen that shows outdated news and information
a tool that helps us correct the mistakes of the past
a service that reminds us of what our friends enjoyed
a stream of suggestions limited to what we already liked
items.exp: 과거 선택만 학습한 시스템은 그 선택을 조금 다른 형태로 되돌려 줄 뿐이라서 탐정 드라마를 보면 또 탐정 드라마만 보여 준다고 했어요. 따라서 이미 좋아했던 것에 갇힌 추천을 뜻해요. yesterday를 '오래된 정보'로 본 ②는 매력적인 오답이에요.

items.passage: Many managers save their feedback for the yearly performance review, believing that a single, careful conversation is more professional than frequent comments. In practice, this approach often fails the very people it is meant to help. By the time the review arrives, the details of a project from ten months earlier have faded, and the employee can no longer connect the comment to what actually happened. Worse, a mistake that could have been corrected in a day may have been repeated for months. Feedback given soon after an event works differently. The situation is still fresh in both people's minds, so the conversation can focus on specific actions rather than vague impressions. It also feels less threatening, because a short remark about one task is easier to accept than a long list of problems delivered all at once. In this sense, the value of feedback depends less on how formal it is than on how quickly it follows the work it describes.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 피드백은 일이 끝난 직후에 주어야 효과적이다.
연간 평가는 직원의 실수를 줄이는 데 가장 효과적이다.
관리자는 피드백을 줄 때 공식적인 형식을 지켜야 한다.
부정적인 피드백은 긍정적인 피드백과 함께 주어야 한다.
items.exp: 마지막 문장에서 피드백의 가치는 형식보다 일을 한 뒤 얼마나 빨리 주느냐에 달려 있다고 했어요. 연간 평가는 오히려 실패하는 방식으로 제시되었으므로 ②는 반대예요.

items.passage: Anyone who has watched very old film footage has probably noticed that the people in it seem to rush about with jerky, comical speed. It is tempting to conclude that life simply moved faster back then, or that early cameras were poorly made. The real explanation lies in how films were shot and shown. In the early silent era, cameras were usually cranked by hand, and operators commonly filmed at around 16 to 18 frames per second, sometimes changing the speed as they worked. Today's projectors and video systems, however, generally play films at 24 frames per second or more. When footage recorded at a slower rate is played back at a faster one, every movement is squeezed into less time, so walking turns into scurrying. Film restorers now correct this by carefully adjusting the playback rate, and the results can be surprising: once shown at the right speed, the people of a century ago move as naturally and gracefully as we do.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the decline of hand-cranked cameras in modern filmmaking
why early films were made without any recorded sound
how a mismatch in frame rates makes old films look fast
the high cost of restoring damaged film collections
differences in the pace of daily life between past and present
items.exp: 초당 16~18프레임으로 찍은 옛 필름을 24프레임 이상으로 재생하면 움직임이 짧은 시간에 압축되어 빨라 보인다는 내용이므로 ③이 알맞아요. 옛날 삶이 더 빨랐다는 생각은 글에서 틀린 추측으로 소개되었으므로 ⑤는 주제가 될 수 없어요.

items.passage: When a painting is cleaned and restored, visitors often expect it to look the way it did on the day the artist finished it. But that goal is harder to reach than it sounds. Over centuries, some pigments fade while others darken, and the varnish laid over the surface turns yellow. Earlier restorers may have painted over damaged areas with colors that have since changed as well. A modern restorer must therefore make many judgments: which layers belong to the artist and which were added later, how bright a faded blue was originally, and whether a crack should be filled or simply left alone. Different experts can reach different answers. For this reason, many museums now follow a principle of restraint. They remove only what clearly damages the work, record every step, and use materials that a future restorer can take away. The aim is not to recreate a lost original but to protect what remains honestly.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Restoring Art: Careful Choices, Not Perfect Copies
Why Varnish Is an Artist's Best Friend
The Secret Colors of Famous Painters
How Museums Decide Which Paintings to Buy
Modern Technology Brings Old Paintings Back to Life
items.exp: 작품을 완성 당시 그대로 되살리기는 어렵고, 복원가는 많은 판단을 해야 하며 박물관은 절제의 원칙으로 남은 것을 정직하게 보호한다는 내용이에요. 따라서 '완벽한 복제가 아닌 신중한 선택'이 알맞아요.

items.passage:
Cedar Lake Paper Lantern Festival 2027

Light up the summer night with handmade lanterns! Families and friends of all ages are welcome.

items.q: Cedar Lake Paper Lantern Festival에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
items.exp: 입장권은 온라인으로만 살 수 있고 입구에서는 팔지 않는다고 했으므로 ④가 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 안내문 내용과 같아요.

items.passage: Vertical farms grow crops indoors on shelves stacked from floor to ceiling, often in buildings in the middle of cities. Instead of soil, the plants are usually grown in water ①[that] contains carefully measured nutrients, and LED lights replace the sun. Supporters point out that such farms use far less water than traditional fields, because the water is collected and ②[reused] again and again. They also allow lettuce and herbs to be harvested every few weeks, no matter ③[what] the weather is like outside. Yet the method has clear limits. Lighting and climate control require large amounts of electricity, which makes it expensive to grow anything beyond small leafy plants. Crops such as wheat and rice, ④[which] need much space and light to produce grain, ⑤[remaining] far cheaper to grow outdoors. For now, vertical farming is best seen as a useful addition to traditional agriculture rather than a replacement for it.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: 주어 Crops such as wheat and rice에 이어지는 문장의 본동사 자리이므로 remaining이 아니라 remain이 와야 해요. ①은 water를 꾸미는 주격 관계대명사, ②는 is collected와 병렬된 과거분사, ③은 like의 목적어 역할을 하는 what, ④는 계속적 용법의 관계대명사라서 맞아요.

items.passage: A news headline has only a few words to do its job, so every choice matters. Studies of online news have found that readers often share articles after seeing only the headline, without ①[opening] the story itself. This gives headlines a power that goes well beyond their length. A headline that says 'Study Links Coffee to Longer Life' may be technically accurate, yet the article might explain that the link was ②[weak] and that many other factors were involved. Readers who stop at the headline walk away with a much ③[stronger] belief than the research supports. Editors face pressure here, because dramatic headlines attract more clicks, and clicks bring in advertising money. Some news organizations have responded by setting rules that require headlines to reflect the ④[main] finding and its limits, even at the cost of a few readers. Such rules recognize that for many people, the headline is not the beginning of the story but the ⑤[least] of it.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 많은 사람이 제목만 보고 기사를 공유한다고 했으므로, 그들에게 제목은 이야기의 시작이 아니라 '전부(whole)'예요. 따라서 ⑤ least를 whole이나 entirety로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: In the hot, humid regions of Southeast Asia, many traditional houses stand on wooden posts, with their floors raised well above the ground. Visitors sometimes assume this design is mainly a defense against floods, and in some places it is. But the raised floor serves another purpose that matters every single day: it lets air ___ freely beneath and through the house. Breezes pass under the floor and rise through gaps between the floorboards, carrying heat away from the living space. Steep roofs with wide openings near the top allow warm air to escape, drawing cooler air in from below. Walls made of woven bamboo or thin wooden panels let the wind pass through rather than blocking it. Long before electric fans and air conditioners, builders used these simple principles to keep homes comfortable in extreme heat, and modern architects are now studying them again to design buildings that need less energy.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 바람이 바닥 밑으로 지나가 틈새로 올라가고, 지붕으로 더운 공기가 빠지며 시원한 공기가 들어온다고 했으므로 공기가 '순환하도록(circulate)' 한다는 말이 알맞아요. stay, settle, remain still은 공기가 머무는 것이라 반대예요.

items.passage: In recent decades, many musicians have tried to perform older music "authentically," using copies of period instruments and studying old manuals to recover how a piece sounded when it was first played. This effort has revealed much that had been forgotten: lighter bows, gut strings, and tempos far livelier than nineteenth-century habits had allowed. Yet the goal of perfect authenticity hides a difficulty. Even if we could rebuild every instrument exactly, we could not rebuild the listeners. An audience in 1720 heard a piece against the background of the music they knew, and a harmony that struck them as daring may sound gentle to ears familiar with jazz and film scores. Moreover, the performers' choices about which old sources to trust, and how to fill the gaps those sources leave, inevitably reflect present-day ideas of what sounds beautiful and convincing. A historically informed performance, then, is less a return to the past than ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a faithful copy that removes the need for further research
a rejection of the instruments used by earlier composers
an attempt to make old music sound exactly like modern pop
a conversation between the past and the tastes of our own time
a lesson that audiences have always heard music the same way
items.exp: 옛 악기는 복원해도 옛 청중의 귀는 복원할 수 없고, 어떤 자료를 믿고 빈틈을 어떻게 채울지에 오늘날의 취향이 반영된다고 했어요. 그러니 역사적 연주는 과거로의 단순한 복귀라기보다 과거와 현재 취향 사이의 대화라는 ④가 알맞아요. ①은 완벽한 복원이 가능하다는 뜻이라 글의 논지와 반대예요.

items.passage: Walk through a subway station in many cities and you may feel raised yellow patterns under your feet, a design created to guide people who are blind or have low vision. These tactile paving blocks are easy to overlook if you can see, but for many travelers they serve as a map drawn on the ground. ① The blocks come in two main types, each sending a different message through the soles of the feet or the tip of a cane. ② Long raised lines indicate a safe direction to walk, leading travelers along platforms and toward exits and stairs. ③ Patterns of small round bumps, by contrast, act as a warning, appearing at the edge of a platform, at the top of a staircase, or just before a crosswalk. ④ Many stations have also installed colorful murals that make long underground walls more pleasant for daily commuters. ⑤ Because the blocks are usually bright yellow, they also help people with partial sight, who can follow the strong color contrast even when they cannot read signs.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 시각장애인을 안내하는 점자 보도블록의 두 종류(방향을 알리는 선형, 위험을 알리는 점형)와 색의 역할을 설명하는 글이에요. 역 벽에 그린 벽화가 출퇴근객에게 즐거움을 준다는 ④는 역 시설 이야기지만 보도블록의 안내 기능과는 관계가 없어요.

items.passage:
People who move into an apartment beside a busy road often complain that they cannot sleep because of the noise. Yet after a few weeks, many of them say they hardly notice the traffic at all.

(A) This filtering is useful, because it frees attention for things that may actually matter. It also explains why a sudden silence, such as the moment a loud refrigerator stops humming, can catch our attention as sharply as a new noise.

(B) In other words, the brain gradually learns that the sound carries no new information. Once a sound is classified as unimportant, the brain reduces its response, and the noise is filtered out before it reaches conscious attention.

(C) The sound has not changed, and their ears still detect it just as well as before. What has changed is how the brain responds to a signal that repeats constantly without ever bringing danger or surprise.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 몇 주 뒤 소음을 거의 느끼지 못한다는 주어진 글 뒤에, 소리 자체는 그대로이고 뇌의 반응이 바뀌었다는 (C), 그것을 In other words로 풀어 소리가 걸러진다고 설명하는 (B), 이 걸러 냄(This filtering)의 쓸모를 말하는 (A)가 이어져요.

items.passage: Every winter, road crews spread salt on icy streets, and within a short time the ice begins to turn into slush. ( ① ) The reason has to do with the way water molecules behave at the surface of ice. ( ② ) Even near zero degrees Celsius, the surface of ice is never completely still: some molecules break away into a thin layer of liquid, while others in that liquid rejoin the solid. ( ③ ) When salt dissolves in this thin layer, its particles get in the way, making it harder for liquid molecules to attach themselves to the ice. ( ④ ) Melting continues while freezing slows, so the balance shifts and more and more ice turns to liquid. ( ⑤ ) This is why salt can melt ice even when the air is several degrees below freezing, although it becomes much less effective in extreme cold, when very little liquid forms on the surface at all.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Normally, at zero degrees, these two movements happen at the same rate, so the amount of ice stays the same.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 these two movements는 ③ 앞 문장의 '떨어져 나가 액체가 되는 분자'와 '다시 얼음에 붙는 분자'를 가리켜요. 평소에는 두 움직임이 균형을 이룬다는 내용 뒤에 소금이 그 균형을 방해하는 문장이 와야 하고, ④ 뒤의 the balance shifts도 주어진 문장이 앞에 있어야 이해돼요.

items.passage: In an experiment at a university dining hall, researchers served the same vegetable dishes over several weeks but changed the names on the menu board. On some days, the dishes had plain, health-focused labels such as 'Low-Fat Carrots' or 'Light Green Beans.' On other days, the same dishes appeared with descriptive names that highlighted flavor, such as 'Sweet Garlic-Roasted Carrots' or 'Zesty Lemon Green Beans.' The recipes, portions, and prices did not change. Nevertheless, students chose the vegetables noticeably more often when they carried flavor-focused names. Many also rated the dishes as tastier after eating them, even though nothing about the food itself was different. The researchers concluded that labels emphasizing health may quietly signal that a food is a sacrifice, while labels that promise pleasure set up expectations that shape both the choice and the actual experience of eating it.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

The way a dish is (A) ___ can influence not only whether people choose it but also how (B) ___ they find it.
items.exp: 요리법·양·가격은 그대로 두고 메뉴 이름만 바꿨더니 선택 횟수와 맛 평가가 달라졌으므로 (A)는 described, (B)는 enjoyable이 알맞아요. 요리 방법과 가격은 바뀌지 않았으므로 cooked, priced는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
For decades, athletes were told to warm up by stretching: holding a hamstring or calf stretch for thirty seconds or more before training or competition. The idea seemed obvious. Looser muscles, it was thought, would move more freely and be (a)[less] likely to be injured. In recent years, however, sports scientists have taken a closer look at this habit, and the results have been surprising.

Several studies have found that long, static stretches performed right before activity can temporarily (b)[reduce] the force a muscle produces. A sprinter who holds deep stretches just before a race may actually run slightly slower, and a jumper may not leave the ground quite as high. The effect appears to come partly from changes in the muscle and tendon, which become briefly less springy, and partly from the nervous system, which sends weaker signals to the stretched muscle for a short time afterward.

As a result, many coaches have shifted toward dynamic warm-ups. Instead of holding positions, athletes perform controlled movements that resemble their sport, such as leg swings, light skipping, and gradually faster runs. These movements raise body temperature, increase blood flow, and (c)[prepare] the nervous system for the patterns it will soon need.

This does not mean static stretching is useless. It remains (d)[valuable] for improving flexibility over the long term, especially when done after training or as a separate session. The lesson from the research is not that one method is good and the other bad, but that timing matters. The same exercise that helps an athlete in the evening may (e)[improve] performance if it is done in the minutes before a race.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Stretching Every Day: The Key to Lifelong Health
How Coaches Prevent Injuries in Young Athletes
Right Exercise, Wrong Moment: Rethinking the Pre-Game Stretch
Dynamic Warm-Ups Make Static Stretching Dangerous
items.exp: 경기 직전의 정적 스트레칭은 근력을 일시적으로 떨어뜨릴 수 있지만 훈련 후에는 유연성에 도움이 되므로 '시기'가 중요하다는 글이에요. 정적 스트레칭이 쓸모없지 않다고 했으므로 ⑤의 '위험하다'는 지나쳐요.

items.passage:
For decades, athletes were told to warm up by stretching: holding a hamstring or calf stretch for thirty seconds or more before training or competition. The idea seemed obvious. Looser muscles, it was thought, would move more freely and be (a)[less] likely to be injured. In recent years, however, sports scientists have taken a closer look at this habit, and the results have been surprising.

Several studies have found that long, static stretches performed right before activity can temporarily (b)[reduce] the force a muscle produces. A sprinter who holds deep stretches just before a race may actually run slightly slower, and a jumper may not leave the ground quite as high. The effect appears to come partly from changes in the muscle and tendon, which become briefly less springy, and partly from the nervous system, which sends weaker signals to the stretched muscle for a short time afterward.

As a result, many coaches have shifted toward dynamic warm-ups. Instead of holding positions, athletes perform controlled movements that resemble their sport, such as leg swings, light skipping, and gradually faster runs. These movements raise body temperature, increase blood flow, and (c)[prepare] the nervous system for the patterns it will soon need.

This does not mean static stretching is useless. It remains (d)[valuable] for improving flexibility over the long term, especially when done after training or as a separate session. The lesson from the research is not that one method is good and the other bad, but that timing matters. The same exercise that helps an athlete in the evening may (e)[improve] performance if it is done in the minutes before a race.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 경기 직전의 정적 스트레칭은 힘을 떨어뜨린다고 했으므로, 저녁에는 도움이 되는 운동이 경기 몇 분 전에 하면 수행 능력을 '해칠(harm)' 수 있다고 해야 해요. 따라서 (e) improve가 적절하지 않아요.

items.passage:
(A)
When Jiwoo got home from school on Friday, the gate to the backyard was swinging open, and Mango, her family's small brown puppy, was nowhere to be found. She called his name up and down the street, but there was no answer. Her younger brother, Seojun, burst into tears, saying (a)[he] must have left the gate unlatched that morning. Jiwoo hugged him and said it was no one's fault. Then she grabbed her bike. "We'll find him," she promised, though her own heart was pounding.

(B)
At last, as the streetlights came on, an elderly man named Mr. Ortiz called the number on one of the posters. He explained that a brown puppy had been sleeping under his porch all afternoon and that (b)[he] had given it a bowl of water. Jiwoo and Seojun ran the three blocks to his house. Mango was curled up on an old blanket, and when he heard Jiwoo's voice, he leaped into her arms, tail wagging wildly. Mr. Ortiz smiled and waved away their thanks.

(C)
First, Jiwoo rode to the park where they usually took Mango for walks, checking under every bench and bush. A woman walking a large dog told her that she had seen a small puppy running toward the river path about an hour earlier. Jiwoo followed the path until it ended at a busy road, but there was no sign of Mango. She thought of her brother waiting by the window at home and how worried (c)[he] must be. Tired and anxious, she decided she needed a different plan.

(D)
Back home, Jiwoo and Seojun made posters with Mango's photo and their phone number. Seojun, who had stopped crying, insisted on drawing a big red heart on each one, and Jiwoo let (d)[him] do it. They taped the posters to lampposts and shop windows all around the neighborhood. Hours passed without a call, and Seojun asked quietly whether Mango would ever come home. Jiwoo held (e)[his] hand and said they had to keep hoping.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 자전거를 타고 나선 (A) 뒤에, 먼저(First) 공원과 강변길을 찾아보다 다른 방법이 필요하다고 느끼는 (C), 집으로 돌아와 전단지를 붙이는 (D), 마침내(At last) 전단지를 본 Mr. Ortiz의 전화로 Mango를 찾는 (B)가 이어져요.
