choices: Seojun은 아침에 문을 확실히 잠갔다고 말했다.
Mr. Ortiz는 강아지가 오후 내내 자기 집 현관 밑에서 잤다고 했다.
Jiwoo는 강아지를 데리고 자주 산책하던 공원부터 찾아갔다.
개를 산책시키던 여자는 강아지가 강변길 쪽으로 가는 것을 보았다.
전단지를 붙인 뒤 몇 시간 동안 전화가 오지 않았다.
items.exp: Seojun은 아침에 자기가 문을 잠그지 않고 둔 것 같다(must have left the gate unlatched)며 울었으므로 ①이 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 지문 내용과 같아요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Howard,

My name is Daniel Brooks, and I coordinate a small group of retired residents who meet to play chess at the Maple Street Community Center. For the past two years, we have used Room 3 every Thursday afternoon, and your staff have always been kind and helpful. Recently, however, the center announced that Room 3 will be turned into a storage area for the new after-school program starting next month. We fully understand the need for more storage, and we have no wish to stand in the way of programs for children. Still, our members, many of whom live alone, have come to depend on these weekly games for company as much as for the chess itself. I am writing to ask whether we could be given another space in the building, even a corner of the main lounge, at the same time each week. We would gladly set up and put away the tables ourselves. I would truly appreciate any consideration you can give to this request.

Sincerely,
Daniel Brooks
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 체스 모임이 사용할 대체 공간을 요청하려고
체스 모임의 신규 회원 모집을 홍보하려고
items.exp: 필자는 3번 방이 창고로 바뀌게 되자 매주 같은 시간에 쓸 다른 공간, 라운지 한구석이라도 내어 줄 수 있는지 묻고 있어요(I am writing to ask whether we could be given another space). 방과 후 프로그램을 방해할 생각은 없다고 했으므로 반대하려는 글이 아니에요.

items.passage: Yuna had spent the whole weekend on her first article for the Riverside Weekly, where she was working as a summer intern. It was a short piece about a family-run shoe shop that had served the neighborhood for forty years, and she was sure it was the best thing she had ever written. On Monday morning, the editor, Mr. Grant, returned it to her desk. Red ink covered almost every paragraph. Whole sentences were crossed out, and in the margin he had written, "Where is the shoemaker's own voice?" Yuna's face burned. She slid the pages into a drawer and stared at her screen, wondering whether she had any talent at all. Late that afternoon, Mr. Grant stopped by her desk. "I only spend this much ink on stories worth saving," he said. "Go back tomorrow and let him do the talking. You've found a good story." Yuna took the pages out again. The red marks no longer looked like wounds; they looked like a map. She smiled and began writing a list of questions for the shoemaker.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Yuna의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: Yuna는 빨간 펜으로 뒤덮인 기사를 받고 얼굴이 달아오르며 자신에게 재능이 있는지 의심했어요. 그러나 편집장이 살릴 가치가 있는 기사라서 고친 것이라고 말하자 빨간 표시를 지도처럼 여기며 미소 짓고 질문을 적기 시작했어요. 따라서 낙담했다가 용기를 얻은 것이고, 처음부터 희망에서 실망으로 바뀐 것이 아니므로 ⑤는 답이 아니에요.

items.passage: When students review a test, most of them look only at the questions they got wrong, copy the correct answer, and move on. This habit feels efficient, but it leaves the real problem untouched. A wrong answer is rarely random; it usually comes from a specific misunderstanding that will appear again on the next test unless it is named. For this reason, teachers should ask students to write a short explanation of why each mistaken choice seemed attractive and where their reasoning went off track. A student who writes, "I chose this because I confused the cause with the result," has discovered something far more useful than the correct letter. At first, students may resist, saying it takes too long. Yet a few minutes spent tracing a single error can save hours of repeating the same mistake. Correcting an answer fixes one question; understanding an error fixes a way of thinking. Reviewing tests should therefore become a habit of explaining, not merely a habit of correcting.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 시험 직후 정답을 바로 확인하는 습관을 들여야 한다.
오답 복습 시간을 줄이고 새로운 문제를 더 풀어야 한다.
학생들이 시험 결과를 친구와 비교하지 않게 해야 한다.
교사는 시험 문항의 난이도를 학생 수준에 맞춰야 한다.
학생들에게 자신이 틀린 이유를 글로 설명하게 해야 한다.
items.exp: 필자는 teachers should ask students to write a short explanation of why each mistaken choice seemed attractive라고 하며, 정답을 베끼는 대신 틀린 이유를 설명하게 해야 한다고 주장해요. 복습 시간을 줄이자는 ②는 글의 방향과 반대예요.

items.passage: A promising young athlete who suffers a serious injury often faces more than physical pain. If running has been the whole of her identity, losing it can feel like losing herself. Psychologists describe this kind of narrow self-definition with the image of a building resting on a single pillar: when one pillar holds up the entire structure, any crack threatens everything. People with a wider range of roles, such as friend, student, musician, and volunteer, tend to recover more quickly from setbacks in any one area, because a failure in one role does not erase the others. This does not mean we should avoid deep commitment. Passion for a single pursuit can lead to remarkable achievement. The point is that commitment and identity are not the same thing. One can give everything to a sport while still knowing that one is also a sister, a reader, and a curious learner. In short, it is wise to [keep more than one room in the house of the self], so that when one door closes, there is still somewhere to live.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [keep more than one room in the house of the self]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: maintain several sources of self-worth beyond a single role
avoid committing deeply to any one activity
share one's personal space with friends and family
change one's goals frequently to prevent boredom
focus on recovering from physical injuries first
items.exp: 글은 정체성이 하나의 역할에만 기대면 그 역할이 무너질 때 전부가 흔들리므로, 친구·학생·봉사자처럼 여러 역할을 지니는 것이 좋다고 말해요. 따라서 밑줄은 한 가지 역할 외에도 자기 가치를 찾을 여러 원천을 지니라는 뜻이에요. 깊은 몰입을 피하라는 ②는 This does not mean we should avoid deep commitment와 반대예요.

items.passage: Bird eggs come in a surprising variety of shapes, from the nearly round eggs of owls to the long, pointed eggs of sandpipers. For years, scientists explained this variety in terms of nesting: pointed eggs, for example, were thought to roll in tight circles and so stay safely on narrow cliff ledges. A large study of thousands of species, however, pointed to a different factor: how birds fly. Species that are strong, frequent fliers tend to lay more elongated or asymmetric eggs. The likely reason lies in the body. Birds built for powerful flight have streamlined, narrow bodies, which limit the width of the passage through which an egg must travel. To hold enough nutrients for the growing chick, the egg must become longer rather than wider. Nesting habits may still matter for some species, but the shape of an egg seems to carry a quiet record of the life its parents lead in the air.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the link between birds' flying ability and the shape of their eggs
the reasons birds choose cliff ledges as nesting sites
the nutritional needs of chicks before hatching
the methods scientists use to classify bird species
the dangers that rolling eggs face in narrow nests
items.exp: 비행을 잘하는 새일수록 몸이 좁고 유선형이어서 알이 길쭉하거나 비대칭이 된다는 내용이므로, 비행 능력과 알 모양의 관계가 주제예요. 절벽 둥지 이야기는 예전 설명으로 잠깐 나올 뿐이라 ②, ⑤는 주제가 아니에요.

items.passage: Most people think of a job as a fixed list of duties written by someone else. Yet researchers who study the workplace have found that many employees quietly reshape their work from the inside, a practice known as job crafting. A hospital cleaner, for example, may see her task not simply as removing dirt but as part of the patients' recovery, so she chats with lonely patients and learns which rooms need extra care. A bank clerk who enjoys teaching may volunteer to train new staff. Neither of them changes the official job description, but both change what the job means to them. Such adjustments usually take three forms: altering the tasks themselves, changing whom one works with, and rethinking the purpose behind the work. Studies suggest that workers who craft their jobs in these ways tend to feel more engaged and are less likely to quit. In other words, a satisfying job is not always something we find; often it is partly built by the very person doing it.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Official Job Descriptions Matter More Than Ever
The Hidden Struggles of Hospital Cleaners
Training New Staff: The Key to Lower Turnover
Shaping Your Work: How Employees Remake Their Own Jobs
How to Find the Perfect Job Before You Apply
items.exp: 직원들이 공식 직무 기술서는 그대로 둔 채 업무, 함께 일하는 사람, 일의 목적을 스스로 바꿔 일을 의미 있게 만든다는 job crafting을 설명하는 글이에요. 그래서 ④가 제목으로 알맞아요. 병원 청소부와 신입 교육은 예시일 뿐이고, 공식 직무 기술서의 중요성을 말하는 ①은 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: Elena Marlow was born in 1912 in a small fishing town on the northern coast of Scotland. Her father repaired boats, and as a child she spent hours shaping clay from the riverbank into tiny animals. At sixteen, she moved to Edinburgh to work in a pottery studio, where she swept floors for two years before she was allowed to use the wheel. In 1938, she opened her own workshop and became known for bowls glazed in the gray-green colors of the northern sea. During the war, when materials were scarce, she taught pottery classes to children for free. Her work gained international attention in 1957, when a set of her bowls won first prize at an exhibition in Copenhagen. Marlow continued working until the age of eighty, and she donated her workshop to a local art school before her death in 1995.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 에든버러의 도자기 공방에서 2년 동안 바닥 청소를 했다.
따뜻한 남쪽 바다의 색을 띤 그릇으로 알려졌다.
전쟁 중에 아이들에게 무료로 도예를 가르쳤다.
사망하기 전에 작업실을 지역 미술 학교에 기증했다.
items.exp: Marlow는 북쪽 바다의 회녹색(the gray-green colors of the northern sea) 유약을 바른 그릇으로 알려졌으므로 ③이 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 각각 아버지의 직업, 2년간의 청소, 전쟁 중 무료 수업, 작업실 기증 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage: On the steep island of La Gomera in the Canary Islands, shepherds once faced a practical problem: deep valleys separated their farms, and walking from one side to the other ①[could take] hours. Their solution was a whistled form of Spanish called Silbo Gomero. Instead of using their vocal cords, speakers whistle through their fingers or lips, ②[turning] the rise and fall of spoken words into changes in pitch. Because a whistle carries much farther than a shout, a message can travel several kilometers across a valley. Whistled languages are not codes with a limited set of signals; they are complete versions of ordinary languages, ③[which] means that almost anything that can be said can also be whistled. Similar systems have been found in mountainous or forested regions of Turkey, Mexico, and Nepal, wherever people needed to communicate over long distances. In 2009, UNESCO recognized Silbo Gomero as part of humanity's cultural heritage, and today it ④[is taught] in local schools so that the tradition ⑤[surviving] for future generations.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: so that 뒤에는 주어와 동사를 갖춘 절이 와야 하므로 ⑤ surviving은 동사 survives(또는 will survive)로 고쳐야 해요. ②는 분사구문, ③은 앞 절 전체를 받는 계속적 용법의 which, ④는 언어가 '가르쳐지는' 것이므로 수동태로 맞아요.

items.passage: Long before European ships entered the Pacific, Polynesian navigators were crossing thousands of kilometers of open ocean to settle islands as distant as Hawaii and New Zealand. They had no compass or written charts, yet their voyages were far from ①[random]. Navigators memorized the points on the horizon where dozens of stars rose and set, and used them to hold a ②[steady] course through the night. During the day they read the ocean itself: the pattern of swells, felt in the rocking of the canoe, revealed the direction of the wind and of distant islands. Even when land was still out of sight, signs such as certain seabirds or clouds gathered over a peak told them an island was ③[near]. This knowledge was not written down but passed from teacher to student through years of training and song. In the twentieth century, some scholars doubted that such long voyages could have been ④[intentional], but modern sailors using only traditional methods have since repeated them, ⑤[undermining] the navigators' reputation.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 현대 항해사들이 전통 방법만으로 그 항해를 다시 해냈다는 것은 폴리네시아 항해자들의 능력을 입증하는 일이므로 ⑤ undermining(약화시키는)은 confirming(확인하는)으로 바꿔야 해요. ④ intentional은 학자들이 의도된 항해였음을 의심했다는 뜻으로 알맞아요.

items.passage: A public library operates on a remarkable assumption: that strangers will return what they borrow. Every day, thousands of books leave the building with nothing more than a card and a promise. Of course, some books go missing, and many libraries have charged small fees to encourage returns. But the system could never work through penalties alone; the fees are far too small to cover the true value of the books. What really keeps the system running is a shared sense that the collection belongs to everyone, and that keeping it for oneself would be a betrayal of one's neighbors. Interestingly, several libraries that removed late fees altogether found that more books came back, not fewer, as people who had stayed away out of embarrassment returned with their overdue items. Such cases suggest that the library is held together less by rules than by ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 벌금 같은 규칙만으로는 유지될 수 없고 '장서가 모두의 것'이라는 공동의 인식과 이웃에 대한 믿음이 도서관을 지탱한다는 내용이므로 mutual trust가 알맞아요. 벌금을 없앴더니 오히려 책이 더 돌아왔다는 사례도 이를 뒷받침해요. strict supervision은 규칙 쪽에 해당해 빈칸 앞 less by rules와 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: We usually think of an opponent in an argument as an obstacle standing between us and the truth. Yet there is a sense in which our opponents do us a service that no ally can provide. A belief that has never been challenged is held, in a way, on credit: we accept it, but we have never had to pay for it with reasons. Such a belief may even be true, but our grasp of it is weak, because we do not know what would count against it or why those objections fail. When someone presses us with a serious counterargument, we are forced to examine the foundations we had taken for granted. Sometimes we discover that our view needs revision; at other times we find that it survives, and we then hold it more firmly and with greater understanding than before. In either case, the encounter leaves us better off. The critic, then, is not merely an enemy of our beliefs but ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a reminder that every belief we hold is ultimately false
the one who turns our borrowed convictions into earned understanding
someone whose views must be accepted to avoid conflict
a source of doubt to be avoided until our views are fixed
proof that agreement is more valuable than argument
items.exp: 도전받지 않은 믿음은 이유로 값을 치르지 않고 '외상으로(on credit)' 가진 것인데, 반론을 받으면 믿음을 고치든 더 깊이 이해하든 우리가 나아진다고 했어요. 따라서 비판자는 빌려 온 확신을 스스로 얻은 이해로 바꿔 주는 사람이에요. 믿음이 살아남을 수도 있다고 했으므로 모든 믿음이 결국 틀렸다는 ①은 지나쳐요.

items.passage: Deep inside a frozen mountain on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, more than a million packets of seeds are stored in a vault designed to last for centuries. ① The Svalbard Global Seed Vault serves as a backup for seed banks around the world, holding duplicate samples of crops such as rice, wheat, and beans. ② If a national collection is lost to war, flood, or simple mismanagement, the stored seeds can be returned to the country that deposited them. ③ This actually happened in 2015, when researchers whose seed bank near Aleppo had been cut off by the Syrian war withdrew samples to rebuild their collection in other countries. ④ Wheat was first domesticated about ten thousand years ago in the region known as the Fertile Crescent, where wild grasses grew in abundance. ⑤ And because the vault sits in permafrost, the seeds would remain cold even if its cooling system failed, giving the world's crops a safety net that does not depend on constant human care.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 스발바르 국제 종자 저장고가 세계 종자은행의 예비 보관소 역할을 하며 영구 동토 덕분에 안전하다는 내용의 글이에요. ④는 밀이 처음 재배된 지역의 역사를 말하고 있어 저장고의 역할이라는 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤는 And로 저장고의 또 다른 장점을 덧붙이므로 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage:
When archaeologists dig up a piece of charcoal from an ancient fireplace, they can often tell how long ago the fire burned. The secret lies in a rare form of carbon known as carbon-14, which is constantly produced high in the atmosphere.

(A) By measuring how much of it is left in a sample and comparing that amount with the level found in living things, scientists can therefore calculate how long ago the plant or animal died. The method works for remains up to about 50,000 years old; beyond that, too little carbon-14 is left to measure.

(B) Every living plant takes in this form of carbon from the air, and animals take it in by eating plants. As a result, as long as an organism is alive, the share of carbon-14 in its body stays roughly the same as that in the atmosphere.

(C) Once the organism dies, however, it stops taking in new carbon, and the carbon-14 already inside begins to break down at a steady, known rate. After about 5,700 years, only half of the original amount remains.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 탄소-14를 소개한 주어진 글 뒤에 살아 있는 생물이 이 탄소를 받아들인다는 (B)가 와요. (C)의 Once the organism dies, however가 (B)의 살아 있는 동안과 대조되고, (A)의 how much of it is left와 therefore는 (C)의 일정한 속도로 줄어드는 내용을 받으므로 (B)-(C)-(A) 순서예요.

items.passage: In the mid-nineteenth century, few buildings rose higher than five or six stories. ( ① ) The reason was not that builders lacked the skill to go higher, but that people were unwilling to climb so many stairs. ( ② ) Lifting machines did exist, but they were used mainly for goods, because everyone knew that if the rope broke, the platform would crash to the ground. ( ③ ) In 1854, at an exhibition in New York, an inventor stood on a raised platform in front of a crowd and ordered the only rope holding it to be cut. ( ④ ) Instead, the platform dropped only a few centimeters before stopping, held by a spring-loaded catch that locked into notches along the sides of the shaft. ( ⑤ ) Once people trusted that a lift would not fall, the upper floors of a building, once the least desirable, became the most valuable, and cities began to grow upward.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

As the rope was cut, the crowd gasped, expecting to see him fall.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 the rope was cut은 ③ 뒤 문장의 밧줄을 자르라는 지시를 받고, 그가 떨어질 거라는 예상은 ④ 뒤의 Instead(그 대신) 문장과 대조를 이뤄요. 그래서 ④에 들어가야 해요. ⑤는 이미 플랫폼이 멈춘 뒤라 떨어질 것을 예상하는 내용이 올 수 없어요.

items.passage: Walk through almost any park or college campus and you will find narrow dirt trails cutting across the grass, often running right beside a paved path. These trails, sometimes called desire paths, form when enough people choose a shorter or more natural route than the one designers provided. Planners have traditionally treated them as a nuisance, putting up fences or signs to keep people on the official walkways. Such efforts rarely succeed for long, since people keep walking where their feet lead them. A growing number of designers now take the opposite approach. On some new campuses, they leave the ground unpaved for the first few months, watch where people actually walk, and only then lay down permanent paths along the lines worn into the grass. The result is a layout that people use willingly, because it reflects their real habits rather than an architect's guesses.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Rather than trying to (A) ___ how people move, some designers now build paths based on the routes people (B) ___ choose.
items.exp: 예전에는 울타리와 표지판으로 사람들을 공식 보도에 묶어 두려 했으니(A)에는 control이, 이제는 사람들이 실제로 자연스럽게 걷는 길을 보고 길을 낸다고 했으니 (B)에는 naturally가 알맞아요. rarely나 reluctantly는 사람들이 그 길을 스스로 즐겨 고른다는 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage:
When a new technology first appears, it rarely looks new. The earliest printed books in Europe were designed to (a)[resemble] handwritten manuscripts, with the same letter shapes, the same layouts, and even spaces left for decorations to be painted in by hand. The first automobiles were called "horseless carriages," and many of them looked exactly like that: carriages with an engine where the horse used to be. Early electric lamps were often shaped like the gas lamps they replaced. Again and again, inventors and users have dressed the new in the clothes of the old.

There are good reasons for this pattern. People understand unfamiliar things by comparing them to familiar ones, so a design that looks like something they already know feels (b)[safer] and easier to accept. Makers, too, are trained in the old craft and naturally (c)[borrow] its forms. In this sense, imitation serves as a bridge that carries users from one way of doing things to another.

The bridge, however, can also become a trap. Because early designers copy the limits of the old technology along with its appearance, the new one often (d)[exceeds] its true potential for years. Carriage-shaped cars, for example, sat high and narrow, a form that made sense for horses but not for engines. Only when designers began to ask what the machine itself needed did cars become lower, wider, and faster. The real revolution of a technology, then, usually comes not at the moment of its invention but later, when people stop (e)[imitating] the past and start exploring what the new tool can uniquely do.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How Printing Changed the Way People Read
Old Clothes on New Machines: How Imitation Shapes Innovation
Why Inventors Should Never Copy the Past
The Horseless Carriage: A Failed Experiment
Gas Versus Electricity: A Battle for City Streets
items.exp: 새 기술은 처음에 옛 기술의 모양을 흉내 내며(옛 옷을 입으며) 받아들여지지만, 그 모방이 한동안 잠재력을 가로막기도 한다는 글이므로 ②가 알맞아요. 모방이 다리 역할을 한다는 장점도 말했으므로 절대 과거를 따라 하지 말라는 ③은 지나쳐요.

items.exp: 옛 기술의 한계까지 그대로 따라 하기 때문에 새 기술이 수년 동안 자기 잠재력에 미치지 못한다는 흐름이므로, (d) exceeds(넘어서다)는 falls short of(미치지 못하다)로 바꿔야 해요. 뒤에 나오는 마차 모양 자동차가 엔진에 맞지 않았다는 예도 이를 뒷받침해요.

items.passage:
(A)
Every summer, Lena spent a week at her grandmother's farmhouse in the countryside. Grandma Rose's garden was the heart of the place, with rows of tomatoes, beans climbing wooden poles, and sunflowers taller than the fence. Lena, who cared more about her phone than about plants, usually watched from the porch while (a)[her grandmother] pulled weeds and watered the beds. "Someday you'll want to know how to do this," Grandma Rose would say, and Lena would only shrug.

(B)
On the last day of August, Lena drove with her mother to the rehabilitation center, carrying a basket of ripe tomatoes. Grandma Rose, now walking with a cane, met them in the lobby. She picked up a tomato, turned it slowly in (b)[her] hands, and took a bite. For a moment she said nothing. Then her eyes filled with tears. "It tastes like my garden," she whispered. Lena laughed and hugged her. "It is your garden, Grandma. I just borrowed it for the summer."

(C)
That spring, however, Grandma Rose slipped on the icy back steps and broke her hip. The doctors said (c)[she] would need months of treatment at a rehabilitation center far from home. When Lena heard that the garden would be left to the weeds, she surprised everyone, including herself, by offering to spend the summer at the farmhouse. On her first morning there, she stood in the overgrown garden, unsure where to begin. Then, in the tool shed, she found a worn notebook filled with Grandma Rose's handwriting.

(D)
The notebook told her everything: when to plant beans, how deep to set tomato seedlings, and which flowers kept harmful insects away. Each morning, Lena read a page and followed it carefully. Every evening, she called her grandmother to report on the day, and (d)[the old woman] answered every question with growing delight. Blisters formed on Lena's hands and then slowly hardened. By July, the tomato plants had grown so heavy that (e)[she] had to tie them to wooden stakes, just as the notebook instructed.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Lena가 정원 일에 관심이 없었다는 내용 뒤에, That spring, however로 할머니가 다치고 Lena가 정원을 맡아 헛간에서 공책을 찾는 (C)가 와요. 이어서 The notebook으로 그 공책대로 정원을 가꾸는 (D), 마지막으로 8월 말 토마토를 들고 할머니를 찾아가는 (B) 순서예요.

choices: Lena는 매년 여름 할머니의 농장 집에서 일주일을 보냈다.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Alvarez,

I have been a season ticket holder at the Riverside Playhouse for more than ten years, and I have enjoyed nearly every production your company has staged. Over the past few years, however, my hearing has gradually declined, and even with hearing aids I now miss much of the dialogue, especially when actors speak quickly or turn away from the audience. I know that I am not alone; several friends of my age have stopped attending for the same reason. I recently learned that some theaters offer captioned performances, in which the actors' lines appear on a small screen beside the stage. I would like to ask whether the Playhouse could offer at least one captioned performance of each production next season. I believe it would allow many loyal audience members to keep enjoying your wonderful work. Thank you for considering my request.

Sincerely,
Harold Bennett
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 공연 중 관객의 소음 문제를 지적하려고
자막이 제공되는 공연을 마련해 달라고 요청하려고
items.exp: 필자는 청력이 약해져 대사를 놓친다고 설명한 뒤, 다음 시즌 각 작품마다 적어도 한 번은 대사가 화면에 나오는 자막 공연을 열어 달라고 부탁하고 있어요. 보청기는 필자의 상황을 설명하는 말일 뿐 문의 대상이 아니므로 ③은 알맞지 않아요.

items.passage: When the judges read out the names of the three finalists, mine was not among them. I sat frozen in my seat while the audience clapped. For two months I had practiced my speech every night in front of the mirror, and now it was over in a single sentence. I wanted to slip out of the hall before anyone could see my face. As I reached the door, someone tapped my shoulder. It was Mr. Alvarez, one of the judges. "Your opening story about your grandfather was the most moving thing I heard today," he said. "You lost points only because you rushed the ending. Slow down next time, and you'll be standing on that stage." He handed me his scoring sheet, covered with notes. I read them on the bus home, one by one. They were not just criticism; they were a map. By the time I got off the bus, I was already planning a new ending. Next year's contest suddenly felt within reach.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 결선 진출자에 이름이 없자 'I'는 얼어붙고 몰래 빠져나가고 싶어 할 만큼 낙담해요. 심사위원의 조언과 메모를 읽은 뒤 새 결말을 계획하며 내년 대회가 손에 닿을 듯하다고 느끼므로 'disheartened → hopeful'이 알맞아요.

items.passage: Beginners in the kitchen often treat a recipe as a set of laws. They measure every spoonful exactly and panic when the store has no fresh basil. Experienced cooks see it differently. They know that the person who wrote the recipe worked with a particular oven, particular tomatoes, and a particular taste. Your oven may run hotter, your tomatoes may be sweeter, and your family may like more salt. Following the instructions word for word therefore does not guarantee the same result; it only guarantees that you have ignored the conditions in front of you. Skilled cooks taste as they go, adjust the heat, and swap ingredients when they must, using the written steps as a guide rather than a contract. Over time, many of their versions drift so far from the original that they become new dishes with their own names. For them, [a recipe is a starting line, not a finish line].
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a recipe is a starting line, not a finish line]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: cooking should begin only after every ingredient has been measured
a good recipe must be followed exactly to produce the same dish
beginners should avoid difficult recipes until they gain skill
the speed of cooking matters more than the quality of the result
written instructions are a base to be adapted to one's own conditions and tastes
items.exp: 숙련된 요리사는 레시피를 계약이 아닌 안내로 삼아 맛을 보며 불과 재료를 조정하고, 결국 새 요리를 만들기도 한다고 했어요. 따라서 밑줄은 레시피가 자신의 조건과 입맛에 맞게 바꿔 나갈 출발점이라는 뜻이에요. 정확히 따라야 한다는 ③은 초보자의 태도로, 글이 비판하는 내용이에요.

items.passage: Many organizations assume that a longer meeting means more careful decisions. In practice, the opposite is often true. When a meeting is scheduled for an hour, discussion tends to expand to fill the hour, with participants repeating points that have already been made and drifting into side topics. Attention, meanwhile, fades steadily; by the final twenty minutes, few people are thinking as clearly as they were at the start. Teams that deliberately shorten their meetings, setting a strict limit of fifteen or twenty minutes and sharing materials in advance, often report that they reach decisions just as sound and far more quickly. The time limit forces everyone to prepare, to state their views directly, and to separate essential issues from minor ones. What improves a decision is not the number of minutes spent around a table but the quality of focus that people bring to it. A short, well-prepared meeting respects both the problem and the people trying to solve it.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 회의는 모든 구성원의 의견을 듣기 위해 충분히 길어야 한다.
중요한 결정은 회의보다 개인이 혼자 내리는 것이 낫다.
회의 시간을 짧게 제한하고 미리 준비하면 결정의 질과 효율이 높아질 수 있다.
회의 자료를 미리 나누면 오히려 토론이 줄어든다.
회의 참석자 수를 줄여야 집중력을 유지할 수 있다.
items.exp: 긴 회의는 시간을 채우느라 반복과 잡담이 늘고 집중력이 떨어지지만, 시간을 15~20분으로 제한하고 자료를 미리 나누면 결정이 똑같이 타당하면서 더 빠르다고 했어요. 결정을 좋게 하는 것은 시간이 아니라 집중의 질이라는 것이 요지예요. 참석자 수 이야기는 나오지 않으므로 ⑤는 근거가 없어요.

items.passage: Living near an active volcano seems like an obviously dangerous choice, yet some of the most densely populated farming regions on Earth lie on the slopes of volcanoes. The reason lies in the ground itself. When a volcano erupts, it spreads ash and broken rock over the surrounding land. As these materials weather, they release minerals such as potassium, phosphorus, and magnesium that plants need to grow. Volcanic soils also tend to be loose and porous, allowing roots to spread easily while holding enough water for dry seasons. In places such as the island of Java in Indonesia, farmers can harvest rice several times a year from these rich soils. Of course, the same mountain that feeds them can one day destroy their villages. Generation after generation, people have accepted this uncertain bargain, trading the risk of a rare disaster for the reward of fertile land every season.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: methods scientists use to predict volcanic eruptions
why fertile volcanic soil draws people to live near volcanoes
the damage that volcanic ash causes to crops
the history of rice farming on the island of Java
how farmers protect their villages from lava flows
items.exp: 화산재와 암석이 풍화되며 식물에 필요한 무기질을 내놓고 토양이 푸석하고 물을 잘 머금어, 위험을 감수하고도 사람들이 화산 근처에 산다는 내용이므로 ②가 주제예요. 자바섬은 하나의 예일 뿐이어서 ④는 지엽적이에요.

items.passage: If you point at a cup, a dog will usually look at the cup, not at your finger. This may seem like a small thing, but it is surprisingly rare in the animal world. Even chimpanzees, our close relatives, often fail to follow human pointing gestures in experiments unless they have been specially trained. Dogs, by contrast, seem to do it naturally, and even young puppies with little human contact can follow a pointing hand. Many researchers believe this skill developed during thousands of years of living alongside people. Dogs that could read human signals, such as where a person was looking or pointing, were more likely to receive food and care, and they passed this ability on to their offspring. Wolves raised by humans, in comparison, tend to perform less well at the same tasks. In other words, dogs may have evolved a special talent not for understanding the world in general, but for understanding us.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Chimpanzees: The Smartest Animals on Earth
Why Wolves Make Better Companions Than Dogs
Born to Read Us: Dogs' Inherited Skill at Following Human Cues
Training Puppies to Point at Objects
How Humans Learned to Communicate With Gestures
items.exp: 개는 훈련 없이도, 심지어 어린 강아지도 사람의 손짓과 시선을 따르는데, 이는 사람과 함께 살며 진화한 능력이라는 글이므로 ③이 알맞아요. 사람 손에 자란 늑대는 이 과제를 더 못한다고 했으므로 ②는 반대이고, 강아지 훈련법 이야기도 아니에요.

items.passage:
Harbor Book Swap Festival 2027

Bring the books you have finished and take home stories you have never read! Join your neighbors for a weekend of sharing and reading by the sea.

• When: Saturday, September 18 – Sunday, September 19, 10 a.m. – 5 p.m.
• Where: Harbor Park Pavilion (Hall B in case of rain)
• Admission: Free for everyone

How to Swap
• Bring up to 10 books in good condition and receive one token for each book.
• Exchange each token for any book on the swap tables.
• Textbooks and magazines are not accepted.

Special Events
• Story time for children: 11 a.m. each day
• Book-cover drawing contest: Saturday only (registration required on site)

Notes
• Books left over after the festival will be donated to local schools.
• Visit www.harborbookswap.org for more information.
items.q: Harbor Book Swap Festival 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 책 한 권당 토큰 한 개를 받는다.
축제 후 남은 책은 지역 학교에 기부된다.
items.exp: 안내문에 Textbooks and magazines are not accepted라고 했으므로 교과서와 잡지도 교환할 수 있다는 ④가 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 운영 시간, 우천 시 장소, 토큰 규칙, 남은 책 기부 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage: Medieval stained glass windows were far more than decoration. In an age when few people could read, they ①[served] as picture books, telling stories that worshippers could follow from panel to panel. To make them, craftsmen first melted sand and wood ash and then added metal oxides ②[colored] the glass: copper for red and green, cobalt for deep blue. The colored sheets were then cut into small pieces, ③[which] were painted with details such as faces and folds of cloth and fired again so that the paint fused with the glass. Next, the pieces were joined with strips of lead, a soft metal that could be bent easily ④[to follow] the curves of each shape. Because glass made in this way was uneven in thickness, the light ⑤[passing] through it shimmered and changed throughout the day, giving the windows a living quality that modern, perfectly flat glass cannot easily copy.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ②는 금속 산화물을 넣은 목적(유리에 색을 내기 위해)을 나타내야 하므로 to부정사 to color로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 주어 they의 과거 동사, ③은 pieces를 받는 계속적 용법의 관계대명사, ④는 '~하도록'의 목적을 나타내는 to부정사, ⑤는 the light를 꾸미는 현재분사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: English spelling often seems designed to confuse learners. Why is there a k in "knight," a gh in "night," and a b in "doubt"? Much of the answer is that, over the centuries, spelling has been far more ①[changeable] than pronunciation. In the fifteenth century, words like "knight" were actually pronounced with a k sound, and the gh stood for a sound similar to the one in the German word "ich." When printing arrived in England around that time, early printers ②[fixed] many spellings in place, just as speech was beginning to shift. Over the following centuries, the k and gh sounds ③[disappeared] from speech, but the letters stayed on the page. Other silent letters have a different origin. Scholars of the sixteenth century, eager to show the Latin roots of English words, ④[added] letters that had never been pronounced at all, such as the b in "doubt," taken from the Latin "dubitare." Silent letters, then, are not random errors but ⑤[traces] of the language's long history.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 발음이 바뀌는 동안 철자는 인쇄로 고정되어 그대로 남았다는 흐름이므로, 철자가 발음보다 훨씬 '안정적'이었다고 해야 해요. 따라서 ① changeable은 stable로 바꿔야 해요. 나머지는 고정하다, 사라지다, 덧붙이다, 흔적으로 모두 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: Most of us have stood in front of a glass door, pushed when we should have pulled, and felt a little foolish. Yet the fault usually lies not with us but with the designer. A well-designed object tells us how to use it through its shape alone. A flat metal plate on a door can only be pushed, so our hands know what to do without thinking. A vertical handle, on the other hand, invites us to grab it and pull. Problems begin when designers choose a handle simply because it looks elegant, placing identical handles on both sides of a door that opens only one way. To fix the confusion, someone then tapes up a sign reading "PUSH" or "PULL." Designers sometimes say that such a sign is a confession of failure: if an everyday object needs written instructions, the design itself has not done its job. The best designs make instructions ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 좋은 디자인은 모양만으로 사용법을 알려 주고, 문에 '미시오/당기시오' 안내문이 필요하다면 디자인이 실패한 것이라고 했어요. 따라서 최고의 디자인은 설명을 불필요하게(unnecessary) 만든다는 ⑤가 알맞아요. 안내문을 잘 보이게 하는 것은 실패를 보완하는 것일 뿐이므로 ④는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: A sofa priced at $1,200 may seem out of reach to a young couple furnishing their first apartment. Offered instead at "$50 a month," the same sofa suddenly appears affordable, and many buyers who would have walked away from the full price sign up without hesitation. Nothing about the sofa has changed, and if interest or fees are added, the total paid may even be higher. What has changed is the number the buyer is asked to evaluate. A single large figure invites comparison with savings, income, and the other things the money could buy; a small monthly figure is compared instead with the cost of a lunch or a movie ticket, and against that standard it looks trivial. Retailers have learned that the question customers ask themselves is less often "Is this worth the price?" than "Can I manage the next payment?" Installment plans therefore do more than spread a cost over time. By breaking a price into pieces, they lead buyers to ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: compare products more carefully before making a purchase
save money in advance in order to avoid paying interest
refuse any purchase whose total cost they cannot calculate
judge a purchase by the size of each payment rather than its total
value the quality of a product more than its brand name
items.exp: 같은 소파도 한 달 50달러로 제시되면 점심값 정도와 비교되어 사소해 보이고, 손님은 '이 값어치가 있나'보다 '다음 할부금을 낼 수 있나'를 묻게 된다고 했어요. 그래서 전체 가격이 아니라 한 번에 내는 금액으로 구매를 판단하게 된다는 ④가 알맞아요. ①은 할부가 오히려 따져 보지 않고 사게 만든다는 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: When you step out into a cold wind or hear a thrilling piece of music, tiny bumps may suddenly appear on your arms. ① These goosebumps are produced by small muscles attached to the base of each hair, which tighten and pull the hairs upright. ② Human hair grows at roughly one centimeter per month, and each hair passes through cycles of growth and rest that can last several years. ③ In our furry ancestors, and in many mammals today, raised hair traps a thicker layer of air next to the skin, which helps hold in body heat. ④ The same reaction also makes an animal look larger, which is why a frightened cat's fur stands on end when it faces an enemy. ⑤ Humans have lost most of their body hair, so goosebumps no longer keep us warm or make us look threatening, but the reflex has remained as a reminder of the bodies our ancestors once had.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 소름이 털을 세우는 작은 근육 때문에 생기고, 털 많은 조상에게는 체온 유지와 몸을 커 보이게 하는 역할을 했으며, 지금은 흔적으로 남았다는 흐름이에요. 털이 한 달에 약 1센티미터 자라고 성장 주기가 있다는 ②는 털에 관한 내용이지만 소름의 원리·역할과는 관계가 없어요.

items.passage:
Long before photography was invented, people knew that a dark room could produce a picture of the world outside.

(A) Despite this odd reversal, artists found the device extremely useful. By tracing the projected images, some painters were able to capture perspective and proportion with remarkable accuracy, and later inventors added lenses and, eventually, light-sensitive plates, turning the dark room into the first cameras.

(B) The image it produced, however, had one strange feature: it was upside down. This happens because light travels in straight lines, so rays from the top of a tree pass through the hole and land near the bottom of the wall, while rays from its base land near the top.

(C) If a small hole is made in one wall of a darkened room, light from the bright scene outside passes through it and forms an image of that scene on the opposite wall. This arrangement came to be called the camera obscura, Latin for "dark room."
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 어두운 방이 그림을 만든다는 주어진 글 다음에, 작은 구멍으로 상이 맺히는 원리와 camera obscura라는 이름을 소개하는 (C)가 와요. 그 장치(it)가 만든 상이 거꾸로라는 (B)가 이어지고, '이 이상한 뒤집힘(this odd reversal)'에도 화가들이 유용하게 썼다는 (A)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Before a symphony concert begins, the audience hears a curious ritual: one instrument plays a single long note, and the rest of the orchestra tunes to it. ( ① ) That note is an A, and in most orchestras it is played by the oboe. Why should this one instrument, rather than a powerful trumpet or a piano, have the honor? ( ② ) Tradition is part of the answer, since the oboe has led orchestral tuning for centuries. ( ③ ) First, once its reed is set, the oboe's pitch is relatively hard to change, so it offers the players a stable reference. ( ④ ) Second, its bright, penetrating sound cuts clearly through the noise of dozens of musicians warming up on stage. ( ⑤ ) Once every section has matched this note, the hall falls silent, the lights dim slightly, and the conductor walks out to begin the performance that the audience has been waiting for all evening.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Yet sound musical reasons also explain why the custom has lasted.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 Yet ... also로 앞의 이유(전통)에 덧붙여 음악적 이유도 있다고 말해요. ③ 앞에는 전통이라는 이유가, ③ 뒤에는 First, Second로 그 음악적 이유가 나열되므로 ③에 들어가야 해요. ②에는 아직 앞선 이유가 없어 also가 어울리지 않아요.

items.passage: When artists move into a run-down neighborhood, they are usually looking for one thing: cheap space. Old warehouses and empty shops offer large rooms for studios at rents that more central areas cannot match. Over time, however, their presence changes the area. Galleries open, cafés follow, and the neighborhood begins to appear in magazines as an exciting place to visit. Developers and wealthier residents take notice, property values climb, and rents rise accordingly. Eventually, many of the artists who made the area attractive can no longer afford to stay, and they move on in search of cheaper space elsewhere, where the cycle often begins again. Some cities now try to break this pattern by building permanently affordable studios or by helping artist groups buy their buildings together, so that creative communities are not pushed out by the very success they helped create.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Artists who settle in neglected neighborhoods often make them more (A) ___, which eventually raises costs and (B) ___ the artists themselves.
items.exp: 예술가들이 들어오면 갤러리·카페가 생겨 동네가 매력적인 곳이 되고(desirable), 임대료가 올라 결국 그 예술가들이 떠나게 된다(displaces)고 했어요. 따라서 ⑤가 알맞아요. 예술가들이 버티지 못하고 밀려난다고 했으므로 supports나 protects는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Today, audiences at a classical concert sit in near-total silence, hesitate even to cough, and know that applause between the movements of a symphony is frowned upon. It is easy to assume that music has always been heard this way, but these customs are surprisingly (a)[recent]. In the eighteenth century, concerts and operas were lively social events. People talked with friends, ate and drank, walked about, and sometimes demanded that a favorite passage be played again on the spot. Composers did not always (b)[resent] such reactions; Mozart wrote happily to his father about an audience that burst into applause in the middle of a new symphony.

During the nineteenth century, however, attitudes changed. Music, especially instrumental music, came to be seen as a serious art that deserved the same (c)[respect] as great literature or painting. Large concert halls were built, printed programs explained the works, and critics urged listeners to follow a piece attentively from beginning to end. Some composers and conductors went further, dimming the lights in the hall so that attention would be (d)[scattered] across the room. Gradually, silence became a sign of good manners and serious listening.

This history does not mean that the modern way of listening is wrong. Deep concentration can reveal details that a noisy room would hide. But it does suggest that our concert habits are a cultural (e)[choice] rather than a law of nature. Some orchestras now experiment with more relaxed concerts, inviting audiences to clap whenever they feel moved, and many listeners find the experience refreshing.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Hush! How Silent Listening Became a Concert Custom
The Lost Art of Writing Symphonies
Modern Concert Halls: Better Sound Through Technology
items.exp: 18세기에는 떠들썩했던 공연 관람이 19세기에 음악을 진지한 예술로 보게 되면서 조용히 듣는 관습으로 바뀌었고, 이는 문화적 선택이라는 내용이므로 ①이 알맞아요. 모차르트는 박수에 기뻐했다고 했으므로 ②는 글과 반대예요.

But it does suggest that our concert habits are a cultural (e)[choice] rather than a law of nature. Some orchestras now experiment with more relaxed concerts, inviting audiences to clap whenever they feel moved, and many listeners find the experience refreshing.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 공연장 조명을 어둡게 한 것은 관객의 주의를 무대에 모으기 위해서이므로, (d) scattered(흩어진)는 focused(집중된)로 바꿔야 해요. (b) resent는 모차르트가 관객의 박수를 기뻐했다는 예와 이어져 '늘 불쾌하게 여긴 것은 아니다'라는 뜻으로 알맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
The night train to the coast was nearly full when Owen found his seat by the window. He was seventeen and traveling alone for the first time, on his way to a summer job at his uncle's seaside café. Across from him sat an elderly man in a gray coat who was carefully unwrapping a sandwich. The man smiled and nodded, and Owen nodded back before putting on his headphones and turning toward the dark window.

(B)
About an hour into the trip, the train stopped suddenly in the middle of a forest. A voice announced that a fallen tree was blocking the tracks and that the delay might last several hours. Owen groaned. His phone battery was almost dead, and he had no way to tell his uncle. The elderly man, noticing (a)[his] worried face, pulled a small charger from his bag. "Here," he said. "I always carry one for my grandchildren."

(C)
At dawn the train finally reached the coast. On the platform, Owen's uncle was waving, and beside him stood an elderly woman holding a bunch of flowers. "Walter!" she called, and the man in the gray coat hurried toward her. Owen stared at them in surprise. "You two know each other?" (b)[his] uncle asked, laughing. It turned out that the woman was a regular customer at the café, and the old man had been on his way to visit her, his younger sister. Owen shook (c)[his] new friend's hand warmly, sure that this would not be the last time they met.

(D)
While the phone charged, the two began to talk. The man, whose name was Walter, had worked as a railway engineer for forty years and knew the line by heart. (d)[He] explained how trains were cleared after storms and told stories of snowy nights stuck in mountain tunnels. Owen, who had planned to sleep the whole way, found himself asking question after question. Hours passed, and when the train jerked forward again near midnight, (e)[he] was almost disappointed that the delay was over.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Owen이 노신사와 마주 앉은 뒤, 기차가 숲에서 멈추고 노신사가 충전기를 건네는 (B)가 와요. 휴대폰을 충전하는 동안(While the phone charged) 이야기를 나누는 (D)가 이어지고, 새벽에 해안에 도착해 Walter의 여동생을 만나는 (C)가 마지막이므로 (B)-(D)-(C)예요.

(C)
At dawn the train finally reached the coast. On the platform, Owen's uncle was waving, and beside him stood an elderly woman holding a bunch of flowers. "Walter!" she called, and the man in the gray coat hurried toward her. Owen stared at them in surprise. "You two know each other?" (b)[his] uncle asked, laughing. It turned out that the woman was a regular customer at the café, and the old man had been on his way to visit her, his younger sister. Owen shook (c)[his] new friend's hand warmly, sure that this would not be the last time they met.

(D)
While the phone charged, the two began to talk. The man, whose name was Walter, had worked as a railway engineer for forty years and knew the line by heart. (d)[He] explained how trains were cleared after storms and told stories of snowy nights stuck in mountain tunnels. Owen, who had planned to sleep the whole way, found himself asking question after question. Hours passed, and when the train jerked forward again near midnight, (e)[he] was almost disappointed that the delay was over.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 가리키는 대상이 나머지 넷과 다른 것은?
items.exp: (a), (b), (c), (e)는 모두 Owen을 가리키지만, (d)는 철도 기술자로 일했던 노신사 Walter를 가리켜요.

The man smiled and nodded, and Owen nodded back before putting on his headphones and turning toward the dark window.

(B)

items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Owen은 처음으로 혼자 기차 여행을 하고 있었다.
쓰러진 나무가 선로를 막아 기차가 멈췄다.
Owen의 삼촌은 승강장에서 손을 흔들고 있었다.
items.exp: (D)에서 기차가 다시 움직인 것이 자정 무렵이고, (C)에서 해안에 도착한 것은 새벽(At dawn)이므로 ⑤가 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 (A)의 첫 혼자 여행, (B)의 쓰러진 나무, (C)의 손 흔드는 삼촌, (D)의 40년 철도 기술자 내용과 일치해요.
